adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solutions might use O(n^2) construction (e.g., rotating array for each position) leading to TLE.
adversarial.why_effective: Uses maximum input size to amplify time complexity differences; O(n) solution finishes in milliseconds, O(n^2) will exceed time limit.

adversarial.description: Odd n=3 with specific patterns to test construction algorithm correctness
adversarial.attack_vector: Some constructions might produce invalid order for small n, e.g., sums differing by more than 1.
adversarial.why_effective: Small n makes it easy to verify sums manually; if construction is wrong, it will be caught. Also checks that output is a permutation of 1..6.

key_coverage_gaps: No test for n=1 (not required)
No test for extremely large output verification (but can be inferred from construction)

random.description: Random small test cases with n ≤ 5, w ≤ 10, individual array lengths up to w, values in [-10, 10]. Useful for verification against brute force.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random n in [1,5], w in [1,10], then for each array generate random li in [1,w] and li random integers in [-10,10]. Compute expected output by brute force enumerating all placements for each column independently.

random.description: Large random test with n=1000, w=1000, total length approximately 1e5, values in [-1e9, 1e9]. Stress test for time efficiency.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n and w with total length constraint. Randomly choose array lengths such that sum ≤ 1e6. Fill with random int64 values. Compute output using efficient algorithm (prefix/suffix maxima + difference array).

boundary.description: Maximum constraints: n=1e6, w=1e6, total length exactly 1e6 by setting each array to length 1. Values can be large positive or negative. Tests ability to process many arrays with minimal per-array overhead.
boundary.test_values: n=1000000, w=1000000, each array length 1, values from -1e9 to 1e9. Expected answer per column is sum of all max(0, a_i) because each array can contribute to any column (since length 1, it can slide anywhere).
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of large n with small arrays

boundary.description: Minimum width: w=1, n can be large but total length ≤ 1e6. Each array must have length 1. No sliding possible, each array forced to cover the only column. Values can be negative. Tests that the algorithm correctly forces inclusion of negative values when exclusion is impossible.
boundary.test_values: n=5, w=1, all arrays length 1, values: -5, -2, 0, 3, -1. Expected answer: -5 + -2 + 0 + 3 + -1 = -5.
error_types_caught: incorrect assumption that exclusion is always possible

boundary.description: Single array with length equal to width. No sliding flexibility; each column gets the corresponding element. Values can be negative. Tests that the algorithm correctly handles the case where the array cannot be shifted.
error_types_caught: Assuming full array availability for middle columns

adversarial.description: Arrays with large negative values but one large positive at the edge, to test that the prefix and suffix maxima computations correctly pick the positive value and that the middle range update uses the global maximum.
adversarial.attack_vector: Test maximum selection when the array has a single large positive element at one end and all other elements are very negative. The global maximum is that positive. For columns where the positive is not accessible due to sliding constraints, the algorithm must correctly fall back to negative values (or zero if negative).
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that only consider prefix and suffix maxima without properly restricting the accessible range will incorrectly assign the positive value to all columns, resulting in overestimation for columns where it cannot be placed.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of sliding window boundaries
not taking max with zero for negative values

adversarial.description: Many arrays of length 1 with mixed signs, and w very large. This tests scalability of the difference array approach for constant range updates. The contribution from each length-1 array is a single value (max(0,a_i)) added to every column because they can slide anywhere. This should be handled efficiently without iterating over all columns for each array.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit O(n*w) naive solution by making n and w both large (e.g., 1e5 each) but total length small because each array length 1. Expected efficient solution uses difference array to add constant to entire range.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive algorithm that iterates over all columns for each array would time out because O(n*w) is huge. The efficient algorithm should process each array in O(1) by adding its contribution to the whole range using difference array.
error_types_caught: inefficient range update (e.g., using for loop over w)
memory blow if storing ans as full array of size w (which is fine as w ≤ 1e6)

adversarial.description: Array with alternating positive and negative values and length exactly w, so no sliding possible. Tests that the algorithm correctly uses the array as a fixed assignment to columns, and that max(0, a_j) is applied per column.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive algorithm might assume that sliding is always possible and compute global maximum for all columns, leading to incorrect answer.
adversarial.why_effective: If the algorithm incorrectly uses prefix/suffix maxima and assumes a sliding window, it might output 20 for all columns because global max is 20, but actually the 20 is only at column 3, and other columns cannot get that value because the array is fixed.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of arrays with length equal to width
forgetting to consider the fixed placement when li == w

key_coverage_gaps: Test with very sparse arrays (many zeros)
Test with arrays where all values are negative and w > 1 to ensure zero is chosen when possible
Test with w=2 and various lengths

random.description: Small random instance (n=3) with varied probabilities to test correctness of inclusion-exclusion and modular arithmetic. Can be verified by brute-force enumeration of all 2^9 = 512 possible graphs.
random.generation_strategy: Set n=3. For each i,j in [0,2], assign p_ij as a random integer from 0 to 100.

random.description: Medium random instance (n=7) with uniform probabilities (e.g., 50%) to stress-test performance and modular inverse calculations. Useful for checking time limits and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Set n=7. For each i,j, set p_ij = 50 (or any constant between 1 and 99 to avoid triviality).
error_types_caught: Modular inverse miscalculation due to large exponent

boundary.description: Minimum n (n=1) with zero probability. Edge case: no edge can exist, so perfect matching probability is 0.
boundary.test_values: n=1, p=0. Output must be 0.
error_types_caught: Incorrect sign in inclusion-exclusion for n=1

boundary.description: Maximum probability (all 100). Graph is complete, perfect matching always exists, probability=1.
boundary.test_values: n=2, all p=100. Output must be 1.
error_types_caught: Sign errors leading to negative probability

adversarial.description: Sparse graph with some probabilities very small (1%) and others large (99%). Tests numeric stability and sign accuracy in inclusion-exclusion when terms range widely.
adversarial.attack_vector: The large variation in probabilities can cause catastrophic cancellation in inclusion-exclusion sums if modulo arithmetic is not handled with proper inverses.
adversarial.why_effective: The inclusion-exclusion sum involves terms that are close to 1 and close to 0, leading to potential rounding errors (though modulo is exact). Naive implementations might lose precision.
error_types_caught: Precision loss when converting to rational
Incorrect modular inverses for small numbers
Sign errors due to large cancellations

adversarial.description: Uniform non-power-of-100 probabilities (e.g., 33%). Tests correctness when the probability denominator is not a simple divisor of 100.
adversarial.attack_vector: The inclusion-exclusion requires converting probabilities to fractions with denominator 100^{n^2}. Using 33/100 leads to mod inverses that are not trivial; bugs in computing products mod MOD can occur.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive implementation might treat 33% as 0.33 and use floating point, causing precision issues. Even modular implementations must correctly compute (33 * inv100 mod MOD) raised to powers.
error_types_caught: Off-by-one in inclusion-exclusion for repeated probabilities

key_coverage_gaps: n large (e.g., n=10) not covered
Probabilities with many zeros to test sparse graph efficiency
Probabilities near 0 or 100 but not exactly (e.g., 1 or 99) already covered

random.description: Random small values to verify basic correctness
random.generation_strategy: Generate b, g, n randomly from 1 to 10 such that n <= b+g (if possible) and also include cases where n > b+g to check zero answer.

random.description: Random large values near constraints to test performance and edge handling
random.generation_strategy: Generate b and g from 9000 to 10000, n from 1 to 10000, covering both feasible and infeasible participant counts.

boundary.description: Empty interval when n exceeds total number of people (b+g)
boundary.test_values: b=2, g=3, n=6: n > b+g, so no feasible number of boys; answer should be 0.

boundary.description: Single possible composition when L = R

adversarial.description: Case where naive formula b+g-n+1 fails (when n < min(b,g))
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit simplistic formula that does not limit between 0 and min(n,b).
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solution might compute answer = b+g-n+1 = 9, but correct answer is 3 because only up to n=2 boys can attend.

adversarial.description: Case where L becomes negative if max with 0 is omitted
adversarial.attack_vector: Missing max(0, n-g) leading to negative L and inflated answer.
adversarial.why_effective: If L computed as n-g = -5, then answer becomes R-L+1 = 3 - (-5) + 1 = 9 instead of 4.

key_coverage_gaps: Very large n near 10000 but b+g small
Extreme where b or g is 1 and the other is large
When answer is minimal (1) due to L=R with small numbers

random.description: Small random tree with moderate weights and queries to verify correctness of DSU-based solution.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random tree with n=10, edge weights in [1,20], and m=5 queries with values in [1,20]. Ensure all weights are distinct for easier manual verification.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect component merging
WA due to off-by-one in pair counting

random.description: Larger random tree (n=1000) with random weights and queries to stress test performance.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random tree using Prufer sequence or random edge addition, assign random weights in [1,1e9], generate m=2000 random queries in [1,1e9].
error_types_caught: MLE due to storing all pairs

random.description: Random tree with duplicate weights and queries equal to some edge weights to test equality handling.
random.generation_strategy: Generate tree with n=20, assign weights from a small set (e.g., {1,3,7}) with repetitions, queries include these values and values in between.
error_types_caught: WA when query threshold equals edge weight

boundary.description: Minimum n=2 and minimum m=2, single edge with weight w, queries below and above w.
boundary.test_values: n=2, edge weight=5, queries: 4, 5
error_types_caught: Off-by-one in pair counting when n=2

boundary.description: Maximum n=200000 and m=200000, all edge weights equal to 1e9, all queries equal to 1e9, expecting maximum number of pairs.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, m=200000, edge weights all 1e9, queries all 1e9
error_types_caught: TLE due to large input reading
Overflow in pair count (n*(n-1)/2 fits in 64-bit)

boundary.description: Star tree (one center connected to n-1 leaves) with edge weights from 1 to n-1, queries covering all thresholds.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, star: center=1, leaves=2..n, edges weight = leaf index-1, queries=1,2,...,n-1
error_types_caught: WA when merging only two nodes at a time

boundary.description: Path tree (1-2-3-...-n) with edge weights strictly increasing, queries include values between weights.
error_types_caught: WA when merging along a path
TLE if solution is O(n^2) per query

adversarial.description: Path tree with alternating large and small edge weights to test DSU merging order after sorting.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solutions that process edges in input order instead of sorted order will merge incorrectly.
adversarial.why_effective: If edges are processed unsorted, merging results in wrong component sizes and incorrect pair counts.
error_types_caught: WA due to not sorting edges before DSU

adversarial.description: All edge weights equal but queries given in decreasing order (if solution processes queries in online order).
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that answer queries online without sorting may recompute from scratch each time, causing TLE.
adversarial.why_effective: The naive O(n^2) per query leads to O(m n^2) time.
error_types_caught: TLE due to online processing without sorting

adversarial.description: Tree where queries exactly match edge weights in descending order to test handling of equality and sorting stability.
adversarial.attack_vector: If DSU merging uses ≤ instead of <, or if sorting doesn't handle ties properly, answers may be off by one.
adversarial.why_effective: For query=2, edge weight 2 should be included; if merging condition is strict <, it will be excluded, giving wrong answer.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect comparison (strict vs non-strict)
WA due to unstable sorting of edges with equal weight

adversarial.description: Large tree with many queries such that each query requires merging many components; designed to test DSU path compression efficiency.
adversarial.attack_vector: If DSU lacks path compression or union by size, operations may become O(n) each, leading to TLE.
adversarial.example_input:
200000 200000
(edges: all weight distinct, tree is a line)
(queries: increasing, each step adds a new edge)
adversarial.why_effective: In a line, each query merges two components, but without union by size, the tree can become skewed, causing deep recursion.
error_types_caught: TLE due to inefficient DSU (no path compression or union by rank)

key_coverage_gaps: Large memory usage when storing all queries in multidimensional array
Integer overflow when n=200000 (pairs = 19999900000 > 2^31)
Handling of duplicate edge weights in sorting
Offline vs online processing of queries

random.description: Small random strings to verify basic correctness and manual validation.
random.generation_strategy: Generate s and t with lengths between 1 and 10. Ensure t is a subsequence of s by randomly selecting positions in s. Include edge cases where t equals s or t is a single character.

random.description: Large random strings (length up to 200) to stress test performance and correctness on bigger inputs.
random.generation_strategy: Generate s of length 200 with random lowercase letters. Then generate t by randomly selecting a subsequence of s (preserving order) with length between 1 and 200. Ensure variety in characters.
random.example_input: s = "a" repeated 200 times, t = "a" repeated 100 times
error_types_caught: time limit issues due to O(n^2) implementation

boundary.description: Both strings have minimum length 1.
boundary.test_values: s length = 1, t length = 1, t is a subsequence of s.

boundary.description: Both strings have maximum length 200 and are identical.
boundary.test_values: s and t both length 200, identical string. Expected output 0.
boundary.example_input:
s = "a" repeated 200 times
t = "a" repeated 200 times

boundary.description: t is a single character that appears many times in s.
boundary.test_values: t is a single character, s of max length 200 with all same character
error_types_caught: forgetting that only one character of t needs to remain
inability to compute maximum removal when t is short

boundary.description: t appears at the beginning of s, so maximum removable substring is at the end.
boundary.test_values: s = "abc...", t = "ab" (first two chars)
error_types_caught: off-by-one when removal is at the end

adversarial.description: t has repeated characters, s has many occurrences; optimal removal requires careful selection of which occurrences to keep.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solutions that only consider nearest matches may miss larger removal opportunities.
adversarial.why_effective: Common approach: precompute left[0]=0, left[1]=first 'a', left[2]=next 'b' after that, etc. For removal, check gaps. If left positions are chosen greedily forward, the gap between left[1] and right[2] might be underestimated. Here, the optimal removal is to remove substring from index 2 to 4 (0-indexed) giving "aaa" and t "aba" is subsequence. Output 3.

adversarial.description: Multiple possible removals of same maximal length; algorithm must correctly find any maximum.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that only consider one direction or stop early may miss the maximum.
adversarial.why_effective: The maximum removable substring length is 3 (remove either "abc" from positions 3-5 or positions 0-2). A naive solution that only checks removal from the beginning or end might output 0 or 2.
error_types_caught: failing to consider all possible removal positions
incorrect handling of multiple subsequence matches

adversarial.description: A large gap between consecutive t characters in s, causing maximum removal to be large.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that only compute gaps but have off-by-one errors may output incorrect length.
adversarial.why_effective: The maximum removal is the entire middle block of 'x's (100 characters). Off-by-one errors could output 99 or 101.
error_types_caught: off-by-one errors in gap length calculation
handling of strings with many identical characters in s

key_coverage_gaps: cases where t is empty (not allowed per constraints)
multiple test cases (not required per problem description)

random.description: Small random tree with matched multisets and varying mismatches
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random tree with n up to 20. Assign initial colors a_i randomly from 1 to 3. Generate desired colors b_i by randomly permuting the multiset of a_i. This ensures multiset match. Output can be Yes or No depending on structure; we need to compute actual answer using correct algorithm, but for pattern we generate both cases.

random.description: Large random tree with all initial equal to desired (k=0)
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random tree with n up to 200000 (total sum of n across test cases <= 2e5). Set a_i = b_i = random integer from 1 to 1e6 for all i. No mismatches.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of k=0 output format

boundary.description: Single city (n=1) with mismatched colors (impossible)
Two cities connected by edge, initial and desired swapped (possible)
Maximum total n (200000) with random mismatches, multiset match
boundary.test_values: n=200000 total across test cases, e.g., one test with n=200000. Generate tree as path to maximize depth. Colors: a_i = i mod 10, b_i = same permuted such that multiset matches and exactly 100000 mismatched vertices.

adversarial.description: Long path with mismatched vertices only at the two ends
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive BFS or DFS might explore entire tree when solution requires path between two far vertices
adversarial.example_output:
Yes
100000
1 2 ... 100000 (or a route that goes from end to end)
adversarial.why_effective: The minimal subtree covering mismatched vertices is the whole path. A solution that tries to simulate swaps along each possible path may be slow if not optimized. The length of the walk is large, and output must be correct.
error_types_caught: output format error for large route

adversarial.description: Star tree with many mismatched leaves requiring pairing
adversarial.attack_vector: Complex pairing logic; solution might incorrectly assume that any even number of mismatched vertices works
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution that tries all possible pairings or uses recursion may blow up on a star with many leaves because the number of permutations is large. But given that problem can be solved efficiently, this pattern tests the algorithm's ability to handle many mismatched vertices with same colors (requires grouping by color).

adversarial.description: Large tree with all colors distinct but multiset matches, forcing a long walk that covers many edges
adversarial.attack_vector: Outputting the route (list of vertices) for large k may be memory-heavy; naive solutions might try to store the whole walk in memory or output incorrectly.
adversarial.why_effective: The walk length can be O(n^2) if not optimized? Actually optimal walk length is at most 2*(n-1) maybe? For a line with mismatched ends, walk length is n. For all mismatched, walk might be longer but still O(n). But outputting 100000 integers is fine. However, if solution incorrectly constructs a walk that repeats many times, length could be huge. This pattern tests that the algorithm correctly identifies the minimal walk length.

key_coverage_gaps: Cases where multiset matches but number of mismatched vertices is odd (should not occur, but testing ensures)
Large number of test cases (t up to 2e5? Actually t can be large but sum n <= 2e5) to test per-test-case overhead

random.description: Small random inputs with moderate values to verify basic correctness.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate n (1..1000), d (1..100), e (1..100) to keep brute force feasible for verification.

random.description: Large random inputs with values up to 1e8 to stress-test performance and check for TLE.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate n, d, e in [1, 100000000] using uniform distribution, ensuring coverage of various ranges.

boundary.description: Minimum input values where n=1, d and e are large so no bill can be bought.
error_types_caught: incorrect assumption that at least one bill can be bought

boundary.description: Maximum input values with d=1 so answer must be 0 (since 1-dollar bills allow exact exchange).
error_types_caught: overlooking that dollar bills can make any integer amount due to 1-dollar bill

boundary.description: Both prices equal and n is a multiple of that price, so answer is 0.
error_types_caught: incorrect modulo handling when d and e equal

adversarial.description: Test that forces iteration over a large number of 5-euro bills when d is large and e is small, to catch solutions that limit iterations to a fixed small constant.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits the assumption that optimal number of 5-euro bills is small (e.g., <200).
adversarial.why_effective: Optimal solution may require many euros (20000000 rubles in euros) to minimize remainder, but a solution that only checks up to, say, 1000 euro bills will miss the optimal and output incorrect remainder.

adversarial.description: Test with small d and large e, where optimal is to use only dollars, but naive BFS might get stuck.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits that dollar denominations can make any amount, but some solutions might try to use euros unnecessarily.
adversarial.why_effective: Since d=2 and e huge, it's best to spend all on dollars. Solutions that iterate over euros might waste time or choose a suboptimal euro amount.
error_types_caught: lack of considering dollar's full coverage

adversarial.description: Large values that cause overflow in multiplication if not using 64-bit integers.
adversarial.attack_vector: Overflow when computing n - y*e or y*e.
adversarial.why_effective: Multiplication n*e could exceed 32-bit, but 64-bit is safe. Yet some solutions might use int and overflow.

key_coverage_gaps: Test cases with both d and e very small (e.g., 1) to exercise full coverage
Test cases where n is prime and d, e are large to ensure modulo handling

random.description: Small random rectangles with coordinates in [0,10] to verify basic logic.
random.generation_strategy: Generate white rectangle with random bottom-left (x1,y1) and top-right (x2,y2) such that x1<x2, y1<y2 and coordinates between 0 and 10. Similarly generate two black rectangles. Compute expected output by checking if white is completely covered by the union of black rectangles. Use exact geometry for cover check.

random.description: Large random coordinates spanning full range [-1e9,1e9] to stress test performance and overflow.
random.generation_strategy: Generate white rectangle with random coordinates, ensure x2-x1 >= 1 and y2-y1 >= 1. Generate black rectangles similarly. Use 64-bit integers to avoid overflow. Typical sizes: up to 1e9.
error_types_caught: Time limit exceed due to inefficient algorithm
Wrong handling of large negative coordinates

boundary.description: Minimal white rectangle (1x1) and black rectangles placed to test edge touching and exact coverage.
boundary.test_values: White: (0,0) to (1,1). Black1: (0,0) to (1,1) covers exactly. Black2: irrelevant. Also test edge touching: white (0,0)-(1,1), black1 (1,0)-(2,1), black2 (0,1)-(1,2) => visible.
error_types_caught: Assuming black rectangle must be inside white to cover
Not considering that a single black rectangle can cover whole white

boundary.description: Extreme values: white occupies full coordinate range, black rectangles in corners.
boundary.test_values: White: (-1e9,-1e9) to (1e9,1e9). Black1: (-1e9,-1e9) to (0,0). Black2: (0,0) to (1e9,1e9). Union exactly covers white (note: line x=0 or y=0? Actually union includes boundaries? Since white includes boundaries, points on the line are in both? The line x=0 from y=-1e9 to 0? Actually black1 includes x from -1e9 to 0, black2 includes x from 0 to 1e9. The line x=0 is included in both? If boundaries are inclusive, then union covers whole white. But careful: 'strictly outside' condition: point on white boundary that is also on black boundary is not strictly outside. So if white is covered by union including boundaries, then no visible point. So expected output NO. But if white is only covered by interiors? Usually boundaries are considered part of rectangles, so union covers all. So this should be NO.
error_types_caught: Neglecting that boundaries of black rectangles cover white points
Handling of zero-width/height rectangles? Not applicable

adversarial.description: White rectangle exactly covered by union of two disjoint black rectangles that meet at a line (no overlap).
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits naive check that only considers each black rectangle individually and not their union.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solution might check if white is inside each black rectangle and conclude visible because not fully inside either, but union covers all. Also, boundary at x=1 is shared: are points on x=1 considered covered? Since black rectangles include boundaries, the line x=1 from y=0 to 2 is covered by both. So no visible point.
error_types_caught: Failure to consider union of black rectangles

adversarial.description: Black rectangles overlap and together cover white, but one black rectangle is completely inside the other or they overlap significantly.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits incorrect area-based covering check or incorrect handling of overlapping regions (e.g., subtracting intersection twice).
adversarial.why_effective: Some might think that since second black is small and inside first, white is covered. But they might incorrectly compute union area as sum minus intersection, but if they don't check that union exactly covers white, they might output YES if there is any uncovered area. Here union exactly covers everything because first black covers all white. So should be NO. But naive area-based check might think union area is less than white area if they subtract too much? Actually here union area = area of first black = 100, white area=100, so equal. But if they only check if area(union) >= area(white), it would work. But if they check only if white is subsets of each black individually, they would output YES incorrectly (since not subset of second).
error_types_caught: Not checking exact coverage by union

key_coverage_gaps: Overlapping black rectangles that cover white with complex shape (e.g., L-shaped union)
Negative coordinates with minimal white
Large coordinates and many test cases for time limit verification

random.description: Random test cases with small constraints for verification of correctness
random.generation_strategy: Generate t (1-10) test cases, each with n (1-10) blows, h (1-100), d_i and h_i (1-100). Use random values.

random.description: Stress test with maximum constraints to test performance and overflow
random.generation_strategy: Generate t=1000 test cases, each with n=100 blows, h up to 1e9, d_i and h_i up to 1e9. Random values.
random.example_input:
2
100 1000000000
... (100 lines of random d_i and h_i)
100 1000000000
... (another 100 lines)
random.example_output: Some integer or -1 per test case

boundary.description: Single blow type that can defeat the dragon in one hit (d_i >= h) with small h
boundary.test_values: h=1, n=1, d_i=1 or larger; also h=1e9 with d_i>=h

boundary.description: All blows have d_i <= h_i (net non-positive) and no one-shot possible, so impossible
boundary.test_values: h large, d_i small, h_i large; ensure d_i < h for all

adversarial.description: Best final blow (max d_i) is not the same as best reduction blow (max d_i - h_i). Checks if solution correctly uses different blows for reduction and kill.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solution might use same blow for both or incorrectly compute number of blows by using max_d alone.
adversarial.why_effective: The blow with max d_i (90) has net reduction 5, blow with max net reduction (9) has d_i=10. Optimal: use the net reduction blow 9 times to reduce heads from 100 to 100-9*9=19, then final blow with d_i=90 kills (since 90>=19). Total 10 blows. If a solution uses max_d for reduction (90) and then final blow also max_d, it would use 1 blow? But 90<100 so cannot one-shot. If it uses max_d repeatedly, each blow reduces by 5, need ceil((100-90)/5)=2 blows after one max_d? Actually that totals 3 blows, but wrong because after first max_d, heads become 100-90+85=95, then next max_d makes 95-90+85=90, never decreases. So incorrect. This catches solutions that don't consider net reduction properly.

adversarial.description: Cases where after using net reduction blows, the remaining heads exactly equal max_d, requiring correct ceiling calculation.
adversarial.attack_vector: Off-by-one errors when (h - max_d) is exactly divisible by max_net_reduction.
adversarial.why_effective: Max_d=9 (net=1), max_net=2 (from second blow). h - max_d = 1, which is divisible by max_net? 1/2=0.5, ceil=1, plus final blow = 2. But careful: alternative strategy: use max_net blow twice? 10-3+1=8, 8-3+1=6, then final? Actually check: after two reduction blows: 10->8->6, still >9? No, 6<9, so final blow kills, total 3? That's worse. Correct answer is 2: one reduction blow (3-1=2 net) reduces to 8, then final blow 9 kills (9>=8). If solution uses floor instead of ceil, it might compute (h - max_d) / max_net = 1/2=0 (floor), then +1 =1, wrong. Also if it computes incorrectly because max_d is not enough to kill after zero reductions? Actually after 0 reductions, heads=10, max_d=9<10, so need at least one reduction. This catches ceiling errors.

key_coverage_gaps: Missing pattern for multiple test cases with identical repeated values
Missing pattern for very large net reduction but low max_d

random.description: Random cactus graph with vertex-disjoint cycles, moderate size (n up to 1000, cycles up to 20). Costs uniformly random in [0, 1000000].
random.generation_strategy: Generate a tree backbone with n nodes, then attach additional edges to form cycles ensuring each vertex belongs to at most one cycle. Randomly assign costs.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect cycle handling

random.description: Random cactus with many small cycles (each cycle length 3-5), n large (100000), cycles up to 30. Costs random large values up to 1e9.
random.generation_strategy: Use a tree as base, then add random small cycles on random nodes, ensuring no vertex in two cycles. Assign high costs.
error_types_caught: TLE due to large FFT domain

boundary.description: Tree (no cycles). The only repair set is all edges, so cost is xor of all edge costs, number of ways is 1.
boundary.test_values: Graph as a tree with n=1000, m=n-1. Costs vary.

boundary.description: Single cycle graph (n=m, each vertex in exactly one cycle). Linear time solution exists: take all edges, then remove one edge; min xor is min xor of spanning tree (remove one edge). Number of ways = count of edges achieving that min.
boundary.test_values: Cycle with n=3, costs 10^9, 10^9, 10^9 (all equal). Min xor = 0, ways = 3.
error_types_caught: Failing to consider all possible removals

boundary.description: Graph with zero-cost edges. Zero can be included and affects xor and counting.
boundary.test_values: Cycle with costs 0, 1, 1. Min xor = 0 (remove zero-cost edge), ways = 1.

adversarial.description: Graph where each cycle has costs that cause many possible xor values, leading to large FFT size and potential TLE or memory issues if not optimized.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit FFT by having cycle xor values covering a wide range, e.g., each cycle's xor has high bits set, causing convolution size to be large (up to 2^20).
adversarial.why_effective: Multiple cycles with xor sums that are powers of two cause the FFT convolution to require large arrays (e.g., size up to 2^20) if naive, leading to TLE.

adversarial.description: Graph where multiple cycles have identical xor values, testing the counting modulo 1e9+7 and ensuring correct combination count (using DP or FFT).
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit small number of distinct xor values but many cycles, causing counting combinatorics to be large and modulo handling.
adversarial.why_effective: Multiple identical cycle xor values can cause incorrect counting if not handled properly (e.g., using DP incorrectly with combinatorics).

key_coverage_gaps: Graph with cycles where some cycles have length > 10
Graph with costs near upper bound (10^9) combined
Graph where minimum xor is achieved by multiple combinations due to zero-cost edges

random.description: Random small n (n up to 10) with uniformly random d_i. Used for correctness verification.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n between 1 and 10, then generate n random integers d_i in [0, n-1] uniformly. Build tree using known constructive algorithm to validate output satisfies distance constraints.

random.description: Random large n (n=100000) with random d_i to test performance and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Set n=100000, generate d_i uniformly in [0, n-1]. Ensure the generation algorithm runs in O(n log n) or better.

boundary.description: Minimum n (n=1). Only one pair of vertices.
boundary.test_values: n=1, d_1 can be 0 only (since d_i <= n-1 =0). The tree must have 2 vertices and 1 edge.

boundary.description: All d_i = 0. Each pair must be directly connected.
boundary.test_values: n arbitrary (e.g., 5). d_i all 0. The construction must connect each i to i+n, plus additional edges to ensure connectivity (since a tree must be connected, and direct connections alone form n disjoint edges). Known solution: after sorting, the chain of vertices 1..n is built, and for d_i=0, the vertex i+n is directly attached to i.
error_types_caught: Assuming direct edges alone suffice (forgetting tree must be connected)

boundary.description: Maximum d_i values (d_i = n-1). Requires long paths.
boundary.test_values: n=10, all d_i = 9. The tree must have a path of length at least n-1 to accommodate distances. The known solution places vertices with large d_i at the beginning of the chain.
error_types_caught: Violation of distance constraint when d_i large

adversarial.description: Sorted descending d_i with many equal large values. Tests stability of sorting and handling of duplicate distances.
adversarial.attack_vector: Some solutions assume that after sorting by d_i, the order of equal d_i doesn't matter, but they might break if indices are not properly tracked.
adversarial.why_effective: If the solution uses stable sort but relies on original order, it may produce different chain order; the distance constraint must still hold. This pattern checks that any valid order works.
error_types_caught: Sorting instability leading to invalid tree

adversarial.description: Large n with alternating small and large d_i values to stress the construction algorithm.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive O(n^2) algorithms will TLE; also tests for correct handling of positions when d_i vary widely.
adversarial.why_effective: The solution must process each pair efficiently; any O(n^2) step will time out.

adversarial.description: d_i values that cause the chain to have gaps (e.g., d_i sorted descending, but some d_i are zero after a large one). Tests correctness of linking 'spare' vertices.
adversarial.attack_vector: Some solutions might incorrectly attach vertices when d_i is zero and the chain length is already full.
adversarial.why_effective: The first two pairs (d=4) need to be placed at positions 1 and 2 of the chain; the zeros must be attached at positions 3,4,5. If the algorithm does not handle the 'gap' between the main chain and the extra vertices correctly, it may produce incorrect distances.
error_types_caught: Incorrect attachment logic for zero-distance pairs

key_coverage_gaps: Non-integer or invalid d_i (not applicable since input guarantees integer)
Very large n with specific patterns like all d_i = n-1 (covered)
Edge case n=2 (not explicitly covered, but similar to n=1)

random.description: Mixed small random operations with random array values and random add/count operations. This tests basic correctness under typical usage.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n and m up to 10 (for verification) with random values in [1,10000]. Generate random operations: add with random l,r,d (d <= 10000, ensuring final values <=10000) and count with random l,r. Small size allows manual verification.

random.description: Large-scale random test with n=100000, m=100000. Operations are random but balanced between add and count to stress test performance and data structure correctness.
random.generation_strategy: Generate array of size 100000 with random values in [1,10000]. Generate 100000 operations: approximately half adds, half counts. Ensure validity: for adds, l,r in [1,n], d in [1,10000] such that after all adds each element does not exceed 10000 (track cumulative adds). Counts are random intervals. Expected output can be computed by brute force for small n,m, but for large we rely on correctness of generator.

boundary.description: Minimum constraints: n=1, m=1. Single element array and single operation. Tests edge case of minimal input.
boundary.test_values: n=1, m=1, array value=1 (non-lucky), operation='count 1 1'

boundary.description: Maximum constraints: n=100000, m=100000, all adds over entire array, then a final count. Tests ability to handle large input and updates.
boundary.test_values: n=100000, m=100000. Array initial values all 1. Operations: 99999 adds 'add 1 100000 1', then a final 'count 1 100000'. After 99999 adds, each element becomes 100000, but the guarantee says after all operations values <= 10000. So we must scale: initial=1, add 1 each time for at most 9999 times to keep final <=10000. We'll limit d=1 and number of adds to 9999, but then m=100000 includes many counts. Better: use initial=5000, add d=1, and only 5000 adds to reach 10000. For simplicity, we design a pattern with initial=1, d=1, and only 9999 adds, with remaining operations as counts. But to hit max m, we can interleave counts. For the example, we show a minimal version with n=1, m=2: add 1 1 9999 then count 1 1. Output: 0 if 10000 is not lucky, or count depending. Actually 10000 is not lucky, so output 0. But to have lucky numbers, we could set initial=4, add 1 each time to cross 7, etc. But we want boundary of maximum values. Let's make a small concise example: n=1, m=2, initial=1, add 1 1 9999, count 1 1. Output 0.

boundary.description: All count operations with no adds. Tests that count works correctly on static array, and that operations parsing handles missing add.
boundary.test_values: n=10, m=10, array with mix of lucky and non-lucky numbers. All operations are count on various intervals.

adversarial.description: Repeated add and count on the same small interval to exploit lazy propagation or segment tree update bugs.
adversarial.attack_vector: Frequent updates on a small subarray cause many modifications; if a data structure uses lazy propagation, errors may appear due to incorrect propagation or accumulated values.
adversarial.example_input:
3 10
4 7 44
add 1 2 1
count 1 3
add 1 2 1
count 1 3
add 1 2 1
count 1 3
add 1 2 1
count 1 3
add 1 2 1
count 1 3
adversarial.why_effective: Naive O(n) per operation would pass for small input in this example but large similar patterns with many operations on same interval can expose O(n*m) time. Also, segment tree with lazy must correctly maintain lucky count after multiple increments; if threshold crossing is not tracked correctly, answer will be wrong.

adversarial.description: Add operations that cause array values to repeatedly cross lucky number boundaries (e.g., from 4 to 7, then 7 to 44, etc.). This tests if the interval tree correctly updates the count of lucky numbers when values change near the boundary.
adversarial.attack_vector: Manipulate values to frequently flip lucky status. For example, initial values just below a lucky number, then add 1 repeatedly.
adversarial.why_effective: This sequence of adds causes both elements to remain lucky after first add, and then both become non-lucky after second add. A naive interval data structure that only stores sum of lucky flags might incorrectly propagate updates if it does not recalculate after each add. Specifically, a segment tree that stores the number of lucky numbers in a segment and uses lazy addition must be able to recompute whether the count changes when the values shift across lucky thresholds. This pattern checks if the algorithm correctly handles such transitions.
error_types_caught: failure to recompute lucky status after add
off-by-one errors in lucky number set

key_coverage_gaps: Maximum value (10000) and minimum value (1) not both covered in same test for boundary? Covered in boundary_2 and boundary_1.

Multiple adds that cause values to cross multiple lucky numbers in one operation (e.g., adding 1000 to 4 to get 1004, which is not lucky, but crosses many numbers). This is partially covered by adversarial_2.
Long sequence of count-only operations with many queries to test query-heavy scenarios.
Interleaved adds and counts on disjoint intervals to test range segmentation.
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: At least 6 patterns: 2 random, 2 boundary, 2 adversarial. Additional patterns for specific coverage gaps may be added.

random.description: Random test with small n (e.g., n=3) for quick verification of correctness.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random positive integers a_i (e.g., in range [1,100]), then compute matrix b[i][j] = a_i * a_j for i != j, with zeros on diagonal.
error_types_caught: logical errors in handling small n

random.description: Random test with large n (e.g., n=1000) and random a_i up to 10^9 to stress performance and overflow handling.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n random positive integers a_i in range [1, 10^9], compute matrix b with 64-bit integers. Example with n=3 for illustration, but actual test uses n=1000.
random.example_output: Actual output would be computed from a_i. Example: if a=[1e9,2e9,3e9], but need consistent. Let's use simpler: a=[2,3,5] produce small products.

boundary.description: Minimum n=2 case. Only one off-diagonal pair, so a1 and a2 are determined uniquely as the square root? Actually a1*a2 = b12, but multiple solutions exist? The problem guarantees a solution, and we can output any. Common solution works.
boundary.test_values: n=2, a1 and a2 positive integers. Example: a1=1, a2=10^9.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of n=2 where only one equation

boundary.description: Maximum n=1000 with all a_i equal to the same value (e.g., 10^9). Tests performance and handling of repeated values.
boundary.test_values: n=1000, a_i = 10^9 for all i. Off-diagonal entries are 10^18. Example shown for n=3.

adversarial.description: Input designed to cause integer overflow in intermediate multiplication when computing a_i using the formula a_i = sqrt(b[i][j]*b[i][k]/b[j][k]) without careful order.
adversarial.attack_vector: Use large a_i (e.g., 10^9) so that b[i][j] is about 10^18. Then b[i][j]*b[i][k] exceeds 64-bit range (≈9e18) before division.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive implementations compute numerator b[1][3]*b[2][3] = 10^36, which overflows 64-bit signed integer (max ~9e18). Only solutions that divide first (e.g., compute a3 = b[1][3] / (b[1][2]/b[2][3])?) or use 128-bit integers survive.

adversarial.description: Input where all a_i share a common factor, causing the gcd of a row to be a_i * common_factor, leading to wrong answer if a_i is taken as row gcd.
adversarial.attack_vector: Set a_i such that the set of all a_j for j!=i has a common divisor greater than 1. For example, a = [2, 6, 10] (gcd of {6,10}=2). Then row gcd for row1 = gcd(12,20)=4, but a1=2. So outputting row gcd yields wrong.
adversarial.why_effective: Some naive solutions attempt to compute a_i = gcd of row i (or column i) without considering that the gcd includes a common factor from other a_j. This input directly breaks that logic.

key_coverage_gaps: Case where n=2 with large products
Case where a_i are not all distinct

random.description: Random pairs covering all possible d_a and d_b combinations, including impossible cases
random.generation_strategy: Generate random d_a and d_b from 1 to 9. Compute expected output based on the logic: if (d_a < d_b and d_b == d_a+1) or (d_a == d_b) or (d_a == 9 and d_b == 1) then output a and b as described; else output -1.
error_types_caught: Mistakes in constructing a and b for equal digits

random.description: Random large values with specific exponent choice (e.g., 10^8-based) to ensure numbers within 10^9
random.generation_strategy: For possible pairs, use construction with 8-digit tail (10^8) to produce numbers exactly within bound. For impossible pairs, output -1.
error_types_caught: Off-by-one errors in constructing a and b

boundary.description: Extreme digits: d_a=9, d_b=1 (the carry case that many miss)
boundary.test_values: d_a=9, d_b=1. This is the only case where first digit increases from 9 to 1 due to carry.

boundary.description: Boundary of impossible: d_a=9, d_b=9 (equal digits, possible) and d_a=1, d_b=9 (impossible because d_a < d_b but not d_a+1, and not 9,1)
boundary.test_values: d_a=9,d_b=9 (possible, a=900000000,b=900000001) and d_a=1,d_b=9 (impossible)
error_types_caught: Incorrectly treating d_a=9,d_b=9 as impossible due to carry fear

adversarial.description: All impossible cases except one: this tests if the solution correctly identifies all 9*9 - (number of possible cases) impossible pairs
adversarial.attack_vector: Provide a list of all 81 pairs and expect -1 except for 17 possible pairs (9 equal + 8 consecutive + 1 carry = 18? Actually: 9 equal (1-1,...,9-9) =9; consecutive (1-2,...,8-9) =8; carry (9-1) =1; total 18. So 81-18=63 impossible. This pattern tests if the solution handles all impossible cases correctly.
adversarial.why_effective: A common mistake is to think that any d_a < d_b is possible, or that any d_a == d_b is impossible due to carry. This pattern catches overgeneralization.
error_types_caught: Missing the condition d_b == d_a+1 for d_a < d_b

adversarial.description: Edge case with numbers exactly at 10^9 boundary: d_a=9,d_b=1 requires b=1000000000. Some solutions may use a=9*10^8-1=899999999 for other cases but fail here.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit naive construction that might produce b > 10^9 for d_a=9,d_b=1 if they use 10^8-based construction.
adversarial.target_error: WA or RE (if they use incorrect exponent)
adversarial.why_effective: Some solutions might try to use the same exponent for all cases, e.g., a = d_a*10^8 + (10^8-1) for d_a < d_b, but for (9,1) that would give a=9*10^8+99999999=999999999, b=1000000000? Actually that works, but if they use a = d_b*10^8 - 1 for consecutive, they might get a=1*10^8-1=99999999 for (9,1) which is wrong. This pattern catches such inconsistency.
error_types_caught: Failure to handle numbers exactly at 10^9

key_coverage_gaps: Testing all 81 input pairs
Verifying numbers within 1e9 limit
Ensuring the algorithm works for both consecutive and equal digits

random.description: Small number of warehouses (n=2 to 5) with simple convex shapes like triangles and quadrilaterals placed in different quadrants around the origin, not intersecting, and not containing origin.
random.generation_strategy: Place each polygon in a different angular sector relative to origin, ensuring they are convex and non-overlapping. Use simple polygons with 3-4 vertices for easy manual verification.

random.description: Large number of warehouses (n=1000) with moderate number of vertices each (5-10), placed at various distances and angles, ensuring no intersections and no warehouse containing origin. This stresses the algorithm's performance and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Use a spiral-like placement or random radial sectors. Ensure polygons are convex and non-overlapping by generating them in separate angular sectors and at increasing radii. Use random convex polygon generation algorithm.
random.example_input: 10 polygons with 5 vertices each, placed in a spiral pattern around origin, not intersecting.
error_types_caught: floating point precision in angle sorting

boundary.description: Single warehouse with minimum number of vertices (k=3). This tests the simplest case.
boundary.test_values: n=1, k=3, vertices (1,1),(2,0),(1,0) in clockwise order. Origin (0,0) is outside.

boundary.description: Maximum total vertices (up to 2e5) with one warehouse having many vertices or many small polygons. Stresses input handling and large-scale geometry.
boundary.test_values: total vertices ~200000, e.g., single polygon with 100000 vertices forming a circle, or many small triangles summing to 200000 vertices.
boundary.example_input:
1
100000 (x y pairs for 100000 vertices forming a convex polygon approximating a circle centered at (10000,0) with radius 5000)

adversarial.description: Office lies on the extension of an edge of a warehouse (collinear ray). This tests handling of degenerate intersections where the ray exactly coincides with an edge line.
adversarial.attack_vector: Division by zero or incorrect handling of tangent rays.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive angle sorting may produce duplicate angles or division by zero when origin lies on line extension. Hitting a vertex exactly can cause incorrect edge count.

adversarial.description: Complete occlusion of a far warehouse by a nearer one. The far warehouse is hidden behind the closer one from the origin.
adversarial.attack_vector: Overcounting area by ignoring occlusion.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive geometric algorithms may sum all polygon areas without considering occlusion, leading to overcounting. Proper occlusion requires angular sweep and distance comparison.

key_coverage_gaps: Patterns with multiple overlapping polygons at different distances
Origin exactly on a vertex of a polygon
Large number of polygons with few vertices (e.g., many triangles)
Polygons with collinear edges (not strictly convex)

random.description: Small random test case with n between 2 and 10, d between 1 and 10, and b_i between 1 and 20. Ensures basic correctness of greedy logic and formula for number of moves.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly choose n in [2,10], d in [1,10], then generate n random b_i in [1,20]. Compute expected output by simulating greedy algorithm.

random.description: Large random test case with n=2000, d up to 1e6, b_i up to 1e6. Tests performance and integer overflow (should use 64-bit).
random.generation_strategy: Randomly choose n=2000, d in [1,1000000], then generate n random b_i in [1,1000000]. Compute expected output with 64-bit integers.

boundary.description: Minimum constraints: n=2, d=1, b_i=1 and 2 (already increasing). Output should be 0. Tests extreme small input and early exit optimization.
boundary.test_values: n=2 (minimum), d=1 (minimum), b_i=1 and 2 (minimum values, already increasing). Edge case: sequence already increasing.
error_types_caught: assuming at least one move needed

boundary.description: Maximum constraints with decreasing sequence: n=2000, d=1, b_i = 1000000, 999999, 999998, ... (strictly decreasing). This yields many moves and tests overflow with large intermediate values.
boundary.test_values: n=2000 (maximum), d=1 (minimum increment), b_i from 1000000 decreasing by 1 each step. The total number of moves is huge, potentially exceeding 32-bit signed int (max 2^31-1 ~ 2.1e9). Requires 64-bit.
error_types_caught: incorrect formula when many moves needed

adversarial.description: All elements equal with large d. Tests formula when successive moves increase quickly.
adversarial.attack_vector: Equal values cause each step to require increasing number of moves, revealing bugs in move count calculation or overflow.
adversarial.why_effective: Even though all values are same, after first move the previous value increases, making subsequent moves harder. Naive solutions might incorrectly assume same number of moves per step.
error_types_caught: failure to update previous value correctly

adversarial.description: Already decreasing sequence with large values and d=1. Simulates the worst-case for number of moves and tests overflow.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits maximal number of moves per step due to large differences and small d, leading to final values exceeding 32-bit range.
adversarial.why_effective: The first element is large, then all subsequent are very small. Each step requires many moves (first step: (1000000-1)/1+1=1000000 moves, subsequent steps similar). Sum of moves > 2^31? Actually for n=2000, total moves can exceed 2^31, causing overflow if using int.

key_coverage_gaps: Zero moves (already increasing)
Single element (not allowed, n>=2)
Large d with small b_i differences

random.description: Small random test case with n between 5 and 10, all values bounded by 10, to verify correctness of greedy heap solution.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n (5-10), k (0-10), g (1-10), a_i (0-10), c_i (0-10). Ensure validity (positive g and non-negative others). Use brute-force or known correct algorithm to compute expected output.
error_types_caught: incorrect greedy selection (e.g., buying cheapest future instead of immediate need)

random.description: Large random test case with n near 100000 to stress test time complexity and heap performance.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=100000, k=0, g=1, a_i = i (increasing linearly), c_i random between 1 and 1e9. This forces many drink purchases. Expected output can be computed by greedy heap, but for test generation, output is computed by a reference solution.

boundary.description: Single day test case, checking minimal and maximal constraints.
boundary.test_values: n=1, k=0 (min), k=10^9 (max simulated), a_i=0 (min), a_i=10^9 (max), g=1 (min), g=10^9 (max), c_i=0 (min), c_i=10^9 (max).
error_types_caught: forgetting to check initial strength before any drinks

boundary.description: Zero requirement days and zero initial strength, testing when no drinks are needed throughout.
boundary.test_values: n=10, k=0, all a_i=0, g and c_i arbitrary. Expected output 0.
error_types_caught: incorrect loop condition while strength < a_i for zero

adversarial.description: Costs decreasing over days, but initial requirement forces purchase of expensive early drink.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive algorithm that tries to skip buying early expensive drinks, expecting to buy cheaper later, fails because strength needed immediately.
adversarial.why_effective: On day 1, strength=0 < 1, so must buy a drink. Only option is day1 drink costing 100. Naive algorithm might think to wait for day2 (cost 1) but then cannot meet day1 requirement.
error_types_caught: incorrect greedy that only considers future cheapest without respecting day order

adversarial.description: Large gaps in required strength forcing many drinks, with cheap drinks at very end, to test proper prioritization of earlier drinks.
adversarial.attack_vector: Algorithm that does not maintain a heap of past costs and instead buys drinks in chronological order may overspend.
adversarial.why_effective: To meet day1 (1), must buy day1 (10) -> strength=50. Day2 needs 100, need +50, so must buy day2 (20) -> strength=100. Day3 needs 101, need +1, buy day3 (30) -> 150. Day4 needs 102, already met. Total=60. If algorithm tried to skip day2 hoping to use day4 cheap (5), it would fail because day2 requirement cannot be met without a drink before day2.
error_types_caught: not using min-heap of all past costs

key_coverage_gaps: Test with g=1 and large a_i values requiring many drinks to ensure sum of costs does not overflow 64-bit integer
Test with all c_i equal to check that any drink selection works (cost constant)
Test with k extremely large (10^9) to ensure no overflow when checking if strength < a_i

random.description: Small random test case with n=3, random initial and target matrices, random bar pattern. This tests basic functionality and ensures solution is found when exists.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=3, initial matrix, target matrix, and bar string randomly from 0/1. Solve using correct algorithm; if solution exists, output operations; else output -1. Include both solvable and unsolvable cases.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect XOR logic

random.description: Large random test case with n=1000, random matrices and bar, designed to stress test time and memory limits.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=1000, each matrix and bar as random strings of '0' and '1' of length n. Ensure the instance is solvable by constructing from known operations: generate random r[i], c[j] and compute target from initial. Then output operations. This avoids unsolvable cases for stress.
random.example_input:
1000
... (omitted for brevity, but would be a large input of 1000 lines each of 1000 chars, plus bar line)
random.example_output:
10
row 0
col 5
... (but actual operations would be many; we can note that output will have up to 2000 operations)
error_types_caught: TLE due to inefficient algorithm O(n^2) or worse
Memory overflow from storing data structures

boundary.description: Minimum n=1 with various bar patterns: bar='0', bar='1'. Tests base case.
boundary.test_values: n=1, bar either '0' or '1'. Initial and target can be 0 or 1.
error_types_caught: Missing handling of bar='0' which toggles nothing

boundary.description: All zeros bar (bar string all '0'). In this case, row operations have no effect on any cell (since bar[j]=0), and column operations have no effect on any cell (since bar[i]=0). Thus no transformation possible unless initial equals target. Tests detection of impossible cases correctly.
boundary.test_values: bar = '0'*n for various n; initial and target differ at some cell -> impossible.
error_types_caught: Incorrectly assuming operation can change cells when bar is all zeros
Error in checking consistency for cells where both bar[i] and bar[j] are zero

boundary.description: All ones bar (bar string all '1'). This means every operation toggles entire row/column. The problem reduces to standard toggling rows and columns. Test large n with this to ensure algorithm handles full dependence.
boundary.test_values: n=10, bar='1111111111', initial all zeros, target random. Operations will be many.
boundary.example_output:
20
row 0
row 1
... (all rows and columns needed to match target)
(but actual output would be determined by solving; we can just note it will be many)
error_types_caught: Incorrect handling of fully determined system
Not outputting optimal number of operations

adversarial.description: Bar pattern with many zeros and ones such that many cells are never changed, creating independence. Tests if algorithm correctly identifies impossible cases when conflicting constraints arise in a cycle.
adversarial.attack_vector: Create a cycle of constraints that forces inconsistency, e.g., bar with alternating pattern that causes a cycle of odd length in the graph of r[i] and c[j] relations.
adversarial.why_effective: In a 2x2 with bar='10', the cells (0,0): bar[0]=1, bar[0]=1 -> r0 xor c0 = A00 xor B00 = 0 xor 0=0. (0,1): bar[0]=1, bar[1]=0 -> only column operation? Actually bar[0]=1, bar[1]=0, so cell (0,1) affected only by column 1? Wait: bar[1]=0, so row op on row0 uses bar[1]=0 no effect; col op on col1 uses bar[0]=1 so effect. So equation: c1 = A01 xor B01 = 0 xor 1=1. (1,0): bar[1]=0, bar[0]=1 -> only row op on row1: r1 = A10 xor B10 = 1 xor 0=1. (1,1): bar[1]=0, bar[1]=0 -> both zero, so A11 must equal B11: 1 vs 0 -> impossible. So output -1. This tests detection of impossible due to unchanged cells.
error_types_caught: Failing to check cells where both bar are zero

adversarial.description: Large n with bar alternating 0 and 1 (e.g., '0101...'). This creates a bipartite graph with many independent components. Tests algorithm's ability to handle many independent assignments without exponential blowup.
adversarial.attack_vector: Force many independent variables; naive backtracking would be exponential, while correct algorithm does linear greedy.
adversarial.example_input: n=1000, bar='01'*500, initial and target chosen such that solvable (e.g., all zeros to all zeros). Then we can output empty operations. But to make it adversarial, we can make it solvable but need to assign many variables. The naive approach might try to assign all possibilities.
adversarial.why_effective: Bar with alternating pattern creates many cells where only one operation affects, giving direct assignments, and cells where both affect, leading to constraints that form many disjoint chains. Correct algorithm assigns in O(n^2) by processing each cell once, but mistaken algorithm might re-check many times.
error_types_caught: Inefficient DFS on large graph with many nodes

key_coverage_gaps: Test cases with n=2 and bar='00' (impossible if initial != target)
Test cases with bar='1'*n but n odd/even to check parity issues
Test cases where solution requires both row and column operations on same cell

random.description: Small random unicyclic graphs for correctness verification
random.generation_strategy: Generate N in [3, 20]. Start with a random cycle of length between 3 and N. Then attach remaining vertices as trees to random cycle nodes. Ensure graph is connected and exactly N edges.

random.description: Large random unicyclic graphs for stress testing performance
random.generation_strategy: N = 200000. Generate a random cycle of length between 3 and N (e.g., 100000). Attach remaining vertices randomly to cycle nodes. Shuffle edges order.

boundary.description: Minimum N (3) forming a triangle cycle
boundary.test_values: N=3, cycle: 0-1,1-2,2-0. All nodes have degree 2. Optimal sum: start at any node, potentials: 3,2,1 sum=6.

boundary.description: Large pure cycle (all nodes degree 2) to test cycle DP
boundary.test_values: N = 200000, cycle edges forming a single ring. Each node has exactly 2 neighbors. Optimal sum: starting anywhere gives same pattern; potentials sum = N + (N-1) + ... + 1 = N*(N+1)/2.

boundary.description: Cycle with a single long chain attached to one node
boundary.test_values: N=200000, cycle of length 2? No, cycle must be at least 3. So cycle of 3 nodes, one node has a chain of length 199997 attached. Optimal: kick-start at leaf of chain, then go along chain, then cycle.

adversarial.description: Optimal kick-start is a leaf far from cycle, not on cycle
adversarial.attack_vector: Many solutions assume the kick-start must be on the cycle, but here starting at a leaf of a very long chain yields higher sum.
adversarial.why_effective: If algorithm only considers kick-start on cycle nodes, it will miss the optimal starting point (leaf 9 in chain). The optimal sum is computed by starting at leaf and going up chain then cycle.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect kick-start selection

adversarial.description: Cycle with many equal-sized subtrees attached to each cycle node
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that do not correctly compute potentials during activation may double-count or misorder subtrees of equal size.
adversarial.why_effective: Each cycle node has two leaves attached, but there is also deeper structure. A naive DP might treat all subtrees equally and produce wrong order.

key_coverage_gaps: Graphs with multiple cycles (not applicable since unicyclic)
Very large ratio of tree to cycle (covered by boundary)
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: At least 10 random small, 5 random large, all boundary cases, and 5 adversarial/hack cases

random.description: Small random test case for verification of basic correctness, with n up to 10 and m up to 20.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate n between 2 and 10, m between 1 and 20, and randomly assign query types (1 or 2) ensuring at least one type 2. For each query, randomly generate a and b between 1 and n. Simulate the forced online decoding to compute expected output.
error_types_caught: Incorrect decoding of vertices using ans

random.description: Large random test case for stress testing performance, with n up to 200000 and m up to 200000.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=200000, m=200000. Randomly assign types with 70% type 1 and 30% type 2 to ensure many connectivity checks. Randomly generate a,b in range [1,n]. Simulate to get expected output (or verify with correct solution).

boundary.description: Single vertex graph (n=1) to test self-loop and minimal graph handling.
boundary.test_values: n=1, m=3: queries consist of type 2 with a=b=1, type 1 with a=b=1, and another type 2. Since n=1, all decoded vertices are 1. Self-loops: connectivity always true for type 2, so ans becomes 1 and remains 1.

boundary.description: Maximum n with single query to test edge-case of large n and minimal m.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, m=1: only one type 2 query. With a=1,b=1 (self-loop) output '1'; with a=1,b=2 output '0'.
error_types_caught: Missing at least one type 2 query guarantee

boundary.description: Repeated edge toggling on two vertices to test correctness of toggle logic and ans impact on decoding.
boundary.test_values: n=2, m=10: alternating type1 and type2 queries on the same edge. The ans alternates due to connectivity changes, affecting subsequent decoding.

boundary.description: All queries are type 2 (no edge modifications) to test connectivity on empty graph.
boundary.test_values: n=5, m=3: three type2 queries with random vertices. Since no edges ever exist, only self-loop queries return 1; all others return 0.

adversarial.description: Alternating ans to cause decoding shifts that test correctness of forced online decoding.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit that ans changes between 0 and 1, causing same input numbers to decode to different vertices. Naive hardcoded decoding might not recompute ans correctly.
adversarial.why_effective: The same input '1 2' decodes to different vertex pairs depending on ans. Without correct online update, answers may be wrong.

adversarial.description: Many self-loop queries to stress connectivity logic and decoding when ans=1.
adversarial.attack_vector: Self-loop queries always return 1, locking ans to 1. Subsequent queries are decoded with ans=1, which may produce different vertex indices. This can break assumptions that decoding is simple.
adversarial.why_effective: First three self-loops set ans=1. The fourth query (1,2) decodes with ans=1 to (2,3) not (1,2). If naive code ignores ans, it will check (1,2) and return 0 incorrectly.

adversarial.description: Star graph construction followed by connectivity queries between leaves to test DSU with rollback performance.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive recomputation of connectivity after each query will be slow due to many edges being toggled. Efficient dynamic connectivity is required.
adversarial.why_effective: Each connectivity query after building the star requires checking if leaves are connected, which is true via center. Recomputing from scratch is O(m) per query, leading to O(m^2) time.
error_types_caught: TLE due to inefficient connectivity checks

key_coverage_gaps: Large m with all type 1 queries (no output) to test edge toggle only
Multiple self-loops with type 1 toggles
Patterns with very high number of type 2 queries relative to type 1

random.description: Small random test for correctness verification
random.generation_strategy: Generate random string of length n (1≤n≤10) with lowercase letters. Generate q (1≤q≤10) random queries, mixing type 1 (update) and type 2 (query) with equal probability. For each type 2, compute answer by brute force for verification.

random.description: Large random stress test with maximum constraints
random.generation_strategy: Generate random string of length n=100000 with all lowercase letters. Generate q=100000 random queries, 70% type 2 (query) and 30% type 1 (update). For type 2, l and r uniformly random in [1,n]. For type 1, i uniformly random in [1,n] and c uniformly random letter. This stresses time and memory.
error_types_caught: TLE in segment tree / BIT with slow query per character
MLE from storing too many sets

boundary.description: Minimum length string and single query
boundary.test_values: n=1, q=1 (type 2 on the only character)

boundary.description: Maximum length string with all same character, alternating updates and queries
boundary.test_values: n=100000, all 'a', then many updates to 'b' and queries. This tests worst-case for bitmask updates (26 bits) and range queries.
boundary.example_input:
aaaa... (100000 'a')
100000
1 1 b
1 100000 b
... (many updates and queries)
error_types_caught: TLE from O(n) per update in naive segment tree
failure to handle update of same character

boundary.description: String with all 26 distinct characters, query full substring repeatedly
boundary.test_values: n=26, s='abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz', q=100000 all type 2 queries on [1,26].
error_types_caught: range query returning wrong count when all characters present

boundary.description: Single character substring queries (l=r) for many positions
boundary.test_values: n=100, s random, q=100 all type 2 with l=r for different i.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of l==r in range query
off-by-one in segment tree leaf index

adversarial.description: Maximum interleaving of updates and queries to exploit naive O(n) per query solutions
adversarial.attack_vector: Alternate between updating many positions and querying large ranges, forcing O(n) per query if solution recomputes from scratch.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that recompute distinct count in O(n) per query will be O(n*q) > 1e10 operations.
error_types_caught: TLE due to O(n) per query

adversarial.description: Updates on same character (no change) to fool lazy implementations
adversarial.attack_vector: Many updates where the new character equals the old one, causing unnecessary updates if not handled.
adversarial.example_input:
ab (n=100000, alternating 'a' and 'b')
100000
1 1 a
1 2 b
1 3 a
... (all updates identical to current char)
adversarial.why_effective: If the data structure updates even when no change, it may still do heavy work; proper solution should skip if same character.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of update with same char (should not change state)

adversarial.description: Many updates on same position to test segment tree leaf performance
adversarial.attack_vector: Concentrate all updates on one position, then query many ranges covering that position.
adversarial.example_input:
a (n=100000, all 'a' initially)
100000
(repeat 50000 times: 1 1 b, then 1 1 a)
 then 50000 queries: 2 1 1
adversarial.example_output: 1 (for each query, since final char is 'a')
adversarial.why_effective: If segment tree updates are O(log n) per update but repeated many times on same leaf, it's fine, but naive recompute would be O(n) per update. However, this tests constant factors in update logic.
error_types_caught: TLE due to high constant factor in update

key_coverage_gaps: Empty string? Not allowed (n>=1).
Queries with l>r? Not allowed.
Multiple updates on same position with same character.
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: At least 10 test cases: 2 random (small, large), 4 boundary, 3 adversarial, plus 1 for each edge case (n=1, q=1, all same, all distinct).

random.description: Typical random test with moderate n and k, diverse friend IDs.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n (e.g., 1000) and k (e.g., 100). Fill a_i with random integers from 1 to 10^5, ensuring some repeats but also many distinct IDs.
error_types_caught: logic error in updating screen order

random.description: Large random test at max constraints (n=200000, k=200000) to stress time and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Set n=200000, k=200000. Generate a_i as random integers from 1 to 10^9, with many distinct IDs to fill screen quickly.
error_types_caught: TLE due to O(n*k) or O(n log n) with large constant
MLE due to storing all IDs

boundary.description: Minimum constraints: n=1, k=1.
boundary.test_values: n=1, k=1: only one message from a friend.

boundary.description: Maximum n, minimum k: n=200000, k=1. Each new message replaces the previous one.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, k=1: screen always shows the most recent message.

boundary.description: All messages distinct, n=k=200000. Screen will contain all messages in reverse order.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, k=200000, all IDs distinct from 1 to 200000.
error_types_caught: forgetting to remove from set when evicting

boundary.description: All messages from same friend, n=200000, k=200000. Screen stable after first message.
error_types_caught: incorrectly updating screen when friend already present

adversarial.description: Repeated cycle of k+1 distinct IDs to cause frequent evictions and reinsertions. Exploits O(n) linear search in naive implementations.
adversarial.attack_vector: Cyclic pattern of IDs that are not on screen, forcing every message to trigger eviction and insertion. If implementation uses vector::erase/insert at front, each operation is O(screen size), leading to O(n*k) total.
adversarial.why_effective: Each message from a new ID (4) forces removal; repeated IDs (1,2,3) are already on screen but after eviction they reappear, causing many front operations.
error_types_caught: TLE due to O(n*k) instead of O(n)
incorrect set update when ID already present

adversarial.description: Large number of distinct IDs with small k (e.g., n=200000, k=10). Exploits memory and time in naive list-based implementations that store all messages or use O(k) per operation.
adversarial.attack_vector: All messages from distinct IDs, forcing eviction after first k messages. Each new message causes removal from back and insertion at front. If implementation uses a list and tracks presence with a set, still O(1) per operation, but if using vector and linear scan, it's O(k) per message leading to TLE.
adversarial.why_effective: Every message after the second causes a removal from back and insertion at front. A naive solution with vector front insertion O(k) will be very slow.
error_types_caught: RE due to accessing invalid indices if screen size tracking wrong

adversarial.description: Alternating between two IDs that are already on screen, causing no action but testing that order is not changed incorrectly. Exploits implementations that mistakenly reorder when a message is already present.
adversarial.attack_vector: Two IDs that are initially placed on screen. Then alternate messages from these two. A correct algorithm should do nothing. A buggy algorithm might move the existing conversation to top, which would change order over time.
adversarial.why_effective: If algorithm incorrectly moves existing friend to top on subsequent messages, the order will become [1,2] after third message instead of [2,1] after second message. Final screen would be [1,2] instead of [2,1], causing WA.
error_types_caught: incorrect order when friend already on screen

key_coverage_gaps: Large k but few distinct IDs causing repeated checks for existence (already covered by boundary_4 and adversarial_3)
Extreme ID values (1 and 1e9) to test hash functions or overflow in indexing (not in patterns)
Test with k=200000 and IDs that are all 1 (boundary_4 does this)

random.description: Small random test cases for verification of basic logic. L is small (1-5) and N has up to 10 digits. Covers simple period increment and length adjustment.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly choose L in [1,5]. Generate N as a random integer with length in [1,10]. Ensure N has no leading zeros. For each case, compute expected output manually or via reference algorithm.
error_types_caught: off-by-one when comparing candidate with N
not handling case where N is already periodic
incorrect period extraction when len(N) not multiple of L

random.description: Large random test cases for stress testing performance and memory. L up to 100, N up to 1000 digits. Ensures algorithm handles large strings efficiently.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly choose L in [1,100]. Generate N as a random integer with length in [L, 1000]. Use random bytes for digits, ensure first digit non-zero. Output is not computed here due to size; can be verified by reference algorithm.
error_types_caught: time limit exceeded due to inefficient string operations
memory limit exceeded by storing large intermediate numbers
integer overflow when converting period to integer (should use strings)

boundary.description: L=1, testing smallest period length. Covers repdigit behavior and edge cases like N=1, N=9, N=99.
boundary.test_values: L=1, N=1 (smallest N); L=1, N=9 (largest 1-digit); L=1, N=99 (largest 2-digit repdigit)
error_types_caught: off-by-one when period increments cause digit length increase

boundary.description: N has fewer digits than L. Must output smallest L-digit number (10^(L-1)).
boundary.test_values: L=10, N=123 (N short); L=100, N=1 (very short N)
error_types_caught: trying to form period from N's digits when N is too short
incorrectly outputting N or extending N with zeros

boundary.description: N has length exactly L and is the largest L-digit number (all 9's). Answer must be the smallest 2L-digit periodic number.
boundary.test_values: L=3, N=999; L=1, N=9 (all 9's, but L=1 gives next repdigit with 2 digits: 11, not 2L? Actually for L=1, 9 -> 11, which is 2-digit, which is 2L. So consistent)
error_types_caught: not incrementing repetition count when period overflows

boundary.description: N is already periodic with period all 9's and length multiple of L. Tests overflow to next repetition count.
boundary.test_values: L=2, N=9999 (period 99 repeated twice); L=3, N=999999 (period 999 repeated twice)
