boundary.description: Minimum length: m=1 with b=0, s='a'.
All b_i are zero: all positions must be filled with largest available letter.
Maximum b_i: when all positions have letters in descending order, e.g., t='zyx...', b_i can be large.
boundary.test_values: m=5, t='edcba' gives b = [10,6,3,1,0]? Compute: positions: e(0),d(1),c(2),b(3),a(4). b0 = sum distances to later letters (d,c,b,a): (1-0)+(2-0)+(3-0)+(4-0)=10; b1: distances to c,b,a: (2-1)+(3-1)+(4-1)=6; b2: distances to b,a: (3-2)+(4-2)=3; b3: distance to a: (4-3)=1; b4:0. So max b = 10. Length s=5 all distinct descending.

boundary.test_values: s='aaaa', m=4, b all zero

adversarial.description: Multiple largest letters repeated in s, and b zeros exceed count of largest letter, forcing use of second largest.

adversarial.why_effective: If algorithm assigns 'z' to both zero positions but there is only one 'z', it fails; correct is assign 'z' to one zero, then after removal, remaining zero becomes 'a'.
error_types_caught: Not updating b after partial assignment

adversarial.description: Large alphabet variation: s contains many distinct letters with low frequencies, forcing careful selection.
adversarial.attack_vector: Choosing letters in wrong order (e.g., not iterating from largest to smallest).
adversarial.why_effective: If algorithm picks 'c' first instead of 'z', then b values for remaining positions may not match. Correct order: zeros must be largest letters.

adversarial.description: Multiple test cases with shared large s length but each small m, to test resetting state.
adversarial.attack_vector: Incorrect global counters or carry-over between test cases.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution uses a single global frequency map without resetting, it may produce wrong output for second case.

adversarial.attack_vector: Off-by-one in conditional when r is exactly n or n-1
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions that use condition r < n incorrectly when r = n-1 (should use r < n formula) or use r <= n incorrectly when r = n (should use r >= n formula) will fail on these edge cases. Also tests the triangular number calculation.

boundary.description: Minimum length binary string: '1' (n=1).
boundary.test_values: The smallest possible input: length 1, binary '1'.

boundary.description: Power of two with many trailing zeros (n = 2^k).

error_types_caught: failure to handle carry across all bits

adversarial.description: Long run of consecutive ones followed by zeros, testing carry propagation.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits incorrect handling of carry when a block of ones ends with zeros; naive algorithms may fail to propagate carry correctly.
adversarial.why_effective: A block of three ones followed by zeros triggers a carry that must be propagated. Solutions that treat each one individually will output 3 terms instead of 2.

adversarial.description: Very long alternating pattern (e.g., '101010...') to cause TLE in O(n^2) DP solutions.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits algorithms that use DP with O(n^2) complexity by providing input of maximum length (1e6).
adversarial.example_output: Output m = number of ones (500000) with alternating +2^x terms; runtime should be O(n).
adversarial.why_effective: Alternating bits create no consecutive ones, so the optimal solution is simply all positive terms. DP algorithms that consider all pairs will be O(n^2) and exceed time limit.

adversarial.description: Maximum value input (all ones of length 1e6) to cause overflow in solutions that convert binary string to integer.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that try to parse the entire binary string into a numeric type (e.g., Python int, Java BigInteger) which may cause memory/time issues, or overflow in C++.
adversarial.why_effective: The number is too large to fit in standard 64-bit integers, causing overflow or requiring arbitrary precision arithmetic that may be slow or incorrect.
error_types_caught: wrong output due to truncated value

key_coverage_gaps: Inputs with leading zeros (not allowed as per problem, but could appear in malformed inputs).
Inputs with exponent near limits (2^0 and 2^999999) - covered by boundary.
Inputs with multiple isolated groups of consecutive ones like '1110111' - not explicitly covered, but similar to adversarial_1.

error_types_caught: incorrect cost decreasing by more than 1

error_types_caught: wrong logic when bomb positions are at end

adversarial.description: Bombs are placed at positions of the largest elements first, causing immediate removal. This tests whether the algorithm correctly handles rapid decreases in cost.
adversarial.attack_vector: Force maximum removals early; the cost should drop quickly. Naive solutions that recompute from scratch each time will be slow.
adversarial.example_output: 100000 99999 99999 ... (see pattern: after first bomb, cost becomes n-1; after second, remains n-1 until bomb at position n-1? Actually need to compute)
adversarial.why_effective: For each new bomb, the set changes drastically. An O(n^2) simulation would be too slow. Also, solutions that track only the maximum may get confused when multiple bombs remove the same element.

adversarial.description: Bombs are placed at positions that never correspond to the current maximum, so cost stays high for many steps. This tests tracking of next candidate when a bomb removes a non-maximum element.
adversarial.attack_vector: Make bombs target small values that are never the largest, so cost remains n until a bomb finally hits the largest element.
adversarial.why_effective: The first nine bombs are at positions 9..1 (values 9..1). They never remove the largest element (10) because 10 is at position 10. So cost stays 10 until the tenth bomb at position 10 removes 10. A naive simulation that only checks if the bomb index matches the current max might incorrectly remove earlier.
error_types_caught: WA when bomb does not affect current maximum but affects future maximum

Patterns with duplicate bombs? Not possible because q is permutation.

A naive solution that simulates moves might think Alice can win if she picks correctly, but optimal play leads to Bob win. Many might incorrectly output DA.

A solution that checks only for existence of both characters (and not their counts) might incorrectly output DA for '00' because it sees both zeros but no move. Also tests parity on odd cases.

random.generation_strategy: For each test case, generate n uniformly from 1 to 10, m from 0 to min(20, n*(n-1)/2). Randomly assign type=1 with probability 0.5, rest type=0. Ensure no duplicate edges and no self-loops. For directed edges, randomly choose u<v or not; ensure no directed cycles by checking with topological sort after generation (if cycle, regenerate). Output a feasible orientation by topological ordering.

random.description: Random large graph with many vertices and edges, stress test for performance and correctness.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=100000, m=200000 (sum across test cases). Use few test cases (e.g., 2 cases each with half edges). Randomly assign type=1 with probability 0.3, rest 0. Ensure no directed cycle by building directed edges in a topological order (assign random order to vertices, direct edges from lower order to higher order). Then add undirected edges randomly. For the second test case, include a directed cycle to produce NO.
random.example_input:
2
50000 100000
(edges generated as described, but for brevity not shown)
50000 100000
(edges including a directed cycle)

random.description: Random graphs where all edges are undirected, testing ability to assign arbitrary directions without creating cycles.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n up to 1000, m up to 2000. All edges type=0. Ensure graph is acyclic by creating edges only from lower numbered vertex to higher (like a DAG). Then shuffle order but maintain acyclicity by using a topological order. Alternatively, simply generate a tree (undirected) and assign directions arbitrarily (e.g., always from smaller to larger, which is safe if no directed edges).
error_types_caught: incorrect assumption that undirected edges alone can always be oriented
overly complex algorithm when no directed edges

boundary.description: Minimum vertices and edges: n=1, m=0. Test single vertex with no edges.
Maximum vertices and edges within constraints: n=200000, m=200000 across all test cases. Single test case to stress memory and time.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, m=200000, all edges type=0 (undirected) to avoid cycle checks on directed edges. But need to ensure acyclic orientation exists; generate as a tree (n-1 edges) plus additional edges but ensure no cycle by using a topological order.
boundary.example_input:
1
200000 200000
(edges generated as a DAG: for i from 1 to 200000-1, edge 0 i i+1; for remaining edges, random pairs with u<v and no duplicates)
error_types_caught: time limit exceeded due to O(n^2) algorithm

boundary.description: Edges count zero: both n=1,m=0 and n=100000,m=0. Multiple test cases with only vertices.
boundary.test_values: m=0 across all test cases

boundary.description: Only directed edges that form a cycle, making answer NO.
boundary.test_values: n=3, m=3, directed edges forming a cycle: 1->2, 2->3, 3->1. Also test with larger cycle.
error_types_caught: trying to orient undirected edges to break cycle (nonexistent)

adversarial.description: Graph with directed edges that form a directed cycle, but some undirected edges also present. Naive algorithm might try to orient undirected edges to break cycle, but that's impossible because directed edges are fixed. This catches algorithms that only check for cycle after orienting all edges.
adversarial.attack_vector: Direct cycle among directed edges, with additional undirected edges. The answer must be NO immediately.
adversarial.why_effective: Some solutions try to assign directions to undirected edges first and then check for cycle, or they might attempt to break the directed cycle by reversing the directed edges, which is not allowed. Since directed edges cannot be changed, the answer is always NO if a directed cycle exists.
error_types_caught: not considering that directed edges are fixed

adversarial.description: Disconnected components: one component has a directed cycle, others are fine. Overall answer is NO.
adversarial.attack_vector: Graph with multiple components, one of which has a directed cycle. Algorithms that process each component independently and combine results might wrongly output YES if they miss the cycle in one component.
adversarial.example_input:
1
5 4
1 1 2
1 2 1
0 3 4
0 4 5
(cycle in component 1-2, undirected edges in component 3-4-5)
adversarial.why_effective: Some algorithms might only check cycles on the whole graph or assume connectivity. This tests that all components are considered.

adversarial.description: Large test case with many test cases (t=20000) each with small n,m (e.g., n=1,m=0). This tests the ability to handle many small test cases efficiently and reset data structures properly.
adversarial.attack_vector: Time limit due to O(t * something) overhead, or memory not reset between cases.
adversarial.why_effective: Many solutions use global data structures and forget to reinitialize per test case, leading to memory leaks or incorrect results. Also, if input parsing is O(total characters) it's fine, but if there's per-test-case overhead, it may time out.

adversarial.description: Undirected edges that must be oriented to avoid a cycle, but the orientation must follow a topological order of directed edges. This tests that the algorithm correctly uses the directed edges' order to orient undirected edges.
adversarial.attack_vector: Directed edges already define a partial order. Undirected edges connecting vertices with conflicting order (e.g., an undirected edge between two vertices that are already connected by a directed path in one direction) must be oriented consistently. Some naive algorithms might pick the wrong direction and create a cycle.
adversarial.example_output:
YES
1 2
3 4
2 3
1 4   (or 4 1, but must be consistent with topological order: 1->2->3->4, so 1->4 is fine, 2->3 fine)
adversarial.why_effective: If the algorithm orients undirected edges arbitrarily (e.g., always from smaller to larger), it might create cycle 1->2->3->4->1 if 4->1 is chosen. Only topological ordering ensures correctness.

key_coverage_gaps: Cases where undirected edges form a cycle that cannot be oriented without creating a directed cycle (e.g., a cycle of undirected edges with directed edges preventing a consistent orientation).
Large test case with maximum sum n,m = 2e5 and many test cases (e.g., t=2e4, each with n=10,m=10).
Graphs with self-loops (not allowed per problem, but some generators might accidentally create them).

random.description: Small grid with a mix of G and B, typical case where blocking around B's does not trap G's.
random.generation_strategy: Set n,m between 2 and 5. Place a few G and B randomly, ensuring exit is empty. Randomly assign remaining cells as '.' or '#' with low probability of walls. Ensure the pattern is solvable by manually verifying with the standard algorithm.

random.description: Larger grid (e.g., 5x5) with multiple G and B, testing scalability of BFS and correct handling of multiple blockers.
random.generation_strategy: Set n,m between 5 and 10. Place 2-3 G and B randomly. Add some random walls. Ensure the pattern is solvable by manually verifying.

boundary.description: Minimum grid size (1x1). The only cell is the exit, which is empty. No good or bad persons. Output should be Yes.
boundary.test_values: n=1, m=1, grid with '.' only

boundary.description: Maximum grid size (50x50) with all empty cells except one good person at (1,1). Path exists, so output Yes.
boundary.test_values: n=50, m=50, grid full of '.' except cell (1,1) is 'G'. Exit at (50,50) is '.'.

boundary.description: No bad persons, only good persons. Output should always be Yes as long as each G can reach exit. Simple case with one G.
boundary.test_values: n=2, m=2, grid with one 'G' at (1,1) and rest '.'
error_types_caught: incorrectly returning No when no B present

boundary.description: No good persons, only bad persons. Must block all B's from reaching exit. Adjacent blocking possible, so output Yes.
boundary.test_values: n=2, m=2, grid with one 'B' at (1,2) and rest '.'; exit at (2,2). Block exit to stop B.
error_types_caught: assuming No when no G present
forgetting that exit can be blocked if no G needs it

adversarial.description: Bad person adjacent to both a good person and the exit. This forces an impossible situation because we cannot block the good person's cell nor the exit without trapping the good person.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits the condition that a good person adjacent to a bad person is a direct conflict; also the exit is adjacent to the bad person, making blocking either impossible.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions may block empty cells around B without noticing that blocking the exit would also block G, or they may not consider that B can step into G's cell.
error_types_caught: incorrectly blocking exit even when a G needs it
failing to check that B can use G cells

adversarial.description: Multiple bad persons surrounding a good person, forcing many blocks that trap the good person.
adversarial.attack_vector: By placing bad persons so that their required blocks create a wall around the good person, making the good person unable to reach the exit.
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions that block all adjacent cells to each bad person independently may inadvertently block all paths for a good person; also, they may fail to detect that a good person is cut off.
error_types_caught: overblocking without verifying good person reachability
incremental blocking that doesn't consider global effect

key_coverage_gaps: All patterns cover common pitfalls; additional adversarial patterns could target more complex wall configurations

random.description: Random small n (1 to 10) for verification of formula correctness and basic modulo operations.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random integer n in [1,10] using uniform distribution. Compute expected output as (n! - 2^(n-1)) mod 1e9+7.

random.description: Random large n (up to 1e6) to stress test performance and modulo operations with large numbers.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random integer n in [1, 1000000] using uniform distribution. Compute expected output using precomputed factorials and modular exponentiation.

boundary.description: Minimum value n=1 to test base case where answer is 0.
boundary.test_values: n=1 (smallest constraint)

boundary.description: Maximum value n=1000000 to test large input handling and performance.
boundary.test_values: n=1000000 (largest constraint)

boundary.description: n=2 to verify that answer is 0 for small n where no permutation is cyclic.
boundary.test_values: n=2 (second smallest, also yields 0)

adversarial.description: Smallest n=1 to detect off-by-one error in exponent (using 2^n instead of 2^(n-1)).
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit common mistake of using 2^n instead of 2^(n-1) in formula.
adversarial.why_effective: For n=1, 2^(n-1)=1, 2^n=2. Wrong formula gives 1!-2=-1 mod M which is 1000000006, not 0.

adversarial.description: Large n to test correctness of modular subtraction, especially when factorial is smaller than exponent before mod.
adversarial.attack_vector: Catch cases where (n! % M) < (2^(n-1) % M) and subtraction yields negative if not handled properly.
adversarial.why_effective: At large n, factorial mod M may be smaller than power mod M, so direct subtraction without adding M gives negative. Ensures use of (a - b + M) % M.

key_coverage_gaps: n=3 to test first non-zero output (answer=2)
n=1000000 already covered

random.description: Small random arrays with values in [1,5] and length in [1,10] for verification of correctness across diverse cases.
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, randomly generate n (1-10) and array elements (1-5). Multiple test cases to cover various shapes.

random.generation_strategy: Generate a single test case with n=200000, values random in [1,200000]. Alternatively, multiple test cases summing to 200000.

boundary.description: Single element array: always good, answer 0.
boundary.test_values: n=1, any value (e.g., 100)
error_types_caught: assuming array must have at least 2 elements

boundary.description: Two-element arrays: both [1,2] and [2,1] are good, answer 0.
boundary.test_values: n=2, all possible orders (combined in one test suite)
error_types_caught: thinking only non-decreasing arrays are good

boundary.description: All equal elements of length 200000: always good, answer 0.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, all values same (e.g., 1)
error_types_caught: time limit for large constant array
incorrect handling of equality in comparison

boundary.description: Strictly decreasing array of length 200000: answer n-1 = 199999.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, values decreasing from 200000 to 1
error_types_caught: misunderstanding of good array for decreasing sequence

adversarial.description: Array where almost all elements must be deleted: strictly decreasing except the last element is very large. This forces a large prefix deletion.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive O(n^2) simulation would be too slow for large n. Also some algorithms might incorrectly stop at the first decrease.
adversarial.why_effective: The longest good suffix is the last two elements [1,200] (non-decreasing), so answer = 98. A solution that only checks from the beginning or uses a single loop might over- or under-estimate.
error_types_caught: wrong answer due to incorrect suffix detection

adversarial.description: Array that is not good as a whole, but the longest good suffix is not simply the decreasing part from the end. It requires the two-phase scan to correctly identify.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that only implement the first phase (decreasing from end) or do not handle the transition correctly.
adversarial.why_effective: The two-phase scan correctly finds i=2 (0-indexed: delete first 2). A one-phase scan stopping at first increase would give i=3, overcounting deletions.
error_types_caught: wrong answer due to insufficient scanning of both phases

adversarial.description: Many small test cases (t=20000, each n=1) to test input parsing and overhead of processing many cases.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that initialize large structures per test case may cause overhead; also checks robust input reading.
adversarial.why_effective: Each test case is trivial, but the number of cases is maximal. O(t) overhead can cause TLE if not efficient.
error_types_caught: time limit exceeded due to high constant per case

key_coverage_gaps: very large values near constraint boundaries
arrays with multiple peaks/valleys (though handled by algorithm)
mixed test cases with varying n and values to ensure robust output formatting

error_types_caught: Logic errors in basic happiness index constraints

random.generation_strategy: Generate a random tree (e.g., using random parent for each node) with n=200000. Assign p_i uniformly in [0, 1e9] but sum m up to 1e9. Then compute valid h_i by simulating moods: start from leaves upward, assign good/bad such that conditions hold. Output single test case.

1
200000 1000000000
[200000 random integers summing to 1e9]
[200000 valid h_i computed]
[199999 edges]

boundary.description: Single city (n=1). All people live in capital. Happiness index must satisfy parity and range.
boundary.test_values: n=1, m from 1 to large, p_1=m, h_1 must be in [-m,m] with same parity.
error_types_caught: Missing check for n=1 root condition

boundary.description: Linear chain (path) with maximum depth n=200000 to test recursion and cumulative sums.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, tree is a path from 1 to n. p_i uniformly distributed, total m=1e9. Compute valid h_i. Could also include invalid case where g_i < sum_g_child at some node.
error_types_caught: Stack overflow due to deep recursion if using recursive DFS
Time limit for large linear trees

boundary.description: Extreme values for p_i and h_i near 1e9 and -1e9, including zero populations.
boundary.test_values: p_i can be 0 or up to 1e9, h_i near 1e9 or -1e9. Check parity and bounds.
error_types_caught: Integer overflow in (sub_p + h_i) if using 32-bit

boundary.description: Multiple test cases with total n=200000, many small trees (t up to 10000) to test initialization overhead.
boundary.test_values: t=10000, each n=20, total n=200000. Random valid/invalid cases.
error_types_caught: Incorrect clearing of data structures between test cases
Memory leak or reuse of values

adversarial.description: Parity mismatch at a node: (sub_p + h_i) is odd, but solution may forget to check parity and get fractional g_i.
adversarial.attack_vector: Missing parity check in condition for g_i.
adversarial.why_effective: For city 1, sub_p=3, h_1=2 → (3+2)/2=2.5 not integer. City 2: sub_p=2, h_2=-1 → (2-1)/2=0.5. Should output NO.

adversarial.description: g_i < sum_g_child at some node, violating mood worsening constraint (good people cannot increase downwards).
adversarial.attack_vector: Parent node has lower g than sum of children's g, meaning more good people come from children than entered parent.
adversarial.why_effective:
Leaf g_3 = (1+0)/2=0.5? Wait check parity: p3=1, h3=0, so sub_p(3)=1, g3=(1+0)/2=0.5 not integer. Let's fix: use even numbers. Better: n=3, p=2,2,2, h=2,2,? Actually construct: Path 1-2-3. p1=2, p2=2, p3=2, total m=6. Compute sub_p: 3:2, 2:4, 1:6. Set h3=2 -> g3=(2+2)/2=2. h2= ? For valid, g2 >= g3. If h2= -2? Then g2=(4-2)/2=1, which is <2. So invalid. Example: p=[2,2,2], h=[?, ?, 2]. To make g2 < g3, set h2=-2 gives g2=1, so output NO. The example input: 
1
3 6
2 2 2
? -2 2
1 2
2 3
 Output NO.
error_types_caught: Missing check that g_i >= sum of children g

adversarial.description: Capital (city 1) with h_1 out of range: g_1 negative or larger than m.
adversarial.attack_vector: For root, sub_p=m, so g_1 must be between 0 and m. If h_1 too large or too small, condition fails.
adversarial.why_effective: Root sub_p=5, h1=6 -> g1=(5+6)/2=5.5 (non-integer) actually 5.5 not integer. Better: use h1=6 with m=5 gives odd sum. Or h1=5: g1=5 but must be <= m=5, ok but then children? Let's make h1= -6: (5-6)/2=-0.5 no. For g1 negative: (5 + (-10))/2 = -2.5. So example: p=[3,2], h=[-10,?] -> output NO.

adversarial.description: Large values causing overflow in 32-bit signed integer when computing (sub_p + h_i) or multiplication.
adversarial.attack_vector: Use maximum p_i (1e9) and large tree so sub_p can exceed 2^31 (~2.1e9). sum of p over subtree can be up to 1e9 (since total m <= 1e9). Wait m <= 1e9, so sub_p <= 1e9, safe in 32-bit signed? 1e9 < 2^31-1 (2147483647). So no overflow for sum. But h_i up to 1e9, sum sub_p + h_i up to 2e9, still within signed 32-bit. However, if using 32-bit unsigned, it's fine. But some solutions might use int and overflow when adding two large numbers? Actually 2e9 is safe. But to be adversarial, we can have negative h_i down to -1e9, then sub_p + h_i could be 0 or small. No overflow. However, if m is up to 1e9, sub_p <= 1e9, so no overflow. But if someone uses int for m (1e9 fits in int). So overflow is unlikely. Instead, we can test for long long requirement? The problem statement doesn't specify 64-bit, but values up to 1e9 fit in 32-bit signed. So overflow not a big risk. But we can still include a pattern with m=1e9 and large h to ensure handling of large arrays.
adversarial.target_error: WA (if using wrong data type for intermediate multiplications? There are no multiplications.) Actually, no multiplication needed. So this pattern may not be necessary. Replace with adversarial pattern for tree depth and recursion.
adversarial.why_effective: Instead, use deep recursive DFS that may cause stack overflow if not iterative.
adversarial.example_input:
1
200000 200000
[200000 p_i each 1]
[200000 valid h_i computed]
[linear chain edges]
error_types_caught: Recursion stack overflow (RE) in languages like Python or with defined recursion limit

key_coverage_gaps: No tested case for disconnected graph (not allowed, tree guaranteed)
No explicit test for multiple test cases with large total n but many small trees
No test for zero p_i in all cities except root? (possible but trivial)

adversarial.why_effective: Naive check might accept because there is a 1 diagonally, but condition requires directly below or right.

random.description: Random test with moderate n and random d, simulating typical interactive binary search.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random n between 2 and 100, random d in [1,n]. Simulate response logic: first query response ignored, subsequent responses are 1 if |x_prev - x_curr| >= d else 0.

random.description: Large n (up to 1000) with d near middle, to test query efficiency and memory usage.
random.generation_strategy: Set n = 1000, d = random in [100,900]. Simulate queries as per problem.

boundary.description: Minimum n (n=1). Only one color, so d must be 1. First query is meaningless, then no further queries needed because d=1 is known? But algorithm may need to confirm. Typical behavior: query color 1, get meaningless response, then cannot query again (color already used), so output d=1.
error_types_caught: Trying to query more than allowed

boundary.description: Maximum difference d=n. For n large (e.g., 1000), d=n means any color change will have absolute difference < n, so all responses after first are 0.
error_types_caught: Assuming there is always a change
Incorrect binary search when all zeros

boundary.description: n=2 with d=1 and d=2 separately, small boundary.
boundary.example_output:
For d=1: first response meaningless, second response 1
For d=2: first response meaningless, second response 0

adversarial.description: Attack on algorithm that reuses same color or doesn't track used colors. Provide sequence where the same color appears twice.
adversarial.attack_vector: The adversary can respond to queries in a way that a naive solver might try to reuse a color, violating constraint. The test case ensures that the solver must not reuse colors.
adversarial.why_effective: If algorithm reuses color 1, it breaks rule; if it doesn't, it must detect and avoid. Some solvers might assume it's allowed, leading to wrong judgment.

adversarial.description: Attack on algorithms that interpret the first response as meaningful. Provide a case where first query response is 1, which might mislead if not ignored.
adversarial.attack_vector: The adversary gives a response for the first query that is the opposite of what binary search expects, causing convergence to wrong d.
adversarial.why_effective: If solver uses first response, it might infer d<=|2-1|=1 from first response, but actually d could be 1. But if first response is 1 for d>|2-1|? Actually first response is meaningless, so it should be ignored. If not ignored, solver may think that change >=d, but if d=1, second response also 1; if d=2, second response should be 0, but solver might incorrectly set bounds. Example: d=2, first response 1 (ignore), second response 0 (correct). If solver uses first response as meaningful, it might set d<=1 and then contradict with second 0.

adversarial.description: Attack on binary search that doesn't handle the case where all responses are the same (e.g., d=1 or d=n). This can cause infinite loop or incorrect answer if algorithm doesn't have proper termination condition.
adversarial.attack_vector: Provide a case where d is at extreme so all responses after first are same (all 0 or all 1). Some binary search implementations may not converge or may output wrong d.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive binary search might keep narrowing range but never confirm d because it expects a change point. Without proper check for all-same responses, algorithm may query too many times or incorrectly assume d=mid.

key_coverage_gaps: Large-scale interactive simulation with varying query patterns
n=1 edge case with no second query
Multiple queries with same color reuse detection

100000 200000 50000

boundary.test_values: n=1, m=0, k=1, c=[100], no edges. Special vertex is 1.

boundary.description: Two vertices connected by one edge, only one special vertex. Simple directed case.
boundary.test_values: n=2, m=1, k=1, c=[10,20], w=[1], edge 1-2, special vertex 1.
error_types_caught: incorrect profit computation with one special vertex

boundary.description: Tree graph with all vertices special. Requires all edges to be undirected to ensure mutual reachability.
boundary.test_values: n=4, m=3, k=4, c=[5,5,5,5], w=[2,2,2], edges form a tree (1-2,2-3,2-4). All vertices special.
error_types_caught: assuming all vertices can be saturated without cost
misunderstanding of saturation for complete special sets

adversarial.description: Cycle graph with high cost edges and special vertices placed to mislead greedy orientation.
adversarial.attack_vector: Greedy algorithms that orient edges cheaply may fail because later need to leave expensive edges undirected to connect special vertices.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might orient all edges (cost 0) but fail to saturate vertices because orientation may not guarantee mutual reachability. The optimal solution leaves one edge undirected (cost 10) but gains all three vertices (15-10=5). If all edges are directed, at least one vertex might not be reachable from all specials, leading to lower profit. The correct solution must consider orientations.

adversarial.description: Star graph with many special vertices on leaves, high edge costs, and high vertex rewards. Tests efficiency of DFS and DP.
adversarial.attack_vector: If solution performs many recomputations for each vertex, it will TLE. Also, handling of high costs may cause integer overflow if not using 64-bit.
adversarial.why_effective: The center vertex is not special, but all leaves are special. For each leaf, the optimal solution may involve directing edges away from center or leaving undirected, but with high costs, most leaves will be left undirected. Naive algorithms that recompute from scratch for each vertex will be O(n^2). Efficient solution uses tree DP and rerooting, O(n). This pattern tests for TLE if not optimized.
error_types_caught: TLE due to O(n^2) per vertex processing

key_coverage_gaps: Graphs with multiple biconnected components
Different distributions of c_i and w_i (all small, all large)
Graphs where special vertices form a subset of a cycle
Large disconnected graphs (though problem says connected, but might still be useful)

random.description: Random strings with moderate proportion of '?' to simulate typical contest data
random.generation_strategy: For given n, generate s where each character is randomly chosen from {'0','1','?'} with probabilities adjusted so that '?' appears with probability 0.3, and '0','1' each 0.35. This mimics partially known results.

random.description: Large random string with all '?' to stress test optimal assignment
random.generation_strategy: Generate string of length 1000000 consisting entirely of '?' characters. This tests the algorithm's ability to quickly compute maximum sets as floor(n/x) for each x.
error_types_caught: overflow in computing floor(n/x) for large n
incorrect handling of last incomplete set

boundary.description: Minimum n: n=1 with all possible characters
error_types_caught: off-by-one: for x=1 answer should be 1 if round is known

incorrect handling of incomplete set: answer always 0? Wait: if n=1 and x=1, a set can be completed (1 consecutive win), so answer=1. For x>1, answer=0. Output should be n=1 integer: the answer for x=1 only? Actually output n integers for each x from 1 to n, so for n=1 output one integer. For s='0', possible to have one set (Alice wins 1 round) => answer for x=1 is 1. For x=1, yes. So output '1'.

boundary.description: Maximum n: n=1000000 with all same known character
error_types_caught: TLE due to O(n^2) per x
incorrect answer when x > n (should be 0)
edge case: when n is large and all same, answer for x is floor(n/x), but algorithm must handle large loops efficiently

boundary.description: Alternating pattern known
boundary.test_values: n=100, s alternating '01'
error_types_caught: incorrectly assuming streaks of length 2 can be formed
greedy that doesn't consider alternating pattern prevents any x-length streak

adversarial.description: String with many '?' that can be assigned to create long streaks but also have known characters that break potential sets
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive greedy that fills '?' to extend current streak without considering future sets may produce suboptimal count.
adversarial.why_effective: For x=2, a naive algorithm might try to assign first '?' to 1 to get a streak of 1s, but the known 0s break that; optimal assignment might group sets differently. This tests proper DP or interval covering approach.

adversarial.description: Large n with pattern that causes O(n log n) per x to become O(n^2) if binary search not properly implemented
adversarial.attack_vector: For very large n (1e6) and all x from 1 to n, if algorithm uses binary search over next possible start for each x, but that binary search is O(log n) per step, total O(n log n * something) might be okay. But if implementation uses nested loops, it will TLE. Specifically, design input where there are many possible streak starts and ends to stress the data structure.
adversarial.example_input:
1000000
0?1?0?1?0?1?... (alternating '0' and '?' with known '1' every other? Actually better: pattern that forces many small segments: e.g., all '?' except one known character at end, causing many potential sets).
adversarial.why_effective: Naive algorithm that for each x tries to find next streak start by scanning linearly from current position will be O(n^2) and TLE. Efficient solution uses precomputation of longest uniform segment and jumps using binary search or two pointers.

key_coverage_gaps: Test with very small x (x=1) and large x (x=n) should be explicitly covered
Mix of known and unknown where '?' can create multiple possible set arrangements not caught by simple greedy
Cases where answer for some x is zero due to insufficient characters to form a streak of length x

random.description: Small random test cases with n and a_i in small ranges to verify correctness and cover both winning conditions.
random.generation_strategy: Generate t random games with n between 1 and 5, a_i between 1 and 10. Ensure a mix of cases where max > sum_rest and max <= sum_rest, and both parities of total stones.
error_types_caught: incorrect win condition when max > sum_rest

random.description: Large random test cases with n up to 100 and a_i up to 100 to stress test performance and correctness.
random.generation_strategy: Generate t=100 games, each with n=100, a_i random between 1 and 100. Compute expected output using solution logic.

boundary.description: Single pile of varying sizes. First player always wins.
error_types_caught: incorrectly thinking HL wins for even single pile

boundary.description: Two piles with equal stones. Total stones even, so second player should win (HL) for all positive integer values.
boundary.test_values: n=2, a=[k,k] for k=1,2,3,... (including large values)
error_types_caught: incorrectly thinking T wins for equal piles due to parity misapplication
not checking max > sum_rest condition (here equal, so parity applies)

boundary.description: Largest pile greater than sum of others. First player wins regardless of total parity.
error_types_caught: incorrectly applying parity when max > sum_rest

boundary.description: All piles equal with odd total stones. First player wins (since max not > sum_rest, total odd => first wins).
boundary.test_values: n odd such that total odd, e.g., n=3, a=[1,1,1] (total 3 odd); n=3, a=[2,2,2] (total 6 even => second wins).

adversarial.description: Largest pile exactly equal to sum of rest. This edge case (max == sum_rest) is tricky because it's not greater, so parity decides. Many naive solutions might incorrectly treat it as if max > sum_rest or ignore equality.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits ambiguity around strict vs non-strict inequality in max > sum_rest condition.
adversarial.why_effective: Some solutions might use >= instead of >, causing them to output T for these cases, but correct answer is HL (since total even).

adversarial.description: Multiple piles all equal with total stones even (e.g., n=4, all 1's). This is a simple case but frequently miscalculated because some solvers think first player wins when piles are equal, ignoring the cannot-pick-same-pile rule.
adversarial.attack_vector: Misunderstanding of optimal play for equal piles.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive parity-only solutions may see even total and assume second wins, but they might also think that with equal piles first can force win. Correct answer is HL.

adversarial.description: Case where max > sum_rest but total stones odd. Some might think parity overrides the dominance condition, leading to wrong output.
adversarial.attack_vector: Testing if the dominance condition is correctly prioritized over parity.
adversarial.why_effective: Total stones is 9 odd, but max=5 > sum_rest=4, so first wins. Solutions that check parity first might incorrectly output 'T' anyway, but we need to ensure dominance is checked.

key_coverage_gaps: Large number of games (t up to 1000) not covered (though n may be small)
Very large stone counts (up to 1e9) if problem constraints allow
Cases where multiple piles are equal to max but not all
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: At least 10 random small, 5 random large, all boundary and adversarial patterns included, totalling ~20 test cases for basic coverage.

random.description: Small random tree for verification of basic logic.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a tree with n between 2 and 10, random edges ensuring connectivity and root at 1. Assign random weights from 1 to 10. Choose S randomly between 0 and total initial sum.
error_types_caught: missing update of sum after halving

random.description: Large random tree for stress testing performance and overflow.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a tree with n=100000 (single test case) using a random parent for each new node, ensuring tree is rooted at 1. Assign random weights up to 1e9. Choose S small enough to require many moves.
error_types_caught: TLE due to inefficient data structures
integer overflow in sum or gain

boundary.description: Minimum tree size: n=2, single edge.
boundary.test_values: n=2, S=0, weight=1
error_types_caught: division by zero when weight becomes 0
handling of root being leaf? root has child so not leaf

boundary.description: Maximum tree size and large weight, S=0 requiring many moves.
boundary.test_values: n=100000, S=0, all weights=1e9, tree is a line (1-2-3-...-n) so leaves only leaf at node n. Total sum = 1e9*(n-1) ~ 1e14. Each move halves edge weight, need about log2(1e9) * (n-1) ~ 30*99999 ~ 3e6 moves, but problem expects output as integer.
error_types_caught: TLE if algorithm is O(n * log(max weight)) instead of O((n + moves) log n)
handling of large number of moves

boundary.description: All weights equal to 1, S just below total sum.
boundary.test_values: n=10, all weights=1, leaf count varies, S=total_sum-1
error_types_caught: handling of small weights where halving does nothing (weight 1 becomes 0)

adversarial.description: Tree where halving an edge changes gain for many other edges, and greedy order matters. Naive solution may choose edge with large initial gain that becomes less effective later.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit gain updates: after halving an edge, the leaf count in its subtree changes if that edge was on paths to multiple leaves, but actually leaf count per edge remains constant. The gain per edge changes only due to weight change. However, a mistake is to not recompute gains after each move. This pattern has many edges with same initial gain, ties broken arbitrarily, but the optimal strategy requires specific order.
adversarial.why_effective: If the algorithm does not correctly update the gain of affected edges after halving, it may not pick the most beneficial edges later.

adversarial.description: Deep tree with a single leaf, requiring many moves on the same edge. Some implementations may track the number of leaf paths incorrectly (should be 1 for all edges).
adversarial.attack_vector: Miscomputation of leaf count for edges. In a line, all edges have leaf count 1. If code incorrectly counts leaves, it may underestimate gain.
adversarial.why_effective: Each edge must be halved until weight becomes 0; total moves = sum over edges of floor(log2(weight)) + 1? Actually weight 100: moves: 100->50->25->12->6->3->1->0: 7 moves per edge? Wait careful: 100->50(1), 50->25(2), 25->12(3), 12->6(4), 6->3(5), 3->1(6), 1->0(7). So per edge 7 moves, 3 edges: 21 moves? But sum initially is 300, need sum ≤0, so each edge must become 0. Moves per edge = number of times halved until 0: ceil(log2(w+1))? Actually for w=100, floor(log2(100))=6, but we need 7 moves to get to 0. So total moves=21. In example I'll set S=0 and weight 1 -> minimal? Let's just give a small example where leaf count miscomputation leads to wrong answer.
error_types_caught: incorrect leaf count for edges not directly connected to leaves
overcounting leaf paths in non-leaf subtrees

key_coverage_gaps: Edge cases with weight becoming 0
Multiple test cases with varying n
Large S where no moves needed

random.description: Small random test with N and M up to 10, random initial powers and operations, to verify correctness against brute force simulation.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random N between 1 and 10, M between 1 and 10. Generate initial powers as random integers from 1 to N. Then generate M random operations: each with 70% chance type 1 (query) and 30% chance type 0 (update), with valid parameters (a and b between 1 and N).
error_types_caught: Off-by-one errors in last hole index

random.description: Large random test with maximum N=100000 and M=100000, random operations, to stress test performance and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Set N=100000, M=100000. Generate initial powers uniformly random from 1 to N. Generate operations: 50% type 1, 50% type 0, both random. Ensure updates produce valid b (1 to N). Use efficient generation to avoid timeouts.
error_types_caught: Time limit exceeded (TLE) due to O(N) simulation

boundary.description: N=1, single hole. Minimal case to test base logic.
boundary.test_values: N=1, M=1: hole 1 only. Initial power can be 1 (since max N=1). Test query and update.

boundary.description: Maximum power values: all a[i]=N. Every ball exits immediately from the starting hole.
boundary.test_values: N=100000, all initial powers = N. Then a query from hole 1 should output last hole = 1, jumps = 1. Also test update changing some powers away from N.
error_types_caught: Handling of jumps less than or equal to remaining distance
Output last hole when exit immediate

boundary.description: Long chain: all a[i]=1. Query from hole 1 gives N jumps and last hole N. Tests large jump count and propagation.
boundary.test_values: N=100000, all a[i]=1. Then query from hole 1. Jumps = 100000, last hole = 100000. Also update some middle hole to break chain.
error_types_caught: Incorrect jump count when path is long
Last hole incorrectly computed when exit

adversarial.description: Frequent updates on a single hole, forcing many recomputations in sqrt decomposition or similar data structures.
adversarial.attack_vector: Update the same hole repeatedly, potentially beyond the block boundary, causing cascading updates in block-based solutions.
adversarial.why_effective: In block decomposition, each update on hole 3 may require recomputing the entire block if the jump target crosses block boundary; repeating many times multiplies cost.

adversarial.description: Random updates that cause chain splitting and merging, creating many 'forward jumps' that are not monotonic, testing correctness of result propagation.
adversarial.attack_vector: Alternate between setting powers to 1 (long chain) and powers to large value (short circuits) on the same set of holes, forcing incorrect last hole or jump count if update is not propagated correctly.
adversarial.why_effective: After changing hole 2's power from 1 to 3, hole 1's path changes drastically; if update doesn't propagate correctly, query from 1 gives wrong result.
error_types_caught: Wrong answer due to missed propagation of updates to predecessor holes

key_coverage_gaps: No pattern specifically targets memory usage with large block size (extreme N with high updates)
No pattern with all updates then all queries

random.description: Small random test with few words and short strings, intended for verifying correctness of algorithms.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n (1≤n≤5) strings with lengths between 1 and 5, uniformly random lowercase letters. Compute expected output using brute force enumeration of all deletion choices and distinct sequence counting.

random.description: Large random test with many words and total length close to 1e6, to stress test time and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n ≈ 1e5 strings, each of length approximately 10, uniformly random. Ensure total length ≤ 1e6. Use hashing and DP to compute expected answer (or reference implementation).

boundary.description: Test with only one word. The number of valid sequences equals the number of distinct strings obtained by deleting at most one character (since no ordering constraint).
boundary.test_values: n=1, single word of varying lengths (1, 2, 3).
error_types_caught: not considering empty string from length 1 word

boundary.description: Test with maximum n possible given total length constraint of 1e6: many strings of length 1. Each word is a single letter. Deleting the only letter gives empty string. Non-decreasing condition on sequences of single letters and empty strings.
boundary.test_values: n=1e6, each word a single lowercase letter (e.g., all 'a'). Each word can become either 'a' or empty. Need to count sequences non-decreasing lexicographically.

boundary.description: Test with a word of length 1 leading to empty string. Ensure empty string is considered correctly in lexicographic order (empty string is smallest).
boundary.test_values: Word 'a' becomes empty upon deletion. Compare empty vs non-empty.

boundary.description: Test with all words identical after deletion, e.g., all 'aa' (any deletion gives 'a'). Many ways to delete but only one distinct string per word. Sequence is non-decreasing if all are same. So answer is 1 (only one distinct sequence).
boundary.test_values: All words same pattern with duplicates removed.
error_types_caught: overcounting duplicate deletions as distinct sequences

adversarial.description: Strings with many repeated characters, causing many deletion positions to yield identical resulting string. E.g., 'aaaaa' (length 5) gives only one distinct deletion result: 'aaaa'. If a word has length L and all characters same, then there are L deletion positions but only 1 distinct resulting string. Counting distinct sequences must ignore duplicate deletion choices.
adversarial.attack_vector: Overcounting naive solutions that treat each deletion position as distinct resulting string.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions may iterate over all L deletions and treat each as a separate state for DP, leading to exponential or large counts. Correct solution must identify identical strings from different deletions and treat them as one option.

adversarial.description: Words that are nearly identical but differ in tricky ways, causing lexicographic comparisons to be costly. E.g., long strings that are prefixes of each other. Also, strings that become identical after deletion. This tests the hashing/comparison efficiency.
adversarial.attack_vector: Time limit due to O(L^2) comparisons if not using efficient string comparison (hashing or suffix arrays).
adversarial.why_effective: Many comparisons between strings after deletion require comparing large portions that are identical. Without precomputed hash or LCP, each comparison takes O(L) leading to O(total length^2) = 1e12.

adversarial.description: Input where no deletion sequence yields a non-decreasing order, causing answer 0. This tests early termination and handling of impossible cases.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions may assume there is always at least one valid sequence, or loop infinitely.
adversarial.why_effective: Simple greedy or incorrect DP might produce a positive number incorrectly. Need to check all possibilities.

adversarial.description: Large number of valid sequences (exponential in n), but modulo requires correct arithmetic. E.g., each word has many distinct deletion options and all can be ordered non-decreasingly. This tests modulo and DP correctness under large counts.
adversarial.attack_vector: Overflow or modulo errors.
adversarial.why_effective: Number of ways can be huge; naive enumeration of all combinations may overflow or miscount. Correct DP must accumulate modulo correctly.

key_coverage_gaps: strings with mixed case (only lowercase given)
very large n but small total length? Not possible
randomized pattern for specific edge in hashing collisions

random.description: Small random test cases with n up to 10, for manual verification and correctness of logic.
random.generation_strategy: Generate t=10 test cases, each with n between 1 and 10, x between 1 and 20, a_i between 1 and 20. Compute expected output by brute-force enumeration of all subsets (since n small).

random.description: Large random test cases with n up to 100000, to stress test performance and large input handling.
random.generation_strategy: Generate t=1 test case with n=100000, x=1000, a_i uniformly random between 1 and 10000. Expected output computed by correct greedy algorithm.
error_types_caught: time limit exceeded due to O(n^2)

boundary.description: Single programmer with skill equal to or greater than x, and skill less than x.
All programmers have skill 1, with various x values to test floor division or grouping logic.
boundary.test_values: n=100000, all a_i=1. For x=1, answer=n; for x=2, answer=floor(n/2); for x=100001, answer=0.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of teams when all skills equal
integer overflow when n up to 1e5 and x up to 1e9

boundary.description: Maximum x and maximum skill, testing team formation with highly skilled individuals.
boundary.test_values: n=100000, x=1e9, all a_i=1e9. Each programmer forms a team of size 1, answer=n.

boundary.description: Impossible case: no team can be formed because even the largest possible team size (n) multiplied by the maximum skill is less than x.
boundary.test_values: n=10, x=1e9, a_i=100 each. Since 10*100=1000 < 1e9, no team possible, answer=0.
error_types_caught: incorrect edge case when answer is 0
division by zero or invalid logic

adversarial.description: Test case where a greedy algorithm that sorts ascending instead of descending would fail.
adversarial.attack_vector: Misordered sorting: if a solution sorts skills ascending, it will form teams inefficiently, leading to fewer teams.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive ascending sorting will fail to form any team because it starts from small skills and can never satisfy the condition with the large ones at the end, while descending allows forming teams with high-skilled individuals first.
error_types_caught: incorrect greedy strategy that processes from smallest to largest

adversarial.description: Test case with many test cases and small n to exploit slow I/O or repeated sorting overhead.
adversarial.attack_vector: High test case count with small n each, total sum n = 1e5. If solution uses expensive operations per test case (e.g., allocating large arrays or sorting unnecessarily), it may TLE.
adversarial.why_effective: Many test cases with minimal work per case can expose overhead in reading input, writing output, or reinitializing data structures.

adversarial.description: Test case where the product size * min_skill can overflow 32-bit integer if using int in C++.
adversarial.attack_vector: Integer overflow in the condition check.
adversarial.why_effective: If a solution uses int for the product, when size=100000 and min_skill=1e9, product=1e14 > 2^31-1 (~2.1e9), causing overflow and incorrect comparison.

key_coverage_gaps: More test cases with random large x and random skills to cover extreme combinations
Case where answer is maximized by using many small teams vs few large teams
Test with duplicate skills to ensure deterministic behavior

random.description: Small N and M for correctness verification. N=3, M=1 with one blue point inside the only red triangle, so answer should be 0.
random.generation_strategy: Generate 3 red points forming a non-degenerate triangle and 1 blue point strictly inside it. Ensure no three collinear.

random.description: Larger random N and M (e.g., N=500, M=500) to stress performance and check that solution handles maximum constraints without TLE or MLE.
random.generation_strategy: Use random integer coordinates within [-1e9, 1e9], ensure no three collinear by rejection sampling if needed. Generate up to 500 red and 500 blue points.
random.example_input:
500 500
... (500 random red points)
... (500 random blue points)

boundary.description: N < 3: no triangles can be formed. Test with N=0,1,2 and arbitrary M.
M = 0: no blue points, so all C(N,3) triangles are valid. Test with maximal N=500, output C(500,3)=20708500.
boundary.example_input:
500 0
... (500 red points in general position, e.g., on a convex curve to avoid collinearity)

adversarial.description: All red points are vertices of a convex polygon (e.g., on a circle), and many blue points are placed inside the polygon. This forces many triangles to contain blue points, testing the ability to correctly exclude them. Also tests angular sweep DP for convex sets.
adversarial.attack_vector: Red points in convex position; blue points inside the convex hull but placed such that they are close to many triangle edges, possibly causing floating point errors if using double.
adversarial.why_effective: With convex hull, many triangles contain the interior points. Naive O(N^3) would be slow; DP solutions must correctly handle point-in-triangle tests without false negatives when points are near edges.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of points on edge (though problem says no three collinear)

adversarial.description: Red points arranged in two clusters far apart, with blue points scattered. This tests that solutions correctly compute triangles that cross clusters, and that the DP does not produce integer overflow when computing cross products with large coordinates.
adversarial.attack_vector: Large coordinate differences (up to 1e9) in red points, causing cross product values near 2e18, testing for 64-bit overflow if using signed 64-bit (still safe) but risky if using 32-bit or floating point.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that use 32-bit ints will overflow. Also, the triangle spans large area, but the blue point is inside, so answer should be 0. Solutions using double might lose precision.

key_coverage_gaps: Complex scenarios where blue points are on the boundary (but not collinear) are not tested because problem forbids collinearity.

random.description: Random sequence of moderate length (N=10) with values in a reasonable range to verify correctness.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate N between 5 and 20, then generate N random integers between -100 and 100.

random.description: Large random sequence (N=5000) with values spanning the full range to stress test performance and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Set N=5000, generate each a_i uniformly random from [-1e9, 1e9].

boundary.description: Single element sequence (N=1). Already non-decreasing, answer is 0.
boundary.test_values: N=1, a_i= any number, e.g., 5

boundary.description: Maximum N with all equal values. Already non-decreasing, answer 0.
boundary.test_values: N=5000, all a_i = 0

boundary.description: Maximum N with decreasing sequence (worst-case for DP). Requires many steps.
boundary.test_values: N=5000, a_i = 5000 - i (i from 1 to 5000), strictly decreasing from 4999 to 0

adversarial.description: Sequence that forces many distinct values after compression, with alternating high and low values to test DP correctness.
adversarial.attack_vector: Large number of distinct values (N distinct) and a pattern that may mislead greedy approaches.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive greedy (e.g., adjust each element to previous) fails because optimal might change middle values.

adversarial.description: Sequence with large magnitude values (close to 1e9) to trigger integer overflow if using 32-bit for sums.
adversarial.attack_vector: Extreme values causing sum of steps to exceed 2^31-1.
adversarial.why_effective: Answer is 2e9, which fits in 64-bit but not 32-bit; naive solutions may overflow.

key_coverage_gaps: All equal values already non-decreasing
Single element
Maximum N decreasing
Large magnitude values
Many distinct values

random.description: Random arrays with various sizes, covering both YES and NO cases. The generation ensures that the condition (elements not divisible by min are already in correct sorted position) is sometimes met and sometimes not.
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, pick random n between 1 and 100, random array of positive integers up to 1e9. Then decide with 50% probability to make it a YES case by ensuring that for each index i, if a[i] != sorted[i] then a[i] is divisible by min. Otherwise, randomly flip some elements to violate the condition.

random.description: Stress test with maximum constraints: t=10000, sum n=100000. Each test case has n=1 or small n to maximize number of test cases, or few large n. Random arrays with values up to 1e9.
random.generation_strategy: Generate t test cases such that sum n = 100000. Vary n from 1 to 1000. Randomly assign a_i with uniform distribution in [1, 1e9]. Include both YES and NO cases by construction.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of many test cases

boundary.description: Single element array (n=1). Always YES because it's trivially non-decreasing.
boundary.test_values: n=1, any positive integer

boundary.description: Minimum element equals 1. Since 1 divides everything, the array can always be sorted to non-decreasing order using the operation (because gcd(1, x) = 1 for any x, so we can swap any two elements). Thus output should always be YES.
boundary.test_values: m=1 in every test case

boundary.description: Array already sorted non-decreasing. Should output YES.
boundary.test_values: sorted array of any length

boundary.description: Maximum values: large a_i up to 1e9, large n=100000 with sum n constraint. Also include n=1e5 in a single test case to test memory and time.
boundary.test_values: n=100000, a_i=1e9 (or random large values)

adversarial.description: Array where all elements are multiples of the minimum, but some non-minimum elements are not in correct order. Since they are all divisible by min, they can be rearranged using min as pivot, so answer is YES. A naive solution might mistakenly think that if all elements are multiples of min, it's always YES (which is correct), but some might incorrectly check positions of non-min elements. This tests that awareness.
adversarial.attack_vector: Tricking solution that might do additional unneeded checks.
adversarial.why_effective: All elements are multiples of 2, but the array [2,4,6,8] is already sorted so it's easy. But we need a case where it's not sorted but still YES: e.g., [4,2,8,6]. Since all divisible by 2, we can swap 4 and 2 (gcd=2), then 8 and 6, etc. So a naive solution might think it's NO because 4 is at index 1 but sorted would have 2 at index1; but it's actually YES. So example: [4,2,8,6] expected YES.

adversarial.description: Array where non-multiples of min are already in correct positions relative to sorted order, but a naive solution might only check divisibility of the entire array and miss that non-multiples must be fixed. This is a classic WA pattern.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploiting incomplete condition: checking that all elements are divisible by min, without verifying that non-divisible elements are in correct places.
adversarial.why_effective: Min=2. Sorted = [2,3,4]. Original: [2,3,4] is already sorted? Actually original is [2,3,4] sorted yes. But we need a case where original differs from sorted but non-multiples are correct. E.g., [2,4,3] min=2, sorted [2,3,4]. Original: position1=2 matches, position2=4 (should be 3) is multiple of 2, position3=3 (should be 4) is not multiple of 2? Wait 3 is not multiple of 2, and it's at position3; sorted position3 is 4, so original[3] != sorted[3] and original[3] not multiple of 2 -> NO. That's correct. Actually to trick, we need a case where non-multiple is in correct place. Example: [2,3,4] is sorted. Another: [3,2,4] min=2, sorted [2,3,4]; original[1]=3 not multiple of 2, and it's at position1 where sorted has 2 -> mismatch, so NO. But if we have [2,3,4] already sorted, condition holds. So adversarial case: an array where one non-multiple is out of place but the solution might think it's okay because it's divisible? But non-multiples are never divisible. So the trick is to have a non-multiple in a position that matches sorted, but another element (multiple) is out of place. For instance: [4,2,3] min=2, sorted [2,3,4]; original[1]=4 (multiple of 2) but should be 2, so can be swapped; original[2]=2 (min) correct; original[3]=3 (non-multiple) and it's at position3 where sorted has 4, so mismatch! Actually 3 is not multiple of 2 and at position3, but sorted[3]=4, so original[3]==3 !=4, so condition fails -> NO. So we need a scenario where non-multiple is correct: e.g., [4,3,2] min=2, sorted [2,3,4]; original[1]=4 (multiple, out of place), original[2]=3 (non-multiple) is at position2 where sorted has 3 -> correct; original[3]=2 (min) in wrong place? Actually sorted[3]=4, but original[3]=2. So 2 is min, which is divisible by itself, so it can be moved. So overall, we can sort: swap 2 and 4 (gcd=2) -> [2,3,4]. So YES. boundary.test_values: n=5, m=0, all l_i=2, r_i=2
error_types_caught: Incorrect application of constraints (must be satisfied by each chosen mercenary)

adversarial.description: Large n, m=0, all intervals [1,n], to test exponentiation and large number handling. The output is (2^n - 1) mod MOD.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exponential brute force failure
adversarial.why_effective: Naive O(2^n) methods will timeout. Efficient algorithms must use fast exponentiation or combinatorial formulas.

adversarial.description: Conflicts form a large clique (complete graph on k nodes) with n=k+C where C is small. Intervals all [1,n]. Tests handling of large conflict graphs.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that iterate over all possible conflict subsets or fail to compress cliques.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive inclusion-exclusion over m pairs would be too slow. Correct solution must use DSU and combinatorial counting for cliques.
error_types_caught: Wrong answer due to incorrect conflict handling
Memory limit exceeded from storing large graph

adversarial.description: Intervals are all tight to a fixed size k, and conflicts form a perfect matching. Tests the interaction between exact size constraints and conflicts.
adversarial.attack_vector: Forces correct handling of size constraints and conflicts simultaneously, especially when subset size is forced.
adversarial.why_effective: If the solution does not correctly enforce that each chosen mercenary's interval is satisfied, it may count subsets of wrong size. Also, matching conflicts reduce the number of valid subsets.
error_types_caught: Incorrect counting of subsets with exact size

key_coverage_gaps: Tests with both tight intervals and dense conflicts
Edge cases where l_i or r_i equals n
Cases with repeated identical intervals and conflicts

random.description: Random small numbers for verification: n between 1 and 1000, s between 1 and 100.
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, generate n uniformly in [1, 1000] and s uniformly in [1, 100]. Compute expected answer via straightforward increment (feasible for small n) or algorithm.

random.description: Random large numbers to stress efficiency: n up to 10^18, s up to 10^9.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n uniformly up to 10^18 and s uniformly up to 10^9. Ensure some cases where digit sum already <= s (answer 0) and some where large increments are needed.
error_types_caught: wrong handling of carries across many digits

boundary.description: Minimum n=1 with various s values (including min s=1 and max s=10^9).
boundary.test_values: n=1, s=1, s=2, s=10^9. All should output 0 because digit sum of 1 is 1.
error_types_caught: missing early exit when sum <= s

boundary.description: Maximum n=10^18 with various s (including min s=1 and max s=10^9).
boundary.test_values: n=10^18, s=1, s=10^9. Digit sum of 10^18 is 1, so answer 0 for both.

boundary.description: Minimum s=1 with various n that require rounding to power of 10.
error_types_caught: failure to handle carries beyond first non-zero digit

boundary.description: Maximum s=10^9 with various large n. Since max digit sum of n (18 digits) is 162, all answers should be 0.
error_types_caught: incorrectly assuming large s requires big moves

boundary.description: n with many trailing zeros and small s, testing carry propagation.
error_types_caught: incorrect rounding when trailing zeros present
failure to increment to next power of 10 efficiently

adversarial.description: n with many trailing zeros and s small, causing large moves and testing carries.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits naive increment-based solutions or incorrect carry logic. Naive solutions would count each increment, leading to TLE for large moves.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive increment from n to next power of 10 (10^18) would require 5e17 moves, impossible within time limit.
error_types_caught: incorrect algorithm that doesn't jump to next power of 10

adversarial.description: n with all digits 9 and s small, forcing rounding to next power of 10 with minimal moves.
adversarial.attack_vector: Tests correct handling of carry across all digits: increment by 1 makes all digits become 0 and first digit becomes 1. Solutions that incorrectly compute moves may output huge number instead of 1.
adversarial.why_effective: Many naive algorithms would try to increment digit by digit, resulting in wrong answer or huge number.
error_types_caught: wrong answer due to miscalculation of required increment

adversarial.description: Large number of test cases (t=20000) to stress input/output and time limit.
adversarial.attack_vector: Multiple test cases with maximum t, each with large n and s, can cause slowdown if I/O is not optimized or algorithm is O(log n) per case but with large constant.
adversarial.why_effective: Ensures solution reads and writes efficiently and algorithm runs in O(t * log n) without too much overhead.

adversarial.description: n where digit sum already equals s, edge case of equality.
adversarial.attack_vector: Tests if algorithm correctly returns 0 when sum <= s, including equality. Some solutions might treat sum < s only.
adversarial.why_effective: Equality case is often missed; sum of digits of 500 is 5, equal to s=5, answer 0.
error_types_caught: off-by-one in condition sum <= s vs sum < s

key_coverage_gaps: very small s (1) combined with large n requiring big jumps
n with alternating digits requiring precise carries

random.description: Small random test with few rooks, no two sharing row or column. Covers basic correctness.
random.generation_strategy: For n between 5 and 10, randomly select m (1 to n). Choose m distinct rows and columns, then pair them randomly ensuring no rook on diagonal (optional) or allow some on diagonal. Simulate algorithm to compute expected output.

random.description: Large random test with n=100000, m=100000, random permutation. Stresses time and memory, checks handling of large input.
random.generation_strategy: Set n=100000, m=100000. Generate a random permutation of 1..n, then place rooks at (i, p[i]). If p[i]==i, it's on diagonal. Use solution to compute answer (number of rooks not on diagonal + number of cycles of length >1).

boundary.test_values: n=100000, m=100000, rooks forming one big cycle

adversarial.description: Swap of two rooks (cycle of length 2). Common mistake: output 2 instead of 3.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits naive assumption that each rook moves once.
adversarial.why_effective: Many beginners think each rook moves directly: (1,2)->(1,1) and (2,1)->(2,2) takes 2 moves, but they attack each other after first move, so need 3 moves.
error_types_caught: incorrect answer due to overlooking attack after move

adversarial.description: Mixed scenario: two cycles of length 2 and one cycle of length 3, plus isolated diagonal rooks. Tests correct counting of moves.
adversarial.attack_vector: Confuses cycles vs single non-diagonal rooks.
adversarial.why_effective: First test: two swaps (each costs 3) plus one diagonal (cost 0) = 6. Second test: cycle of length 3 (cost 4) plus swap (cost 3) plus diagonal (0) = 7. Naive solution might count each rook not on diagonal as 1, giving 5+4=9, wrong.

adversarial.description: Large input with many isolated non-diagonal rooks and no cycles. Tests performance and correctness for simple case.
adversarial.attack_vector: Large m but no cycles; trivial answer = m.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solution might use O(m) time, but if it uses adjacency matrix or deep recursion, might exceed memory/time. This tests that algorithm efficiently handles many disjoint cycles.
error_types_caught: TLE due to O(n) per test

adversarial.description: Test with single large cycle of length close to 10^5. May cause stack overflow if using recursion for DFS.

adversarial.why_effective: Recursive DFS on a cycle of length 100000 can exceed recursion limit. Iterative solution or union-find works.
error_types_caught: incorrect cycle length due to recursion termination

random.description: Small random permutations with n between 1 and 10

boundary.description: Maximum n (n=200000) with already optimal permutation

200000

boundary.test_values: n >= 1. Permutation is identity: p[i]=i for all i.

boundary.description: Single cycle of length n (full cycle)
boundary.test_values: n >= 1. Permutation is a single n-cycle, e.g., p[i]=i+1 for i<n, p[n]=1.
error_types_caught: Min swaps when current cycle length is larger than optimal; need to split cycle into smaller cycles

adversarial.description: Multiple optimal partitions for n mod 3 = 1 with different swap distances
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits the fact that for n mod 3 = 1, there are two optimal cycle length multisets (e.g., one 4-cycle + rest 3-cycles, or two 2-cycles + rest 3-cycles). Some algorithms may always target one, missing the other that requires fewer swaps.
adversarial.why_effective: The identity permutation (all cycles of length 1) needs to be transformed to a permutation with product 12. Options: (3,3,1) product 9 not maximal; (3,2,2) product 12; (4,3) product 12. Min swaps: from 7 1-cycles to a 3-cycle and two 2-cycles: need at least 2 swaps (e.g., swap 1 and 2 creates a 2-cycle, etc.). To a 4-cycle and a 3-cycle: need at least 3 swaps? Actually from 7 1-cycles to a 4-cycle: need to merge 4 elements into a cycle, which requires at least 3 swaps (since each swap can increase cycle length by at most 1? Actually starting with all fixed points, each swap can create a 2-cycle; to get a 4-cycle, you need at least 3 swaps). So optimal is 2 swaps. Algorithm that only considers one target may output 3 swaps.
error_types_caught: Incorrect handling of multiple optimal partitions
Greedy min swaps not exploring both options

adversarial.description: Large product overflow modulo check
adversarial.attack_vector: The product of cycle lengths can be huge, but modulo 998244353. However, some solutions might compute product without modulo, causing overflow. Also, when computing min swaps, algorithms may use large numbers incorrectly.
adversarial.why_effective: Simple case but product is 3, small. For large n, product modulo must be correct. An adversary input with n=200000 and product requiring modulo computation.

adversarial.description: Permutation where current cycle structure is already optimal but requires swaps due to alternative optimal?
adversarial.attack_vector: If the permutation already achieves the maximum product, swaps=0. But some algorithms may incorrectly compute swaps >0 if they misinterpret the target.
adversarial.why_effective: Permutation has two 3-cycles (product 9). Optimal product for n=6 is 3*3=9. So swaps=0. An algorithm that always tries to make all cycles length 3 or something may still output 0, but if it tries to change cycle lengths unnecessarily, it might output positive swaps.

key_coverage_gaps: Cases with n mod 3 = 0 where product is pure 3's but current cycle lengths are mixed (e.g., many 2-cycles and fixed points) to test min swaps combining multiple cycles
Large n with many cycles of various lengths to stress test efficiency and correctness of min swaps calculation

random.description: Small random test cases with n up to 10, segments in various positions, k moderate.

boundary.description: Minimum n=1, k=1, various segment positions.

Also [0,0] and [0,1] => initial intersection 0 (since point and segment? Actually intersection of point [0,0] and [0,1] is length 0 because point length 0? adversarial.description: Test where naive solution that only works on one pair at a time fails because spreading steps across many pairs is more efficient.
adversarial.attack_vector: Greedy focusing on single pair vs distributing steps. For example, large n=100, initially no intersection per pair (segments are disjoint). k is moderate. Spreading steps across many pairs to achieve small intersection each may be cheaper than concentrating on one pair.

(First: each pair initial intersection = min(10,10)-max(0,5)=5? Actually [0,10] and [5,15] overlap from 5 to 10, length 5. So each pair gives 5, total 10 >=5, steps=0. Second: disjoint, need steps.)
adversarial.why_effective: Naive greedy might try to work on a single pair without considering the cheap initial overlap from many pairs. For first case, answer is 0, but some solutions might incorrectly compute steps needed based on single pair.

adversarial.description: Test that explores precision/overflow in step calculation when n, k, and segment lengths are large.
adversarial.attack_vector: Large numbers causing overflow in intermediate multiplication: n * (something) may exceed 64-bit? n up to 2e5, k up to 1e9, steps per pair could be up to 2e9, so total steps up to 4e14, which fits in 64-bit signed (9e18). But if using Python it's fine. In C++, use long long. But overflow can occur if someone uses int. Also, when calculating steps, formula may involve multiplication n*(gap) if they incorrectly compute. So test with n=200000, large distance, large k.
adversarial.why_effective: If a solution uses int for intermediate calculations, it will overflow. Also, if they incorrectly compute steps by summing n times something, they might get huge numbers.

adversarial.description: Test where segments are identical but initial intersection is exactly 0? Actually if identical, they overlap. So test with segments that are points at same coordinate? [0,0] and [0,0] give intersection length 0, but then answer depends on k.

adversarial.why_effective: If a solution assumes initial intersection = length of segment, it will be 0 here, correct. But some might compute wrong step count for points.

adversarial.description: Two clusters: first cluster dense but spread wider than k, second cluster dense. Greedy that picks global best interval first fails because optimal uses two overlapping intervals in first cluster to cover all points.
adversarial.attack_vector: Greedy algorithm that picks the best single interval and then best non-overlapping interval.
adversarial.why_effective: The best single interval covers 4 points (e.g., [0,3]). Then the best remaining interval covers 4 points (in second cluster). Total 8. But optimal uses two intervals in first cluster (covering all 6 points) plus second cluster (4 points) = 10.

adversarial.description: Points spread far apart so that at most two points can be covered by two platforms.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that assume many points can be covered or miscalculate the maximum possible.
adversarial.why_effective: Each point is isolated; a single platform can cover at most one point. With two platforms, max is 2. Naive solutions might overcount or think single platform covers multiple.

adversarial.description: Large platform length that covers all points with one platform.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that miscalculate the interval length or fail to handle large k.
adversarial.why_effective: With k large enough, all points are within one interval. Some solutions might incorrectly think two platforms are needed or make off-by-one errors.
