Modular arithmetic errors for large powers

adversarial.description: All elements zero (a_i=0 for all i) with x=0. For n>0, no valid sequence exists.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive counting may incorrectly allow the all-zero sequence when x=0 because any non-empty subsequence XORs to 0.
adversarial.why_effective: Programs that for x=0 count sequences where 0 is not in the span of basis may forget that a zero element itself forms a subsequence of XOR 0.
error_types_caught: Logic error in condition: missing that presence of 0 itself violates condition when x=0

adversarial.description: k=0, n=1, x=0: only possible sequence is [0], but subsequence XOR=0, so answer 0.
adversarial.attack_vector: Special case k=0 where only possible element is 0; many solve for k≥1 only.
adversarial.why_effective: If not handled separately, solution might output 1 (since only one sequence) or crash due to division by zero.

adversarial.description: Many test cases with small n, sum of n up to 3000, but with t=1000 each n=3, to test performance of initialization per test case.
adversarial.attack_vector: High number of test cases (up to 1000) could cause O(t * something) solutions to be slow if something is O(k^2) per test case.
adversarial.example_output: null (each output would be some number)
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions that precompute factorials or powers up to max n per test case may recompute 1000 times, causing TLE.
error_types_caught: Performance issue: high constant factor per test case

key_coverage_gaps: Large n with k=30 and x=2^k-1
Combination of n=3000 and many test cases not covered (only single large test case)
Edge case where x is not in range [0, 2^k-1] (not needed because input guarantees x<2^k)

random.description: Random valid triple with moderate n (e.g., 10-50). Permutation constructed by starting with sorted [1..n], then reversing subsegments [l, k-1] and [k, r]. Serves as general verification for correct identification of l, k, r.
random.generation_strategy: Pick random n between 3 and 50, random l between 1 and n-2, random r between l+2 and n, random k between l+1 and r-1. Generate permutation by reversing p[l..k-1] and p[k..r] (where p is initially identity).

random.description: Random valid triple with maximum n=200 to stress test query limit (max 40 queries) and large inversion counts.
random.generation_strategy: Pick random n=200, random l, r, k satisfying constraints. Ensure the permutation has many inversions to test integer overflow or query timing.
error_types_caught: slow binary search due to large n

boundary.description: Minimal n=3 (smallest possible valid triple). Only possible l=1, k=2, r=3. Tests handling of minimal reversal lengths.
boundary.test_values: n=3, triple (l=1,k=2,r=3)
error_types_caught: edge case where k equals l+1 or r-1

boundary.description: Maximum n=200 with l=1, r=n=200, k near middle (e.g., 100). Tests binary search on full range and high inversion counts.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of zero inversion queries on full array

boundary.description: n=2 (invalid triple but possible input). Program should either handle gracefully or be guaranteed not to receive. Tests robustness for unexpected input.
boundary.test_values: n=2 (no valid triple exists)
boundary.example_output: ! 1 1 1 (dummy output indicating no valid triple, though problem likely won't give n=2)
error_types_caught: infinite loop if no valid l,k,r

adversarial.description: Many small test cases (1000 test cases, each n=3). Tests overhead of resetting state, query handling per test case, and ability to stay within total query budget (though per-case limit is 40, total not specified).
adversarial.attack_vector: Stress interactive system with many rapid small cases; potential for leftover state from previous case.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions may not properly flush output or reset variables between test cases, causing cumulative errors or delays.
error_types_caught: failure to flush output after each case

adversarial.description: Large n with first reversed segment very short (l=1, k=2, r=n). Tests binary search when inversion count changes abruptly only at first element.
adversarial.attack_vector: Binary search for k may be fooled because the inversion count from l to k-1 is small (only 1 inversion if segment [1,1] reversed) and the transition at k is subtle.
adversarial.why_effective: Many solutions assume a minimum number of inversions in reversed segments; a length-1 reversal has no inversions, causing false negatives when searching for k.
error_types_caught: assuming any reversed segment has at least one inversion
incorrect detection of k when l+1 == k

adversarial.description: Both reversed segments are very short: l=1, k=2, r=3 (n big, e.g., 200). This results in a permutation close to identity, with only two inversions at positions 1-2-3. Tests detection of small inversion counts and precise binary search.
adversarial.attack_vector: Inversion counts on subsegments may be zero or one, making it hard to distinguish boundaries.
adversarial.why_effective: Binary search relying on finding a point where inversion count jumps may fail because the jumps are small (e.g., from 0 to 1). Solutions that use threshold-based detection may miss these.
error_types_caught: inability to detect small inversion counts
incorrect binary search when inversion count is constant over large ranges

key_coverage_gaps: Test cases where l and r are not at extremes (e.g., middle of array) but k is close to l or r
Test cases with multiple test cases of varying sizes to test memory management
Test cases where the permutation is not sorted initially but reversed segments are applied to a non-identity permutation (though problem defines starting as sorted)

random.description: Small random test cases with n up to 10 and small values to verify correctness using brute force.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random n between 3 and 10, random a_i between 1 and 20. Compute expected answer by brute force enumeration of all pairs and checking condition.

random.description: Large random test cases with total n up to 200000 to test performance and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a single test case with n=200000, random a_i in range [1, 10^9]. Ensure 2*sum divisible by n for valid pairs (optional, can also include cases without validity). Compute answer using frequency map O(n).

boundary.description: Minimum n (n=3) with various scenarios to test edge cases of small arrays.
boundary.test_values: n=3 is the smallest n where deletion leaves non-empty array. Test arrays where valid pairs exist and where they don't.
error_types_caught: division by zero if n=2 is tested

boundary.description: All elements equal to the same value, leading to maximum number of valid pairs.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, all a_i = 5. Then target = 2*S/n = 2*5*n/n = 10. Pair sum must be 10, and each pair sums to 10 because 5+5=10. So all pairs are valid: n*(n-1)/2. This tests handling of large counts.

boundary.description: Target value not integer (2*S % n != 0), ensuring answer is 0.
boundary.test_values: n=3, a=[1,2,4] (sum=7, 2*7=14 not divisible by 3). Answer must be 0.
error_types_caught: incorrect use of floating point to compute target

boundary.description: Extreme values: a_i = 1 and 10^9, large sum potentially causing overflow in intermediate calculations.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, half elements 1 and half 10^9. Sum = 100000*1 + 100000*1e9 = 1e5 + 1e14 = 1.00000000001e14, well within 64-bit. But if using 32-bit for sum, overflow occurs. Check that solution uses 64-bit (long long in C++, int in Python fine).

adversarial.description: All elements equal to target/2, but with many repeated values to test frequency counting and avoid double counting or O(n^2) loops.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits naive O(n^2) solutions by having many valid pairs, causing TLE. Also tests correct handling of combinations (n choose 2).
adversarial.example_input:
1
200000
(repeat 1000000000 200000 times?) Actually target? Let's make target = 2*mean. If all equal to x, then sum = n*x, mean = x, target = 2x. So pair of any two elements sums to 2x, so all pairs valid. Answer = n*(n-1)/2 ~ 2e10, which fits 64-bit. For n=200000, answer = 19999900000. A naive O(n^2) would take forever. So this is TLE attack.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution that loops over all pairs would execute ~2e10 operations, far exceeding time limit.
error_types_caught: incorrect counting of pairs by multiplication

adversarial.description: Case where target = half of a_i + a_j pair, but many elements are close to target/2, testing hash map collisions or sorting stability.
adversarial.attack_vector: If using unordered_map with poor hash function, many collisions could degrade performance to O(n^2). Also tests floating point precision if target computed as double.
adversarial.example_input:

random.description: Large random test with n=100000, many colors, sizes up to 1e9, to stress performance and ensure linear-time algorithm works.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=100000. For each cube, assign random color in [1,50000] and random size in [1,1e9]. Ensure at least two colors are used.
random.example_output: Expected output: a valid optimal tower. The exact values depend on random generation; the test should verify that the algorithm completes within time and gives a consistent result.

boundary.description: Minimum n=2 with two cubes of different colors. Tests the simplest valid tower.
boundary.test_values: n=2, colors 1 and 2, sizes 5 and 7. The only possible tower uses both cubes (order may vary).

boundary.description: Maximum n=100000 with all but one cube of the same color. Extreme imbalance: one color has 99999 cubes, another has 1 cube. Tests handling of large majority color.
boundary.test_values: n=100000. Cube1: color1, size=1000000000. Cubes 2-100000: color2, size=1. So one huge cube of color1 and many tiny cubes of color2. Optimal tower: take the top two cubes from color2 (size 1 each) and the huge cube from color1, giving height 1000000002. Alternatively, start with color1: huge, tiny, huge? But only one huge, so can't. So tower of 3 cubes: color1, color2, color1? Actually two colors: we have more of color2. So possible sequences: start with color2 (tiny, huge, tiny) height = 1+1e9+1 = 1e9+2. Or start with color1 (huge, tiny) height = 1e9+1. So optimal is 3 cubes. Output indices must show that order. Also ensure algorithm uses prefix sums correctly to pick top two from majority.
error_types_caught: Incorrectly computing candidate towers when one color has many cubes

adversarial.description: Two colors only, each with many cubes of the same size. Tests that algorithm correctly considers all cubes and does not miss optimal sum by only picking top few.
adversarial.attack_vector: All cubes of color1 have size 1, all cubes of color2 have size 2. Both colors have equal large count (e.g., 50000 each). The optimal tower should use all cubes from both colors? Actually max length: since counts equal, max tower length is 2 * 50000 = 100000 cubes (alternating). The sum would be 50000*1 + 50000*2 = 150000. But note: we must output indices from bottom to top. The algorithm must correctly compute prefix sums and decide on the tower structure (can start with either color, sum same). This tests handling of large equal counts.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive algorithm that only considers the largest cubes from each color might miss that all cubes are used. Or if it assumes maximum tower length is limited by min(count) without considering that all cubes are used, it may produce a suboptimal sum. This input forces the algorithm to consider using all cubes when counts are equal.
error_types_caught: Index ordering when all cubes used

adversarial.description: Multiple colors, each with exactly two cubes: one very large (1e9) and one very small (1). Tests that algorithm considers taking both cubes from a color, not just the largest.
adversarial.attack_vector: Consider three colors: A, B, C. Each has cubes: (A: big=1e9, small=1), (B: big=1e9, small=1), (C: big=1e9, small=1). The optimal tower could use two colors, taking all four cubes (big+big+small+small) from two colors, sum = 2e9+2. Alternatively, taking only the two big cubes gives 2e9, which is less. So the algorithm must consider using the small cubes as well.
adversarial.why_effective: A solution that only considers the largest k cubes from each color (e.g., using only top 1 cube per color) will miss the small cubes and output a lower sum. This pattern forces correct handling of multiple cubes per color.
error_types_caught: Incorrect greedy that picks only top cube
Failure to consider all cubes in a color

adversarial.description: Colors with varying counts: one color has many medium cubes, another has one huge cube, a third has many small cubes. Tests decision between using a color with many cubes versus one with a single huge cube.
adversarial.attack_vector: Color A: 1000 cubes of size 1000. Color B: 1000 cubes of size 1. Color C: 1 cube of size 10^9. The optimal tower should pair color C with color A (since A has medium sizes) rather than with B. The tower using C and A can take up to 3 cubes: the huge from C and two largest from A (1000+1000) = 10^9 + 2000. Using C and B gives 10^9 + 1 + 1? Actually, B has many small, but we can take at most 3 cubes: huge from C and top two from B (1+1) = 10^9+2, which is less. Also pairing A and B could yield many cubes but sum is smaller. So the optimal pair is A and C. This tests if the algorithm compares sums correctly across pairs.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution that only considers the single largest cube from each color might pair color C with a color that has a large cube but ignore the benefit of taking two cubes from a color with many cubes. This tests correct evaluation of all possible pairings and lengths.
error_types_caught: Failure to consider multiple cubes from a color

random.description: Small random test case with n between 1 and 5, t between 1 and 5, houses with xi in [-10,10] and ai in [1,5]. Used for verifying correctness against brute force.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate n, t, and houses ensuring no overlap: for each pair of houses, ensure |xi - xj| >= (ai + aj) / 2. Then compute expected output by brute force: for each house, consider left candidate (xi - (ai + t)/2) and right candidate (xi + (ai + t)/2). For each candidate, check that it touches at least one house (distance to that house equals (ai + t)/2) and does not overlap any house (distance to other houses strictly greater than (ai + t)/2). Count distinct valid candidates.

adversarial.description: Duplicate candidate positions: two houses placed symmetrically such that the right candidate of the left house equals the left candidate of the right house. Tests deduplication of positions.
adversarial.attack_vector: Two houses with same side length and symmetric placement cause a candidate position to be generated from both houses. Naive solutions that count two positions per house will double count this position.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution counting two candidates per house without deduplication would output 4, but the correct answer is 3 because the position at 3.0 is generated from both houses and should be counted once.

adversarial.description: Interior candidates invalid due to overlapping neighbours: three houses equally spaced such that only the outermost positions are valid. Tests overlap checking with both left and right neighbours.
adversarial.attack_vector: Houses are placed close together so that interior candidates (e.g., right of leftmost house) overlap with the next house. Solutions that only check one neighbour or assume all candidates are valid will overcount.
adversarial.why_effective: A solution that considers each house gives two valid positions would output 6, but only the leftmost left candidate and rightmost right candidate are valid. Correct output is 2.

adversarial.description: Edge case where the optimal bit is not the least significant, testing correct bit enumeration
adversarial.attack_vector: Range [1, 6] (binary: 1,10,11,100,101,110). Counts: bit0: 1,3,5 ->3; bit1: 2,3,6 ->3; bit2: 4,5,6->3; all equal, answer=3. But if solution stops at bit 1 (since 2^2=4<6, thinks bit 2 not needed) it would output 3? Actually all 3 bits give count 3, so answer=3. However, consider range [4,5] (100,101): bit2 count=2, bit1=0, bit0=1, optimal is bit2 with count 2, answer=0. A common mistake: consider only bits up to floor(log2(r)). But [4,5] has bit2 set. Another tricky case: l=2, r=3 -> [10,11]: bit1 count=2, bit0 count=1, answer=0. Some might think need to delete 1. Also range [2,4] -> [10,11,100]: bit2 count=1 (only 4), bit1 count=2 (2 and3), bit0 count=1 (3). Max=2, answer=1. If solution always picks bit0, it would say count=1, answer=2, wrong. So adversarial: l=2, r=4.
adversarial.why_effective: The range [2,4] has binary: 10, 11, 100. Bit1 (2's place) appears twice, bit0 and bit2 appear once each. The optimal bit is 1, giving count 2, so answer = 3-2=1. A naive solution that only considers bit0 might output 2.

Corner cases where l and r are powers of two
Cases where answer is zero for non-trivial ranges (e.g., l=4, r=7)
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: At least 50 test cases to cover various ranges, including at least 10 boundary cases and 10 adversarial cases.

random.description: Small random test cases with k=2 or 3 and short strings (length <= 10) to verify correctness of LCS computation.
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, choose k from {2,3}. Generate strings of random length between 1 and 10 over alphabet of lowercase and uppercase letters, ensuring each character appears at most twice. Use brute force or known correct algorithm to compute expected output for verification.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect DP logic

random.description: Large random test cases with k=6 and strings of length up to 100 to stress test DP with bitmasks.
random.generation_strategy: Generate strings of length between 50 and 100, using all 52 letters, each at most twice. Use random assignment of positions. This tests state space size (52 * 2^6 = 3328 states) and transition logic.
random.example_output: Expected: some long LCS, length at least 1 if common letters exist. Exact output depends on generation.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect bitmask transitions

boundary.description: Test case with minimum number of strings (k=1) and a single character string.
error_types_caught: assuming LCS requires at least two strings

boundary.description: Test case with maximum number of test cases (t=1000) each with k=1 and short strings.
boundary.test_values: t=1000, each test case: k=1, s1='a'
boundary.example_output: For each test case: '1' and 'a' on separate lines, total 2000 lines.
error_types_caught: TLE due to overhead per test case
incorrect output formatting for many cases

boundary.description: Strings where each character appears exactly twice in all strings, testing maximal occurrence constraint.
boundary.test_values: k=2, strings 'aabb' and 'abab' (each character twice)
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of two occurrences per character
DP state loops due to multiple transitions

boundary.description: Strings with no common characters, testing output for zero-length LCS.
boundary.test_values: k=2, strings 'ABC' and 'xyz'
error_types_caught: forgetting to output empty line after zero

adversarial.description: Strings where characters appear twice but in conflicting order across multiple strings, forcing DP to choose correct occurrences.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits greedy choice of first occurrence, which may lead to suboptimal LCS.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that always pick the first occurrence of 'a' would get 'a' only, missing longer subsequence.

adversarial.description: k=6, each string has many characters but only a single long common subsequence exists, testing that DP doesn't miss it due to large state space.
adversarial.attack_vector: Large number of strings with sparse common characters; some solutions might prune incorrectly or run out of time.
adversarial.example_input:
1
6
aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa
... (5 more strings, each with same pattern of 'a's but with some differences to force unique LCS)
adversarial.example_output: Expected: length 100 (if each string has 100 'a's and no other conflicts) but in adversarial version, only one common subsequence of length 50, and others have many 'a's but not all. Example: each string has 100 'a's but positions differ such that only 50 can be aligned.
adversarial.why_effective: Forces DP to consider many states (up to 2^6 * 52) and transitions; naive memoization might overflow or become slow.
error_types_caught: TLE due to inefficient state exploration
WA due to incorrect state transitions when characters appear twice

adversarial.description: Case sensitivity test: strings contain both uppercase and lowercase letters that are distinct.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that treat letters case-insensitively will produce wrong LCS.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution ignores case, it would think LCS length is 1 (only 'a' or 'A') but actual length is 2.
error_types_caught: incorrect mapping of characters to indices

key_coverage_gaps: Extremely long strings (close to 104) with all characters twice
k=6 with maximum test cases t=1000
Randomized mix of uppercase and lowercase
Strings with repeated characters that are not common to all strings
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: Minimum 10 test cases: 2 random small, 2 random large, 4 boundary, 3 adversarial (some may overlap)

random.description: Random small arrays with various lengths and patterns (strictly increasing, decreasing, duplicates, etc.) to verify correctness on manageable inputs.
random.generation_strategy: Generate t up to 10, each n between 1 and 10, a_i random between 1 and 20. Mix of even/odd lengths and varied sequences.
error_types_caught: Misunderstanding of LIS length for non-strictly increasing subarrays

random.description: Large arrays to stress test performance and ensure O(n) solution works within time limits.
random.generation_strategy: Generate t=1, n=100000, a_i random between 1 and 1e9. Ensure n is even to guarantee YES, but also include odd n with a non-increasing adjacent pair to verify.
random.example_input:
1
100000
[100000 random integers, e.g., 1..1e9, ensure even length]
error_types_caught: Time limit exceeded due to O(n^2) splitting or O(n log n) per subarray

boundary.description: Single element array (minimum n=1). Must output NO.
boundary.test_values: n=1, a_i=5 (any value >0). Expected NO because XOR of LIS of single subarray is 1.
error_types_caught: Assume splitting into empty subarrays allowed

boundary.description: Many small test cases with n=1 to test handling of large t and sum of n limit.
boundary.test_values: t=10000, each n=1. Total n = 10000 ≤ 1e5. For each test case, a_i random between 1 and 1e9. All outputs should be NO.
error_types_caught: TLE due to overhead in reading many test cases
Not resetting variables correctly across test cases

boundary.description: All elements equal. For any n, answer is YES because any adjacent pair is non-increasing (equal).
boundary.test_values: n=99999 (odd), all a_i=1. Should output YES.
error_types_caught: Miscomputing LIS length for equal elements as length of subarray
Assuming that only strictly decreasing pairs count as non-increasing

adversarial.description: Strictly increasing array of odd length. This is a classic counterexample where naive solutions might incorrectly output YES.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits common misconception that any odd-length array can be made YES by splitting into subarrays with LIS 1. But strictly increasing forces each subarray's LIS to equal its length, making XOR non-zero for odd splits.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution might try to compute if it's possible to get XOR=0 by splitting, but the correct condition is either n even or existence of non-increasing adjacent pair. This array has neither, so answer NO.
error_types_caught: Wrong answer on strictly increasing odd n
Incorrectly assuming that splitting into smaller subarrays always yields some with LIS 1

adversarial.description: Array of odd length that is strictly decreasing from start to end. This tests that the solution correctly identifies that a non-increasing pair exists (every adjacent pair is decreasing) so answer is YES.
adversarial.attack_vector: Some solutions might think that decreasing arrays are like increasing and require special handling, but LIS of each subarray with length>1 is still 1 because no increasing pair.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive algorithms might incorrectly compute LIS for subarrays with decreasing order as length 2 due to misunderstanding of LIS (strictly increasing).
error_types_caught: Assuming that non-increasing means LIS length > 1

adversarial.description: Large odd n with only one non-increasing pair at the very end. This tests that the solution checks all pairs, not just early ones.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that only check first few pairs or stop early.
adversarial.example_input:
1
100001
[50000 increasing from 1 to 50000] 50000 [then] 50000 50001 50002 ... 100000? Actually design: first 100000 elements increasing, last element 1 (decrease). More precisely: n=100001, first 100000 elements are 1..100000 (strictly increasing), last element is 50000 (so a_100000=100000, a_100001=50000). This gives one non-increasing pair at (100000,100001). Answer should be YES.
adversarial.why_effective: A solution that only checks first few pairs or processes in O(n) but misses the last pair may output NO incorrectly.

key_coverage_gaps: n=2 with all equal (covered in random but not as boundary)
Large even n with strictly increasing (should be YES, but important to ensure algorithm handles both even and odd conditions correctly)

random.description: Small random tree with known and unknown edges, consistent queries
random.generation_strategy: Generate a small tree (n <= 10), assign some edges fixed values, set others to -1, then generate queries that are consistent with a chosen assignment of node parity.
error_types_caught: WA due to misunderstanding parity constraints

random.description: Small random tree with inconsistent queries
random.generation_strategy: Generate a small tree and queries that are inconsistent with the edge parities. For example, fix all edges to have parity 0 but query requires path parity 1.

boundary.description: Single node tree with no edges and no elves
Two-node tree with unknown edge and a consistent query
boundary.test_values: n=2, m=1, edge w=-1, query p=0

boundary.description: No elves, all edges known – should always be YES
boundary.test_values: m=0, edges have fixed values

boundary.description: All edges known with inconsistent query (using large w values to test overflow handling)
boundary.test_values: w up to 2^30-1, parity mismatch

adversarial.description: Long chain with many queries covering the entire path, designed to test performance and correctness of DSU with path compression
adversarial.attack_vector: Chain tree of 5 nodes with unknown edges, many queries on the same pair (1,5) with parity 1. This forces many parity updates.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution that recomputes paths each time would be very slow. Also, if DSU does not handle parity correctly, it might output inconsistent assignment.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect parity from long chain

adversarial.description: Implicit inconsistency through a cycle of constraints using queries only (no known edges). This tests the ability to detect contradictions from constraints on node parities.
adversarial.attack_vector: Using queries to create a cycle of parity constraints that sum to 1, causing contradiction. For a tree, such cycle is impossible if only queries on actual paths? Actually constraints on node parities can create cycles even though underlying graph is a tree. This pattern creates a set of constraints that imply x1≠x4, but also x1=x4 via transitivity.
adversarial.why_effective: Some solutions may not propagate constraints correctly, missing the contradiction.
error_types_caught: WA due to inconsistency detection failure

adversarial.description: Maximum constraints with all unknown edges and many queries, to stress both time and memory
adversarial.attack_vector: Use maximum allowed n and m (within sum) in a single test case. For example, a star tree with 100000 nodes and 100000 queries randomly assigned. But to keep example small, we provide a schematic input with n=5, m=5 as a proxy.
adversarial.why_effective: Large input tests recursion depth (if using DFS) and memory usage. Also tests that solution handles many disjoint constraint sets.
error_types_caught: MLE due to storing entire graph twice

key_coverage_gaps: No pattern specifically tests multiple test cases with varying sizes mixed together (sum constraints)
No test for tree with only one edge and many queries (boundary but covered partially by chain)
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: 10 test cases per pattern, plus additional random stress tests

random.description: Small random test cases for manual verification and basic correctness.
random.generation_strategy: Generate t=5 test cases with n between 1 and 10, each a_i random between 1 and 100. Compute expected output using standard solution.

random.description: Large random test cases to stress test performance and check for TLE.
random.generation_strategy: Generate t=10000 test cases with total n=300000. For each test case, n uniform 1 to 1000 (but sum <=300k). a_i uniform from 1 to 1e9.
error_types_caught: Incorrect handling of large a_i mod

boundary.description: Single element with a1 divisible by 2 (minimum n).
boundary.test_values: n=1, a=[2] -> output NO. Also include n=1, a=[1] -> YES to ensure symmetry.

boundary.description: Maximum n (300000) in a single test case with all a_i = 1 (trivially YES).
boundary.test_values: t=1, n=300000, all a_i=1. Sum n matches constraint.

boundary.description: Extreme a_i values: a_i = 1e9 and a_i = 1.
boundary.test_values: n=10, a = [1e9, 1, 1e9, 1, ...] alternating. Should check if large numbers cause overflow or mod issues.

adversarial.description: Elements are consecutive LCMs to guarantee impossibility for each position.
adversarial.attack_vector: Each a_i is divisible by all numbers from 2 to i+1, so it can never be erased. This targets solutions that do not check all possible indices.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might only check divisibility at current index or a few indices, failing to see that no index works.
error_types_caught: Assuming element can always be moved left

adversarial.description: All elements are 1, which is the easiest case; any correct solution should output YES.
adversarial.attack_vector: If a solution incorrectly requires an element to be not divisible by something at its original index only, it might wrongly output NO for elements that can be erased after shifting.
adversarial.why_effective: Common mistake: only check a_i % (original position+1) == 0 and conclude NO, forgetting that index can decrease.

adversarial.description: Mixed scenario: first element impossible, rest possible, to see if solution short-circuits correctly.
adversarial.attack_vector: If a1%2==0, whole sequence is impossible because a1 can never be erased. This checks that solution doesn't proceed after first element.
adversarial.why_effective: Some solutions might try to erase other elements first and forget that the first element can never be erased if it's stuck.
error_types_caught: Assuming first element can always be removed

key_coverage_gaps: Multiple test cases with varied n
Edge case where n=1 and a1=2 (NO)

random.description: Small random test case (n=5) with non-trivial winner set. Strengths are distinct and arranged such that both the player with highest a and the player with highest b can win, but others cannot.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n random distinct integers for a and b independently, ensuring no duplicates within each map. Then shuffle indices. Use the known algorithm to compute expected output.

random.description: Large random test case (n=1000) with random distinct strengths. Useful for performance testing and verifying correctness under stress.
random.generation_strategy: Generate 1000 unique random integers in range [1, 1e9] for each map. Sort? Actually, random order. Then compute expected output using the known algorithm.
random.example_input:
1
1000
[1000 random distinct a_i]
[1000 random distinct b_i]

boundary.description: Single player (n=1). The only player can always win.
boundary.test_values: n=1, a=[1], b=[1] (any value works)

boundary.description: Two players (n=2) with various strength relations: one player dominates on both maps, and both players have a map each where they are stronger.
boundary.test_values: n=2, two players with extreme strengths to test all possible outcome patterns (10, 11).
error_types_caught: logic error when one player beats the other on both maps

adversarial.description: Strictly increasing b when sorted by descending a. This creates a chain where all players can win, potentially fooling solutions that only consider the top players.
adversarial.attack_vector: Weakens naive solutions that output '1' only for the maximum on each map without considering propagation through chains.
adversarial.why_effective: Each player has a higher b than all players with higher a, so they can beat the previous strongest on map2, creating a chain that allows all to win. A naive solution might only mark the first and last players as winners.

adversarial.description: A critical player acts as a bridge. Players with high a and low b, players with low a and high b, and a moderate player that can beat both top players. The weakest player in terms of both strengths cannot win.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that overestimate winners due to direct edges from top players, or underestimate due to not considering indirect chains.
adversarial.why_effective: Player4 (97,98) is directly beaten by player1 on map1 (since a1=100) and by player2 on map2 (b2=100). But player4 cannot beat any top player directly, and there is no chain to eliminate them. Naive BFS from top players would incorrectly include player4.

key_coverage_gaps: Multiple test cases in one input
n=100000 with all players winning
n=100000 with only one player winning

random.description: Random small test with moderate n and q, covering all query types and mixture.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n between 1 and 10, q between 1 and 20. Initialize a_i and b_i randomly in [0,10]. Generate queries randomly from types 1-4, with valid parameters (l,r within bounds, x in [0,10]). Ensure at least one query of each type. Output results for type 4 queries.

random.description: Large random test with maximum constraints to stress test performance and scalability.
random.generation_strategy: Set n=100000, q=100000. Initialize a_i and b_i randomly in [0,1e9]. Generate queries: type 1-3 each with probability 0.25, type 4 with probability 0.25, ensuring ranges are random and x in [0,1e9]. Use a pseudorandom generator with fixed seed for reproducibility.
random.example_input: (Omitted due to size; would be generated programmatically)
error_types_caught: TLE due to inefficient data structure
incorrect lazy propagation with multiple update types

boundary.description: Minimum size array (n=1) and single query.
boundary.test_values: n=1, q=1, a=[0], b=[0], query type 4 l=1 r=1. Output should be 0 because a_i*F_b = 0*F0 = 0.
error_types_caught: handling of single element in segment tree

boundary.description: All arrays values zero; every query type 4 yields zero.
boundary.test_values: n=5, q=3, a=[0,0,0,0,0], b=[0,0,0,0,0], queries: type 1 set 1 5 10 (but a becomes 10), then type 4, then type 3 set 1 5 100, then type 4. Actually we want zero after updates? Better: no updates, just type 4. But include a type1 set to zero to ensure update works. Let's do: type1 set a to zero, type4, type3 set b to zero, type4. Example: n=2 q=4, a=[1,2], b=[3,4]; then type1 set a[1..2]=0; type4; type3 set b[1..2]=0; type4; expected 0 and 0.
error_types_caught: handling of zero values in multiplication
lazy tags not clearing or resetting properly

adversarial.description: Many type 3 (set b) queries with large x values to force many Fibonacci exponentiations.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit expensive Fibonacci computation on each update if not optimized with precomputation or caching.
adversarial.why_effective: Each type 3 requires computing F_x for large x (up to 1e9). If the solution recomputes Fibonacci from scratch for each element in segment tree, it will TLE. Proper solution should use matrix exponentiation with log x per update, but if number of updates is large, even that could be heavy; but with lazy propagation, only O(log n) exponentiations per update. However, if implementation is naive (e.g., as each segment tree node recomputes), it may time out.
error_types_caught: TLE due to repeated expensive Fibonacci calculations

adversarial.description: Alternating type 1 and type 2 updates with type 3 updates to test lazy propagation correctness.
adversarial.attack_vector: Cause conflicts in lazy tags: set a, then add a, then set b, etc. If lazy tags are not properly combined or applied, results will be wrong.
adversarial.why_effective: The sequence: first set a1=5, add a2=3: a=[5,3], b=[0,0] -> sum = 5*0+3*0=0. Then set b1=10: a=[5,3], b=[10,0] -> sum = 5*F10+3*0 = 5*55 = 275? Wait F10=55. But my expected output 25? Let me recalc: I made mistake. Actually F10=55, so 5*55=275. But I said 25. Let me revise: This should be 275. Then set a1=2: a=[2,3], b=[10,0] -> sum=2*55+3*0=110. Then add a2=1: a=[2,4], b=[10,0] -> sum=2*55+4*0=110. So outputs: 0, 275, 110, 110. But I wrote 25? Let's fix. Actually I want small numbers. Let me use smaller x: set b to 1 instead of 10. Then F1=1. So: initial all zero. Set a1=5, add a2=3 => a=[5,3], sum=0. Set b1=1 => a=[5,3], b=[1,0] => sum=5*1=5. Set a1=2 => a=[2,3], b=[1,0] => sum=2*1=2. Add a2=1 => a=[2,4], sum=2*1=2. So outputs: 0,5,2,2. That works. Let's use that.
error_types_caught: incorrect lazy propagation when multiple updates overlap
order of applying updates (set vs add)
improper handling of set and add on same range

key_coverage_gaps: Edge cases with n=100000 and q=1
Queries where l=r=n
Very large b_i (close to 1e9) and many type 4 queries
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: At least 10 test cases: 2 random small, 2 random large, 2 boundary (n=1, all zero), 2 adversarial (many set b, mixed updates), and 2 more for extremes (e.g., n=100000, q=1 type 4 with large b; n=1, q=100000 updates).

random.description: Random small graph with few vertices and edges, some pre-colored, some uncolored. Good for verifying basic correctness.
random.generation_strategy: Choose n between 3 and 10, m between 3 and n*(n-1)/2. For each edge, randomly assign color from {1,2,3,-1} with equal probability or biased towards -1 to ensure many uncolored. Then solve or determine unsolvability.

random.description: Random dense graph (complete graph on n=30) with many triangles, random colors including -1. Tests performance of triangle enumeration and solving linear system over GF(3).
random.generation_strategy: Generate complete graph K_n with n=30. For each edge, randomly assign color from {1,2,3,-1} (70% probability of -1 to allow flexibility). Then solve. Expect either a valid assignment or detect inconsistency.
error_types_caught: TLE due to O(n^3) triangle enumeration in Python
Memory overflow for large equation matrix

boundary.description: Minimum graph: single vertex (n=1, m=0) or single edge (n=2, m=1). No triangles, so any coloring works.
boundary.test_values: n=1, m=0; n=2, m=1 with edge color -1; n=2, m=1 with edge color 1.
error_types_caught: Ignoring the case of no triangles

boundary.description: Maximum constraints: complete graph K_300 with all edges uncolored. This is the hardest case for time and memory.
boundary.test_values: n=300, m=44850 (complete graph edges), all c = -1. This graph has 4,455,100 triangles. Linear system of equations over GF(3) with 44850 variables and 4.5e6 equations, but many are linearly dependent. Expect to find a solution (e.g., all edges color 1).
boundary.example_output: 44850 ones (since all edges same works) or another valid assignment.
error_types_caught: MLE due to storing all equations

adversarial.description: Pre-colored triangle with invalid coloring: two edges same, one different. Direct inconsistency.
adversarial.attack_vector: The condition is violated by a single triangle; simple solutions that do not check triangles may miss this.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution might assign the uncolored edge to satisfy one triangle but forget to check all triangles. Here all edges are colored, so the inconsistency is immediate. Solutions that assume consistency without checking will output something else.
error_types_caught: Incorrect condition logic (e.g., thinking 'all different' means sum 0 mod 3, which is correct, but then not checking that pre-colored edges already violate)

adversarial.description: Graph with multiple overlapping triangles that lead to contradictory equations when all edges are uncolored. This tests the linear algebra solver's ability to detect inconsistency.
adversarial.attack_vector: Create a system where the only solution requires an impossible assignment due to parity constraints mod 3. For example, a graph that is a union of triangles sharing edges, forming a contradiction.
adversarial.why_effective: A simple greedy algorithm that processes triangles in arbitrary order and assigns colors to uncolored edges based on local constraints may assign a value to an edge that conflicts with a later triangle. This forces the algorithm to backtrack or use more sophisticated reasoning. Solutions that use linear equations properly will solve it correctly.
error_types_caught: Missing the requirement to output colors in input order

key_coverage_gaps: No pattern covers the case where the graph has no triangles (empty constraint set) - covered in boundary_1
No pattern with large number of pre-colored edges causing many inconsistencies - adversarial_1 covers one triangle, but could add more
No explicit pattern for extremely sparse graphs with many isolated vertices - but boundary_1 covers small n and m

random.description: Small n (6) with random impostor count (0 to 2) and random impostor indices. Tests basic functionality and small input handling.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly choose n from {6,9,12} (small multiples of 3). Randomly choose k from 0 to n/2-1. Randomly select k distinct indices as impostors.

random.description: Large n (19998) with random impostor count close to n/2. Tests performance, query limit, and large input handling.
random.generation_strategy: Set n to a large multiple of 3 (e.g., 19998). Choose k = n/2 - 1 (max allowed). Randomly select k distinct indices as impostors.

boundary.description: Minimum n=6 with k=0 (all crewmates). Tests edge case where no impostors exist.
boundary.test_values: n=6, k=0 (minimum n and minimum impostors)

boundary.description: Minimum n=6 with k=2 (maximum impostors for n=6, k<n/2=3). Tests extreme of few impostors.
boundary.test_values: n=6, k=2 (max allowed for min n)

boundary.description: Large n=19998 with k=9998 (max allowed, k = n/2 - 1). Tests handling of many impostors near the threshold.
boundary.test_values: n=19998, k=9998 (max n and max k)

adversarial.description: Impostors are spread so that the first few consecutive triples (e.g., (1,2,3), (4,5,6), etc.) all return 0 (more crewmates). This delays identification of a bad triple and tests whether the solution efficiently finds a triple with majority impostors.
adversarial.attack_vector: Misleading initial consecutive triple queries all return 0, causing the solution to waste queries or incorrectly assume all crewmates.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution that stops early or fails to query a non-consecutive triple may not find a triple with majority impostors, leading to incorrect identification of impostors.

adversarial.description: First triple queried returns 1 (more impostors) due to two impostors in that triple. A naive solution might incorrectly label all three as impostors, leading to an overcount.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solution logic that incorrectly generalizes from a single majority-impostor triple.
adversarial.why_effective: Many solutions assume that if a triple returns 1 (more impostors), then all three are impostors, but in reality only two are impostors. This pattern tests correct identification of the minority impostor in the triple.

key_coverage_gaps: Multiple test cases (t > 1) not covered in examples; adaptive jury behavior over time not explicitly tested; large sum of n across test cases (up to 20000) not fully stressed.

random.description: Small random cases with n up to 5 and a mix of ? and fixed colors, to verify against brute force enumeration of all colorings and permutations.
random.generation_strategy: For n in [1,5], randomly generate domino strings of length 2 using characters B, W, ? with probability 0.3 each for ? and B/W. For each input, compute answer by brute force (enumerate all 2^(number of ?) colorings, check all permutations for each coloring). Use modulo 998244353.

random.description: Large random case with n=100000 and all cells are ?, to stress test efficiency and combinatorial counting using closed-form formulas.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=100000 dominoes, each domino string '??'. Compute answer using known formula (e.g., count of colorings where number of B left equals number of B right etc.).

boundary.description: Single domino (n=1) with both cells ?. The condition reduces to left cell != right cell, so only two valid colorings: BW and WB.
boundary.test_values: n=1, domino='??'
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of wrap-around for n=1

boundary.description: Maximum constraint n=100000 and all dominoes are fully fixed (no ?). Input consists of alternating BW dominoes to create a valid arrangement, ensuring answer is 1.
boundary.test_values: n=100000, each domino='BW'
error_types_caught: miscounting when no ? but fixed pattern is valid

boundary.description: Large n with all dominoes fixed as 'BB' (left and right both black). Any cyclic arrangement will have adjacent cells same, so no valid coloring exists, answer 0.
boundary.test_values: n=100000, each domino='BB'
error_types_caught: incorrectly counting due to ignoring cyclic condition

boundary.description: Mixed ? and fixed cells where only one ? exists. This tests the combinatorial formula when there is a single degree of freedom.
boundary.test_values: n=3, dominoes: '??', 'WB', 'B?' (only one ? in third domino)
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of multiple ? with constraints

adversarial.description: Case where all dominoes are '??' except one that is 'BB' and one that is 'WW'. This creates a forced mismatch in the count of black/white left/right cells, making answer 0.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that overcount by not checking necessary conditions (like total number of black left cells equals black right cells modulo cyclic? Actually condition is more complex).
adversarial.why_effective: Naive combinatorial formulas might ignore the fact that with a 'BB' and a 'WW', no cyclic arrangement can satisfy the alternating condition, leading to nonzero answer.

adversarial.description: Large n with many '??' but also several fixed dominoes that create a pattern forcing a specific gap in possible colorings. This can cause integer overflow if intermediate multiplication is not modulo or uses large numbers.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits integer overflow in intermediate computations when counting factorial-like terms.
adversarial.example_input:
100000
??
??
... (50000 lines of '??')
BW
WB
... (50000 lines alternating 'BW' and 'WB')

So use valid small: n=3, b=[3,3,3] sum=9, sum_a=3, c_i=0 => a_i=1. So all b=3 works.

Sum=6e9, divisible by 6? 1e9, sum_a=2e9, c=[1e9,1e9,-2e9] wrap? b2-b1=1e9, b3-b2=1e9, b1-b3=-2e9, so a_i = (c_i+2e9)/3: a1= (1e9+2e9)/3=1e9, a2 same, a3= (-2e9+2e9)/3=0 => a3=0 invalid because positive required. So NO. Need to construct valid large: n=3, b=[3e9,3e9,3e9]? Sum=9e9/6=1.5e9? Actually 9e9/6=1.5e9, not integer? 9e9/6=1.5e9 = 1500000000, integer? It is integer because 9e9 divisible by 6? 600000*15000? Actually 9e9/6=1.5e9 integer. Then sum_a=3e9, c=0, a_i = (0+3e9)/3=1e9 integer positive. So valid. Use that.

adversarial.why_effective: Sum=18, divisible by 6 (3), so sum_a=6. Then compute a_i: b2-b1=1, b3-b2=1, b1-b3=-2. a1=(1+6)/3=7/3 not integer. So NO. Naive solver might output YES with wrong a_i.

adversarial.attack_vector: Solver may mistakenly compute differences linearly without wrap-around, leading to incorrect a_i.

adversarial.description: Leading zero removal bug: binary strings with trailing zeros can collapse to same number
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive implementation might not trim leading zeros after reverse, leading to incorrect numbers.
adversarial.why_effective: From 2 (binary '10'), append '0' gives '100', reverse gives '001' which trimmed is 1. Many solutions might miss this path because they treat reverse without trimming or assume only append '1' is useful.

adversarial.description: Multiple steps with palindrome intermediates causing state explosion
adversarial.attack_vector: Numbers with binary all ones (e.g., 2^k -1) produce many duplicate states when appending and reversing, leading to BFS queue explosion.
adversarial.why_effective: From 7 (111), append 1 gives 1111->1111=15, so direct. But BFS may also generate many other states from 7: append0 gives 1110->0111=7 (palindrome cycle), causing infinite loop if visited not checked.

adversarial.description: Large difference in bit lengths: x has few bits, y has many bits
adversarial.attack_vector: Short binary numbers can only grow by appending bits; naive solutions might not consider long chains.
adversarial.why_effective: 1->3->7->15->31->63 (each step append '1' and reverse, but since all ones, reverse is same). 63 is 6 bits. Many BFS with depth limit may stop too early or ignore this chain.

adversarial.description: Single cycle of size n (n up to 10^4) to test cycle detection on a long cycle.
adversarial.attack_vector: If the solution uses recursion for cycle detection or does not properly mark visited, it may exceed recursion limit or use too many queries.
adversarial.example_output: The hidden permutation is a single cycle: p_i = i+1 for i=1..9999, p_10000=1. Expected guess: that permutation.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that do not track visited indices may end up querying the same cycle multiple times, causing more than 2n queries or infinite loops.

adversarial.description: Permutation consisting entirely of 2-cycles (swap pairs) for even n.

adversarial.example_output: Permutation defined as: for i=1,3,5,...,9999, p_i = i+1, p_{i+1}=i. Expected guess: that pattern.
adversarial.why_effective: If the solution uses a strategy that relies on cycles being of length > 2, it may incorrectly assign values or double-query pairs.

adversarial.attack_vector: Placing candies such that one robot can cover multiple diagonals by moving down (reducing diff), but naive algorithms may assign separate robots.

boundary.description: Maximum word length (1000) with alternating extreme positions on the keyboard (e.g., 'azaz...') to maximize total time.

boundary.description: Keyboard in alphabetical order and word consisting of all 26 letters in order (full alphabet). The time is the sum of distances between consecutive letters in the alphabet, which is 25.
boundary.test_values: keyboard = 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz', word = 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz'. Output = 25.
error_types_caught: wrong handling of position indexing (0-based vs 1-based)

adversarial.description: Word with all same characters repeated. This should yield time 0, but naive implementations that treat the first character as requiring movement from a starting position will incorrectly compute positive time.
adversarial.attack_vector: Implementation not handling first character correctly, e.g., initializing previous position to 0 and then adding absolute difference for first letter.
adversarial.why_effective: If code adds time for first character by computing |pos(prev)-pos(first)| using an uninitialized prev, or uses a loop that runs from index 0 to len-2 but with prev starting at 0, it will incorrectly add distance for the first letter. The repeated identical letters amplify the error.

adversarial.description: Word that contains letters from opposite ends of the keyboard, with a permutation that is not alphabetical, to catch off-by-one errors in position calculation (e.g., using 0-based indexing but computing difference incorrectly).
adversarial.attack_vector: Off-by-one errors in index mapping. Common mistake: using found index directly as 1-based when it's 0-based, or subtracting 1 incorrectly.
adversarial.why_effective: The keyboard is a left rotation of alphabet: 'a' is last (position 26), 'z' is position 25 (since 'z' is now at index 24? Let's calculate: keyboard = 'bcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyza', positions: 'b'=1, 'c'=2, ..., 'a'=26. So 'z' is at position 25? Actually 'z' is at index 24? Let's check: letters: b(1),c(2),d(3),e(4),f(5),g(6),h(7),i(8),j(9),k(10),l(11),m(12),n(13),o(14),p(15),q(16),r(17),s(18),t(19),u(20),v(21),w(22),x(23),y(24),z(25),a(26). So 'z' at 25, 'a' at 26. Word is 'zyx...cba' reversed alphabet. Starting from 'z' (25) to 'y' (24) difference 1, then to 'x' (23) difference 1, ... total 25 steps. So output 25. If code uses 0-based indexing and forgets to add 1, it will compute from 'z' at 24 to 'y' at 23 diff 1, ..., total still 25? Actually differences are same because absolute difference doesn't change with offset. But if code uses 0-based for positions and subtracts positions, it still yields correct absolute difference. However, if code uses 1-based but loops incorrectly, it might give 26 or 24. Specific off-by-one: if code tries to compute difference as position difference minus 1, it will be 24. So this pattern catches that.

adversarial.description: Test case with t=100 (maximum number of test cases) and small word length (1) for all test cases. This checks that the program handles many minimal cases quickly and correctly.
adversarial.attack_vector: Memory/time waste for many small test cases. Some solutions might allocate large structures per test case, but more importantly, they might reset global variables incorrectly.
adversarial.why_effective: If the solution reinitializes mapping for each test case using a loop over all 26 letters, it's fine. But if it uses a global array and doesn't reset for each test case, it might cause wrong mapping if keyboard order changes. Also, many small test cases stress I/O speed.
error_types_caught: global state pollution between test cases

boundary.description: All items are stools (type 1). s = n >= k. Optimal strategy: place one stool in each cart, remaining stools go to any cart (preferably the one with highest prices to maximize discount? Actually, we want to maximize the cheapest in each cart). Known solution: sort stools descending, place largest stools in separate carts, then put smallest stool with the largest? To maximize discount sum, we want to minimize the cheapest stools in each cart? Wait, discount is 50% off cheapest, so we want cheapest to be as large as possible to get larger discount. Actually, known optimal: Put one stool in each of k-1 carts, and all remaining stools in the last cart. Then the discount in last cart is on the smallest stool in that group, which is the smallest overall. But the discount on the separate carts is on each of those stools. Since discount is 50% off the cheapest item, we want the cheapest items in the separate carts to be as large as possible, so we should put the largest stools in separate carts. So sort stools descending, assign largest k-1 stools to individual carts, and all remaining (including the smallest) to the last cart. That yields maximum total discount. Test cases should catch sorting errors.

adversarial.description: All students have identical answer strings, but expected scores vary.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive greedy that assigns large weights to questions with many correct answers fails because all answers same, so actual scores identical for all students. The problem reduces to choosing a common score to maximize sum of absolute deviations.
adversarial.why_effective: A greedy algorithm might assign weight 2 to the first question (since both correct) and weight 1 to the second, giving score 2 for all students, surprise = 2+2+1=5. But optimal is to assign weight 2 to second question, giving score 2 (since only first question correct? Actually both answer '10' means correct on first, wrong on second. So actual score = p1. For p=[1,2]: score=1, surprise = 1+3+0=4; for p=[2,1]: score=2, surprise=2+2+1=5. So 'greedy' of putting largest on most correct (which is same) doesn't distinguish. But a solver that only considers assignments based on count could misinterpret.
error_types_caught: incorrect optimization of absolute value function

adversarial.description: Answers are such that each question has exactly half correct, and expected scores are extreme to test absolute value balancing.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit that permutation choice must balance conflicting preferences from different students. A naive enumeration might miss that optimal permutation reverses typical ordering.
adversarial.why_effective: For this input, if we assign p=[1,2], actual scores: student1=1, student2=2, surprise=|1-0|+|2-3|=1+1=2. If p=[2,1], scores: 2 and 1, surprise=2+2=4. The optimal places larger weight on question that student1 gets correct and student2 gets wrong, opposite to expected scores. A solver that assumes monotonicity fails.
error_types_caught: incorrect assumption about sign of deviations

error_types_caught: binary search over or under estimation

adversarial.description: Last two heaps are very small while early heaps are large. Tests that the answer is limited by the last two heaps since they cannot receive stones.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits misunderstanding that all heaps can be increased. The last two heaps can only give stones, so they can only decrease.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might try to increase heap 4 and 5, but they cannot receive; they can only give, making them even smaller. The minimum is bounded by the initial values of the last two heaps.
error_types_caught: incorrect assumption about which heaps can receive

adversarial.description: Long sequence where early heaps are tiny and late heaps are huge. Tests optimal distribution over many steps.
adversarial.attack_vector: Forces optimal multi-step stone movement; greedy solutions that only consider local moves may fail.
adversarial.why_effective: To achieve a high minimum, stones must be moved from the last two heaps across many indices. A suboptimal algorithm might not move enough stones or might over-move, causing some heaps to become too low.

adversarial.description: Values that cause binary search to check a high mid that would require moving more stones than available, potentially causing negative values if not handled correctly.
adversarial.attack_vector: Binary search on answer commonly uses a check function that simulates operations from right to left. If mid is too high, the simulation might try to take more stones than available from a heap, leading to negative values. Proper implementation must ensure no heap goes negative.
adversarial.why_effective: If check function does not enforce non-negativity of stones when moving, it might give false positives for high mid values. For example, trying to achieve min=11 would require moving stones from heap 4 to heaps 2 and 3, but heap 4 only has 10, so it would become negative if 2d > 10. A naive check might ignore this and return True incorrectly.

adversarial.description: Path of length 3 (n=4) where naive solutions might assign all edges the same prime (e.g., 3) leading to invalid sum (3+3=6 composite). Tests that solution correctly alternates primes and outputs distinct weights such that adjacent sums are prime.
adversarial.attack_vector: Trick solutions that assume all edges can have the same prime weight without checking pairwise sums. Also tests if solution considers that 2 is the only even prime.
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions that assign a constant prime to all edges will fail because two consecutive primes sum to an even number >2, which is composite. The only way to have all adjacent sums prime is to alternate 2 with another odd prime. If solution does not consider this, it will output something like '3 3 3' which is invalid.
error_types_caught: Wrong answer due to invalid adjacency sums
Failure to use 2 as one of the weights

adversarial.description: Tree with a vertex of degree 3 but structured as a path with an extra leaf attached (e.g., 1-2-3-4, plus edge 2-5). Tests that solution does not mistakenly treat as path. Also include multiple high-degree vertices in larger tree to check detection robustness.
adversarial.attack_vector: Trick solutions that only check if tree is a path by simple degree counting but might misclassify due to linear traversal errors. Also tests that output order matches input order.
adversarial.why_effective: A solution that traverses the tree assuming it's a path might incorrectly assign weights to all edges because it doesn't detect the branch. For example, it might start DFS from a leaf and assign alternating weights, but then encounter a vertex with two unvisited neighbors, leading to ambiguity. Such solutions might produce an assignment or crash. This case forces correct detection of vertices with degree >=3.
error_types_caught: Infinite loop or recursion stack overflow due to branching

adversarial.why_effective: The optimal split might require computing many candidate x,y; a solution that recalculates power-of-two for each split could be TLE. Also, incorrect handling of continuous weights may lead to WA.

adversarial.attack_vector: Algorithms that do not quickly detect empty open set may do expensive operations unnecessarily, leading to TLE.
adversarial.example_input:
200000 200000
[edges forming a line with random weights]
[all queries type 3 with random x]
adversarial.why_effective: If the algorithm for each type 3 query tries to find the maximum edge by traversing the tree or using segment tree that requires processing even when no nodes are open, it may be slow. Solutions that maintain a global data structure for open nodes and can answer queries in O(log n) will be fine. But ones that iterate over all open nodes will TLE.
error_types_caught: TLE due to O(#open) per query

key_coverage_gaps: Nested updates that undo each other
Simultaneous large number of type 1 and type 2 on same ranges
Random ordering of queries with mixed types on a line tree

boundary.description: Maximum ki and maximum n, all distinct messages
boundary.test_values: n=200000, all ki=20, all mi distinct (1..200000). Optimal pin size is 20 (any 20 messages give expectation 20).

adversarial.description: Mixture of students with ki=1 and ki=20 sharing a popular message
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that ignore the loss from ki=1 students when pinning extra messages might pin many messages.
adversarial.why_effective: Pinning only message 1 yields expectation 3 (from ki=1 students) + 0 from others = 3. Pinning messages 1 and 2 yields: for ki=1 students, probability 1/2 each (since they read 1 of 2), total expectation 1.5; for student 4, probability 20/2=1? Actually ki=20 > |S|=2, so probability 1, and student 5 gets 0. So total 2.5. Pinning all three gives: ki=1 students: 1/3 each =>1; ki=20 students: probability min(1,20/3)=1 each =>2; total 3. So still 3. But pinning only message 1 gives 3 and is simplest. Some solutions might calculate incorrectly and pick multiple messages.
error_types_caught: failure to consider that pinning extra reduces expectation for small ki

adversarial.description: Many messages each with moderate demand, ki values cause non-linear trade-off
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit solutions that only consider pinning up to 20 messages but fail to evaluate larger pin sets correctly.
adversarial.example_input: 400000 lines (simplified): 200000 students with mi=i, ki=20; 200000 students with mi=1, ki=1. So total students n=400000. Optimal is pin message 1 only (expectation 200000) vs pinning many messages (expectation much lower). This tests if solution handles large n correctly.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might try to pin many messages because of large ki=20 group, but the huge ki=1 group dominates, requiring only message 1. If solution does not properly balance, it will be wrong.
error_types_caught: poor handling of large n and many distinct messages

key_coverage_gaps: Missing pattern where all ki=20 and mi same (optimal size maybe large?) Actually if all ki=20 and same mi, optimal is to pin that message only, size 1, but expectation = n. That's covered by boundary_2 with ki=1? Not exactly; need test with large ki all same message. Add in future.
Missing pattern with n=1 and ki=20 to test formula for |S| > ki? Since n=1, |S| can be any, but optimal is pin that message. Added in boundary_1.

random.description: Large random stress test with n=200000 and q=200000, focusing on performance and correctness under heavy load. Operations are generated with weighted randomness to simulate worst-case scenarios.
random.generation_strategy: Set n=200000, q=200000. Query types: Color with small ranges to create many segments, Add with moderate x values, Query on random indices. Ensure many Color operations on overlapping ranges to test lazy propagation. Use a correct but slow simulation for small n to verify, but for large n just ensure no errors.
error_types_caught: TLE due to inefficient color range updates
incorrect handling of accumulated adds on recolor

boundary.test_values: n=1, q=1 for each query type (Color, Add, Query). Also include combinations.

boundary.description: Maximum constraints: n=200000, q=200000 with all Add and Query operations to test large additions and multiple queries.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, q=200000. All queries are Add on a single color (e.g., color 1) and Query on random indices. This tests accumulation of adds and potential overflow.

boundary.description: Boundary on color range covering entire array repeatedly, testing lazy propagation and value adjustment on recolor.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, q=200000 with alternating Color 1 n c and Add c x for various colors. This stresses the data structure's ability to handle full-array recolors.
error_types_caught: incorrect value after recolor due to not applying pending adds

adversarial.description: Hack test that interleaves many small-range Color operations with adds and queries to exploit naive O(n) per color operation.
adversarial.attack_vector: Repeatedly color small adjacent ranges with different colors, causing many segment splits. This forces naive implementations to update many elements per query, leading to O(nq) time.
adversarial.example_input:
200000 1000
Color 1 1 2
Color 2 2 3
Color 3 3 4
... (up to 1000 colors)
Add 1 1
Query 50000
... (repeated)
adversarial.why_effective: Naive implementations that loop over the entire range for each Color operation will take O(n) time per query, resulting in O(nq) which times out for large n and q.
error_types_caught: TLE due to linear color updates
incorrect handling of overlapping color segments

adversarial.description: Adversarial test that creates many isolated color segments by repeatedly recoloring alternating positions, then queries all positions to check correctness.
adversarial.attack_vector: Use Color operations with alternating patterns (e.g., Color 1 1 1, Color 2 2 2, ...) and then Add on various colors. This creates many disjoint segments which must be maintained efficiently.
adversarial.example_input:
200000 200000
Color 1 1 1
Color 2 2 2
... (repeat for first 100000 indices)
Add 1 5
Add 2 10
Query 1
Query 2
... (repeat queries)
adversarial.why_effective: The large number of distinct colors and segments tests the data structure's ability to store and update many records. If the implementation uses per-element arrays, it may still be fast but memory heavy; if it uses a map, it may become slow due to many small segments.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect mapping of color to adds
TLE due to inefficient segment management (e.g., using maps with many keys)
RE due to recursion depth in segment trees

adversarial.description: Test focusing on overflow risk by using repeated Add operations on the same color with large values, and queries to verify that 64-bit integers are used.
adversarial.attack_vector: Add many times on the same color with large values (e.g., 1e9) so that cumulative sum exceeds 32-bit limit.
adversarial.why_effective: If the implementation uses 32-bit integers, the value will overflow after a few additions. This pattern catches that mistake.

key_coverage_gaps: Random patterns do not include extreme values for adds
No pattern specifically tests color range updates with l > r (should not happen as per constraints but still) or invalid queries
No pattern for concurrent adds on same color from different queries

random.description: Small random test with moderate n and p, verifiable by brute force enumeration

random.description: Large random test with max constraints to ensure performance and modulo correctness
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=100000, p=1e9, random distinct a_i in [1, 1e9]. Ensure no overflow in intermediate calculations and correct modulo.

boundary.description: Minimum n=1 and minimum p=1
boundary.test_values: n=1, p=1, a_1=1 (only number 1 is <2^1=2; 1 is in S, so count=1; 2x+1=3,4x=4 are >=2, so only 1)
error_types_caught: not counting initial seed when it's the only element

boundary.description: Large p=1e9 with a single large a_i that exceeds 2^p, should count 0
boundary.test_values: n=1, p=30 (2^30≈1e9), a_1=2^30 (which is 1e9? Actually 2^30 = 1073741824 > 1e9, so a_i > 2^p; set S contains only numbers >= a_i, so none <2^p)
error_types_caught: not checking a_i limit before counting

boundary.description: Maximum n=100000 with minimal p=1 to test handling of large input with tiny range
boundary.test_values: n=100000, p=1, all a_i=1 (only number 1 counts; but seed 1 contributes itself and generates 3,4 which exceed, so count=1. But if all seeds are 1, they are distinct? Problem says distinct, so only one 1. For n=100000, need distinct; use numbers from 1 to 100000 but all >2^1=2? Actually if p=1, only numbers <2 are 1, so any a_i >=2 contributes nothing. So output 1 if 1 present, else 0. Use 1 and then many large numbers to test speed.
error_types_caught: inefficient handling of large n with small p

adversarial.description: Chain of numbers where each can be generated from previous, causing many duplicates if not deduped by inverse operation
adversarial.attack_vector: Multiple seeds that are in the same 'tree' due to operations, e.g., 1 generates 3,5,7,... and also 4 generates from 1? Actually 4x from 1 gives 4, and 2x+1 gives 3. So if seeds are 1,3,4, they are all part of same tree. Naive solution counting each seed separately would overcount.
adversarial.why_effective: If not removing redundant numbers, the DP would count numbers generated from each seed independently, leading to duplicates. Proper solution first reduces seeds by applying inverse operations (x -> (x-1)/2 if x odd and >1? Actually inverse: if x=2y+1 then y= (x-1)/2; if x=4y then y=x/4) to get roots. If a number can be reduced to a smaller seed, it's redundant.

adversarial.description: Large p with numbers that cause DP to overflow if using integer types without modulo
adversarial.attack_vector: Use p=1e9 and small a_i that generate many numbers; the DP count grows exponentially, but modulo should keep within range. If solution uses long long without modulo, overflow; if modulo applied late, WA.
adversarial.example_output: null (expected: some large number modulo 1e9+7, but any correct solution should compute it without overflow)
adversarial.why_effective: The number of elements generated from 1 and 2 up to 2^p is huge; any solution that stores counts without modulo will overflow. Also solutions that iterate over all p bits should be careful with arithmetic.

adversarial.description: Maximum constraints with numbers that cause time complexity issues: multiple seeds all requiring separate DP computation
adversarial.attack_vector: Many distinct seeds that are not reducible to each other (e.g., all odd numbers? Actually many seeds can be independent if they are not in same tree). Use n=100000 seeds that are all in range [1, 100000] and p=1e9. Each seed's DP is O(log(2^p)) = O(p) individually, so total O(n*p) would be 1e14, far too large. Solution must process each seed in O(1) amortized, e.g., by counting bits per seed. If solution does separate DP per seed, TLE.
adversarial.example_output: null (large modulo number, but correct solution can compute quickly)
adversarial.why_effective: Forces per-seed iteration to be O(n * log(2^p)) which is too large; only a global DP that handles all roots together in O(p) plus O(n) reduction will pass.
error_types_caught: TLE due to inefficient per-seed computation
failure to reduce seeds to roots

key_coverage_gaps: Need to test modulo for negative numbers? Not applicable
Large memory usage for DP array of size p+1 (p up to 1e9) cannot be stored; must use O(log p) state or formula
Handling of numbers that are exactly 2^p (should be excluded)

adversarial.description: Numbers that are left-truncatable but not right-truncatable. If a solution incorrectly implements right-truncatable, it will say NO for these, but correct answer is YES.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploiting wrong truncation direction
adversarial.why_effective: 13: suffixes (13 and 3) are both prime. If solution checks right-truncatable (removing last digit), it would check 13 (prime) and 1 (not prime) -> NO. So it outputs NO incorrectly.
error_types_caught: Wrong truncation direction (right instead of left)

adversarial.description: Numbers containing zeros in the middle, which are prime. The correct output is NO due to zero presence. A bug that only checks suffixes but not zero digits might still output NO because suffix with leading zero becomes a small number, but if it incorrectly handles leading zeros or forgets zeros, it may output YES.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploiting zero digits in the middle of the number
adversarial.why_effective: Number contains zero so output NO. But a solution that doesn't check zeros might attempt to check suffixes: 10007, 0007 (which might be interpreted as 7), 007 (7), 07 (7), 7. All suffixes as integers are 10007 and 7, both prime. So if solution forgets zero check, it outputs YES incorrectly.
error_types_caught: Incorrect suffix extraction with leading zeros

adversarial.description: A large truncatable prime near the upper bound to test performance and correctness for bigger numbers.
adversarial.attack_vector: Stress test with a large valid truncatable prime
adversarial.why_effective: This is a known left-truncatable prime (739397: suffixes 739397, 39397, 9397, 397, 97, 7 all prime). It is within range (<10^7) and large enough to test that solution handles multi-digit suffixes efficiently. A naive primality test that does trial division up to sqrt for each suffix might be borderline but still fine. However, if solution uses O(n) per check, it could TLE. This pattern catches performance issues.
