boundary.description: Minimum n=1. Only one subarray [1,1]. Both permutations are [1]. MEX of subarray is 2 (since 1 is present). Answer should be 1.
error_types_caught: WA due to not handling n=1
WA due to MEX computation error when array contains all numbers 1..n

boundary.description: Small n=2. Test all possible permutations.
boundary.test_values: n=2, permutations: p=[1,2], q=[2,1]
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect subarray enumeration for small n
WA due to MEX of full array being n+1=3

boundary.description: Maximum n=200000 with extreme structure to test edge handling. For instance, p and q are identical sorted (1..n). Then every subarray has same MEX? Actually MEX depends on elements present. But if both permutations identical, then for any l,r MEX is same because subarrays same. So number of pairs should be n*(n+1)/2. But this is huge (2e10) which fits in 64-bit. Checks if answer fits in 64-bit integer.

adversarial.description: Both permutations are identical (sorted or same order) to exploit naive solutions that might double-count or misinterpret MEX equality.
adversarial.attack_vector: Identical permutations cause many subarrays to have equal MEX. A naive O(n^2) solution must compute MEX for each subarray, which is heavy. But the answer is simply n*(n+1)/2. Hacks can be designed to force incorrect counting if the algorithm does not handle large MEX values (n+1) properly.
adversarial.why_effective: Identical permutations ensure that for any subarray, MEX of p and q are equal trivially. But an algorithm that checks MEX by scanning all numbers from 1 to n may be slow or incorrectly compute MEX when all numbers present (MEX=n+1). Also, if the algorithm uses a sliding window, it may handle this case fine, but if it uses a naive MEX computation for each subarray, it will be O(n^3).
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect MEX of full array
TLE due to O(n^3) subarray MEX computation

adversarial.description: Place 1 at extreme ends to maximize number of subarrays where MEX=1 (since 1 is missing from many subarrays). This tests the algorithm's ability to handle many segments with MEX=1.
adversarial.attack_vector: If the algorithm computes MEX by checking presence of 1 only, it might miscount segments where MEX is 2 or higher. Also, it may cause hash or array accesses that are slow.
adversarial.why_effective: When 1 is at the ends, many subarrays do not include 1, so MEX=1 for those. The algorithm must correctly count these and also handle subarrays that include 1 (MEX>1). An algorithm that only tracks positions of 1 might incorrectly assume MEX=1 for all subarrays that miss 1, but also need to consider other numbers for larger MEX. This pattern stresses the logic of expanding and contracting MEX intervals.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect MEX calculation when 1 is missing
WA due to off-by-one in subarray range boundaries

adversarial.description: Design permutations where MEX of p and q are equal only for a specific set of subarrays, testing the algorithm's precision in handling MEX increments.
adversarial.attack_vector: Create cases where MEX changes frequently and equality occurs only in narrow intervals. For example, align positions of small numbers such that MEX equality only for subarrays containing certain numbers.
adversarial.why_effective: This input forces the algorithm to correctly track the minimum missing number for each subarray. The MEX changes as we include or exclude 1,2,3,... The algorithm must maintain the current MEX efficiently. An incorrect two-pointer or hashmap approach might give wrong counts.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect sliding window logic
WA due to not considering MEX > n

key_coverage_gaps: Need more patterns for non-identical but adversarial MEX changes near boundaries.
Need pattern for large n with many repeated MEX values to test performance.
Need pattern for n=2 with permutations that are not just reversed (all 2 cases).

random.description: Medium-sized board with random king position, covering typical interior cases.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n,m between 10 and 1000, king coordinates random within bounds. Use uniform distribution.
error_types_caught: Logic error in deducing coordinates from query results

random.description: Large board near maximum constraints, king placed in interior to test scalability.
random.generation_strategy: Set n,m to large values like 1e8 or 1e9, king coordinates random but not on boundary.

boundary.description: Minimum board size 1x1, only possible cell.
boundary.test_values: n=1, m=1: only (1,1) is valid. Tests if algorithm handles trivial case.
error_types_caught: Not immediately guessing the only cell

boundary.description: Board of size 1 x large, king on the only row.
boundary.test_values: n=1, m=100000: tests row-only constraint, king can only be on row 1.
error_types_caught: Misinterpretation of distances when one dimension is 1

boundary.description: Board of size large x 1, king on the only column.
boundary.test_values: n=100000, m=1: column-only constraint, king can only be on column 1.
error_types_caught: Misinterpretation of distances when one dimension is 1

boundary.description: Smallest non-trivial square board 2x2, all positions are corners/edges.
boundary.test_values: n=2, m=2: tests edge cases for corner detection and distance calculations.
error_types_caught: Incorrect deduction when all positions are symmetric
Failure to differentiate between adjacent cells

adversarial.description: King at a corner (1,1) to test handling of distance 0 queries.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solutions may assume that the first query will never give distance 0, or mishandle when a query returns 0.
adversarial.why_effective: If algorithm does not account for the possibility that the queried cell IS the king, it may waste queries or make wrong deductions.
error_types_caught: Not checking equality between queried cell and king

adversarial.description: King on edge but not corner, e.g., (1, m/2). Tests edge detection.
adversarial.attack_vector: Algorithms that rely solely on symmetric properties may misjudge when king is on an edge.
adversarial.why_effective: When king is on edge, the distance to some queries may be the same as interior points, causing confusion if algorithm does not consider boundary conditions.
error_types_caught: Not exploiting that distance to a corner gives info about row/column

adversarial.description: King positioned such that multiple query answers are equal, exploiting symmetry to confuse deduction.
adversarial.attack_vector: Choose king at the center of the board (or near center) to make distances to corners symmetric, potentially causing ambiguity.
adversarial.why_effective: If the algorithm's decision tree relies on unique distances from specific queries, symmetric distances may lead to wrong coordinate resolution.
error_types_caught: Incorrect inference when distances are equal

random.description: Small random test cases for verification. k is small (≤20), m is small (≤10), query strings are random short strings of 'a' and 'b'. This allows brute-force checking of results.
random.generation_strategy: Generate k randomly from 1 to 20. Generate m randomly from 1 to 10. For each query, generate a random string of length 1 to min(5, length of f_k) using characters 'a' and 'b'. Ensure total length of queries ≤ 100.

random.description: Medium random test with moderate k (up to 100) and queries of reasonable length to test performance of efficient algorithms.
random.generation_strategy: Generate k between 30 and 100, m between 10 and 100. Query strings length up to 10. Total query length ≤ 1000.

boundary.description: Minimum k value: k=1, f1='a'. Tests base case handling.
boundary.test_values: k=1, m=3, queries: 'a','b','ab'

boundary.description: Small k values: k=2, f2='b'. Also test k=3, f3='ba'.
boundary.test_values: k=2, queries include 'a','b','ba','ab'
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of second Fibonacci string

boundary.description: Maximum k value: k=10^18, with simple queries. Tests that solution can handle extremely large k without overflow or time issues.
Query longer than any Fibonacci string for given k. For k=3 (f3='ba', length 2), query 'aba' (length 3) should give 0.
boundary.test_values: k=3, m=1, query='aba'
error_types_caught: not checking if query length exceeds Fibonacci string length

boundary.description: Single query case: m=1, query='a'. Tests minimal number of queries.
boundary.test_values: k=10, m=1, query='a'

adversarial.description: Many query strings that are prefixes of Fibonacci strings. This tests if the solution correctly handles overlapping occurrences and border counting.
adversarial.attack_vector: Queries are prefixes of Fibonacci strings, which may have many overlapping occurrences. Naive counting may double-count or miss overlaps.
adversarial.why_effective: Fibonacci strings have many self-overlapping substrings. If solution does not correctly account for borders (e.g., using Aho-Corasick without suffix links), occurrences may be miscounted.

adversarial.description: Maximum number of queries (m=10^4) with total length 10^5, all queries are length-2 strings consisting of 'aa','ab','ba','bb'. This stresses time and memory for building automaton and computing counts.
adversarial.attack_vector: Large m with short queries. Solutions that process each query independently (e.g., KMP per query) will TLE. Also tests if automaton building is efficient.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive O(total_length * m) or O(m * k) will exceed time limit. Requires O(total_length + m log k) using automaton and matrix exponentiation.

adversarial.description: Queries that are long and appear very frequently (e.g., single character 'a' for large k). Tests if solution handles large counts and modulo correctly.
adversarial.attack_vector: Single character 'a' occurrences grow like Fibonacci numbers, leading to huge counts. Need modulo and fast recurrence.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution uses 64-bit integers without modulo at intermediate steps, overflow occurs. Also tests if recurrence correctly computes large indices.

key_coverage_gaps: Queries with both 'a' and 'b' mixed to test alternating patterns
Queries that are empty (not allowed per problem, but still might be input)
Very long query strings (close to length of f_k) for moderate k
Multiple queries that are substrings of each other
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: At least 10 test cases to cover basic boundaries, random small, random large, and adversarial cases.

random.description: Randomly generated valid x values (even and (x/2 & x) == 0) to ensure correct a,b computation.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random even numbers x in [2, 10^7] such that (x>>1) & x == 0. Use bitwise check. For each valid x, compute a = x + x//2, b = x//2. Include multiple test cases.
error_types_caught: WA when condition holds but computation wrong

random.description: Randomly generated invalid x values (odd or even but (x/2 & x) != 0) to ensure -1 output.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random odd x and random even x that fail the condition. Mix them.
error_types_caught: WA when outputting numbers for invalid cases

boundary.description: Minimum value x=1 (odd) and x=2 (smallest valid).
Maximum value x=1073741823 (odd) and maximum valid x (approx 715827882).
Even x that are invalid due to condition failure, e.g., x=6, x=12.
error_types_caught: assuming all even x have solution

adversarial.description: Large number of test cases (t=10000) with large valid x to test time and memory.
adversarial.attack_vector: High input size and large numbers to cause TLE or overflow in naive implementations.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution recomputes something per test case inefficiently (e.g., O(log x) per test) it may TLE. Also tests overflow if using 32-bit int without care.

adversarial.description: Tricky invalid x where the parity check might be missed, e.g., x=6 (binary 110) and x=12 (1100) where condition fails only in specific bits.
adversarial.attack_vector: The condition (x/2 & x) != 0 might be mischecked by only checking parity or incomplete bitwise logic.
adversarial.why_effective: These numbers are even but have overlapping bits with half; naive solutions might think they are valid because they are even, or might use a wrong formula.

key_coverage_gaps: No test for x=0 (though not in constraints)
No test with multiple valid and invalid mixed in one test case

random.description: Small random test cases with n between 1 and 5, and small values of a_i and b_i (1 to 10). Used to verify algorithm correctness on trivial cases.
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, choose random n in [1,5]. For each i, choose a_i in [1,10], b_i in [1,10]. Ensure variety in divisibility patterns.

random.description: Large test case with up to 300,000 total n and large a_i, b_i up to 1e9. Stress tests performance and overflow handling.
random.generation_strategy: Generate one test case with n=300000 (or sum=300k across multiple test cases). Randomly assign a_i and b_i in full range, ensuring some variation. Use loop to generate inputs.
random.example_output: null (unknown, but expected to run in time)

boundary.description: Single candy type (n=1) for each test case. The answer should always be 1.
boundary.test_values: n=1 for all test cases; t up to 10000, but sum n <= 300000, so t can be 300000 if each n=1.

boundary.description: All a_i = 1, so d_i must be 1. c_i = b_i. Answer is number of contiguous groups with equal b_i.
boundary.test_values: a_i=1 for all i, b_i arbitrary, but only possible d_i=1.
error_types_caught: assuming d_i can be chosen to make c_i equal when b_i differ
failing to consider that d_i must divide a_i

boundary.description: Maximum values: a_i = 1e9, b_i = 1e9. Product a_i*b_i = 1e18, just in 64-bit range. Groups possible only if LCM of b_i divides 1e18.
boundary.test_values: a_i=1000000000, b_i=1000000000 for all i. Then L = lcm of all b_i = 1e9, G = gcd of a_i*b_i = 1e18. L divides G? Yes, 1e9 divides 1e18. So all can be in one group. Answer=1.
error_types_caught: overflow in lcm when numbers are large

adversarial.description: Cases where LCM of b_i quickly exceeds 1e18, causing overflow if not handled. The algorithm must detect when L > 1e18 and break early.
adversarial.attack_vector: Set b_i such that lcm grows beyond 64-bit. Typically use relatively prime numbers like 1e9, 999999937 (big prime), etc.
adversarial.target_error: overflow (WA or TLE if simulation continues)
adversarial.why_effective: Naive lcm calculation would overflow or become wrong; correct algorithm checks if L > max_a*b (or > 1e18) and starts new group.

adversarial.description: Sequence that forces maximum number of groups. Each pair forces a new group because LCM of b_i does not divide current G.
adversarial.attack_vector: Alternate between two values that are incompatible: e.g., b_i = 2 and 3 alternating, while a_i such that a_i*b_i are all distinct and do not share common divisor? Actually need to break condition. Simple: make each b_i a different prime, and a_i=1, then L will never divide G (since G=1). So each type is its own group.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive algorithms might try to merge adjacent types that are incompatible; correct algorithm should count each individually.
error_types_caught: missing case when L does not divide G

key_coverage_gaps: Edge case where a_i*b_i product overflow in 32-bit (but we assume 64-bit)
Cases where L equals G exactly
Zero values (not allowed)

random.description: Small random test cases for verification (n between 1 and 10, c up to 100)
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate t (1-10), for each test case n in [1,10], c in [1,100], and a_i in [1,20]. Compute expected output via greedy sorting.
error_types_caught: WA due to mistake in cost calculation

random.description: Large random test cases to stress test performance (n up to 200000 total, c up to 1e9, a_i up to 1e9)
random.generation_strategy: Generate t=1, n=200000, c=1e9, a_i random in [1,1e9]. Alternatively multiple test cases with total n=200000.

boundary.description: Minimum n=1, various c and a_i values
boundary.test_values: n=1, c from 1 to 1e9, a_i from 1 to 1e9, checking cost = 1 + a_i vs c
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of 0-index vs 1-index (cost = i+1 + a_i)
edge case when c exactly equals cost

boundary.description: Maximum n=200000 in one test case, extreme values of c and a_i
boundary.test_values: n=200000, c=1e9, a_i=1e9 for all, costs = i+1e9. The smallest cost is about 1+1e9 = 1000000001, which is > c, so output 0.
error_types_caught: integer overflow when adding i to a_i (if using 32-bit)

boundary.description: c large enough to use all teleporters
boundary.test_values: n=200000, c= large (e.g., sum of costs), a_i=1 for all, so costs = i+1, sum up to ~2e10, c could be 2e10. But c max is 1e9, so cannot use all. Actually c max 1e9, so maybe only about sqrt(2e9) ~44721 teleporters. But pattern: all costs equal so greedy picks first n if c big enough.

adversarial.description: Costs such that ignoring index (i) when sorting leads to wrong answer
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solutions may sort only by a_i, not i+a_i. This test has a_i small at high indices, so index dominates.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that sort by a_i only will output 1 instead of 2 because they pick the expensive teleporter first, blocking cheaper ones.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect greedy cost calculation

adversarial.description: Large costs causing integer overflow in 32-bit when computing i + a_i
adversarial.attack_vector: If code uses 32-bit int, adding i (up to 200k) to a_i (up to 1e9) can exceed 2^31-1 (2.147e9) and overflow to negative. This test triggers overflow.
adversarial.why_effective: Some solutions might use O(n^2) or incorrect greedy for many test cases? Actually this is just a normal case. We need adversarial that targets common mistakes like not resetting variables, or miscomputing cost for first teleporter. Another common mistake is assuming teleporter at position i cost = a_i + 1? No, i is not 1-indexed? Actually in problem, points are 1..n, so start at 0, moving to i costs i coins. So cost = i + a_i. A mistake is to use 0-index: cost = i+1 + a_i? If using 0-indexed array, i in code is 0..n-1, then cost = (i+1) + a_i. So if someone uses i directly, they get wrong for first element. So adversarial test: n=1, a1=5, c=5. Correct cost: 1+5=6 >5, can't use. But if uses 0-index cost: 0+5=5, would think can use. So that catches off-by-one. Example: n=1, c=5, a=[0? a_i >=1, so a1=5? Actually a_i >=1, so a1=5, cost=6. So output 0. If someone uses 0-index, they compute 0+5=5 <=5, output 1. So test: 1 5 5 -> expected 0. This is a good adversarial.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect cost formula

key_coverage_gaps: Handling of large number of test cases with small n
Cases where c exactly equals cost of first few teleporters
Duplicate costs

random.description: Small random permutations of size n (3 ≤ n ≤ 10) covering various game outcomes
random.generation_strategy: Generate random permutations of size n, exclude ascending and descending order, compute expected outcome using optimal play logic (or brute force for small n). Ensure variety in counts of misplaced elements for both players.

random.description: Large random permutations (n up to 10^5) to stress test optimal strategy computation without simulation
random.generation_strategy: Generate random permutation of size n (large, e.g., 100000). The expected outcome can be computed analytically by counting misplaced elements for ascending and descending, and checking if one player can force a win within turn limit (if any).
error_types_caught: Time limit exceeded due to simulation

boundary.description: Minimum size n=3 with different outcomes
boundary.test_values: n=3 is the smallest valid size because n=2 would be sorted. Test all three outcomes at n=3.
error_types_caught: Failing to handle input validation for n=3

boundary.description: Maximum size n=500000 with permutation designed to have known outcome (e.g., First wins quickly)
boundary.test_values: n=500000, permutation where almost all elements are in correct ascending position except a few, so First can win in few moves.
error_types_caught: Too many test cases summed over large n

adversarial.description: Permutation where second player can force a win by having many common misplaced elements that first player cannot block
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solutions may think first player has advantage because more elements are in correct ascending position than descending, but second player can use common elements to delay.
adversarial.why_effective: Common misplaced elements (positions where both players need change) are high, allowing second player to sabotage first's progress while advancing own goal.
error_types_caught: Assuming first player always wins if more elements are in place

adversarial.description: Permutation that forces a draw due to symmetric conditions
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that don't consider skip option may think one player wins, but optimal play leads to draw.
adversarial.why_effective: Both players have equal numbers of misplaced elements and common elements are symmetric, so neither can force a win, leading to draw under optimal play.

key_coverage_gaps: Large permutations with precise counts of misplaced elements
Permutations requiring examination of turn limit (if any)

random.description: Small n with diverse a_i values, including extremes and duplicates, to verify basic logic and manual computation.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly select n between 3 and 10. Generate a_i randomly from 1 to n. Generate m between 1 and 3, with k values covering 1 to n. Ensure all a_i ≤ n. Sort for reference output.
error_types_caught: ignoring the constraint that each book must have at least one reader

random.description: Large n (up to 200000) with random a_i and many queries (up to 200000) to stress test time and memory efficiency.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n = 200000. Generate a_i uniformly from 1 to n. Generate m = 200000 queries with k values uniformly from 1 to n. Note: expected output is not provided here, but can be computed by a standard solution.
random.example_input:
200000
1 2 3 ... 200000 (sorted? actually generated unsorted but solution will sort)
200000
1
2
...
200000

boundary.description: Minimum n = 1, with a single reader and various k values.
boundary.test_values: n=1, a_1=1 (minimum requirement). Queries: k=1 (must have one book) and k=0 (if allowed, but problem likely k>=1). Test only k=1.

boundary.description: All readers have minimum requirement a_i = 1. Then any grouping works; answer should be n for any k (since one book can hold all, and each book must have at least one reader).
boundary.test_values: n=5, a=[1,1,1,1,1]. Queries: k=1,2,3,4,5. Expected output all 5.
error_types_caught: assuming that more books always reduce satisfaction

boundary.description: All readers have maximum requirement a_i = n. Only one book can satisfy all; using more than one book splits readers and no one is satisfied.
error_types_caught: forgetting that each book must have at least one reader

boundary.description: Number of books equals number of readers. Then each reader can be alone, so only readers with a_i=1 are satisfied.
boundary.test_values: n=5, a=[1,2,3,4,5]. Query k=5. Expected output = 1 (only the first reader).
error_types_caught: incorrectly assuming all can be satisfied when k=n
not accounting for minimum group size

adversarial.description: Input where a_i is not sorted; naive algorithm that processes in given order may fail.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits that the correct solution sorts a. Unsorted input can cause greedy grouping in given order to produce suboptimal result.
adversarial.example_output:
For k=2: Expected 3 (put three 1's together in one book, the 4 alone; the three 1's satisfied, 4 not). If processing in order, might group 4 with something and fail.
For k=3: Expected 4 (since we can have three books: one for the 4 alone unsatisfied? Actually with 3 books we can have groups: {4,1,1} size 3, {1} size 1; 4 needs 4, not satisfied; the three 1's satisfied -> 3. But optimal: all four could be in one book? With 3 books, we must use all three books. Actually, we have 3 books, must assign all readers. To satisfy the 4, we need group size at least 4, so that group must contain all others. Then the other two books would have zero readers? That violates 'someone should read each book'. So each book must have at least one reader. So with 3 books, we must have three non-empty groups. So we cannot put all four in one book. So best is to satisfy three 1's. So expected output: 3 for k=2 and 3 for k=3? Let's compute k=2: groups: one book can have three 1's (satisfied), the other book has the 4 (alone, not satisfied) => 3 satisfied. k=3: groups: e.g., {1,1,1} (satisfied), {4} (alone), and a third book must have someone, but we only have 4 readers, so we already used all. Actually, we have 4 readers and 3 books. So one book must have at least 2 readers? Minimal non-empty groups: sizes 2,1,1 or 1,1,2. To satisfy three 1's, we could put two 1's together and one 1 alone? But then the group with two 1's satisfies both (size2≥1), the alone one satisfies, but the 4 alone does not. So 3 satisfied. So outputs: 3,3.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive algorithm that doesn't sort may assign the large requirement reader early, causing unnecessary constraints.

adversarial.description: Cases where the answer changes at specific k values, testing binary search precision.
adversarial.attack_vector: Create a scenario where the minimal books needed for x readers is exactly k, testing off-by-one in binary search.
adversarial.example_output: Sorted: [2,2,3]. For k=1: only one book, group size 3, all satisfied? a=3 needs 3, yes; a=2 needs 2, yes. So 3 satisfied. For k=2: With two books, possible groups: sizes 2+1 or 1+2. To satisfy a=3, group size must be 3, so impossible. So we can satisfy at most the two a=2 readers by putting them together (size 2) and the a=3 alone (size1, not satisfied) => 2 satisfied. For k=3: groups must be three non-empty groups: sizes 1,1,1. Then only a=2? Actually each alone, so only those with a=1 satisfied, but no a=1, so 0 satisfied. So outputs: 3,2,0.
adversarial.why_effective: Checks if algorithm correctly handles the transition from satisfying all to satisfying a subset, especially when k equals the requirement of a reader.

adversarial.description: Many queries (up to 200000) with large n to test for TLE or memory issues if algorithm is not O((n+m) log n).
adversarial.attack_vector: Heavy query load, especially if solution recomputes per query without caching.
adversarial.example_input:
200000
1 2 3 ... 200000 (sorted would be 1..200000, but generate unsorted)
200000
1
2
...
200000 (all k values 1 to 200000)
adversarial.why_effective: Naive per-query binary search that scans the entire array each time will be O(n*m) which is too slow. A proper solution precomputes an array of answers for all k or uses binary search with prefix sums after sorting.

key_coverage_gaps: Cases where a_i values are not unique (duplicates) should be covered by random patterns.
Edge case where some a_i > n? Not possible since a_i ≤ n implicitly from satisfaction condition.
Case where k=0 is not in problem but might be considered; not necessary.
Memory exhaustion with large n if not careful; adversarial pattern addresses performance.
Need to cover that each book must have at least one reader; boundary patterns ensure no group is empty.

random.description: Random small test case for verification
random.generation_strategy: Generate t=1, n random between 1 and 10, a_i random between 1 and 20, b random between 1 and 10, x and y random between 0 and n. Ensure constraints satisfied.

random.description: Random large test case for stress testing
random.generation_strategy: Generate t=1, n=200000, a_i random between 1 and 1e9, b random between 1 and 1e9, x and y random between 0 and n. Ensure sum of n over test cases fits but here only one large test.

boundary.description: Single element array
boundary.test_values: n=1. Vary b, x, y.

boundary.description: No operations allowed (x=0, y=0)
boundary.test_values: x=0, y=0, any n

boundary.description: All operations possible (x=n, y=n) but per-element limits restrict each element to max 2 operations total
boundary.test_values: x=n, y=n, large n
error_types_caught: incorrect assumption about total operations vs per-element

boundary.description: Large b that reduces most numbers to zero
boundary.test_values: b larger than max a_i or just very large

adversarial.description: Order-dependent benefits for combined operations
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solutions that consider only one ordering of halve and subtract on same element may produce suboptimal result because halve-then-subtract vs subtract-then-halve differ.
adversarial.why_effective: a_i=5, b=3. halve then subtract: ceil(5/2)=3, subtract 3 -> 0. subtract then halve: 5-3=2, ceil(2/2)=1. Both sequences differ (0 vs 1). Optimal is 0. A solution that only considers one order might output 1.
error_types_caught: WA due to ignoring order dependency

adversarial.description: Equal reduction from both operations on some elements, requiring careful selection of which to apply when counts are limited
adversarial.attack_vector: Greedy algorithms that always apply the operation with larger immediate reduction may fail because applying both to different elements can yield better overall sum.
adversarial.why_effective: For a=20: halve gives 10 (reduction 10), subtract gives 10 (reduction 10). For a=10: halve gives 5 (reduction 5), subtract gives 0 (reduction 10). Greedy by reduction might apply subtract to 20 and 10, using both ops, leaving third unchanged, sum=20. But optimal: apply subtract to 10 (becomes 0) and halve to 20 (becomes 10), sum=10+0+10=20? Actually 20->10, 10->0, 10 unchanged = 20. Wait, better: apply subtract to 20 (10) and halve to one 10 (5), sum=10+5+10=25. Or apply both to 20: halve then subtract: 20->10->0, sum=0+10+10=20. Or both to a 10: halve then subtract: 10->5->0, and subtract to other 10: 0, sum=0+0+20=20. So minimum is 10? Let's compute: we have x=1, y=1. Options: apply halve to 20: 10; apply subtract to 20: 10; apply halve to 10: 5; apply subtract to 10: 0; apply both to 20: halve->10 then subtract->0; apply both to 10: 10->5->0; apply halve to one 10 and subtract to other 10: 20 + 5 + 0 =25; apply halve to 20 and subtract to one 10: 10 + 10 + 0 =20; etc. So minimum is 20? Actually if we apply both to 20: 20->0, other 10,10 unchanged: sum=0+10+10=20. If we apply both to a 10: 10->0, and subtract to other 10: 10->0, and 20 unchanged: sum=20+0+0=20. So minimum is 20. But we said 10? That seems wrong. Let's recalc: Maybe we can do halve then subtract on 20: 20/2=10, 10-10=0; subtract on one 10: 0; other 10 unchanged: sum=0+0+10=10. That uses x=1 (halve on 20) and y=2? No, y=1 only. So we can't do two subtracts. So minimum is indeed 20. So example needs adjustment. Let's find a case where greedy fails. Consider: n=2, a=[20, 20], b=10, x=1, y=1. Greedy by reduction: halve gives 10 reduction, subtract gives 10 reduction. So it might pick either. If it picks halve on first and subtract on second, sum=10+10=20. But optimal: apply both to first: 20->0, second unchanged: sum=0+20=20. Same. Need case where using both on one element is better than one each. Suppose b=1, a=[100, 2]. x=1, y=1. Greedy reduction: halve on 100: reduction 50; subtract on 2: reduction 1 (since 2-1=1, reduction 1). Sum after: 50+1=51? Actually initial sum=102, after greedy: 100 halved =50, 2 subtract =1, sum=51. But if we apply both on 100: 100 halve=50, subtract 1=49, 2 unchanged, sum=49+2=51. Same. Try a=[100, 3], b=50. x=1,y=1. Greedy: halve on 100: 50 (reduction 50); subtract on 3: 0 (reduction 3). Sum=50+0=50. Optimal: both on 100: halve->50, subtract->0, sum=0+3=3. Yes! That's a difference. So example: n=2, a=[100,3], b=50, x=1,y=1. Expected output: 3 (apply both to 100). Greedy output: 50. So this pattern catches WA from greedy by reduction. But note: This is a single element. Better: n>1 to show selection issue. So let's use this example.
error_types_caught: WA due to suboptimal greedy selection

key_coverage_gaps: Large b exactly equal to some a_i
All elements same value
Alternating large and small values

Misunderstanding of clique formation in G_k

random.description: Random small test cases with n,m between 2 and 10, start and end not adjacent, for verification against known results.
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, randomly choose n,m in [2,10] and randomly choose start and end cells such that they are distinct and not adjacent (i.e., Manhattan distance > 1). Compute answer as min(degree(start), degree(end)).

random.description: Random larger test cases with n,m up to 100, including edge cases where n or m is 1, to stress test performance and correctness.
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, randomly choose n,m in [1,100] but ensure start and end are distinct and not adjacent. For n=1 or m=1, ensure the two cells are not consecutive (i.e., |x1-x2|>1 or |y1-y2|>1). Compute answer as min(degree(start), degree(end)).

boundary.description: Minimum grid size: n=1, m=2 with start and end at the two corners, which are adjacent? Actually (1,1) and (1,2) are adjacent, so not allowed. So use n=1,m=3 with start at (1,1) and end at (1,3) (non-adjacent). Also n=2,m=2 with start and end at opposite corners (diagonal).
boundary.test_values: n=1,m=3: start (1,1), end (1,3) -> degree start=1, degree end=1 -> answer=1. n=2,m=2: start (1,1), end (2,2) -> degree both=2 -> answer=2.

boundary.description: Maximum grid size: n=100,m=100, start at top-left corner (1,1), end at bottom-right corner (100,100) (diagonal, not adjacent).
boundary.test_values: n=100,m=100, start (1,1) degree=2, end (100,100) degree=2 -> answer=2.

boundary.description: Edge cells: start on an edge but not corner, end also on an edge but not corner, to test degree 3.
boundary.test_values: n=5,m=5, start (1,2) degree=3, end (5,4) degree=3 -> answer=3.

boundary.description: Interior cells: start and end both interior, to test degree 4.
boundary.test_values: n=10,m=10, start (5,5) degree=4, end (6,6) degree=4 -> answer=4 (they are diagonal, not adjacent).

boundary.description: One cell difference in dimension: n=1,m=100 and vice versa, start at one end, end at the other end (non-adjacent because distance >=2).
boundary.test_values: n=1,m=100, start (1,1), end (1,100) -> degree start=1, end=1 -> answer=1.

adversarial.description: Adjacent start and end cells: (1,1) and (1,2) in a moderate grid, to catch solutions that assume non-adjacent and output min(degree) without checking.
adversarial.attack_vector: The problem does not explicitly forbid adjacent cells. Many solutions assume non-adjacency and compute min(degree), but adjacent cells make it impossible to block the direct edge. The correct output is undefined; however, to break such solutions, we expect them to output min(degree) (e.g., 2) but the actual answer is infinite or requires special handling.
adversarial.why_effective: If the solution outputs 2 (min degree = 2), it is wrong because you cannot block the direct path without blocking start or end. The problem may have hidden constraint that they are not adjacent, so this case is invalid; but if included, it exposes incorrect assumption.

adversarial.description: Start and end on the same row with exactly one cell between them (e.g., (1,1) and (1,3) in a 1x5 grid). The answer is 1 (block middle cell). Some solutions might output min(degree)=1 correctly, but others might output 2 by thinking both ends need all neighbors blocked.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that compute min(degree) correctly will output 1. But those that block all neighbors of both might output 2, which is suboptimal.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that think they need to block all neighbors of start or end will block at least 1 for start (neighbor (1,2)) and possibly more, but the optimal is 1.
error_types_caught: not considering that blocking one cell can isolate start

adversarial.description: Large grid with start at a corner and end very close but not adjacent (e.g., (1,1) and (2,2) in a 100x100 grid, diagonal). Answer is min(2,4)=2. But a solution might consider only degree of start and ignore that end's degree is higher, leading to wrong if it picks the wrong minimum? Actually min gives correct. But a bug could be that they output degree of start or end without taking min.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that output only degree of start or only degree of end instead of the minimum.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution outputs 4 (degree of end) instead of 2, it's wrong. Also if it outputs 2 but for wrong reason it might pass.

adversarial.description: Start and end on the same edge but far apart (e.g., (1,1) and (1,100) in a 1x100 line). Answer is 1 (block (1,2)? Actually to disconnect start from end, you can block (1,2) to isolate start, or block (1,99) to isolate end, but blocking one cell suffices. So answer 1. Some might think need 2 because both ends are on boundary.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that think corners/edges always require 2 or 3 obstacles irrespective of distance.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution outputs 2 (degree of start) they are wrong, because blocking just (1,2) isolates start.
error_types_caught: not recognizing that blocking one neighbor suffices

key_coverage_gaps: Test cases where n or m is 1 but adjacent cells (should be invalid but could break solutions that don't check)
Test cases with very large grids but start and end are both corners (already covered)
Test cases with varying distances to ensure min degree is always correct

adversarial.description: Repeated actions on the same post to test correct handling of moves without removals.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive simulation may incorrectly treat each action as a removal, or fail to update positions properly when a post is already present.
adversarial.why_effective: Many duplicates: actions on already-present posts should only move them to top, not cause removals. Only when a new post (4) appears does the bottom (post 3) get removed at time 10. Posts 1 and 2 are never removed. A naive solution that counts all actions as removals would output wrong removal times.
error_types_caught: incorrect simulation of 'move to top' without removal

adversarial.description: All actions on posts already in the initial feed (no new posts).
adversarial.attack_vector: If the implementation does not correctly identify that no removals happen, it may assign removal times incorrectly.
adversarial.why_effective: All actions are on posts 1..5, which are present from the start. No new post is ever added, so no removals occur. Output should be all -1. A common mistake is to think that after the first cycle, new posts might appear, but here p_i are always ≤ n.
error_types_caught: mapping wrong posts to removal times

adversarial.description: Large number of subarrays with large k to break O(n*k) solutions
adversarial.attack_vector: n=200000, k=99999, array values alternating between two distinct values, but such that symmetric pairs have same parity and same value? Actually alternating doesn't maximize mismatches. To force O(n*k) worst-case, we need each subarray to have many mismatches. Use array where each element equals its index (all distinct). Then every pair (i, j) with i != j will have different values, so mismatches per subarray = floor(k/2). That avoids any early termination.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive O(n*k) solution would compare each pair in each subarray, leading to ~1e10 comparisons, causing TLE. A proper O(n) solution would handle this efficiently.

adversarial.description: Large sum to test integer overflow
adversarial.attack_vector: n=200000, k=100001 (odd), array with all distinct values (e.g., 1 to 200000). Number of subarrays = n-k+1 = 100000. Each subarray has floor(k/2)=50000 mismatches. Total sum = 100000 * 50000 = 5e9, which exceeds 32-bit int but fits in 64-bit.
adversarial.why_effective: If result stored in 32-bit integer, overflow will cause wrong answer. Using long long avoids this.

adversarial.why_effective: Solution may not count the all-zero ticket as lucky because it thinks sum of others is zero but digit is zero, so condition satisfied. But if logic only checks positive matches, it might skip.

adversarial.description: k=1 edge case
adversarial.attack_vector: Often inputs assume k>=2, but problem allows k=1. Only digit 0 possible, all tickets lucky.
adversarial.why_effective: Solution might crash or output incorrect count due to division by zero or loop over k values.

adversarial.description: Large n and k with small mod
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions with O(n*k) time may TLE; those with O(n*k^2) will definitely fail.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive DP with O(n*k^2) would be 100*30*30=90k operations, which is fine. But if k is larger (e.g., 1e9) not in easy version. For easy version, we can only test within limits. Actually, for easy version, n and k are small enough that O(n*k^2) might pass. Let's choose n=100, k=30, mod=2 to stress DP state count.
error_types_caught: Memory limit for large DP arrays

adversarial.description: Case where sum condition modulo k might be miscounted due to modulo wrap
adversarial.attack_vector: Condition: there exists a digit equal to sum of others modulo k. This is equivalent to total sum ≡ 2*digit (mod k). A solution that directly uses this might have errors.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution counts combinations incorrectly due to not considering that digit can be any, or double counting when multiple digits satisfy condition.
error_types_caught: Overcounting when multiple digits are candidates

Response: 3 (vs expected 3? Actually expected 3, so no special? Wait care: pile 2 has special weight=3, so query piles 1,2: expected 1+2=3, actual=1+3=4, diff=1. So response 4)
? 1 2
Response: 3 (pile2 only)
! 2

boundary.test_values: n=1, a_1 = any value 1 to 1e9, special pile is the only pile.

boundary.example_output: ? 100000 1 2 ... 100000 -> response = 100001 (expected 100000, special in first half). Continue binary search, final ! 1

boundary.description: Large stone counts to test overflow in sum calculation.
boundary.test_values: n=2, a_1=1e9, a_2=1e9, special in pile 2. Sum query both: expected 2e9, actual 2e9+1. But if using 32-bit int, 2e9 fits, but sum of many large numbers could overflow.

adversarial.description: Multiple test cases with small n (1) to test query limit resetting and efficiency.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solutions might ask a query for each test case even when n=1, wasting queries; or they might not reset query counter between test cases.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution asks a query for n=1, it uses 5 queries, but that's allowed (30 per test case). However, some solutions might mistakenly use binary search on a single element, causing an extra query. More importantly, if they don't reset the query limit counter, they might think they have used too many queries. But the main vulnerability is solutions that don't handle n=1 specially and try to ask a query, which is fine but might be unnecessary. However, a worse bug: some solutions might not output anything if they think no query is needed, and then miss flushing. This test checks that the solution can handle multiple test cases with minimal work.

adversarial.description: All piles have the same stone count except one, making the weight difference tiny (1 gram). The solution must accurately detect this small difference.
adversarial.attack_vector: If the solution uses floating point or improper comparison, it might misclassify the difference.
adversarial.example_output: Binary search: ? 5 1 2 3 4 5 -> response = 5000000001 (expected 5000000000, diff 1) so special in first half. Continue, final ! 5
adversarial.why_effective: If the solution uses floating point arithmetic or integer division, it might miscalculate expected sums due to overflow or rounding. Using 64-bit integers is necessary. This pattern checks for proper handling of large numbers and small differences.

key_coverage_gaps: Testing interactive timeouts (delayed responses)
Large number of test cases with varying sizes
Edge cases with special stone in middle and binary search exactly on boundaries

(447 lines each with 447 numbers following pattern)

Also tests integer overflow when using 256*i+j: if i,j up to 399 and 499 respectively, 256*399=102144, plus j up to 499, total < 2^31, but to be safe should use 64-bit. Solutions using 32-bit may overflow if they use larger multipliers.

adversarial.attack_vector: Interleaved test cases with very different sizes; tests that global arrays are properly resized.
