adversarial.description: Many test cases with moderately large n to cause TLE if solution is not O(1) per test case.
adversarial.attack_vector: High number of test cases (t up to 10^4) each with n ~10^6. This will cause O(n) per test case solutions to exceed time limit.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive simulation of n operations for each test case would be O(t*n) = 10^4 * 10^6 = 10^10 operations, far too slow.
error_types_caught: TLE: O(n) or O(n log n) per test case

adversarial.description: Special values like powers of two and small numbers to catch errors in pattern detection.
adversarial.attack_vector: Use n = 2, 3, 8, 16, 32. Powers of two may have different behavior. Also include base cases.
adversarial.why_effective: Some incorrect formulas might work for many n but fail at powers of two or specific residues. This pattern checks those.
error_types_caught: WA: incorrect formula for powers of two

key_coverage_gaps: Very large n (near 10^9) combined with high t (like 10^4) is not explicitly covered but can be derived from adversarial_1 with larger n.
Random distribution across all n values (e.g., modulo patterns) not covered but not essential for this problem.
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: 10-15 test cases (including 5-10 random small, 2-3 boundary, 2-3 adversarial) would give adequate coverage.

random.description: Random small k values from 1 to 1000 to verify basic correctness.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random integers k in [1, 1000] using a uniform distribution.

random.description: Random large k values near 10^14 to stress test performance and large number handling.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random integers k in [10^13, 10^14] using a uniform distribution.

boundary.description: Minimum value k=1.
Maximum value k=100000000000000.
k equal to powers of 9: 9, 81, 729, 6561, etc.
error_types_caught: incorrect mapping when leading digit changes

boundary.description: k just before and after powers of 9 to catch off-by-one errors.

adversarial.description: Maximum number of test cases t=10000 with all k at maximum value to stress time limit.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits inefficient per-test-case computation if not O(log k) per case.
adversarial.why_effective: If the solution recalculates large numbers from scratch for each test case, the time may exceed limits.

adversarial.description: Consecutive k from 1 to 100 to test transitions between base-9 representations.
adversarial.attack_vector: Off-by-one errors may appear at boundaries where base-9 digits change.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that try to generate numbers one by one will be extremely slow; also off-by-one errors are exposed at transitions.

key_coverage_gaps: Very small k around 1-10 are covered by boundary min and consecutive adversarial, but random small provides broader distribution.

random.description: Small random test cases with n up to 10 and health values from 1 to 20. These are useful for verifying correctness against brute force solutions.
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, generate a random integer n between 1 and 10, then generate n random integers a_i uniformly from 1 to 20.

random.description: Medium to large random test cases with n up to 300000 (total sum across test cases up to 300000) and health values up to 1e9, to test performance and overflow handling.
random.generation_strategy: Generate t such that total n <= 300000 and each n roughly up to 300000. Generate a_i uniformly from 1 to 1e9. Include moderate chain propagation scenarios.
random.example_input:
3
100000
<100000 random numbers from 1 to 1e9>
100000
<another set>
100000
<another set>
error_types_caught: integer overflow in sum of health or cost

boundary.description: Single monster (n=1). The explosion can kill it directly with power equal to its health, or basic spells can kill it. Minimum MP is exactly the health.
boundary.test_values: n=1, health=1 (minimum) and health=1e9 (maximum).

boundary.description: All monsters have health 1. The explosion can kill all with a single chain starting from any monster with power 1. No basic spells needed, total MP = 1.
boundary.test_values: n up to 300000, all a_i=1.
error_types_caught: incorrect chain propagation for uniform low health
not considering that explosion power can be as low as 1
mishandling of large n with same health

boundary.description: Health values form a strictly decreasing sequence (e.g., n, n-1, ..., 1). The explosion starting from the first monster with power n can chain through all without basic spells. Total MP = n.
error_types_caught: failure to recognize optimal explosion position

boundary.description: Health values form a strictly increasing sequence (e.g., 1,2,...,n). The explosion must be at the end to chain backwards, or need many basic spells. Total MP = sum of health - (1+2+...+n) + n? Actually for [1,2,3] optimal is explosion at 3 with power 3, kills 3 (3), then 2 (2), then 1 (1) -> total MP=3. So total MP = n.
error_types_caught: not considering chain from high health end

adversarial.description: Health values that cause integer overflow in intermediate calculations (e.g., sum of health in chains near 1e14, close to 2^63 limit). Use large health and n.
adversarial.attack_vector: Integer overflow in 32-bit int or even 64-bit long long if not careful.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution uses 32-bit int for summing health or costs, overflow leads to WA. Many contestants might use int for a_i but compute sums in long long. Still, this catches common pitfall.

adversarial.description: Health values that form a 'wave' pattern: increasing then decreasing at the middle, to test if the optimal explosion position is correctly identified. For example, [1,2,3,2,1]. The optimal explosion is at the peak (value 3) with power 3, costing 3.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solutions might try to compute DP only in one direction or fail to consider positions other than global maximum.
adversarial.why_effective: Some greedy algorithms pick the highest health as explosion center, but here the highest is 5 at position 3, but chain cannot propagate left because left neighbor 3 < 4? Actually chain condition: to kill left neighbor, need health <= power -1. If power=5, left neighbor has health 3 <= 4, so it dies, then left-left neighbor has health 1 <= 3, dies. Right neighbor: health 3 <= 4, dies; then next right: health 2 <= 3, dies; last: health 4 <= 2? No, 4 > 2, so it would survive, requiring basic spells. So explosion at position 3 with power 5 kills left side completely, but right side has a monster (6th) with 4 health that cannot be killed by chain (since after killing 5th with power 2, explosion to 6th is power 1, not enough). So we need to reduce 4th health? Actually basic spells can be used before explosion. The optimal solution may involve reducing some health to enable chain. This pattern is designed to test the DP that computes minimal reductions to make a valid chain.

adversarial.description: All health values are very large (1e9) but monotonic decreasing? Actually large health makes chain impossible without many basic spells. The answer is sum of health (since explosion power needed is huge, costing same as basic spells). This tests if solutions mistakenly think explosion can reduce cost.
adversarial.attack_vector: Overestimation of explosion benefit.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution might choose explosion on first with power 1e9, but chain fails because second also 1e9, and explosion power reduces by 1 each step, so never kills. So must use basic spells to reduce them all, total cost 3e9. This catches errors in chain condition logic.

key_coverage_gaps: Large n with identical health (boundary only covers small health=1, not large identical health)
Health values that form a V-shaped pattern (decreasing then increasing) to test bidirectional DP
Extremely large health differences between neighbors
Cases with n=2 and various health values (chain propagation with two monsters)

random.description: Small random arrays with mixed values including 1s and non-1s to test basic correctness and impossibility detection.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n between 1 and 10, a_i between 1 and 20, uniformly at random. Ensure some cases include 1 and other >1 to trigger -1.

random.description: Large random array (n=200000) with values up to 1e9 to stress test time/memory and operation limit.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=200000, a_i random in [2, 1e9]. Only cases with min>1 to ensure possible. Check that output operations count <= 30*n.

boundary.description: Single element array (n=1). Always possible with 0 operations.
boundary.test_values: n=1, a_i=any positive integer

boundary.description: Two-element arrays covering all impossibility and possibility cases: (1,1), (1,>1), (2,2), (2,3), (2, large), etc.
boundary.test_values: n=2, a1=1, a2=2 (impossible); a1=1, a2=1 (possible); a1=2, a2=3 (possible); a1=2, a2=1e9 (possible)
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of 1 with larger numbers
operation count correctness for two elements

boundary.description: Maximum number of test cases (t=1000) with minimal n=1 for each, to test overhead and output handling.
boundary.test_values: t=1000, each test case n=1, a_i=1

adversarial.description: Impossible case with minimum value 1 and a large number. Naive solutions that don't check min==1 condition will try to perform operations and fail or produce infinite loops.
adversarial.attack_vector: Ignoring impossibility condition when min=1 and there is a larger number.
adversarial.why_effective: Some solutions attempt to reduce all numbers to the minimum by dividing by minimum, but if minimum is 1, division by 1 does nothing, so they loop forever or output many operations incorrectly.

adversarial.description: Case where many operations are required, close to 30*n limit. This stresses the operation counting and may expose solutions that exceed the limit due to inefficient algorithm.
adversarial.attack_vector: Operations count overhead: each operation may take O(n) to find max/min, leading to O(30n^2) worst-case.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive algorithm that finds max and min each step could do O(n^2) for n=200000, which is too slow. Efficient solution uses sorting or repeats with same min.

adversarial.description: Array where all numbers are equal and large (e.g., 1000000000) but n is large. Solutions that output operations for equal arrays should output 0; any extra operation is wrong.
adversarial.attack_vector: Unnecessary operations on equal arrays.
adversarial.why_effective: Some solutions may not check equality first and try to reduce all numbers, outputting operations even though they are already equal.
error_types_caught: false positive operations on equal arrays

key_coverage_gaps: Large n with many distinct values requiring many operations but still within limit
Cases where min becomes smaller during operations (e.g., [3,5])

random.description: Small random strings of length 1-10 to verify correctness of dynamic programming or prefix-sum approach.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate a string of length n (1 ≤ n ≤ 10) by choosing each character as uppercase or lowercase with equal probability.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of all-uppercase or all-lowercase options
off-by-one errors in split point iteration

random.description: Moderate-size random strings of length up to 1000 to test performance and ensure correctness on larger inputs.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate a string of length n (100 ≤ n ≤ 1000) with equal probability for each character being uppercase or lowercase.

boundary.description: Minimum length (n=1) string, already fancy.
boundary.test_values: n=1, single character (both 'a' and 'A')

boundary.description: Maximum length (n=100000) string consisting of all the same case (e.g., all lowercase), already fancy.
error_types_caught: memory limit with large strings if using recursion or extra structures

boundary.description: String that is already fancy: all uppercase then all lowercase, or all uppercase, or all lowercase. Here example of uppercase then lowercase.
boundary.test_values: Already fancy, output 0
error_types_caught: not recognizing all uppercase or all lowercase as fancy

boundary.description: Reverse fancy: all lowercase then all uppercase, which is the worst-case for number of changes needed.
boundary.test_values: String where all lowercase precede all uppercase, length up to 100000
error_types_caught: incorrect computation of changes when case blocks are clear
off-by-one errors in split point between blocks

adversarial.description: Alternating case string where uppercase and lowercase counts are equal, forcing the optimal solution to change all to one case (ends of split), which is better than any internal split.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that only consider splits at indices where case changes (i.e., where s[i] is uppercase and s[i+1] is lowercase) and miss the all-uppercase or all-lowercase options.
adversarial.why_effective: For 'aAbBcC', internal splits (at positions 1,3,5) yield costs: split1: prefixLower[0]=0? Actually cost: split at 1: prefix[0] need to be uppercase? Let's compute: split at 1 means first 1 char should be uppercase, so change 'a' to 'A' (1), rest should be lowercase: 'AbBcC' has uppercase at positions 1,2,4? Actually careful: positions: 0 a (lower),1 A (upper),2 b (lower),3 B (upper),4 c (lower),5 C (upper). Split at 1: prefix [0] need uppercase: change a->A (1). Suffix [1..5] need lowercase: change A->a (1), B->b (1), C->c (1) total 3? Actually suffix uppercase count: positions 1,3,5 -> 3, so total 4? Wait: total changes = lowercase in prefix (1) + uppercase in suffix (3) =4. Split at 2: prefix [0,1] need uppercase: change a (1) but A already upper, so 1; suffix [2..5] need lowercase: change B (1), C (1) -> 2; total 3. So internal split min is 3 (at split 2). But all-uppercase: change all lowercase (a,b,c) -> 3 changes; all-lowercase: change all uppercase (A,B,C) -> 3 changes. So internal split also gives 3, but in 'aA' the ends give 1 and internal gives 2. So 'aAbBcC' still has internal split giving same cost? Actually we need a case where ends strictly better. 'aA' is clear. So use 'aA' as example. But longer: 'aAaA'? Let's compute for 'aAaA' (4 chars: a,A,a,A). Split at 0: all lowercase: change all uppercase (2) ->2. Split at 4: all uppercase: change all lowercase (2) ->2. Internal splits: split at 1: prefix[0] need uppercase: change a (1); suffix[1..3] need lowercase: change A and A (2) total 3. Split at 2: prefix[0..1] need uppercase: change a (1) ; suffix[2..3] need lowercase: change A (1) total 2? Actually: prefix chars: a(need change), A(no change) =>1; suffix chars: a(no change? Actually need lowercase? a is lowercase, fine? No, suffix needs lowercase, a is already lowercase, but we also have uppercase A? Wait string indices:0 a,1 A,2 a,3 A. Split at 2: first two indices (0,1) should be uppercase: a->A (1 change), A ok (0). Last two indices (2,3) should be lowercase: a ok (0), A->a (1 change). Total 2. So internal split at 2 also gives 2. So it's not strictly better. So 'aA' is the simplest. For longer, we can make it such that all internal splits are worse. For example, string starting with lowercase and alternating, but with more lowercase at the beginning? Actually the pattern is that ends are always options. If the string is like 'a' then many uppercase, then 'a'? Not sure. We'll stick with 'aA' as a clear case. So adversarial_1 example: 'aA'. Output 1.
error_types_caught: splitting only at boundaries where case changes

adversarial.description: Long alternating string with equal uppercase and lowercase counts to stress-test O(n^2) solutions and verify efficiency.
adversarial.attack_vector: TLE / high runtime
adversarial.why_effective: A naive O(n^2) dynamic programming would iterate over all splits and compute changes in O(n) each, leading to O(n^2)=2704 operations for 52 chars (still small), but for n=100000 it would be huge. We can make a large version. This pattern catches solutions that are not O(n) in length.
error_types_caught: time limit exceeded on large inputs

adversarial.description: String where the optimal split point is at one of the extremes (all-uppercase or all-lowercase) due to minimal changes, but a naive algorithm may not consider split at 0 or n.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits missing edge cases in split point iteration (e.g., loops from 1 to n-1 only).
adversarial.why_effective: For single character, the only splits are at 0 and 1, both give 0 changes. If algorithm only considers splits from 1 to n-1 (i.e., not including ends), it would miss the valid splits and may produce incorrect (non-zero) output. For example, if n=1, splitting from 1 to 0 is empty, so no iteration, might cause undefined behavior.
error_types_caught: not considering split point 0 or n

key_coverage_gaps: Strings with all same case (covered in boundary)
Strings with only one uppercase among many lowercase (or vice versa)
Strings with length exactly 100000 random

random.description: Small random test cases to verify correctness of solution logic for small values.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a, b uniformly random from 1 to 10, with t up to 10.

random.description: Large random test cases to stress test performance and overflow handling.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a, b uniformly random from 1 to 1e9, with t = 100 (or up to 1000). Ensure duplication of extreme values rarely.
error_types_caught: time limit exceeded due to inefficient iteration

boundary.description: Minimum values: both a and b equal to 1.
boundary.test_values: a=1, b=1 (minimum possible coordinates). Expected answer is 2 (no leg increase, two jumps).

boundary.description: Maximum values: both a and b equal to 1e9.
boundary.test_values: a=1e9, b=1e9. Expected answer is around 94968 (based on optimal m ~ 31623).
error_types_caught: incorrect iteration range (too small) leading to suboptimal answer

adversarial.description: Case where optimal leg length is larger than sqrt(max(a,b)) due to large asymmetry.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solution that only checks m up to sqrt(max) might miss a better solution because the optimal m is slightly larger than sqrt due to ceil behavior.
adversarial.why_effective: With a=1, b=1e9, the optimal m is around 31623 (sqrt). Checking m only up to sqrt works fine, but if someone checks only up to, say, 20000, they might miss the optimum. This pattern targets solutions that use an insufficient upper bound.
error_types_caught: wrong answer due to insufficient iteration range

adversarial.description: Case where both a and b are large but not equal; test symmetry handling.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that assume a>=b or use a single max/min incorrectly might fail for swapping.
adversarial.why_effective: The answer should be the same for (1000,1) and (1,1000). If a solution does not treat symmetry correctly (e.g., always compute based on max and min in a certain order), it might produce different answers.

key_coverage_gaps: No pattern specifically targeting very large t (1000) but random large t is covered in random_2 with t=1000? Actually random_2 example has t=3 but generation strategy can include large t.
No pattern for zero values? But constraints start at 1.
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: At least 100 test cases spanning all patterns, with emphasis on boundary and adversarial cases.

random.description: Small random permutation with n=5 to verify basic functionality and query limit
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random permutation of size 5 using a PRNG. Single test case.
error_types_caught: Exceeding query limit on small input

random.description: Multiple small test cases (t=10, each n=3) to cover a variety of small permutations
random.generation_strategy: Generate 10 test cases, each with a random permutation of size 3. Ensures total n sum <= 30.
error_types_caught: Incorrect handling of multiple test cases
Violation of query limit per test case

boundary.description: Minimum n (n=2) to test edge case where only two permutations exist
boundary.test_values: n=2, permutation must be [1,2] or [2,1]; solution should output both directly without queries

boundary.description: Maximum n (n=2000) single test case to stress memory and query limit
boundary.test_values: n=2000, sum of n across test cases is exactly 2000 (since only one test case)

adversarial.description: Reversed permutation (e.g., [n, n-1, ..., 1]) to test handling of symmetric distances
adversarial.attack_vector: The reversed permutation often causes naive solutions to misalign the mapping from distances to positions, especially when using a path graph construction.
adversarial.why_effective: Many solutions assume the first element is 1 or n, which fails when the permutation is reversed. The distances may be misinterpreted, leading to incorrect permutation recovery.
error_types_caught: Incorrect deduction of permutation from distances

adversarial.description: Permutation that is a specific sequence causing many queries needed for disambiguation (e.g., [1,3,2,4] for n=4)
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits the fact that some permutations have ambiguous distance patterns after the standard two type-1 queries, forcing the solution to use more queries to disambiguate, potentially hitting the 30-query limit.
adversarial.why_effective: Standard solution often uses two type-1 queries to create a path, then queries distances from a specific node. For this permutation, the distances might not uniquely determine the order without additional queries, increasing the total number of queries and risking the limit.

key_coverage_gaps: Large t (e.g., 1000) with many small n each n=2
Permutations that are already sorted (1..n)
Permutations with high symmetry (e.g., identity, reversed)

random.description: Random small test case (n <= 20) to verify basic correctness and ensure algorithm handles small inputs.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random n (5-20), random k (1 to n), and random strings of length 1-10 using lowercase letters.

random.description: Large random test case (n=2000, max string length) to stress test time and memory efficiency.
random.generation_strategy: Generate 2000 random strings of length 500 (or max possible) with random letters. Set k = random value between 500 and 1500.
error_types_caught: MLE due to storing full strings

boundary.description: k=1: only one protein selected, no pairs, so representativity is 0.
boundary.test_values: n=5, k=1, any strings (e.g., 'a', 'ab', 'abc')

boundary.description: All strings identical: each pair contributes full length L. Test maximum possible answer for given n and L.
All strings have no common prefix (first character differs). Every LCP=0, answer 0.
boundary.example_input:
10 5
a
b
c
d
e
f
g
h
i
j
error_types_caught: preserving spurious matches due to character case

boundary.description: Minimum string length (1 character). All strings equal: LCP=1 for each pair.
boundary.test_values: n=100, k=50, all strings 'a'

adversarial.description: Strings with many distinct branches (full binary trie-like structure) to force many node merges and challenge DP performance.
adversarial.attack_vector: All strings share a common prefix but then diverge into many branches. For example, strings 'a', 'aa', 'ab', 'ac', ..., 'az', 'aaa', 'aab', etc., creating a large trie with many nodes. This can cause O(n^2) node visits or excessive memory if not handled carefully.
adversarial.example_input:
2000 1000
[2000 strings generated as binary strings of length 10 over {a,b} with all distinct patterns]
adversarial.why_effective: The trie will have up to O(n * L) nodes, and DP merging at each node may become expensive if the DP arrays are not merged efficiently (e.g., O(k^2) per node). Forces the algorithm to use fast merging or risk TLE.
error_types_caught: MLE due to storing too many DP states

adversarial.description: Strings with long common prefixes but then many unique suffixes, testing DP correctness when many strings share the same prefix but diverge late.
adversarial.attack_vector: Create a set of strings where many strings share a long prefix (e.g., first 400 characters identical) and then have random tails. This forces the algorithm to correctly accumulate LCP contributions for strings that share the full prefix. Naive algorithms might double-count or miss contributions from overlapping prefixes.
adversarial.example_input:
10 5
[10 strings: first 400 chars all 'a', then last 100 chars random distinct]
adversarial.why_effective: If the DP does not properly propagate the contribution of the common prefix through all pairs of strings that share it, it may output a wrong sum. Also, it tests the merging of DP arrays from children where each child’s strings share the prefix.

adversarial.description: Strings with very similar structure but slight differences, testing the algorithm's ability to pick optimal subset.
adversarial.attack_vector: Generate groups of strings where each group has high internal LCP but low cross-group LCP. The algorithm must choose k strings from the groups to maximize sum. This tests whether the DP correctly considers both intra-group and inter-group contributions. A greedy selection might fail.
adversarial.example_input:
4 2
'aaa', 'aab', 'abb', 'bbb' (expected: choose 'aaa' and 'aab' LCP=2, sum for pair=2; alternative: 'aaa' and 'abb' LCP=1, sum=1; 'aab' and 'abb' LCP=1; 'aaa' and 'bbb' LCP=0; best is 2)
adversarial.why_effective: Naive DP might not correctly balance contributions from different groups or might incorrectly merge DP arrays. The optimal selection requires considering all possible combinations.
error_types_caught: failure to consider pair sums across groups

key_coverage_gaps: No pattern specifically tests strings with repeated characters only (e.g., all 'a's)
No pattern with k = n and strings all distinct (no common prefix)
No pattern with maximal string length variety (some short, some long)
No pattern tests alphabetical ordering impact on trie (since input order doesn't matter but some algorithms sort)

random.description: Small n, small a_i, small k. Verifies basic correctness and brute-force equivalence.
random.generation_strategy: Set n random between 1 and 5, a_i random between 1 and 10, k random between 1 and product of a_i (if product > 1) else k=1. Generate a few random instances.

random.description: Moderate n (up to 10), moderate a_i (up to 1000), moderate k. Stress test DP with floor values enumeration (O(sqrt) per dimension).
random.generation_strategy: n random 6-10, a_i random between 100 and 1000, k random between 1e3 and 1e6. Use known correct solution (brute force if small enough) to validate.
error_types_caught: missing combinations due to incomplete enumeration

random.description: Large n (near 100), large a_i (up to 1e9), large k (up to 1e9). Performance test for meet-in-the-middle or optimized DP.
random.generation_strategy: n = 100, a_i random from 1e8 to 1e9, k random from 1e8 to 1e9. Ensure product a_i >= k.

boundary.description: n=1, various a1 and k. Simplest case: maximize floor(a1/p1) subject to p1 >= k, p1 <= a1.
boundary.test_values: n=1, a1=10, k=3 => max floor(10/p) for p>=3 is floor(10/3)=3? Actually p=3 gives floor=3, p=4 gives 2, p=5 gives 2, etc. So max is 3. Then output k*3=9. But careful: p must be integer. So optimal p=3 gives volume=3, output=9. Also test k=1: output = a1=10. Also test k > a1: impossible, output 0.

boundary.description: k=1. The answer should be product of a_i, because we can take p_i=1 for all i, giving volume = product a_i, and k=1, output = product a_i.
k equals the product of all a_i. Then we must choose p_i = a_i for all i, giving floor(a_i/a_i)=1, product of ones=1, output = k * 1 = product a_i.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling when k equals product

boundary.description: Some a_i = 1. For those dimensions, p_i must be 1. They contribute factor 1 to volume and p_i. Test both with n=1 and with n>1.
boundary.test_values: n=2, a=[1,5], k=3. Must set p1=1, p2 can be >=3. floor(5/p2) for p2>=3: p2=3 gives floor=1, p2=4 gives 1, p2=5 gives 1. So volume=1, output=3. Also test when a_i=1 forces impossibility? If n=1, a1=1, k>1 impossible -> output 0.

boundary.description: Very large k close to product of a_i. Forces many p_i to be large, min volume small.
boundary.test_values: n=2, a=[100,100], product=10000. k=9999. Need p1*p2 >=9999. Options: p1=100, p2=100 gives 10000, floor=1 each, volume=1, output=9999. Other combos like p1=100,p2=99 gives 9900 <9999. So answer 9999? Actually min volume =1, output=9999. Also check if 1 is max? Could p1=100,p2=100 give volume 1; p1=99,p2=101? p2 cannot exceed a2=100. So yes.
error_types_caught: overflow when computing product of p_i

boundary.description: All a_i=1, n up to 100, k=1 (only possible). Output=1.
boundary.test_values: n=100, all a_i=1, k=1 => product a_i=1, k=1, output=1.
error_types_caught: segfault or long loop due to many a_i=1

boundary.description: Impossible case: product a_i < k. Ensure output 0.
boundary.test_values: n=2, a=[2,3], product=6, k=7 => output 0.

adversarial.description: Large n with many a_i being perfect squares. This generates many distinct floor values per dimension, potentially causing TLE if DP iterates over all floor values instead of grouping.
adversarial.attack_vector: exploit O(sqrt) enumeration per dimension but still large number of combinations due to many distinct floor values. For a_i=10^9, floor values count ~2*sqrt(10^9)≈63245, which is manageable, but combined with n=100 could be heavy if not careful with meet-in-the-middle.
adversarial.example_input:
100 1
1000000000 1000000000 ... (100 times) with k=1 (trivial) but for stress. For non-trivial, set k large enough to require search. Let's use k=2^50? Actually better: n=10, each a_i=10^9, k=10^6 to force non-trivial.
adversarial.why_effective: DP that enumerates all floor values naively will have to consider ~63245^10 ~ huge, causing TLE. Optimized solutions using map merging for meet-in-the-middle also need to handle many states.

adversarial.description: Test with overflow in integer product when computing floor product or p product. Use large numbers that cause 64-bit overflow if not using high-precision or floating-point log comparisons.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit solutions that compute raw products of floor(a_i/p_i) as 64-bit integers, which overflow when product exceeds 2^63-1.
adversarial.example_input: n=20, a_i all=10^9, k=1 (output should be (10^9)^20, huge, but since k=1, answer is product a_i. 64-bit overflow. However, problem expects output as real number, so using floating point double would lose precision. Actually double can represent up to ~1e308, (1e9)^20=1e180, within double range, but precision might be lost for very large numbers. For n=100, product=1e900, double overflows to inf. So test with n=100, a_i=10^9, k=1: answer = 1e900, double gives inf. So need to handle with log or arbitrary precision? Problem expects answer with 1e-6 error; using log and exp might be needed. So this pattern catches missing log-based comparison.
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions comparing raw products will overflow or lose precision on large numbers. Expected behavior is to output a double, but actual answer is huge; many solutions may output a finite value instead of inf due to overflow.

adversarial.description: Specific adversarial with a_i having many factors causing floor values to be same for many p_i, but DP might overcount states.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit inefficiency in state space: when a_i has many divisors, floor(a_i/p_i) can take only few values, but p_i can be many. DP that enumerates p_i directly will be slow.
adversarial.example_input: n=50, a_i= 2^31-1 (prime) gives floor values up to 2^31-1, distinct. But each dimension only O(sqrt) distinct floor values. Actually prime gives many floor values? For large prime P, floor(P/p) for p=1..P takes about 2*sqrt(P) values. So still manageable. Better: use a_i with many small factors like product of many primes? Actually the number of distinct floor values is about 2*sqrt(a_i) regardless of factors. So adversarial_1 is sufficient. Perhaps another: a_i=10^9+7 (prime) and n=100, k=10^9, forcing many p_i combinations.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive DP that scans p_i from 1 to a_i for each dimension will be O(a_i) per dimension, leading to TLE. The pattern forces a_i large.

adversarial.description: Test with n=100 and k=1 (trivial maximum), to ensure that solutions can quickly output product of a_i without heavy DP.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit solutions that always run full DP, ignoring early exit for k=1.
adversarial.why_effective: A solution that does not handle k=1 as special case will do unnecessary work, potentially timing out.
error_types_caught: TLE due to missing early exit

adversarial.description: Test with product of a_i just barely larger than k, so many p_i combinations need to be considered to achieve exactly product >=k.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit DP that only considers p_i combinations that give large floor values, missing those that barely satisfy product condition with slightly smaller floor values but larger product of floors? Actually the objective is to maximize min volume, so we might sacrifice large floor values to meet k. This pattern forces exploration of many marginal combinations.
adversarial.example_input:
3 10
4 4 4 (product=64>10). Optimal? Let's compute: maximize min volume product floor(4/p_i). p_i can be 1..4. Need p1*p2*p3>=10. Maybe p=[2,2,3] gives floor=[2,2,1], product=4, output=40. Or p=[4,2,2] gives floor=[1,2,1]=2, output=20. So max is 40. So example: input: 3 10
4 4 4 -> expected output 40.
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions that greedily choose p_i to maximize floor product without ensuring product of p_i condition may output a higher floor product but not satisfy k. Or they may miss the optimal combination by not considering all p_i sets.

key_coverage_gaps: n=100 with all a_i=1 and k=1 (covered by boundary_6)
n=1 cases covered
impossible case covered
large k near product covered
overflow and precision covered

random.description: Small random test cases (n <= 10) with random colors to verify correctness via brute force enumeration.
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, randomly choose n between 2 and 10, k between 1 and n, and colors between 1 and n. Generate 5-10 such cases per test file.

random.description: Larger random test cases (n close to 100) with random colors to stress test DP O(n^3) complexity.
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, set n = 90-100, k random between 1 and n, colors random between 1 and n. Generate 5-10 such cases ensuring sum n <= 200000.

2
100 7
[100 random integers between 1 and 50]
95 10
[95 random integers between 1 and 30]

boundary.description: Extreme n=1 and n=100 with various k values to test minimal and maximal constraints.
boundary.test_values: n=1, k=1: answer 1; n=1, k=2: answer 1; n=100, k=100: answer 1 (empty path); n=100, k=1: answer 1 (full row).

boundary.description: All tiles same color vs all distinct colors. Tests counting of subsequences and when no color appears k times.
boundary.test_values: All same color: n=10, k=3 -> max length 9, answer = C(10,9) = 10. All distinct: n=10, k=3 -> no color appears 3 times, max length 0, answer 1. One color appears exactly k times: n=5, k=2, colors [1,1,2,3,4] -> max length 2, answer = number of ways to choose 2 positions with color 1 = C(2,2)=1? Actually also could be (2,?) no, only two 1s, so answer 1.
error_types_caught: failing to return 1 when no path possible
overcounting paths for all same color

adversarial.description: Many test cases (t=10000) with small n to test I/O and per-test overhead, especially for O(n^3) solution per test.
adversarial.attack_vector: High number of small test cases to force high constant overhead and potentially TLE.
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions that initialize large arrays per test case or have high per-test overhead (e.g., O(n^3) for each small n) may time out. Sum n=10000, but if initializing O(max_n^2) per test, it's heavy.

adversarial.description: Carefully crafted colors to make DP count multiple paths of maximum length, testing combinatorial accuracy.
adversarial.attack_vector: Multiple frequencies of same color that create many valid combinations of blocks.
adversarial.why_effective: Maximum length is 10, number of paths = C(10,10)=1? Wait k=2, n=10, max length = 10 (multiple of 2). Number of subsequences of length 10 is 1 (the whole row). Actually for all same color, any subsequence of length 10 is just the full row, so only one path. But if n=10, k=2, max length = 10, but we need blocks of 2, so the path must include all 10 tiles in order, so only one. So correct answer is 1. Not 45. For n=10, k=2, all same, number of ways to choose 10 positions from 10 is 1. So binomial coefficient C(10,10)=1. Actually maximum length is 10, so only one path. So to get multiple paths, need n > L where L is max length multiple of k. For example, n=6, k=2, all same: max length = 6, answer = 1. For n=5, k=2, all same: max length = 4, number of subsequences of length 4 from 5 is C(5,4)=5. So answer = 5. So use n=5, k=2, all same. That gives 5 paths. So test that.

key_coverage_gaps: Edge case when n is not multiple of k and all colors same: combinatorial count
Many test cases with n=100 but different k values to test DP efficiency

250000
<250001 integers, first few: 1, another...>
<250001 integers, shifted>

index out of bounds for arrays of size 1

boundary.test_values: d=1, A(x)=ax+b, B(x)=a(x+s)+b. Leading coefficient a not 0 mod MOD.
error_types_caught: incorrect formula for s in linear case

boundary.description: Maximum degree d=250000 with leading coefficient = 1 and shift s = 0 (identical polynomials). Tests that algorithm correctly outputs 0.
boundary.test_values: d=250000, A(x) = x^250000 + ... (random) but B identical to A.
error_types_caught: inefficient computation of differences for large d

boundary.description: Leading coefficient equals MOD-1 (mod prime) to test modular inverse computation.
boundary.test_values: d=2, A(x)=(MOD-1)x^2 + ... (leading coeff MOD-1). Compute s=123, then generate B.

2
<three values for A from leading coeff MOD-1>
<three values for B shifted by 123>

sign issues when leading coefficient mod prime

adversarial.description: Specific degree 2 case designed to catch off-by-one errors in the shift formula using differences. Uses A(x)=x^2, B(x)=(x+1)^2, so s=1.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit potential off-by-one in indices when computing (d-1)-th difference at 0 and 1.
adversarial.why_effective: Many solutions compute delta = (first difference of B at 0) - (first difference of A at 0) and then divide by (d! * leading coefficient). If they mistakenly use the first difference at 1 instead of 0, or miscompute the constant factor, s may be wrong.
error_types_caught: incorrect scaling factor in shift formula

adversarial.description: Large shift s near MOD-1, with d large. Tests that s can be any value modulo MOD, not just small.
adversarial.attack_vector: Assume s is small; this breaks if algorithm limits s or uses direct comparison for small s.
adversarial.example_input:
2
0 1 4
<values for B with s=MOD-1, e.g., A(x+MOD-1) mod MOD>
adversarial.why_effective: If algorithm estimates s by some heuristic or assumes s < d, it will fail.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of large s modulo MOD
overflow in intermediate steps when using signed integers

adversarial.description: d=1 with shift s=0, leading coefficient 1. Simple but can catch failures in handling zero shift.
adversarial.attack_vector: Zero shift leads to identical sequences; some solutions may produce division by zero or infinite loop.
adversarial.why_effective: If algorithm computes s = (ΔB - ΔA)/ (d!*lead) and both differences equal, numerator 0 leads to s=0, but if they incorrectly compute denominator or fall into division by zero (if lead is 0 but guaranteed not), they might still output nonsense.
error_types_caught: division by zero when differences are equal
infinite loop if trying to find s by iteration

random.description: Small random test cases for verifying correctness against a brute-force simulation of all possible merging sequences (feasible for n <= 8) or against a known manual computation.

boundary.description: Large n (close to 1e5) with values that cause powers of 2 to be used at large exponents. Tests modular exponentiation and inverse correctness.
boundary.test_values: n=100000, all a_i = 1 (or any small value). The weighted sums involve large powers of 2 modulo MOD.

adversarial.description: A sorted array where the optimal split point is not the median. This tests that the algorithm considers all splits.
adversarial.attack_vector: Greedy that only checks a few splits (e.g., only median) may fail.
adversarial.why_effective: The optimal split might be between 1 and 100 rather than at median. A naive algorithm that only checks splits near the middle would miss it.

adversarial.description: Large numbers close together but with large weighted difference. Tests that solution uses exact modular arithmetic, not floating point.
adversarial.attack_vector: Using double for weights leads to precision errors.
adversarial.why_effective: Double cannot represent 2^{-large} exactly, leading to small errors that compound. Modular arithmetic avoids this.

adversarial.description: Large n with n=100000 and multiple test cases summing to 100000. Tests that solution is O(n log n) not O(n^2).
adversarial.attack_vector: If solution computes weighted sums from scratch for each split, it is O(n^2) and TLE.
adversarial.why_effective: n=100000 => 10^10 operations if naive, exceeds time limit.

adversarial.description: Many test cases with large n where exponent of 2 is near n. Tests that modular exponentiation with exponent up to 1e5 is computed efficiently and correctly.
adversarial.attack_vector: Repeatedly computing pow(2, n, MOD) naively causes TLE; incorrect precomputation of powers leads to wrong answer.
adversarial.why_effective: If powers of 2 are computed from scratch for each split, cost becomes O(n^2). Precomputation of all powers in O(n) is required.

key_coverage_gaps: No pattern specifically tests n=3 (small odd n) with non-trivial optimal split.

No pattern tests multiple test cases with varying n to ensure reset of global arrays.

boundary.test_values: n=3, values=1,2,4

adversarial.description: Many duplicates of a single value under geometric progression with many ratios
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit naive iteration over ratios: for each value, iterate over possible b up to sqrt(max/min). With many duplicates, counts become large and may cause overflow if using 32-bit ints.
adversarial.why_effective: All values are same so no distinct triple, many naive implementations might accidentally count permutations of same index (i,j,k) or fail to check distinctness condition. Also, if not optimized, iterating over b for each value is unnecessary.

adversarial.description: Geometric progression with large ratio and many occurrences
adversarial.attack_vector: Target solutions that iterate over all possible b up to sqrt(MaxVal) for each element. For large values, this can be expensive if many elements are large.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solution that loops over all b from 2 to sqrt(MaxVal) for each distinct value will be too slow. Optimized solutions use divisor enumeration or frequency maps.

adversarial.description: Sequence with all identical values and one different value to test distinctness condition
adversarial.attack_vector: Misunderstanding of pairwise distinct: must have three different indices, not necessarily three different values. But condition says 'pairwise distinct' meaning values are distinct. So three indices with same value are not allowed. This pattern checks if the code incorrectly allows three same values.
adversarial.why_effective: If code counts triples like (5,5,5) even though values are not distinct, or if it counts (5,5,10) where 5 and 5 are not distinct, it will output wrong. The correct output should be 0 because there is no triple with three distinct values in geometric progression.

Test with very large frequency for a value to ensure count combination formula

adversarial.description: A path of length n=200000 so that recursive DFS causes stack overflow. Solutions must use iterative approach.
adversarial.attack_vector: Deep recursion leading to stack overflow if solution uses recursion for DP or DFS.
adversarial.why_effective: Many contestants implement recursive DFS for tree DP. Python recursion limit is ~1000, so n=200000 will cause recursion depth error. Even with sys.setrecursionlimit, memory may blow up.

adversarial.description: A tree with a long main path and many branches attached to intermediate nodes. This tests if solution correctly computes expected visits for vertices not on the s-t path.
adversarial.attack_vector: Many branches cause some solutions to incorrectly assume that only vertices on the path between s and t have non-zero expected visits.
adversarial.why_effective: Many contest solutions incorrectly assume that vertices not on the unique path from s to t have zero expected visits, but they can be visited as the chip wanders.
error_types_caught: WA for vertices off the main path

adversarial.description: Starting vertex equals target vertex, but tree has many branches. Some solutions may still try to run DP and get division by zero or incorrect initialization.
adversarial.attack_vector: Handling s==t case specially is necessary; some solutions may not handle it and produce wrong outputs or crash.
adversarial.why_effective: The expected number of visits for the starting/target vertex should be 1 (initial counter) and 0 for others. Some DP formulations that assume movement may incorrectly produce different values or divide by zero because the random walk does not start.

adversarial.description: String where multiple divisors give same minimal changes, testing deterministic selection.
adversarial.attack_vector: A solution that picks the first divisor without comparing all might output a suboptimal string or miscompute changes.
adversarial.why_effective: The string is already balanced for d=3 (each of a,b,c appears 2). Divisors of 6: 1,2,3,6. d=1 has changes 4, d=2 has changes 2 (if pick a,b), d=3 changes 0, d=6 changes 3. If algorithm checks d in increasing order and stops at first with minimal? But d=1 has 4 > d=3, so it would continue. But if it stops at first feasible d without comparing, might pick d=2 (changes 2) instead of optimal d=3. So this catches improper stopping condition.

adversarial.description: Large n with many divisors but best d is not obvious due to frequency distribution.
adversarial.attack_vector: A solution that checks divisors in arbitrary order or uses greedy selection of characters without considering divisor count may fail.
adversarial.why_effective: s has a:5, b:6, c:1. Divisors: 1,2,3,4,6,12. d=1: changes=7 (keep max b 6, change 6 to b? Actually keep b, changes=12-6=6? Wait max freq=6 (b), changes=6. d=2: need 6 each, pick b and a: keep 6 b, 5 a -> keep 11, changes=1. d=3: need 4 each, pick a,b,c: keep 4 a, 4 b, 1 c -> keep 9, changes=3. d=4: need 3 each, pick a,b,c,d: keep 3 a,3 b,1 c,0 d -> keep 7, changes=5. So best is d=2 changes=1. But if algorithm only considers divisors up to 26 but miscalculates changes, it might miss d=2. Also, if it picks characters based on count but not considering that for d=2 we need exactly 6 each, it might incorrectly keep 5 of a and 6 of b, then need one more a, so change one b to a -> changes=1, correct. So this tests correct computation of changes for each d.
error_types_caught: incorrect character selection for given d

adversarial.description: String with n=26 and s containing exactly 13 'a' and 13 'b'. Tests that d=2 (each 13) is optimal.
adversarial.attack_vector: A solution that always picks d=1 or d=n without checking all divisors might miss the best.
adversarial.why_effective: The string is already balanced for d=2. Divisors: 1,2,13,26. d=1: changes=13, d=2: changes=0, d=13: each appears 2, but we have only 2 distinct, need 13 distinct? Actually d=13 needs 13 distinct characters each appearing 2 times, so require introducing 11 new characters, changes=24, so worse. So optimal is d=2. A naive solution that always uses one character if n>26 or tries d=n first might output d=1 or d=13 which are wrong.

adversarial.description: Stress test with maximum constraints: n=100000, t=1, string with all 26 letters appearing with frequencies that make many divisors competitive.
adversarial.attack_vector: Performance test: solution must handle large n and compute minimal changes efficiently without O(n * divisors) if divisors are many (max divisors for n<=1e5 is around 128).

100000
[46% a, 20% b, 10% c, 5% each of d, e, f, rest distributed]
adversarial.why_effective: Large n with many divisors (e.g., 100000 has 36 divisors) and string with distinct counts that require careful computation. Naive O(n * 26) per divisor is fine (1e5*26*36 ≈ 93M, borderline), but if solution uses O(n * number_of_divisors * 26), it may TLE. Also, memory for storing frequencies per test case is fine.

adversarial.why_effective:
Only subsequences from [3,1] and [3] and [1]? Actually 3 (binary 11) has 2 bits, 1 has 1 bit. Subsequences without zeros: [3] (2 bits), [1] (1 bit), [3,1] (3&1=1 ->1 bit). So only [3] counts, so answer=1? Wait, recalc: elements: indices: a1=0, a2=0, a3=3 (11), a4=1 (01), a5=0. Non-empty subsequences without zeros: [3], [1], [3,1]. AND: 3 (2 bits), 1 (1 bit), 1 (1 bit). Only [3] has exactly 2 bits. So answer=1. But I said 2 above; correct to 1. Actually example output should be 1. Let me adjust: Maybe use a different set: [0,0,3,0,7] with k=2? 7 has 3 bits, 3 has 2. Then subsequences without zeros: [3] (2 bits), [7] (3 bits), [3,7] (3&7=3 ->2 bits). So count=2. That works. I'll use that. So example_input: 1
5 2
0 0 3 0 7. Output: 2.

adversarial.description: Mixed queries that require careful handling of the condition p[x] > x when the permutation is reversed or shifted by large amounts.
adversarial.attack_vector: When reversing, the condition p[x] > x changes to something like new_pos[x] = n+1 - old_pos[x]? Actually reversal of array means new a_i = old a_{n+1-i}. So positions change. The answer counting must be recomputed efficiently. A bug could be using the same comparison p[x] > x after reversal without updating positions.
adversarial.why_effective:
The reversal changes the relationship between numbers and positions. A common mistake is to treat reversal as just a flip of indices without considering the effect on the condition p[x] > x. The example starts with [4,2,3,1]: p[1]=4>1, p[2]=2<=2, p[3]=3<=3, p[4]=1<=4 => count 1? Actually p[4]=1<=4, so count=1 (only number 1). But initial answer? Wait check: initially a=[4,2,3,1]. So positions: 1 is at cell4, 2 at cell2, 3 at cell3, 4 at cell1. So p[x]: p[1]=4>1 ->1, p[2]=2<=2, p[3]=3<=3, p[4]=1<=4 -> count=1. Output first line? The problem asks to output before each query, so first number is initial answer. Then after first query (reverse), we get new a=[1,3,2,4]. Then p[1]=1<=1, p[2]=3>2, p[3]=2<=3, p[4]=4<=4 -> count=1. Then shift left by 2: from [1,3,2,4] left 2 -> [2,4,1,3]. p[1]=3>1, p[2]=1<=2, p[3]=4>3, p[4]=2<=4 -> count=2. Then reverse: from [2,4,1,3] reverse -> [3,1,4,2]. p[1]=2>1, p[2]=4>2, p[3]=1<=3, p[4]=3<=4 -> count=2. Then shift right by 1: from [3,1,4,2] right 1 -> [2,3,1,4]. p[1]=3>1, p[2]=1<=2, p[3]=2<=3, p[4]=4<=4 -> count=1. So expected output: 1 (initial), then after reverse: 1, after shift left: 2, after reverse: 2, after shift right: 1. So total 5 numbers. But the problem says output q+1 numbers, here q=4 so 5 numbers. Example output in pattern: I'll put deduced: 1
1
2
2
1

adversarial.description: Mimic changes type every stage to a type that appears multiple times, making frequency changes subtle. This exploits algorithms that only look for types that appear exactly once or that increase in frequency.
adversarial.attack_vector: Mimic always changes to a type that currently has the highest frequency, so frequency differences are small and spread across multiple types.
adversarial.example_output: Correct detection involves tracking positions carefully. A naive solution might guess incorrectly. Expected interaction: remove all of type 1 first (since it's unique), then track changes.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive frequency-only algorithms often assume mimic's type changes cause a unique signature (e.g., a type appears or disappears). When mimic chooses a common type, multiple types change frequency simultaneously, causing confusion.

adversarial.description: Mimic stays the same type for two consecutive stages, then changes. This tests compliance with the 'cannot stay same type for more than two stages' rule and checks if algorithm incorrectly assumes mimic changes every stage.
adversarial.attack_vector: Mimic delays change to mislead algorithms that expect immediate frequency shifts.
adversarial.example_output: Algorithm might remove a type expecting mimic to change, but mimic stays, causing eventual misidentification. Correct approach: after first removal, if no frequency change, the mimic might be holding. Then second stage, remove again to force change.
adversarial.why_effective: Some algorithms assume mimic changes after every removal, so they only consider types that changed. If mimic doesn't change, they might miss it or guess too early.

adversarial.description: Permutation with cnt exactly 2 but from same residue class (should be impossible, but if algorithm incorrectly outputs 1)
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit misunderstanding that swapping two misplaced elements always fixes if cnt==2. Actually, if two positions i and j have same residue mod k and both elements are misplaced such that each element's correct residue is not the other's position residue, then swapping may not fix. But can that happen? Let's try to construct. Suppose k=2, n=4. Positions: 1,2,3,4. Residues: 0,1,0,1. Suppose we have elements: at pos1: value2 (residue1), at pos2: value1 (residue0). Then both positions have wrong residues: pos1 should have residue0 but has residue1; pos2 should have residue1 but has residue0. So cnt=2. Swapping pos1 and pos2: after swap, pos1 gets value1 (residue0) correct, pos2 gets value2 (residue1) correct. So it works. Actually they are from different residues? pos1 residue0, pos2 residue1. So different. To have same residue, both positions must have same residue, say both residue0. Then positions 1 and 3. Suppose at pos1: value3 (residue? 3->2 mod2=0, so residue0 correct?) Actually need both wrong. Let pos1: value2 (residue1) should be residue0, wrong. pos3: value4 (residue1) should be residue0, wrong. Both have same incorrect residue? Actually both have current elements with residue1, but positions require residue0. So cnt=2. Swap pos1 and pos3: after swap, pos1 gets value4 (residue1) still wrong, pos3 gets value2 (residue1) still wrong. So swapping does not fix. But does this case have cnt=2? Yes. So output should be -1, not 1. A naive algorithm that outputs 1 whenever cnt==2 would be wrong. So this pattern catches that.
adversarial.why_effective: Standard solution checks cnt but also that the two misplaced positions have residues that correspond to each other's elements. This example has cnt=2 but the swap doesn't fix both because both misplaced positions have same residue. Naive algorithm that outputs 1 whenever cnt==2 fails.

So cnt=0, but the permutation is completely reversed in blocks. A naive algorithm that checks if permutation is sorted or something might output 1 or -1.

adversarial.why_effective: If solution uses DSU, it might need to process each component separately. With 100000 components, overhead per component can add up. Also, if solution uses BFS/DFS from each unvisited node, it will start 100000 BFS, each with small work but constant overhead.

adversarial.why_effective: Cycle sum is 1+1+1+1-5 = -1 !=0. Naive algorithm might use floating point or incorrectly compute sums due to direction reversal.

adversarial.description: Large coordinates and many test cases to trigger 32-bit integer overflow in languages without automatic 64-bit promotion.

adversarial.description: Case where the missing prefix sum is at the beginning, leading to differences that are exactly the permutation (no duplicate). Some naive solutions may assume there must be a duplicate.
adversarial.attack_vector: missing first element: the first difference (a1) is missing, but the computed differences from 0 and S give exactly 1..n. Solutions that always expect a duplicate will fail.
adversarial.why_effective: Many incorrect solutions first compute differences and look for a duplicate; in this case there is no duplicate (differences are 1,2,3 all distinct). They may incorrectly try to find a sum and fail.
error_types_caught: Assuming always a duplicate in differences
Not handling missing first or last element

adversarial.description: Case where the duplicate difference is exactly equal to a number that is also present as a single difference, causing confusion if the algorithm doesn't track multiplicities properly.
adversarial.attack_vector: The combined difference equals one of the other single differences, leading to two copies of that number. Example: permutation [2,3,1] prefix sums [2,5,6]. Missing middle (p[2]=5) gives b=[2,6]. Differences: 0->2=2, 2->6=4, 6->S=6? Wait S=6, so last diff 0? Actually S=6, so differences: 2,4,0? Not correct. Let's construct carefully. Let permutation [1,4,2,3]? Actually we need a duplicate that equals a single number. Let n=4, permutation [1,2,3,4] prefix sums [1,3,6,10]. Missing p[2]=3 gives b=[1,6,10]. Differences: 0->1=1, 1->6=5, 6->10=4, 10->S=10? S=10, last diff 0? Wait S=10, so last diff = 10-10=0, which is invalid. Need a better example. Let's pick n=5, permutation [1,2,3,4,5] prefix sums [1,3,6,10,15]. Missing p[3]=6 gives b=[1,3,10,15]. Differences: 0->1=1, 1->3=2, 3->10=7, 10->15=5, 15->S=15? S=15, last diff 0. So we have differences 1,2,7,5,0 - not a permutation. We need the combined difference to be a number already present. Let's try permutation [2,4,1,3]? But we need to ensure total sum S=10 for n=4. Permutation [2,4,1,3] sums to 10. Prefix sums: [2,6,7,10]. Missing p[2]=6 gives b=[2,7,10]. Differences: 0->2=2, 2->7=5, 7->10=3, 10->10=0. So differences {2,5,3,0} missing 1 and 4. Not a duplicate. Actually we want a duplicate: the combined diff is, say, 4, and also a single diff is 4. That would require an overlap. Let's solve: Suppose we have difference set from valid prefix sums: {a,b,c,d} permutation of 1..4. After removal, we get differences: a, b+c, d (if missing middle). So we want one of a, d equal to b+c. Example: a=4, b+c=4? That would mean b=1, c=3 or b=2, c=2, but b,c must be distinct? Actually b and c are distinct because they are from permutation. So b=1,c=3 gives b+c=4. Then a=4, d=2? Then set would be {4,4,2} not all distinct. So duplicate of 4. So permutation: a=4, b=1, c=3, d=2 => permutation [4,1,3,2] sums to 10. Prefix sums: [4,5,8,10]. Missing middle p[2]=5 gives b=[4,8,10]. Differences: 0->4=4, 4->8=4, 8->10=2, 10->10=0. So differences {4,4,2,0} with duplicate 4 and missing 1,3. So this is adversarial: the duplicate is 4 which is also a single difference. A naive solution might try to find the missing number as the difference between the duplicate and some other number, but may not handle duplicate correctly.
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions that simply check if the set of differences (excluding the last diff from last received to S) is a permutation of 1..n may miss the duplicate because they might not include the final diff correctly. Also, when they see duplicate, they might incorrectly assume the missing number is the one that appears with count 0, but here the missing numbers are 1 and 3, so the sum of duplicate 4? Actually the missing numbers are 1 and 3, and the combined diff 4 is the sum of 1 and 3. So the algorithm needs to check if the duplicate can be split into two missing numbers.
error_types_caught: Incorrect handling of duplicate and missing set
Assuming duplicate is always the sum of two numbers that include the missing number but not considering both missing numbers
Not verifying that the two numbers sum to the duplicate

boundary.description: No toggle events; all events are type 1. The elevators start on and remain on (no toggles). Test basic DP without state changes.
boundary.test_values: Q >= 1, all events type 1. N=10, C_i random. Elevators both on always.

boundary.description: Only type 2 events (toggles) and no persons. Since no persons need service, no elevator movement is required, so answer should be 0. Tests that the solution handles zero-service days correctly.
boundary.test_values: Q >= 1, all events type 2, with toggles that keep at least one elevator on always. N arbitrary.
error_types_caught: incorrectly moving elevators on non-service days

adversarial.description: Frequent toggles that change elevator availability. The naive solution that ignores toggles or replans every toggle will be suboptimal or wrong.
adversarial.attack_vector: The optimal strategy requires knowing future toggles to decide when to move which elevator. Frequent toggles force careful DP.
adversarial.why_effective: If the solution does not account for toggles properly, it may use an elevator that is off at that day, or fail to pre-position an elevator before a toggle disables it.

adversarial.description: C_i alternates between very high and very low values. Optimal moves should be done on low-cost days, but toggles might prevent that. Tests ability to schedule movements on cheap days.
adversarial.attack_vector: The greedy solution that moves on the day of service may overpay. Optimal is to move on the cheapest day before the service.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution might move the elevator on the service day (cost 1000) instead of on a previous cheap day (cost 1). The output 1502 is computed by optimal: move elevator 1 on day 2 (cost 1) from floor 1 to 500 (500*1=500), then serve first person on day 3? Actually day 1 is first event? Need exact. This pattern forces dynamic programming with time-dependent costs.

adversarial.description: One elevator is always off after initial toggles, so only one elevator is usable for all service days. Simplifies DP but tests that solution correctly handles the case where the other elevator is never available.
adversarial.attack_vector: If the solution assumes both elevators are always usable, it may make incorrect moves.
adversarial.why_effective: After first toggle (2 2), elevator 2 is off for day 1? Actually toggle happens at start of day. So on day 2 (first type1), only elevator1 is on. On day 3, both on? But then toggle 2 1 turns off elevator1? Wait need careful. This pattern tests that solution correctly updates state.

key_coverage_gaps: High Q with all type1 events and varying C_i
Large N with many toggles close together
N=2 (minimum non-trivial)

boundary.description: Minimum n (n=1) with k around the only possible comparison value (1).

error_types_caught: Misunderstanding that comparisons for n=1 is 1 (not 0)

boundary.description: Maximum n (2000) with k at extremes: k=1, k=n*(n+1)/2 (max), k=max+1 (0). Also k=1e9 > max.
boundary.test_values: n=2000, k=1 (should output 2000! mod MOD); n=2000, k=2001000 (max, output count of permutations achieving max comparisons, which is 1); n=2000, k=2001001 (output 0); n=2000, k=1000000000 (output 0).
error_types_caught: Summation of DP from k to max (should handle k very large)

boundary.description: Moderate n with k at boundary where number of permutations with >=k is zero or almost all.

adversarial.description: Test with n moderately large and k just below the maximum to catch off-by-one errors in DP transition for maximum comparisons.
adversarial.attack_vector: The number of permutations with exactly max comparisons is 1 (the sorted array? For first pivot, max comparisons is when array is decreasing? Let's assume it's 1 permutation. So k = max-1 should be close to max. This tests the sum over a narrow range.

adversarial.description: Test with n=2000 and k=1e6 (moderate but large enough to cause integer overflow if not using modulo correctly in intermediate steps).
adversarial.attack_vector: Many solutions use combinatorial DP that multiplies large numbers (like factorials and binomial coefficients). Without proper modulo at each step, overflow can occur. This test checks that intermediate multiplications are done modulo MOD.
adversarial.why_effective: The answer might be 0 because k is less than max?? Wait, for n=2000, max comparisons = 2001000, so k=1e6 is still less than max, so answer is non-zero (since many permutations have comparisons >=1e6). Actually answer is non-zero. So this tests that large combinatorial numbers are computed correctly modulo.

adversarial.description: Test with n even and odd to catch errors in recurrence symmetry or parity handling.
adversarial.attack_vector: The DP might have different behavior for odd/even sizes. Test n=3,4,5,6 with k values that produce results that can be verified by brute force.
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions that assume symmetry without proper combinatorial factors may miscount permutations.
error_types_caught: Incorrect combinatorial factor for left/right subtree sizes

adversarial.attack_vector: If binary search upper bound is not large enough, might miss feasible T. Also DP might overflow if sum is large.

adversarial.description: String with first character ')' or last character '(' after some queries
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solutions may not recheck the first and last characters after each query, or may incorrectly think they can still be walkable.
adversarial.why_effective: After first query flip position 4 (from ')' to '('), the last character becomes '(', so answer should be NO. After second query flip position 1 (from ')' to '('), the string becomes "()()", first char '(' and last char '('? Actually after two flips: string becomes "((()", first char '(', last char '(', still NO. After third query flip position 2 (from '(' to ')'), string becomes "()()", first char '(', last char ')', so walkable. Naive solutions that only check once will fail.

adversarial.description: Large number of queries flipping the same index repeatedly
adversarial.attack_vector: Inefficient data structures that do not update quickly or cause O(q log n) to become O(q n) due to repeated flips on same index.
adversarial.why_effective: If the solution recomputes from scratch on each query, it will be O(q n) = 2e5 * 1e5 = 2e10, causing TLE. Efficient updates are needed.

key_coverage_gaps: Tests with alternating flips that change the pattern drastically

boundary.description: Decreasing a_i: expensive at start, cheap at end. Tests whether algorithm chooses the rightmost cheapest operation to maximize all positions.
boundary.test_values: n=5, a=[5,4,3,2,1], k=10. Should use operation i=5 10 times, giving all 10s.
error_types_caught: greedy from left using original costs

adversarial.description: Decreasing costs with large gap between first and later costs. Exploits naive greedy that picks the first cheap operation (leftmost) instead of rightmost cheapest.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive algorithm may stop at the first minimum (index 2) and not realize later index (4) with same cost gives better lexicographic result.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive left-to-right greedy using prefix minima might compute that cost for index 2 is 1, use it as many times as possible (100 times), resulting in [100,100,0,0], which is lexicographically smaller than the optimal [100,100,100,100].
error_types_caught: failure to propagate operations to later indices

adversarial.description: Non-monotonic costs with multiple minima. Exploits algorithm that does not use suffix minima correctly.
adversarial.attack_vector: Algorithm might choose the leftmost minimal cost (index 3) instead of the rightmost minimal cost (index 7) when costs are equal, leading to suboptimal lexicographic array.
adversarial.why_effective: Self-minimum: suffix minima gives 1 at positions 3 and 7. The optimal uses the rightmost (index 7) to increment all positions. A solution that only considers the first occurrence of the minimum (index 3) would increment only first 3 positions, yielding a smaller array.

adversarial.description: Large k with extremely small a_i, testing overflow in calculations like k * (something) or very large numbers looping many times.
adversarial.attack_vector: If algorithm tries to simulate operations one by one (e.g., while k >= min_cost), it will TLE. Also, if it uses integer division, it might overflow if using 32-bit ints.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive simulation of each operation would require 1e9 iterations. Also, if algorithm uses 32-bit ints, k*(count) may overflow.
error_types_caught: TLE due to loop over k

key_coverage_gaps: Very large a_i values not tested (e.g., a_i up to 1e9+ with small k)

But applying each reversal naively would result in different string due to order of reversals (reversals are not idempotent individually, but the net effect is same as one? Doing it three times: 1st: positions 3-5 reversed; 2nd: same positions reversed again -> back to original; 3rd: reversed again -> same as after first reversal. So net effect is one reversal. But if someone processes queries one by one without parity, they might reverse three times sequentially and still get correct result? But if they implement correctly by actually reversing, it's fine but slow. The parity trick would count mod 2. So this pattern tests that parity-based solution gives same result as naive. But 'adversarial' should target wrong solutions. A wrong solution might incorrectly accumulate parity in a way that changes order? Let's think of a scenario: different x values that affect overlapping pairs? Actually due to partition, reversals only affect within one interval, and intervals are disjoint. So different queries in same interval can affect overlapping segments. Counting parity per position works because the transformation is a composition of involutions. So a solution that does not account for which side (left/right) of the segment each character ends up might be wrong. For example, if for a given interval, multiple queries with different x can cause the net effect to be a permutation that is not simply the identity? But the parity approach counts for each pair (i, j) whether the number of times it's flipped is odd. That is correct because each reversal swaps positions i and j. So for each symmetric pair, the net effect is either swap (if odd) or no swap (if even). So parity counting works. An adversarial case might be where a solution incorrectly assumes that reversals commute and just toggles a flag for the whole interval, but then applies reversals in a different order? Actually the parity approach is standard for this problem. So to catch WA, we need a case where the naive reversal approach (applying each reversal sequentially) and the parity approach differ? They should produce same result. So adversarial should target specific implementation mistakes, like off-by-one in computing a and b, or using wrong interval center, etc. Let's create a pattern with many different x values that cause overlapping reversals within an interval to test that the parity computation is correct and not skipping any pair.

n=2 with one large prime and one small number
Test cases where product is an n-th power but individual numbers have exponents not divisible by n

boundary.test_values: n=1000, q=100, all d_i = 2 (min) or all d_i = n-1 (max). Also test all d_i = k for some fixed k.
