adversarial.description: Alternating extreme distances to force back-and-forth operations
adversarial.attack_vector: Forces many operations in alternating directions, testing time and correctness of movement logic.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might recompute distances each time or not handle reversal correctly, causing incorrect distances or extra operations.

adversarial.description: All days require same distance, starting from initial tree that does not match, then no further changes
adversarial.attack_vector: Tests that after first operation, subsequent days are correctly handled with no operation.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution incorrectly thinks it needs to output operation every day or miscomputes when distance matches, it will output extra operations.

adversarial.description: Large tree with many days where d_i equals the distance between the two leaves after the previous operation (so no change needed)
adversarial.attack_vector: Tests that the solution correctly identifies no operation needed after many days, preventing unnecessary operations.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution always performs an operation regardless of current distance, it will violate the 'no more than one operation per day' rule or produce invalid output.

key_coverage_gaps: Test cases with n=2 (though impossible with d>=2) - skip
Test cases with very large q and n but random d_i
Test cases with d_i equal to n-1 repeatedly
Test cases where initial tree is not a simple path (alternative structure) - might reveal bugs in solutions that assume path
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: At least 10 test cases covering random (2), boundary (3), adversarial (3), plus additional to cover gaps

random.description: Moderate-sized test with a mix of values including 1 and 2, and other values, to verify general correctness.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n between 10 and 100, pick values from 1 to 1000 randomly, ensure at least one 1 and one 2 appear.
error_types_caught: using int instead of long long

random.description: Large test case with many repeated values to stress test performance and check overflow in counting.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n close to 200000, pick values from 1 to 10^9, with many repetitions (e.g., 10-20 distinct values repeated many times).
error_types_caught: time limit exceeded due to O(n^2) brute-force

boundary.description: Minimum length n=1, answer should be 0.
boundary.test_values: n=1, a_i any value (e.g., 5).
error_types_caught: assuming at least one pair exists

boundary.description: All elements equal to max value 10^9, no 1 or 2, only equal pairs. Large n to test large answer.
All elements 1, maximizing equal pairs for smallest value.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, all ones.
error_types_caught: treating 1 specially in cross pairs but missing pairs of 1 with 1

boundary.description: Mix only of 1 and 2, with large counts, to test cross pair counting.

adversarial.description: Many 1 and 2 values interspersed with many other repeating values to test hash map collision handling and correctness of special case logic.
adversarial.attack_vector: Use a large number of distinct values that are not 1 or 2 but have same frequency, combined with many 1s and 2s.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions may incorrectly count cross pairs if they confuse frequencies or use global conditions for all values.

adversarial.description: Alternating 1 and 2 to ensure pairs are counted correctly for both equal and cross types.
adversarial.attack_vector: Test that (1,2) pairs are counted only once per distinct i<j.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive approach might count each pair twice or miss some; correct answer: equal pairs: two 1's (1 pair) + two 2's (1 pair) + cross pairs: (1,2) from first 1 with both 2's (2 pairs) + second 1 with the first 2? Actually careful: indices: a1=1, a2=2, a3=1, a4=2. Pairs: (1,2): 1 and 2 -> cross, (1,3): both 1 -> equal, (1,4): 1 and 2 -> cross, (2,3): 2 and 1 -> cross, (2,4): both 2 -> equal, (3,4): 1 and 2 -> cross. That's 1+1+4=6? Wait count: equal: (1,3) and (2,4) → 2 pairs. Cross: (1,2), (1,4), (2,3), (3,4) → 4 pairs. Total 6. My previous output was wrong; correct is 6. So example input should yield 6.

adversarial.description: Large values (e.g., 10^9) without 1 or 2, repeated many times, to test that solution does not attempt to compute 2^a for large a.
adversarial.attack_vector: If solution computes 2^{a_i} modulo something, it may overflow or get wrong answer. Since condition simplifies, correct solution should not compute powers.
adversarial.why_effective: A solution that tries to compute 2^10^9 will overflow even 64-bit; the correct logic only checks equality or (1,2) pairs, so this tests that simplification is used.

adversarial.description: Many distinct small values (e.g., 1..1000) each repeated a few times, to test frequency map performance and correctness of equal pair counting for non-special values.
adversarial.attack_vector: Large number of distinct keys in hash map to test memory and hashing.
adversarial.why_effective: A solution using an array indexed by value would be too large since a_i up to 1e9; must use hash map. This pattern tests hash map performance.
error_types_caught: using array instead of hash map

key_coverage_gaps: Very large test with many distinct values (close to 200k unique values) might cause TLE if hash map is slow; but sum n is 200k so it's fine.
Test with value 2 only? Already covered by boundary_4 but with 1s. Could add pure 2s. But boundary_2 covers all same value.

random.description: Small random test cases (n between 1 and 10) for correctness verification against brute-force enumeration of all start indices and worst-case orders.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random n ∈ [1,10], random a_i ∈ [1,100]. For each test, compute answer by brute force: for each start s, compute required P = max( max_{i≤s} (a_i + n-i), max_{i≥s} (a_i + i-1) ), take min over s. Output answer.

random.description: Large random test case (n=200000) with a_i up to 1e9, to stress test O(n) solution performance and binary search (if used).
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=200000, a_i random in [1, 1e9]. Compute answer using O(n) prefix and suffix maxima.
error_types_caught: time limit exceed due to O(n^2) solution

boundary.description: Single monster (n=1). The spell hits exactly once, so P must equal a_1.
Two monsters with extreme health values: one minimal (1) and one maximal (1e9). Tests scenario where optimal start index is the high-health monster.
error_types_caught: wrong assumption that starting at low-health monster gives lower P
off-by-one in turn count for edge sides

boundary.description: Maximum n with all identical health values (e.g., all 5). Tests that the algorithm correctly computes P = max(a_i) + (n-1) / something? Actually for identical health, the required P from formula: for any s, L(s)=5+n-i minimized at i=n? But careful: For identical, the answer should be 5 + (n-1) because worst-case order will hit one monster last taking n turns. Specifically, if all equal to h, then required P = h + (n-1). Check with n=5: h=4 -> answer 8 as example. So n=300000, h=5 -> answer = 5+299999 = 300004.
boundary.test_values: n=300000, a=[5] repeated 300000 times
error_types_caught: overlooking that worst-case turn introduces n-1 extra damage
incorrect handling of large n in prefix/suffix computations

boundary.description: Strictly increasing health values: a_i = i. Tests that the algorithm correctly handles monotonicity and that optimal start is near the high-health end.
error_types_caught: miscomputing prefix/suffix maxima due to off-by-one

adversarial.description: Adversarial sequence that forces the binary search (if used) to check many values near boundary. Specifically, a sequence where the answer is exactly the maximum a_i + (n-1) scenario, making naive greedy wrong.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that assume the optimal start is always at the maximum health monster; such solutions may underestimate needed P.
adversarial.example_output: 7 (since optimal start at middle? Check: s=2: L(s)=max_{i≤2} (a_i+3-i): i=1:5+2=7, i=2:1+1=2 => L=7; R(s)=max_{i≥2} (a_i+i-1): i=2:1+1=2, i=3:5+2=7 => R=7; required P=7. If start at 1: L= max(5+2,1+1,5+? Actually i≤1 only i=1:5+2=7; R= max_{i≥1} (a_i+i-1): i=1:5+0=5, i=2:1+1=2, i=3:5+2=7 => P=7. Similarly start at 3 gives 7. So answer 7. Naive may think max health 5 but needs 7.)
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution might choose start at monster with max health and set P = max health + something too small, missing that other monsters due to turn order require higher P.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect start selection
WA due to underestimating turn penalties

adversarial.description: Large n with alternating high and low health to test that the prefix/suffix maxima are computed correctly and that the answer is not simply the maximum of all a_i + (n-1).
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that incorrectly model the worst-case turn as always (n-i+1) or i, without considering that the adversary chooses direction to maximize overall requirement.
adversarial.why_effective: The pattern forces the answer to be determined by the high-health monsters near the ends, which are delayed heavily in worst-case order. Naive solutions might underestimate.
error_types_caught: WA due to missing that monsters at both ends can be hit last
WA due to incorrect computation of worst-case turn for ends

key_coverage_gaps: n=0 (not allowed, min 1)
extremely large n=300000 with all a_i=1
n=2 with a1=1e9, a2=1 (symmetric to bound_2)

random.description: Small random directed graph with n <= 6, m <= 10, random a_i. Good for verification against brute force.

random.description: Large random graph with n=5000, m=20000, a_i random up to 1e9. Stress test for performance and correctness.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=5000, m=20000 by randomly selecting directed pairs without self-loops. a_i random [1,1e9].

boundary.description: Single vertex, no edges. Minimum n=1.
Large isolated vertices (n=200000, m=0). Longest path is single vertex with minimum a_i.

adversarial.description: Large strongly connected component (cycle covering all n vertices). Tests SCC size and sum calculation.
adversarial.attack_vector: If solution does not properly identify SCC, it may think path cannot include all vertices.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might not handle SCC condensation and miss that all vertices can be visited in one path.

adversarial.attack_vector: If DP only considers length and not also sum, might pick larger sum path.
adversarial.why_effective: Forces DP to correctly minimize sum when lengths tie.

adversarial.description: Mixed SCC sizes and a DAG path through them. Tests size/sum accumulation across condensation levels.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive approach may incorrectly accumulate sizes or sums.
adversarial.why_effective: Tests that SCC sizes are summed and values summed correctly across multi-level condensation.

adversarial.attack_vector: If solution uses 32-bit integers, sum will overflow.
adversarial.why_effective: Many contestants might use int instead of long long.

boundary.test_values: n=4, a=[1, -2, 2, 1] as in example? Actually example 1 of problem: Output 2? Let's check problem statement: Example test case 1: 4 1 -2 2 1 edges: 1-2,3-2,2-4. Output is 2. not handling compression removing center when two leaves kept

adversarial.description: Path graph with alternating large positive and negative values, testing optimal deletion decisions before compression.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive algorithms that compress first without deletions may miss better sum.
adversarial.why_effective: If the algorithm only considers compression without prior deletions, it would keep vertices 1 and 4 (after compressing 2 and 3) and get sum -900. But optimal is to delete vertex 4 first, then compress, keeping 1 and 3 with sum 200. This tests that deletions are performed before compression and that the order can affect outcome.
error_types_caught: incorrect dp state that doesn't allow deleting leaves

adversarial.description: Star tree with center and three leaves, all leaves have large positive values, center negative. Best to keep all three leaves after compression removes center.
adversarial.attack_vector: Algorithms that cannot handle degree > 2 in final tree; or incorrectly assume only up to 2 children can be kept.
adversarial.why_effective: The optimal is to keep all three leaves; compression removes the center (degree 3? Actually center has degree 3, not 2, so compression does NOT remove it. Wait: compression only removes vertices with exactly 2 incident edges. Center has degree 3, so it remains. Final tree is a star with center and three leaves. Sum = -1+10+10+10=29. But if we delete the center first? Center has degree 3, cannot delete because operation only removes vertices with degree ≤1. So we cannot delete center. So we are stuck with center. So best might be to delete leaves? But leaves are positive. So sum is 29. Alternatively, we could delete two leaves? Then center degree 1, leaf degree 1, compression nothing, sum = -1+10=9. So keep all three gives 29. So expected output 29. Actually we can compress after deletions? If we delete no vertices, compression does nothing (center degree 3). So answer 29. But if we want to test multiple children, we need a different example: center positive, leaves positive? Then keeping all gives high sum. But compression removes only degree 2 vertices. So for center to be removed by compression, center must have degree exactly 2. So we need a node with exactly two neighbors after deletions. Example: star with two leaves: center degree 2 after deletions? Initially center has degree 2? Actually star with two leaves: center degree 2, leaves degree 1. If no deletions, compression removes center (deg2) and connects the two leaves resulting in an edge between them. So final vertices: two leaves. Sum = leaf1+leaf2. So if center is negative and leaves positive, you want to compress. If center is positive, you might want to delete a leaf to make center degree 1? But then compression doesn't remove center. So the optimal is to either keep all (if center positive) or compress (if center negative). So let's make both leaves positive and center negative. Then best is to compress, getting sum of leaves. Example: n=3, star 1-2, 2-3? Actually star with center 2, leaves 1 and 3. a = [10, -5, 10]. Expected output: after compression, remove center (deg2), leaves become adjacent? Actually compression: remove vertex 2, connect 1 and 3, result is an edge between 1 and 3, both kept, sum=20. So answer 20. This tests that algorithm correctly handles compression that removes a node with degree 2. But we already have that in path examples. To test multiple children, we need a node with more than 2 children, but compression only removes deg2 vertices, so nodes with degree >2 are not compressed. So the tricky part is when a node has exactly 2 neighbors after deletions. So we can design a tree where a node initially has degree >2, but after deleting some of its children, its degree becomes 2, then compression may remove it. That tests DP that considers which children to delete. For example, a node with 3 children, but we delete one, making node degree 2, then during compression node gets removed, connecting the remaining two children. So we can choose to remove the node by compression if beneficial. So adversarial: node u with 3 leaves, values: u= -10, leaves=5,5,5. Option1: keep all 4 nodes: sum -10+15=5. Option2: delete one leaf (deg1 -> can be removed), then u has degree 2 (two leaves left), then compress: u removed, two leaves become adjacent, final sum = 5+5=10. Option3: delete two leaves: then u degree 1, compress doesn't remove u, sum = -10+5 = -5. So best is 10. This tests that algorithm considers deleting a leaf to make node degree 2 for compression. So add this adversarial pattern.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of node degree and compression
not considering deletion to enable compression

adversarial.description: Tree that is a long path (n large, e.g., 200000) to test recursion depth limits and stack overflow.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions using recursion for tree DP may exceed recursion limit (default 1000) or cause stack overflow.
adversarial.example_input:
1
200000
(200000 values: alternating 1 and -1)
(199999 edges: i i+1)
adversarial.example_output: expected output: For long path with alternating 1 and -1, optimal might be to delete all negative vertices? Actually need to compute. But we can set values to all positive to make answer sum of all? If all positive, compression will remove internal vertices? Let's compute: path of positive values, a_i = 1 for all. Compression: repeatedly remove degree-2 vertices, which are all internal nodes, leaving only the two endpoints. So sum = 2. But deletions can remove leaves? If we delete one leaf, path becomes shorter. Eventually we can keep only one vertex? Actually if we want to maximize sum, we might keep all vertices initially: sum = n. But after compression, only two vertices remain. So sum is 2. If we delete all vertices except a single vertex, we get 1. So best is 2. So with all positive, answer is 2 for n>1. If we alternate 1 and -1, answer might be higher. For simplicity, we can set a_i=1 for all to get known output 2. So adversarial pattern with long path and all 1: output 2. This tests recursion and time.
adversarial.why_effective: Deep recursion in DFS will cause stack overflow if not using iterative stack or increasing recursion limit. Also, if DP requires visiting nodes in a certain order, path depth may cause performance issues if not O(n).
error_types_caught: time limit due to inefficient traversal

key_coverage_gaps: missing: tests with large number of test cases (t up to 10000) but small n each

missing: tests where optimal involves keeping a node with degree 2 in final tree? Actually final tree has no degree-2 vertices, so not applicable.

random.description: Small random test cases with n up to 10 and random a_i values within [0, 2^30-1]. Used for verifying correctness of solution logic against brute force.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate n between 1 and 10, then randomly generate n integers in [0, 2^30-1]. Compute answer using brute force O(n^2) and compare.

random.description: Large random test cases with n up to 300000 and random a_i values to stress test time and memory efficiency.
random.generation_strategy: Set n = 300000, generate each a_i uniformly random in [0, 2^30-1]. Compute expected output via efficient solution.

boundary.description: Minimum size n=1. Only one subarray. Tests handling of single element.
boundary.test_values: n=1, a_1 = 0 or large number

boundary.description: All elements are zero. XOR of any subarray is 0, so answer is 0. Tests correct handling of zero XOR contributions.
boundary.test_values: n up to 300000, all a_i = 0
error_types_caught: incorrect assumption that XOR of zeros is non-zero
errors in prefix XOR initial state

boundary.description: All elements are max value 2^30-1 (i.e., all bits set). Prefix XORs alternate. Tests handling of large numbers and per-bit computation.

adversarial.description: Array where bits alternate to maximize number of prefix XOR changes, causing many contributions per bit. Exploits solutions that recompute per bit too often.
adversarial.attack_vector: Elements such that each bit toggles frequently, e.g., alternating between 0 and 2^k for each bit. This creates many subarrays where XOR contributes, increasing computation.
adversarial.why_effective: For each bit, the prefix XOR flips on every element, leading to many contributions that naive O(n^2 * bit) solutions must process. Efficient O(n*bit) solutions handle well, but poor implementations may double count or miss contributions.

adversarial.description: Large n with a_i = 2^30-1. Each prefix XOR alternates between 0 and max value. Tests handling of many subarrays with large XOR values. May cause integer overflow in intermediate products.
adversarial.attack_vector: n=300000, all a_i = 2^30-1. The answer involves large numbers, potential overflow if not using 64-bit or modulo carefully.
adversarial.why_effective: Sum of lengths multiplied by XOR values can be huge (about n^2 * 2^30). Without proper modulo handling, integer overflow occurs. Also, per-bit contributions sum up to large numbers.

adversarial.description: Array such that prefix XOR increases monotonically (e.g., a_i = 2^{i mod 30}). This causes many subarrays with non-zero XOR for each bit individually. Tests handling of cumulative counting with many changes.
adversarial.attack_vector: Elements that cause prefix XOR to have many different values, leading to many transitions in bit occurrences.
adversarial.why_effective: Each bit appears independently, so per-bit contributions must be correctly aggregated. Naive solutions may confuse when XOR flips.

key_coverage_gaps: Mixed large and small values
Case where some bits are always 0 or always 1
n=300000 with random values

random.description: Small random test case with n up to 10, strings of length 1-5, digits 0-9. Useful for verifying correctness of brute force or basic algorithm.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n between 1 and 10. For each i, generate a random string of random length 1-5 using random digits 0-9. Then compute expected output using exhaustive enumeration.

random.description: Medium random test case with n up to 10, strings of varied lengths, including some cross-pair lucky tickets. Useful for testing directional counting and sum logic.
random.generation_strategy: Choose n=3 or 4, create strings such that some concatenations are lucky in one order only, and some are lucky in both. Compute expected output by brute force.

boundary.description: Minimum n (n=1). Only pair (1,1) exists. Should always output 1 regardless of string content.
boundary.test_values: n=1, string of length 5 (max length) with digits 9. Output must be 1.

boundary.description: Maximum n (200000) but with all strings identical and of maximum length 5. All ordered pairs are lucky (output = n^2). Tests overflow and time efficiency.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, each string = '99999'. Expected output = 40000000000 (fits in 64-bit).

adversarial.description: Two strings of different lengths (1 and 3) where only one concatenation order yields a lucky ticket. Tests if algorithm correctly evaluates both orders (i,j) and (j,i) separately.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits common mistake of ignoring one order or assuming symmetry between i and j.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive algorithms might only check (i,j) and not (j,i), or might incorrectly assume that if (i,j) is lucky then (j,i) is also lucky. This test ensures both directions are considered independently.

adversarial.description: Large n (200000) of identical strings of length 5 with digit sum 0 (e.g., '00000'). All ordered pairs are lucky, output = n^2. Forces algorithm to use combinatorics (count pairs by group) rather than iterating over all pairs. Also tests 64-bit integer overflow.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits naive O(n^2) vector iteration and 32-bit integer storage.
adversarial.why_effective: Without grouping by length and sum, O(n^2) is too slow. Using 32-bit int for n=200000 causes overflow (n^2=4e10 > 2^31-1). This pattern catches both inefficiency and overflow.

key_coverage_gaps: Strings with maximum length difference (1 and 5) leading to various split positions
Strings with digit sums causing equal halves for some combinations but not others
Large number of strings with same length but different sums

random.description: Small random test cases with n up to 8, covering various combinations of a and b. Useful for verifying correctness against brute force.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random arrays a and b of length n (1<=n<=8). For each, compute expected answer using condition: for each position i, check if there exists j with a_j == b_i and all a_k between min(i,j) and max(i,j) <= b_i. Output YES if all i satisfy, else NO.

random.description: Larger random test cases with total n up to 200000, covering typical input sizes. Helps detect performance issues and TLE.
random.generation_strategy: Generate multiple test cases (t up to 10000) with n chosen such that sum n <= 200000. Randomly generate a and b within [1,200000], ensuring some YES and NO cases by occasionally setting b equal to a or creating blockers.

boundary.description: Single element arrays (n=1). Tests the simplest cases where only equality leads to YES.
boundary.test_values: n=1, a and b values at extremes (1 and 200000) and possible inequalities.

boundary.description: Large n (up to 200000) with all elements set to same value. Tests performance and correctness when arrays are homogeneous.

adversarial.description: Intermediate propagation: a has a value that can be used to set neighboring positions, but some naive solutions might think it's impossible because the target positions don't have exactly that value initially.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solution checks only if a_i == b_i or if there exists a direct source without considering propagation through intermediate positions that become equal to the target after previous operations.
adversarial.why_effective: In first case, middle element 2 can be used to set entire array to 2. In second case, the 3 blocks propagation from the 2 to position 1, so NO.

adversarial.description: Blocking by larger values in a: a is strictly decreasing, b is strictly increasing. Each b value appears exactly once in a, but paths are blocked.
adversarial.attack_vector: Some solutions might assume that if a contains all b values, it's always YES, ignoring that segments crossing larger values are invalid.
adversarial.why_effective: Each target value has a source at a different position, but the segment between them contains larger values (e.g., for position 1 needing 1, source at position 4, segment has 4,3,2 >1). This blocks all operations, so NO.
error_types_caught: assuming existence of value in a is sufficient

random.description: Small random arrays for verification against brute force
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, generate n uniformly from 1 to 10, and each a_i uniformly from -10 to 10. Total sum of n over all test cases ≤ 100. Compute answer by brute force enumerating all partitions (2^(n-1) possibilities).

random.description: Large random arrays for stress testing performance and correctness
random.generation_strategy: Generate a single test case with n = 100000, and each a_i uniformly from -1000 to 1000. Alternatively, split into multiple test cases with total n = 100000.
random.example_output: Expected: computed by optimal algorithm (suffix sum greedy). Not given exactly due to randomness.

boundary.description: Minimum array size n=1
boundary.test_values: n=1, a_i = -1000, 0, 1000 (separate test cases)

boundary.description: All positive numbers (maximum Cypriot value achieved by splitting each element)
boundary.test_values: All a_i = 1000, n up to 100000
error_types_caught: incorrect greedily joining subarrays when not needed

boundary.description: All negative numbers (optimal is single subarray)
boundary.test_values: All a_i = -1000, n up to 100000

boundary.description: Maximum n in a single test case (100000) with random values
boundary.test_values: n=100000, random a_i from -1000 to 1000

adversarial.description: Sequence that misleads left-to-right greedy algorithm
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits naive algorithm that tries to split when prefix sum is positive, ignoring future positive suffix.
adversarial.why_effective: A left-to-right greedy might split after the first element (5>0) resulting in subarray [5] and then combine [-10,10] -> value = 1*5 + 2*0 = 5, which is suboptimal. The correct approach (suffix sum) yields 15.

adversarial.description: Sequence with many zeros and negative numbers to test ignoring non-positive suffixes
adversarial.attack_vector: Zeros and negatives create suffix sums that are not >0, which should not trigger a split.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive algorithms might incorrectly split when encountering a zero or negative suffix, reducing the total. The optimal solution only splits when suffix sum > 0.

adversarial.description: Large positive values causing integer overflow in 32-bit
adversarial.attack_vector: Maximize answer by using many large positive numbers.
adversarial.why_effective: The naive implementation using 32-bit integers will overflow for n large enough (e.g., n=100000, all 1000 gives answer ~5e12 > 2^31). This small example does not overflow but demonstrates the pattern; actual test uses larger n.

adversarial.description: Many small test cases to test performance overhead of reading and processing
adversarial.attack_vector: t=10000 with each n=10 (total n=100000) to stress I/O and small case handling.
adversarial.why_effective: Some solutions may have high overhead per test case (e.g., reading input slowly, resetting data structures) that becomes significant with many small cases.

key_coverage_gaps: Alternating positive and negative sequences reaching zero suffix sums
Maximum elements count per test case (100000) with single test case
Minimum and maximum element values with mixed signs

random.description: Random array with small n (n < 10) and small values (max 20), to verify correctness by brute force.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly choose n between 2 and 8. For each element, randomly choose a_i between 1 and 20. Generate 1-5 test cases per run.
error_types_caught: WA due to wrong counting logic

random.description: Random large array with n up to 200000 and values up to 1e6, to test performance and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Generate one test case with n=200000. Randomly assign a_i from 1 to 1e6. Ensure no constraints on duplicates.

boundary.description: Minimum n (n=1). No pairs possible.
boundary.test_values: n=1, any a_i

boundary.description: All elements equal to 1 (smallest possible value). Since 1 divides everything, no good pairs (0).
boundary.test_values: All a_i = 1, n up to 200000

boundary.description: All elements equal to 1000000 (max value). If n>=2, no pairs because gcd=1000000>1 but importantly, if 1000000 is present, it divides both. So output 0.
Maximum number of test cases with minimal n each (t=10000, each n=1) to test overhead.

adversarial.description: Array where every pair has gcd>1, but there is no element that is a common divisor. Example: all numbers are powers of distinct primes? Actually need to ensure that for every pair, there is some element that divides both. But to trick solvers who might use gcd condition: make numbers pairwise coprime? That would give many good pairs, but naive O(n^2) would fail. Actually for adversarial to catch WA, do: numbers with many multiples but containing an element that divides many pairs. E.g., set containing 2 and also many odd numbers that are multiples of 2? No. Better: Include 1 so all pairs are bad. That catches many. But to catch incorrect use of mobius: make array consist of all numbers from 1 to max 100000? Actually need a case where the frequency array approach might double count. For example, array with duplicates: a= [2,2,3,3]. Good pairs: (2,3) and (2,3) but careful: indices matter. Not pair (2,2) because 2 divides both. So pair (2 from first, 3 from first) is good. (2 from first, 3 from second) also good. So total good pairs = 2*2=4. If algorithm treats duplicates incorrectly, may output 2. So adversarial: many duplicates of small numbers combined with other numbers.
adversarial.attack_vector: Incorrect handling of duplicates and multiples
adversarial.why_effective: Naive algorithm might count unique values only, missing that each pair of distinct values contributes multiple combinations
error_types_caught: WA due to not considering each index separately

adversarial.description: Array with many numbers that are multiples of 2, but 2 is not present. Then many pairs with gcd>1 (even) but no element divides both, so they are good. This tricks algorithms that assume if gcd>1 then bad.
adversarial.attack_vector: Incorrect condition: using gcd>1 as disqualifier instead of checking existence of a common divisor element
adversarial.why_effective: All numbers are even (gcd any pair at least 2), but no even number divides all pairs (e.g., 4 does not divide 6), so all pairs are good. Naive algorithm that checks if gcd>1 might output 0.
error_types_caught: Not considering that common divisor must be an element

adversarial.description: Array that causes TLE if O(n sqrt(max)) per element, e.g., many large primes near 1e6. But O(n log n) is okay. To cause TLE, we could have t=1, n=200000, all a_i=999983 (prime). Then naive factorization would be heavy. But mobius sieve precomputes, so not. Instead, cause memory blow: values up to 1e6, but frequency array of size 1e6+1 is fine. Could cause recursion depth if using DFS-based approach. But typical solution uses loops. So adversarial for RE: use large n and values that cause stack overflow with recursive DFS.
adversarial.attack_vector: Stack overflow from recursion in sieve
adversarial.why_effective: If using recursive mobius computation, recursion depth 1e6 might cause stack overflow.

key_coverage_gaps: Large values but all same
Mixed small and large numbers
Test with multiple test cases of varying sizes

random.description: Random test cases with small n (0 to 1000) for verification of correctness
random.generation_strategy: Generate random n in [0, 1000] using uniform distribution, then compute answer using digit product formula

random.description: Random test cases with large n (1e6 to 1e7) for stress testing performance and overflow
random.generation_strategy: Generate random n in [1e6, 1e7] using uniform distribution, compute answer using precomputed f(d) and multiplication
error_types_caught: TLE due to naive per-digit loop

boundary.description: Minimum value n=0
Maximum value n=10000000
boundary.test_values: n = 10^7 = 10000000, digits: 1 and seven 0s

adversarial.description: All digits equal to 9 (e.g., n=9999999)
adversarial.attack_vector: Maximum digit product: each digit 9 gives f(9)=55, product for 7 digits = 55^7 ≈ 1.5e12, fits in 64-bit but may overflow 32-bit
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions using 32-bit integers will overflow and produce wrong results.

adversarial.description: Numbers with many zero digits and a non-zero digit at the end, e.g., n=1000000, 2000000, etc.
adversarial.attack_vector: Zeros contribute factor 1, so answer should be f(d) for the non-zero digit only. Naive solutions might incorrectly handle zeros as contributing something else.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution iterates over all digits but mistakenly counts zeros as having factor >1, it will produce wrong answers.

adversarial.description: Multiple test cases with total n large and many operations to stress 64-bit integers.
adversarial.attack_vector: Cumulative operations can exceed 2e9, requiring long long.
adversarial.why_effective: If answer is stored in int, overflow leads to negative or incorrect values. This input forces many operations per test case.

random.description: Small random test cases with known solution. Generate a random array a of length n (n small, e.g., 3-10), then compute M_{i,j}=a_i|a_j. This ensures a solution exists. Useful for verifying correctness of solution construction.

random.description: Large random test cases with maximum size constraints to test performance and memory. Sum of n^2 across test cases up to 2e5. Generate a random a for each test case, then M. n close to 447 for single test case, or multiple test cases summing to 2e5.
random.generation_strategy: Generate 1 test case with n=447, or multiple test cases with total n^2 ~2e5. Use random a values in [0,2^30-1].

boundary.description: Minimum n=1. For n=1, the matrix is just a single 0. The solution must be a single integer a1. Since there are no OR constraints, any a1 works, but typically a1 can be 0. Check that implementation handles n=1 correctly.
n=2 with small values including 0 and 1. Test edge cases where values are minimal.
boundary.test_values: n=2, M_{1,2} can be 0 or 1; also symmetric with zeros on diagonal.
error_types_caught: incorrect bitwise logic when all zeros

boundary.description: Values at maximum 2^30-1 (~1e9). Test that bits 0-29 are handled correctly, especially the highest bit.
boundary.test_values: n=3, values set to (1<<30)-1 on off-diagonals, diagonal 0.

adversarial.description: Test case designed to break solutions that incorrectly initialize a_i as the OR of the row instead of AND. For such solutions, the resulting OR will be too large (bits set that don't belong). Example: M has bits that are not in all entries of a row, leading to false positive.
adversarial.attack_vector: Construct a consistent matrix where the constructive algorithm using AND is correct, but using OR would give wrong candidate a and still pass OR check? Actually OR initialization would produce a_i that is larger than correct, and then when computing OR of those a_i, you get larger than M? Or smaller? Let's design: For a given i, if we set a_i = OR of row, then a_i will have bits that appear in any M_{i,j}. But then a_i|a_j may have bits that are not in M_{i,j} because those bits might come from other j's? Example: n=3, a=[1,2,4] -> M: [0,3,5; 3,0,6; 5,6,0]. Here row 1 has OR = 1|4|5? Actually row1: M[1][2]=3, M[1][3]=5 -> OR=7. Then a1 candidate =7, a2 candidate =3|6=7, a3=5|6=7, then OR of any pair gives 7, but M[1][2]=3, not 7. So OR initialization overestimates. So we can use such matrices to catch that bug.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive OR initialization would give a=[7,7,7], leading to OR of pairs=7, not matching M. The correct a is [1,2,4].

adversarial.description: Matrix that is symmetric with zero diagonal but has no solution. Tests that solution correctly outputs NO. Common inconsistency: triangular inequality on bits. For example, if M_{1,2}=2, M_{1,3}=2, but M_{2,3}=0, then bit 2 must be set in both a1 and a2 (due to M12), and in a1 and a3 (due to M13), so both a2 and a3 have bit 2, so M_{2,3} should have bit 2, but it's 0. So no solution.
adversarial.attack_vector: Provide an inconsistent matrix that naive algorithms might mistakenly find a solution for, e.g., by ignoring constraints.
adversarial.why_effective: Tests that solution correctly detects inconsistency. Common bug: missing global consistency check.

adversarial.description: Matrix where all off-diagonal entries are zero except one pair. Tests handling of isolated bits and edge cases.
adversarial.attack_vector: For n=3, set M12=1, all others 0. Then obvious solution: a1=a2=1, a3=0? But M13=0, M23=0, and a1|a3=1|0=1, not 0. Contradiction. So no solution. Check: a1 must be 1 (from M12), a2 must be 1. Then a1|a3 must be 0, but a1=1, so impossible. So only solution if M12=1 and M13=M23=0 is inconsistent. But if M12=1 and M13=0, M23=0, already inconsistent. So output NO. Tests that algorithm catches such inconsistency.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive algorithm might set a1=1, a2=1, a3=0 and check only pairs where M is non-zero, missing the fact that a1|a3 should be 0 but is 1.

key_coverage_gaps: Large n with inconsistent matrix
Matrix with all bits set except one bit
Multiple test cases mixing small and large n

random.description: Small random test cases with few segments (n ≤ 10) to verify correctness.
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, generate n random segments with l_i, r_i uniformly from [0, 100]. Starting position is 0. Use brute force or binary search to compute answer.

random.description: Large random test cases with many segments (n up to 200000) to stress test performance.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n = 200000 random segments with l_i, r_i from [0, 1000000]. Ensure sum n over all test cases ≤ 200000 by using only one test case. Compute answer via binary search.
error_types_caught: TLE due to O(n log n) with high constant

boundary.description: Test case where k=0 is sufficient because the first segment contains the starting point (0) and player never needs to move.
boundary.test_values: n=1, segment [0,0] or [0,5]

boundary.description: Segments are far apart with maximum possible gaps (coordinates 0 and 1e6) to test large k values.
boundary.test_values: n=2, segments [0,0] and [1000000,1000000]. Answer = 1000000. Also test with multiple segments alternating extremes.

boundary.description: First segment does not contain 0, forcing k to be at least the distance to the segment.
boundary.test_values: n=1, segment [10,20]. Minimum k = 10.
error_types_caught: assuming start can be inside first segment

adversarial.description: Segments that force the player into a narrow interval, then require a large jump, causing feasibility to fail at a specific k.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits naive feasibility check that does not correctly handle interval expansion after narrowing.
adversarial.why_effective: After first move, player can be anywhere in [0,100] (if k is, say, 990 but we need compute). Actually let's compute: For k=990: start 0, first move: need to be in [0,100] with dist <=990, so can be in [0,100]. Second move: from [0,100] expand to [-890,1090], intersect with [10,10] -> [10,10]. Third move: from [10] expand to [-980,1000], intersect with [10,10] -> [10,10]. Fourth move: from [10] expand to [-980,1000], intersect with [0,1000] -> [0,1000]. So yes k=990 works. Try k=989: first move same, second: from [0,100] expand to [-889,1089], intersect with [10,10] -> empty. So answer 990. This catches solutions that incorrectly compute intervals or miss narrowing effect.

adversarial.description: Many test cases with small n but large total sum, to test per-test-case overhead.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that allocate excessive memory or have high constant factor per test case.
adversarial.why_effective: Each test case is trivial but processing 10000 of them can cause TLE if the solution uses O(n log MAX) per test case without amortization.

adversarial.description: Strictly increasing segments that require a specific k equal to half the maximum gap? Actually answer is max of (r_i - l_{i-1})? No. For degenerate points: answer is max distance between consecutive points. So create sequence of points with increasing distances to force answer to be a specific value. This catches errors in binary search bound or feasibility logic for monotonic requirements.
adversarial.attack_vector: Ensures that the answer is exactly the maximum step needed, which can be non-intuitive if segments are not degenerate.
adversarial.why_effective: The gaps are 3,4,3,5. Max gap is 5, but answer is 3? Wait compute: start 0. k=3: first move to [0,3] must land in [0,0]? Actually segment1 is [0,0], so must be 0. So after first move at 0. Second move: from 0 expand to [-3,3], intersect with [3,3] -> 3. Third: from 3 expand to [0,6], intersect [7,7] -> empty. So k=3 fails. k=4: first to 0, second to 3, third: from 3 expand to [-1,7], intersect [7,7] -> 7, fourth: from 7 expand to [3,11], intersect [10,10] -> 10, fifth: from 10 expand to [6,14], intersect [15,15] -> empty. So k=4 fails. k=5: first to 0, second to 3, third to 7, fourth to 10, fifth from 10 expand to [5,15] intersect [15,15] -> 15. So answer = 5. So actually max gap is 5. So pattern with degenerate points, answer = max gap. But if segments have width, answer can be less. So this pattern tests that binary search correctly computes answer for monotonic case.

key_coverage_gaps: nested intervals with alternating narrow/wide
cases where feasible interval becomes empty only at specific k due to cumulative constraints

random.description: Small random test cases with mixed YES/NO outcomes for manual verification.
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, randomly choose n between 1 and 10. For each point, randomly generate coordinates in [-100, 100]. Ensure at least one test case is YES (all points satisfy one half-plane) and at least one is NO (points in multiple quadrants).

random.description: Large random test case with n=100, all points in one half-plane (x>=0) to verify correctness on high-stress YES scenarios.
random.generation_strategy: Set n=100. For each point, set x = random integer in [0,100], y = random integer in [-100,100]. All points satisfy x>=0, so answer is YES.

boundary.description: Single point at extreme coordinates.
Maximum number of points (n=100) all at the same extreme coordinate.
boundary.test_values: n=100, all points at (100,100). This is YES.

boundary.description: Points exactly on axes forming a cross pattern.
boundary.test_values: n=4, points: (1,0), (-1,0), (0,1), (0,-1). This is NO because no half-plane covers all.

adversarial.description: Points placed in two opposite quadrants, targeting solutions that only check one axis.
adversarial.attack_vector: The points are symmetric about the origin, e.g., (1,1), (2,-2), (-1,-1), (-2,2). They do not satisfy any single half-plane condition.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution might check if all x have same sign or all y have same sign, but here both axes have mixed signs, so it correctly returns NO. However, a more naive solution that checks only one axis might incorrectly return YES if it only checks, say, x signs (which are mixed) or y signs (which are also mixed). This pattern ensures the solution checks both axes comprehensively.

adversarial.description: Large number of points with both positive and negative x and y, ensuring NO.
adversarial.attack_vector: Randomly generate 100 points with half in quadrant I and half in quadrant III, guaranteeing that no half-plane covers all.
adversarial.why_effective: Tests that the algorithm correctly handles large datasets where the answer is NO, avoiding accidental YES due to random distribution that might inadvertently satisfy a condition.

adversarial.description: Points that are all on the same line through the origin but in multiple quadrants (e.g., diagonal with both positive and negative).
adversarial.attack_vector: Points on line y=x: (1,1), (5,5), (-1,-1), (-3,-3). These have both positive and negative x and y, so answer NO.
adversarial.why_effective: Some solvers might mistakenly think that points on a line through the origin are automatically YES because they can omit one direction, but actually they require both up/down and left/right if they extend in both directions.

key_coverage_gaps: Very large t (e.g., 1000 test cases) not covered by patterns, but likely not needed due to simple per-test-case logic.
Points with repeated coordinates not explicitly tested in adversarial patterns.
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: At least 50 test cases for adequate coverage, including random small, random large, boundary extremes, and adversarial cases.

random.description: Small random test cases with few black cells and small coordinates to verify correct outcome for simple scenarios.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n between 1 and 10, with coordinates r_i, c_i in [1, 10]. Compute XOR of (r_i-1) XOR (c_i-1). Output FIRST if non-zero, else SECOND.

random.description: Large random test case with many black cells and large coordinates to stress test performance and correctness under scale.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n up to 100000, with coordinates r_i, c_i in [1, 10^9]. Compute XOR efficiently. Expected output depends on XOR; example provided with known outcome.
error_types_caught: integer overflow (in languages without big integers)

boundary.description: Single black cell at the minimum coordinate (1,1). Expected winner: SECOND because XOR = 0.
error_types_caught: miscounting the XOR when coordinates are 1

boundary.description: Single black cell at a coordinate where (r-1) XOR (c-1) is non-zero, e.g., (1,2). Expected winner: FIRST.

adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that compute XOR of r_i XOR c_i will output FIRST, which is wrong. This pattern directly catches that mistake.
error_types_caught: incorrect mapping of coordinates to nimbers

1 1
2 2

... (pairwise diagonal cells)
Alternating (1,2) and (2,1) pairs such that overall XOR=0.

random.description: Small random test cases with n up to 10 to verify correctness manually.
random.generation_strategy: Generate t in [1,3], n in [1,10], and distinct a_i in [-10,10]. Compute expected answer using brute-force enumeration of x and inserted element (within small range).

random.description: Large random test cases with n up to 2e5 to stress-test performance and overflow.
random.generation_strategy: Generate t=1, n=200000, and random distinct a_i in [-1e9, 1e9] using uniformly distributed values. Compute answer using correct algorithm.

boundary.description: Single element array (n=1). The answer should always be 1 regardless of the value.
boundary.test_values: n=1, any valid a_1 within range. This is the minimal n.

boundary.description: Maximum n and extreme values to test memory and integer bounds.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, a_i from -1e9 to 1e9 in steps of 1 (arithmetic progression). This ensures largest possible sum differences.

boundary.description: Extreme negative values and positive values mix with large gaps.
boundary.test_values: n=2, a = [-1e9, 1e9]. The gcd of difference is 2e9, but since n=2, answer? Actually with n=2, insert new element, then choose x=gcd=2e9. Check if max-2e9 = -1e9 is already present, so no missing <=max. Insert max+2e9 = 3e9. Answer = (3e9 - (-1e9))/(2e9)*3 - ((1e9-(-1e9))/(2e9) + (3e9-1e9)/(2e9)? Let's compute: target=3e9, min=-1e9, g=2e9. Operations for existing: (3e9 - (-1e9))/2e9 = 2, (3e9-1e9)/2e9=1, total=3 for existing; new: 0; so total 3. But answer should be? Actually editorial: For n=2, the optimal is often insert the missing arithmetic step. Here max - g = 1e9-2e9 = -1e9, which is in set, so insert max+g=3e9. Then total ops = (max_target - min)/g * (n+1) - sum of (a_i-min)/g = (3e9 - (-1e9))/(2e9)*3 - ((1e9-(-1e9))/2e9 + ((-1e9)-(-1e9))/2e9) = (4e9/2e9)*3 - (2e9/2e9 + 0) = 2*3 -1 =6-1=5? Wait, careful: The formula using min might be confusing. Better direct: sum of (target - a_i)/g = (3e9 - (-1e9))/2e9 + (3e9-1e9)/2e9 + (3e9-3e9)/2e9 = (4e9/2e9)+(2e9/2e9)+0 = 2+1+0=3. adversarial.description: All elements form an arithmetic progression with no missing element <= max. This forces insertion of max+g, which is a common edge case.
adversarial.attack_vector: The naive approach might incorrectly assume there is always a missing number below max.
adversarial.why_effective: The arithmetic progression [1,3,5] has g=2. The numbers max-2=3 and max-4=1 are already present, so no candidate <= max. Correct answer inserts 7, resulting in 6 operations. A naive solution that always inserts max-2g or similar might produce wrong answer.

adversarial.description: Negative numbers with large gaps to test the correctness of gcd and handling of negative values.
adversarial.attack_vector: Some solutions might take absolute values or mishandle negative mod.
adversarial.why_effective: The array [-5,-2,1] has differences 3,3, so g=3. max=1. Check max-3=-2 present, max-6=-5 present, so insert max+3=4. Operations: (4-(-5))/3=3, (4-(-2))/3=2, (4-1)/3=1 total=6. A solution that incorrectly handles negative numbers might compute g wrong or output 5.

adversarial.description: Large n with alternating large positive and negative values to cause potential overflow in sum of differences or intermediate calculations.
adversarial.attack_vector: If using 32-bit integers, sum of differences can exceed 2e9, leading to overflow.
adversarial.why_effective: The sum of differences from max to each element can be huge (up to 2e9 * 2e5 = 4e14), which overflows 32-bit int. Solutions using 'int' will produce wrong answer or crash.

random.description: Large random test cases to stress performance and check for overflow.
random.generation_strategy: Generate t=10 test cases. For each, choose a in [1e8, 1e9], b in [1e8, 1e9], n in [50000, 100000], and each x_i in [1, 1e9] randomly. Expected output formula is straightforward but may involve large numbers; ensure correct use of 64-bit integers.

boundary.description: Minimum a = 1. No tool can add any time because a-1 = 0.
boundary.test_values: a=1, b any, n any, x_i any. Expected output = b.
error_types_caught: adding x_i values even when a=1

boundary.description: Maximum a and b = 1e9, n = 1e5, all x_i = 1e9. Test large sum and potential overflow.
error_types_caught: incorrect cap due to off-by-one (using min(x_i, a) instead of a-1)

boundary.description: Single tool (n=1) with various values of a, b, and x.
boundary.test_values: n=1, a, b, x varying. Test that answer is b + min(x, a-1).
error_types_caught: forgetting the cap when b is large

adversarial.description: All x_i = 1 and a is moderately large. Tests if a solution incorrectly simulates using tools consecutively without waiting.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive simulation might try to use all tools in one second when timer is low, but the cap limits immediate gain; optimal is to use them one per second at timer=1.
adversarial.why_effective: Each tool adds at most a-1=4 seconds when used at timer=1. But if used at timer=1, timer becomes 2, then 1 next second. So you can use one tool per second when timer is 1, giving +1 per tool. Total = b + 4*1 = 5. Some might think you can use multiple tools in the same second to get more, but each tool after the first would be less effective.

adversarial.description: Large a (1e9) and large x_i (1e9) but small b (1). Tests if a solution correctly caps each tool at a-1.
adversarial.attack_vector: Some implementations might add x_i directly without min cap, leading to huge overcount.
adversarial.why_effective: If a solution doesn't cap at a-1, it might try to add x_i=1e9 directly, leading to output like 1+3e9=3000000001, which is wrong. Also tests large numbers.

key_coverage_gaps: No pattern specifically targeting very large n with small a (a=2) to test min cap impact
No pattern with b=1 and a=2 to test edge of cap

random.description: Small random test cases with n between 2 and 10 for verification against brute-force O(n^2) solution.
random.generation_strategy: Generate t=10 test cases, each with n uniformly random in [2,10], and generate a random permutation of [0,n-1].

random.description: Large random test case with n=100000 (or up to 1e6) to test performance and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Generate t=1 test case with n=100000, and generate a random permutation of [0,n-1] using Fisher-Yates shuffle.

boundary.description: Minimum n = 1, permutation [0]. Only one cyclic shift, cost = mex([0]) = 1.
n = 2, both permutations [0,1] and [1,0]. The maximum cost across cyclic shifts is 3 (for [0,1]).
error_types_caught: WA: incorrect mex for prefix of length 1
WA: not considering both cyclic shifts

boundary.description: n=1e6 with sorted ascending permutation [0,1,...,n-1]. The maximum cost is n(n+1)/2 (e.g., for n=10, cost=55). This tests large integer output and performance on sorted data.
boundary.test_values: n=1000000, permutation sorted ascending
error_types_caught: TLE: slow simulation on large n
WA: incorrect math for sorted case

adversarial.description: Permutation in decreasing order from n-1 to 0. This pattern is known to cause many updates in naive implementations because each shift changes mex values significantly.
adversarial.attack_vector: Many algorithms recompute mex for each prefix after each shift, leading to O(n^2) time when the permutation is decreasing. A stack-based solution may also struggle if not implemented with amortized O(1) updates.
adversarial.why_effective: The decreasing order forces the mex of most prefixes to stay at 0 until the last element, causing many updates when rotating.
error_types_caught: WA: incorrect cost due to mishandling of large changes

adversarial.description: Permutation where 0 is not at the front, e.g., [1,0,2,3,...,n-1]. The maximum cost occurs for the original shift (starting with 1), not after moving 0 to front. This catches algorithms that incorrectly assume the optimal shift must start with 0.
adversarial.attack_vector: Assumption that maximum cost is achieved when 0 is the first element. This pattern shows a counterexample where the initial shift yields higher cost.
adversarial.why_effective: The mex values for prefixes after the first element are high, leading to a larger sum than when 0 is at front.
error_types_caught: WA: not considering all cyclic shifts

adversarial.description: Many test cases each with n=1. This tests the overhead of per-test-case initialization. If the solution allocates large structures for each test case (e.g., O(n) arrays) even when n=1, it may still be okay since sum n is bounded, but if it uses O(t) time elsewhere, it may TLE.
adversarial.attack_vector: Excessive overhead per test case (e.g., resetting arrays of size n for each test case).
adversarial.why_effective: If the solution does O(n) work per test case even for n=1, with t=100000 it's O(t) work, which is acceptable. However, if it does O(t) unrelated to n, or if it allocates large arrays per test case (e.g., always allocating size 1e6), it may TLE or MLE.
error_types_caught: TLE: unnecessary overhead per test case

key_coverage_gaps: Permutations where the maximum cost is not unique
Permutations with repeated elements (not applicable)
Extreme values of n (already covered)

random.description: Random strings with varying length (2 to 50), ensuring a valid split exists by construction. The suffix number is chosen as a random positive integer without leading zeros, and the prefix is a random string of letters and digits but always containing at least one letter.

Then generate random prefix (ensuring at least one letter) and random suffix as a positive integer (no leading zeros) of appropriate length. Concatenate.

adversarial.description: String with multiple possible splits, where some solutions might incorrectly choose a split that yields an invalid number (e.g., leading zero).

Very long number with leading zeros after first digit? Already covered by random_3

Then generate q=10 random points outside the polygon (e.g., in a bounding rectangle that contains the polygon but not inside). Ensure no point is inside using point-in-convex-polygon test (binary search or winding). Optionally include points on boundary.

random.description: Large convex polygon (n=1000) and many queries (q=200000) to stress test performance and numerical stability.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a convex polygon by sampling 1000 random angles on a circle and adding noise. Scale coordinates to be within [-1e9, 1e9]. Ensure no three collinear. Generate q=200000 queries by randomly selecting points from a uniform distribution over the bounding box of the polygon, rejecting points inside the polygon (using binary search). Some points may lie on edges.

boundary.description: Minimum number of polygon vertices (n=3) forming a triangle. Tests handling of degenerate convex polygons (no three collinear). Queries include points exactly on vertices and edges.
boundary.test_values: n=3, coordinates such that triangle is non-degenerate. Queries: start point on a vertex, end point on another vertex; both on same edge; etc.

boundary.description: Extreme coordinate values (±1e9). Tests overflow and precision in geometric computations (e.g., cross products, distances).
boundary.test_values: n=100, polygon vertices at (1e9, 1e9), (-1e9, 1e9), (-1e9, -1e9), (1e9, -1e9) etc. Queries also at extreme coordinates.

adversarial.description: Query points such that the optimal two-segment path requires computing tangent lines from each point to the polygon. Small deviations in tangent point calculation cause WA due to path crossing the polygon or being suboptimal.
adversarial.attack_vector: Floating-point errors in binary search for tangent points or in angle calculations.
adversarial.why_effective: The naive solution might test tangents using close points; the tangent points are exactly at midpoints of edges (e.g., (-1000,0) or (1000,0)). If the algorithm uses imprecise bisection or cross product checks, it may pick a point slightly inside the polygon, causing the path to intersect interior. The expected output is the straight line distance if it avoids the polygon, but here the straight line passes through the polygon, so optimal is to go to the midpoint of the top or bottom edge. The distance 4000 is exact.

adversarial.description: Optimal path passes exactly through a polygon vertex. Tests if the algorithm correctly handles the case where the turn point is at a vertex (allowed to touch).
adversarial.attack_vector: Handling of collinearity when the turn point is at a vertex; some implementations may incorrectly classify the vertex as inside the polygon.
adversarial.why_effective: For convex polygon, the optimal path from (-5,5) to (5,-5) goes through vertex (0,0) (or (10,10) but longer). The path (-5,5)->(0,0)->(5,-5) is allowed because the segment (0,0) to (5,-5) touches the boundary only at (0,0) but then goes outside? Actually (0,0) is a vertex. The path is valid. Naive solutions that treat vertices as interior might reject this path or compute wrong tangent.

key_coverage_gaps: Cases where start and end points are on the same edge of the polygon (straight line along edge possible)
Cases with many collinear points (though constraints forbid three collinear vertices, queries may have collinear with vertices?)
Large negative coordinate values combined with large positive to test signed overflow

boundary.test_values: p = 1000000007, any n,m within constraints (e.g., 100 100)
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of p^k % MOD when p≡0
misusing modular inverse when denominator is zero mod MOD

adversarial.description: Max rank case: n=m=2000, p=2. The algorithm must compute answer for k=2000 using Gaussian binomial asymptotic. Likely correct but tests overflow in multiplication of large powers.
adversarial.attack_vector: The number of full-rank matrices involves products of (p^n - p^i) for i=0..k-1. For large k, this product may overflow if intermediate multiplication not modded properly.
adversarial.why_effective: Without modular reduction at each step, intermediate values exceed 64-bit.

adversarial.description: n=2000, m=1 (or vice versa). Only possible ranks are 0 or 1. Tests that loop over k doesn't extend beyond min(n,m) and that binomial coefficients for k>m are zero.
adversarial.attack_vector: Code may incorrectly assume symmetric or compute Gaussian binomial with n>m without proper bounds, leading to out-of-bounds array access or incorrect formula.
adversarial.why_effective: If code loops from 0 to n instead of 0 to min(n,m), it will attempt to compute values for k>m, causing array index error or wrong results.
error_types_caught: incorrect Gaussian binomial formula for k>m

random.example_output: Expected output depends on specific generation; for a random permutation, typical minimum size is around 500-700 and number of sets is large modulo MOD. Provide null.

boundary.description: Minimum n = 2 with various interval structures to test base case correctness.
boundary.test_values: n=2. For n=2, there are three distinct up to symmetry: [1,1,2,2], [1,2,1,2], [1,2,2,1].

boundary.description: Maximum n single test case (n=2000) with all intervals disjoint (consecutive pairs) to test scalability and modulo counting.
boundary.test_values: n=2000, colors arranged as 1,1,2,2,...,2000,2000 in order.
boundary.example_output: 2000 <MOD> (specifically, 2000 and 2^2000 mod MOD; e.g., for MOD=998244353, compute power)
error_types_caught: Stack overflow in recursion (if using DFS on intervals)

boundary.description: Maximum nested intervals (each interval contains the next) to test dependency tracking.
boundary.test_values: n=1000, colors arranged as [1,2,3,...,1000,...,3,2,1] exactly symmetric nesting.
error_types_caught: Wrong component detection for nested intervals

adversarial.description: Deeply nested intervals that cause O(n^2) behavior in naive interval merging algorithms, targeting TLE.
adversarial.attack_vector: Create a chain of intervals where each interval is nested inside the previous, leading to many comparisons if solution uses naive pairwise interval intersection.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive algorithms that compare all pairs of intervals will iterate over O(n^2) pairs, but n=500 is small? Actually sum n <=2000 so 500 is moderate; but if n=1000, O(n^2)=1e6 which might be okay. A better attack: intervals that form many overlapping 'components' but the naive merge might still be O(n^2). Actually, a chain of intervals each containing the next is still O(n) if processed with stack. To cause O(n^2), we want intervals that are not nested but partially overlapping in a way that forces many comparisons. For example, intervals that are like [1,2,1,2] repeated: each color's interval is length 0? No, each color appears twice, so interval for color i is between its two occurrences. If we interleave like [1,2,3,...,n,1,2,3,...,n] then intervals are all overlapping at the center? Actually, that pattern gives intervals [1,n], [2,n-1], etc., which are nested. Still O(n) with stack. To get O(n^2) we need intervals that alternate in a way that forces repeated scanning. For example, [1,2,2,1] gives one nesting. But if we have many such independent nestings, each is small. A better adversarial: intervals that form a 'comb' where many short intervals are inside a large one, but counting them still O(n). I think the most dangerous for easy version is stack overflow due to deep recursion if using DFS on interval graph. So we target RE with deep recursion.

adversarial.description: Intervals with many overlapping minimal colors to cause wrong counting of initial sets.
adversarial.attack_vector: Create a structure where many colors form a single component but each color's interval is such that it is 'mandatory' to pick one bulb from that color, but the number of ways is not simply 2^(#colors). The solution needs to compute product of (2 * size_of_group) for certain groups. If solution incorrectly multiplies by 2 for each color inside a group, answer will be off.
adversarial.why_effective: In this example, intervals: color1=[1,4], color2=[2,5], color3=[3,6]. All intervals intersect, so one component. The minimal initial set size is 2 (e.g., pick one bulb from color1 and one from color3? Actually, with careful analysis, min size is 2 and number of sets is 4. Naive: if you think each color contributes independently, you might guess min size=3 and sets=8, which is wrong.

key_coverage_gaps: Test cases with large number of components (e.g., all intervals disjoint) are covered; nested intervals covered; interleaved intervals covered. Missing: test with very small n but large t (t=1000, n=2 each) to stress test read/write performance, but that's more about I/O than algorithm.
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: At least 10 test cases: 2 random small, 1 random large, 2 boundary (min n, max n), 2 boundary (nested, disjoint), 2 adversarial (deep recursion, overlapping counting), plus edge cases like n=2 with different patterns.

random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate n=5-10, m between n-1 and n*(n-1)/2, random edge weights in [1,100], random slowness in [1,1000]. Ensure graph connectivity.

adversarial.description: Optimal path requires multiple bike upgrades; naive single-buy fails.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solution that only buys a bike at start and never upgrades will yield incorrect (larger) time.
adversarial.why_effective: The optimal strategy is to upgrade at each city: buy at city1 (1000), travel to city2 (1*1000=1000), buy at city2 (100), travel to city3 (1*100=100), buy at city3 (10), travel to city4 (1*10=10). Total=1110. A solution that only uses the first bike would compute 3000; one that only upgrades once might miss the best sequence.

adversarial.description: Multiple edges between same pair with different weights; algorithm must consider all.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that ignore parallel edges or only consider one edge per pair may produce wrong distance.
adversarial.why_effective: The direct edge 1-3 is long. The best path is via city2 using the short edge (1) with slowness 10 from city1 (10*1=10) then upgrade at city2 to slowness 1 and take edge to city3 (1*1=1). Total=11. A solution that ignores the shorter parallel edge would output 101 or 1000.

Graph with many cycles and multiple potential upgrade sequences.
Edge case where optimal path includes staying in same city? Not applicable.
