random.description: Small random arrays to verify correctness against brute-force or known solution
random.generation_strategy: Generate t=1..3 test cases with n=2..5, each a_i in [0, 2^5-1]. Compute expected output via brute-force enumeration of all subsequences (2^n).
error_types_caught: incorrect output due to logic errors

random.description: Large random arrays to stress-test flow implementation for performance and memory
random.generation_strategy: Generate t=1 with n=200000, a_i randomly in [0, 2^30-1]. Ensure total elements across tests within limits (e.g., 2e5).
error_types_caught: TLE due to inefficient flow (e.g., BFS/DFS loops)
MLE due to excessive graph size
integer overflow in capacities or distances

boundary.description: All elements are zero. Popcount of OR is 0, value = n (max possible). Empty subsequence also gives 0, but positive n is better.
boundary.test_values: a_i = 0 for all i
error_types_caught: treating zero elements as not contributing

boundary.description: Single element with multiple set bits. Best subsequence is empty (value 0) because non-empty gives negative value.
boundary.test_values: n=1, a_i = 7 (binary 111, popcount 3)
error_types_caught: incorrectly computing negative value as positive

boundary.description: Each element is a distinct power of two. No bit overlap. Value of any subset of size k is k - k = 0. Empty gives 0. All subsets give 0, so max is 0.
error_types_caught: overcounting value when bits are unique
wrongly thinking you can get positive value

adversarial.description: Case designed to force maximum flow to use many augmenting paths, potentially causing BFS/DFS overhead if poorly implemented.
adversarial.attack_vector: Alternating high and low capacity edges? Actually capacities are 1. But we create many elements that share many bits, so the flow network has high connectivity. Optimal solution: pick all elements? But OR gets all bits, so value = n - number_of_bits. If number of bits is small, value is positive. For example, all elements have the same single bit (e.g., all are 1). Then OR has 1 bit, value = n-1. Flow should find min cut = 1? Actually, min cut: either cut all element edges (cost n) or cut bit edge (cost 1) and no element edges (since all elements are subsets of that bit). So min cut = 1, max value = n-1. This is simple. To make it harder, use many bits but with overlaps that force many paths.
adversarial.example_input:
1
100000
1 2 4 8 ... (exactly 16 distinct powers of two) but then 999984 elements that are 65535 (all bits) etc. Actually, we want many edges. Better: all elements are 2^30-1 (all bits set). Then each element connects to 30 bits. Graph has 100000 elements, 30 bits, and 3e6 edges. This stresses memory and flow algorithm (since each BFS will build level graph with many edges).
adversarial.why_effective: Naive flow with adjacency list and dynamic allocation might be slow or memory heavy. BFS/DFS loops over many edges each time.
error_types_caught: TLE due to high edge count
incorrect infinite capacity (too small causing early termination)

adversarial.description: Elements have overlapping bits such that greedy selection (e.g., always pick element with few new bits) fails. The optimal selection may combine elements that together cover many bits but with many elements.
adversarial.attack_vector: Create two types of elements: many elements with bit pattern A, and many with pattern B, where A and B are disjoint. But also some elements with bits A∪B. The optimal might be to take all of one type, but the flow solution handles correctly. For greedy, it might pick mixed.
adversarial.why_effective: A greedy algorithm that always picks elements that increase value may fail: each element alone gives value 0 (size 1, popcount 1). Pairwise: (1,2) OR=3 popcount2 value0; (1,3) OR=3 popcount2 value0; (2,3) OR=3 popcount2 value0; all three: OR=3 popcount2 value1. So optimal is all three. Greedy might not take all three because initial pairs give 0.
error_types_caught: WA due to wrong greedy heuristic

key_coverage_gaps: Very large a_i with 30 bits all set
Multiple test cases with small n
Edge case where n is large but each element is 0

random.description: Small random test cases with n up to 10 and heights up to 10. Useful for verifying basic correctness.
random.generation_strategy: Generate 5 test cases with n randomly chosen between 1 and 10, heights uniformly random between 1 and 10.

random.description: One large random test case with n=100000 and heights uniformly random between 1 and 1000000. Tests performance and correctness on a large random input.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a single test case with n=100000, heights uniform in [1,1000000]. Output is computed by a correct algorithm (e.g., monotonic stack).

boundary.description: Single tree. n=1, height=1. Tests minimum size input.
All heights equal. No jumps possible, so each tree can only reach itself.
Strictly increasing sequence. No jumps possible, each node isolated.
Strictly decreasing sequence. All nodes are mutually reachable, answer is the maximum height (first element).

adversarial.description: Very large strictly decreasing sequence. If a solution does BFS/DFS from each node, it will have O(n^2) edges and time out.
adversarial.attack_vector: TLE via naive graph traversal for each node in a complete directed graph.
adversarial.why_effective: In a strictly decreasing sequence, every pair of nodes has an edge (both forward and backward), so the graph is complete. A naive BFS from each node would be O(n^2).

adversarial.description: Mountain shape: increasing then decreasing. Tests that the solution correctly handles asymmetry: the increasing part is isolated, the decreasing part (including peak) is fully connected.
adversarial.attack_vector: WA due to incorrect connectivity assumptions (e.g., thinking the peak can reach the left side).
adversarial.why_effective: In mountain shape, the left increasing part (indices 1-3) have no outgoing edges, so they can only reach themselves. The peak (index 4) and the decreasing part (indices 5-7) are strongly connected (peak can go forward to lower on right, and lower can go backward to peak). So answer for indices 1-3 is their own height; for indices 4-7 is the maximum height (4). A common mistake is to output the maximum height for all nodes or to connect the left part to the peak.

adversarial.description: Valley shape: decreasing then increasing. Tests that the solution correctly handles the asymmetry: the decreasing part (including bottom) is strongly connected, the increasing part is isolated.
adversarial.attack_vector: WA due to incorrect connectivity between decreasing and increasing parts.
adversarial.why_effective: In valley shape, the decreasing left part (indices 1-4) are strongly connected (from any node you can reach the bottom and then to the top left). So indices 1-4 output the maximum on the left (4). The increasing right part (indices 5-7) have no edges among themselves and cannot reach the left part, so they output their own heights. A naive solution might incorrectly connect the right part to the bottom or assume symmetry.

adversarial.description: Many small test cases: 100000 test cases each with n=1. Tests input parsing speed and handling of large number of test cases.
adversarial.attack_vector: TLE or RE due to slow input parsing or inefficient handling of many test cases.
adversarial.why_effective: If the input processing is O(total_n) but with high constant overhead per test case (e.g., using slow I/O or excessive allocations), this can cause TLE. Also tests that the output format is correct for each test case.

key_coverage_gaps: No pattern specifically tests maximum height values (1e6) with mixed structure
No pattern tests adjacent equal heights in non-constant sequences
No pattern tests n=2 with various height relations

random.generation_strategy: Generate array length n between 1 and 10, each a_i uniformly random between 1 and 1e9. Include both even and odd numbers. Generate t up to 100 to cover many small cases.

error_types_caught: incorrect treatment of single element (no operation possible)
modulo errors when a_i already equals MOD?

boundary.description: All odd numbers (no factors of 2). Then total_power=0, answer for each prefix is just prefix sum of original numbers.
boundary.test_values: n=100000, all odd numbers. Example: sequence of odd numbers from 1 to 199999 (increment by 2).
error_types_caught: incorrect assumption that operation always changes values
failure to handle zero power of two

boundary.description: All numbers are powers of two (odd part = 1). Then max_odd=1 always, total_odd_sum = n, total_power = sum of exponents. Answer = (n-1) + 2^{total_power} mod MOD.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, all numbers = 2^30 (1073741824) to maximize total power (6e6). Or mix different powers.
error_types_caught: incorrect modular exponentiation for large exponent
failure to subtract 1 from max_odd term

adversarial.description: Sequence designed to trick greedy based on current value instead of odd part. Example: a_i where one number has large value but small odd part, while another has smaller value but larger odd part.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit algorithm that chooses recipient based on current value rather than odd part.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solution might try to move factor from 6 to 5 because 6>5? Actually naive might think to give all factors to 6 (largest value) resulting in [3,10] sum=13, but optimal is [3,10]? Wait: 6 odd=3,5 odd=5. Optimal: give factor from 6 to 5: [3,10] sum=13. Actually let's compute: values: [6,5]. Factor: 6 has one factor of 2 (odd=3), 5 has 0 (odd=5). Total power=1, max_odd=5, total_odd_sum=8, sum= (8-5)+5*2=3+10=13. Is that max? Alternative: If we give factor to 6, we get [12,5]=17? But operation: we can only divide an even number. From 6, divide by 2 -> 3, multiply 5 -> 10 gives [3,10] sum=13. From 5, we cannot because it's odd. So we cannot give factor to 6 because source must be even. Actually we can only move from 6. So the only possible operation is from 6 to 5. So it's forced. So the correct answer is 13. But if someone doesn't consider that only even numbers can be divided, they might think we can move from 5 to 6? No. So this test may catch that misunderstanding. But also the greediness: the number with larger odd part is 5, but 5 is smaller value. So a greedy that always tries to accumulate factors into the largest current value would fail if it thought it could move from 5 to 6 (impossible) or if it considered moving from 6 to 6 (not allowed). But simpler: just to test the odd part logic. Another example: [12,9]. 12 odd=3, 9 odd=9, total power=2. Naive might think to keep factors on 12 because it's large, but best is to give to 9: (12-9?) Wait: total_odd_sum=3+9=12, max_odd=9, total_power=2, sum= (12-9)+9*4=3+36=39. Could we achieve 39? Move both factors from 12 to 9: step1: [6,18] sum=24, step2: [3,36] sum=39. Alternatively, keep on 12: [48,9] sum=57? But can we? To keep on 12, we would need to move factors from 9? But 9 is odd and cannot be divided. So we cannot move factors to 12 from 9. But we could move factors from 12 to 12? No. Actually we can only move from 12 to 5? Here only even is 12. So we can only move factors away from 12. So the only possible moves are to 9. So the final state must be either [3,36] or intermediate. So 39 is the max. But what if we don't move? Then sum=21. So greedy that always tries to keep factors on the largest odd part would be correct. So this adversarial is about understanding that only even numbers can be sources. But I'll adjust to a better example: maybe [8,6]. 8 odd=1, power=3; 6 odd=3, power=1. Total power=4, total_odd_sum=4, max_odd=3. Sum = (4-3)+3*16=1+48=49. Achievable? Move all factors to 6: from 8 to 6 repeatedly: [4,12], [2,24], [1,48] sum=49. Or move to 8: from 6 to 8: [16,3] sum=19. So optimal is to give to 6. But naive might give to 8 because it's larger value initially (8>6) but odd part smaller, so sum would be less. So this is a good adversarial. I'll use [8,6] as example.
error_types_caught: incorrect selection of max odd part
assuming optimal recipient is the number with largest value

adversarial.description: Large odd parts and large total power causing modulo subtraction to become negative if not handled. Example: total_odd_sum < max_odd mod? Actually total_odd_sum >= max_odd always, but after modulo, subtract may yield negative.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit failure to add MOD before modulo in subtraction.
adversarial.why_effective: If code does (total_odd_sum - max_odd) % MOD without adding MOD first, when total_odd_sum > MOD, the modulo may cause negative. For instance, total_odd_sum=2e9 mod 1e9+7 = 999999993, max_odd=1e9 mod MOD = 1e9, subtraction yields -7 mod MOD, correct is 999999993? Actually 2e9 - 1e9 = 1e9, modulo is 1e9. But if total_odd_sum and max_odd are taken modulo, then (total_odd_sum_mod - max_odd_mod) could be negative. So we need to ensure correct arithmetic.

key_coverage_gaps: Case where max_odd comes from a number that itself has many factors of 2 (e.g., [8,8] where max_odd=1, total_power=6)
Case where numbers have mixed odd parts and powers near boundary of 2^30
Case where n=200000 and all numbers are 1 (odd, no power) to test performance on trivial operation

not considering multiple states per cell

boundary.description: Minimum constraints: n=1, m=1, k=1. The only section's tastiness can be 0 or 1.
Boundary where total sum is exactly m*k, so Alice can only get 0 if partitions allow, else -1.
boundary.test_values: n=3, m=2, k=5, a=[5,0,5] (sum=10=2*5) -> Alice must take empty piece, but is it partitionable? Left: [5] (>=5), right: [5] (>=5), so yes, output 0. Another: a=[5,5,0] -> left of Alice can be [5] but right [5,0] sum 5, but need exactly 2 pieces? Actually left [5], right [5,0] is one piece sum 5, so total pieces 2, yes. But if a=[0,5,5] similar.
error_types_caught: incorrect feasibility when total sum just meets requirement

boundary.description: Maximum values: a_i up to 1e9, k up to 1e9, n up to 200000, m up to n. Potential overflow if using 32-bit.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, m=1, k=1e9, all a_i = 1e9. Total sum = 2e14, answer = 2e14 - 1e9 = 199999*1e9. Need 64-bit.

adversarial.description: Array with many zeros and a few large values, requiring careful greedy for max pieces.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive greedy without considering zeros may produce incorrect max piece count.
adversarial.why_effective: The only way to get two creature pieces each ≥5 is to take the first and last sections as separate pieces. Then Alice gets the middle three zeros, sum 0. Greedy scanning left to right would take first 5, then see zeros, but to get second piece it must go to end, which it does. Works. But another: if zeros are in between, greedy might skip them incorrectly.

adversarial.description: All values equal to k, m=n. Each creature gets exactly one section, Alice gets nothing. Output 0.
adversarial.attack_vector: Check if solution handles trivially partitionable case where each section is a piece.
adversarial.why_effective: Solvers might try to combine pieces unnecessarily.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of exactly m pieces

adversarial.attack_vector: Check if solution correctly identifies impossibility when total sum < m*k.
adversarial.why_effective: Total sum = 9 < 10, so impossible. Some may try to partition but fail.
error_types_caught: missing early exit for impossible case

adversarial.description: One color has zero pins, but total sum is large. Tests if solution incorrectly requires non-zero of both colors.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploiting solutions that might assume both colors are needed or that largest row must be assignable to either color.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might think that with zero pins of one color, no triangle can be built because all rows cannot be same color? But actually, all rows can be assigned to the non-zero color, so works. This catches those who impose extra color constraints.

adversarial.description: Large input where w+b is just at the limit of 32-bit integer (2e9). Tests for overflow in multiplication or sqrt calculation.
adversarial.attack_vector: Integer overflow when computing L*(L+1)/2 or 8*(w+b)+1.
adversarial.why_effective: Many solutions use 32-bit int and overflow when computing 2e9*... or sqrt of large number. Using 64-bit int is necessary.

random.generation_strategy: Generate n=5 intervals with lengths, left endpoints, and right endpoints chosen uniformly at random from 1 to 10. Ensure coverage of diverse overlap types by re-rolling if all intervals are disjoint or all identical.

adversarial.description: Intervals arranged so that condition holds at all integer points but fails at some non-integer point, catching solutions that only check integer times.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits the fact that covering sets differ at integer endpoints and interior points.
adversarial.why_effective: At integer 3, all three intervals cover, and color 2 appears exactly once (interval 2). At non-integer 2.5, only intervals 1 and 2 cover, both assigned color 1, causing failure. Naive solution checking only integers would accept.
error_types_caught: WA due to integer-only vertex checks

adversarial.description: Deeply nested intervals that cause recursion depth equal to n in a recursive coloring algorithm, leading to stack overflow.
adversarial.attack_vector: Triggers recursion depth limit by creating a chain of nested intervals where each interval contains the next.
adversarial.why_effective: A recursive algorithm that processes intervals in order of left endpoint and calls itself for each nested interval will hit recursion depth of 100000, causing stack overflow if not tail-recursive or if recursion limit is set low.

key_coverage_gaps: intervals with very large length (200000) and many test cases
intervals with overlapping endpoints only (tangential) maybe?

adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that always select all strings or have default selection will get large negative.
adversarial.why_effective: Since 'keran' has all pattern letters but in reverse order, from state0 none match, so each gives -5. Taking none gives 0, which is optimal. A solution that always picks all would output -500000.

adversarial.description: Large n, very small m to test if solution can handle m=2 efficiently, and to catch O(n^2) DP that would TLE.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive O(n*k) DP for Stirling numbers becomes O(n) when k=2, but if solution uses O(n^2) for all k it will TLE. Also tests formula for m=2: answer = 2^n - 1 mod MOD.
adversarial.example_output: Mod(2^100000 - 1, 1e9+7). For concrete: n=100000, output is large; provide null.
adversarial.why_effective: Many contestants implement O(n^2) DP for Stirling numbers, which will time out for n=100000 even with m=2 because they might loop over all k up to m=2 but still O(n^2) if not optimized. Actually with m=2, O(n^2) is 1e10 operations, TLE. Solutions using O(n log n) convolution will pass.

adversarial.description: Both n and m at maximum (100000) to stress-test O(n log n) convolution and memory usage.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit solutions that use O(n*m) memory or O(n^2) time.
adversarial.why_effective: Memory O(n*m) would be 1e10 integers, impossible. Time O(n^2) would be 1e10 operations. Only O(n log n) convolution with O(n) memory can pass.

adversarial.description: Test for correct modular arithmetic and handling of negative values.
adversarial.attack_vector: Use large n and m to cause intermediate multiplication to exceed 64-bit if not taken modulo at each step. Also test that subtraction yields non-negative result.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution multiplies two large numbers before modulo, it may overflow in languages with fixed-width integers (e.g., C++ long long). Also if they compute sum using (a+b)%MOD without ensuring a and b are positive, off-by-one or negative results can occur.

adversarial.description: Test when m is larger than n to ensure sum is up to n only.
adversarial.attack_vector: Misinterpreting sum limit by going up to m instead of min(n,m).
adversarial.why_effective: If solution sums k!*S(n,k) for k=1 to m, it will include terms for k>n which are undefined (S(n,k)=0 for k>n) but if not handled properly, it might compute incorrect factorials or Stirling numbers for k>n leading to wrong result. With m large, naive DP might also be slow if they loop up to m.
error_types_caught: TLE due to O(n*m) when m>n

key_coverage_gaps: Very small n and m with n=m=1 covered.
Large n and m with m=2 covered.
Both large n and m covered.
Edge cases where m > n covered.
Missing: test with n=0? Not allowed.
Missing: test with n and m such that min(n,m) is prime? Not necessary.

adversarial.description: Star graph: center node 1 points to all other nodes (2..n). n=200000, edges: 1->2,1->3,...,1->n. Center has large diff (n-1), leaves have diff=1 (each leaf: 0 descendants, 1 ancestor from center). Minimum diff=1, output all leaves. This tests handling of unbalanced counts and large output.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive O(n^2) reachability per node will TLE for large star; also may incorrectly compute leaf counts if not using DP.
adversarial.why_effective: Star graph is worst-case for algorithms that iterate over all reachable nodes from each node individually (e.g., BFS from each node). Also tests that leaf nodes are correctly identified when center has many outgoing edges.

adversarial.description: Long chain: 1->2->3->...->n. n=200000. For node i, reachable = n-i, reached by = i-1. Diff = |(n-i)-(i-1)| = |n+1-2i|. Minimum diff occurs near middle. For n=200000, there will be two nodes with diff=0 (if n odd, one node). This tests path length and asymmetric counts.
adversarial.attack_vector: Chain forces long propagation; algorithms that do BFS/DFS per node will be O(n^2). Also tests that correct IDs are output near middle.
adversarial.why_effective: Chain is a classic worst-case for naive transitive closure (O(n^2)). Also tests that the solution correctly handles linear dependency and that the minimum difference is computed correctly for symmetric positions.

So optimal is {2,1,3} with cost 102, whereas picking cheap vertices {2,3} is not connected.

Minimum sum is 3 achieved by ?=00 and ?=01. The smallest number among these is 00. Maximum sum is 5 achieved by ?=10 and ?=11, smallest number is 10. So output should be 00 and 10. Some might incorrectly output 01 or 11.

adversarial.description: Many orders with same price and direction, testing aggregation sum correctness.

random.description: Small random tree with moderate size (n=5-10) to verify correctness of matching and minimal raise.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random tree with n=5-10 nodes, assign random heights (1-20), and random miner heights (1-20) with k <= n. Compute expected output using brute-force enumeration of all caves to raise (including 0), simulating the effect on path minima and checking if a perfect matching exists.

random.description: Large random tree (n=10000, k=5000) to stress test performance and correctness with random heights and miner heights.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random tree with n=10000, heights in [1, 1e9], k=5000 random miner heights also in [1,1e9]. Use efficient implementation to compute expected output (binary search on answer + multiset matching).

boundary.description: Single cave (n=1) with one miner. Test simplest case where raising is necessary and possible.
boundary.test_values: n=1, k=1, h1=1, s1=10 -> need to raise by 9. Also h1=10, s1=1 -> output 0.
error_types_caught: wrong handling of n=1 in tree traversal

boundary.description: All ceiling heights extremely small (1) and miners large (1e9), but only one miner can be placed after raising. n=3, tree 1-2, 1-3, k=3. Only possible if we raise a node and place one miner there, but two miners cannot be placed because other nodes still have min=1. So answer -1.
boundary.test_values: h_i all 1, s_j all 1e9, k=n=3. Raising any node only makes that node's own min large, but its subtree's other nodes still have min=1. So only one miner can be placed, thus impossible -> -1.
error_types_caught: assuming raising a node affects entire subtree
incorrectly allowing multiple miners to use same raised node

adversarial.description: Chain tree of length n=1000, where raising a specific deep node (the leaf) is optimal. Naive solution might try raising every node and recompute matching from scratch, leading to O(n^2).
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that recompute minima and matching for each candidate node individually instead of using efficient incremental update.
adversarial.example_input:
1000
(heights: first 999 nodes 10, last node 1)
(edges: chain 1-2, 2-3, ...)
500
(s_j: 499 miners height 5, one miner height 100)
adversarial.why_effective: Naive O(n^2) solutions will timeout on n=1000? Actually n=1000 is small but we can scale to 100000. The pattern: many nodes have high min_on_path except a bottleneck near the root. Raising the leaf only helps that leaf, not others. So we need to check if raising a node deep in chain can place the tall miner. The correct answer is raising the leaf from 1 to 100 (increment 99) to place the tall miner, and the other miners can be placed elsewhere. If we recompute for each node, O(n^2) is heavy.
error_types_caught: incorrectly assuming raising deeper nodes affect ancestors

adversarial.description: Tree where many nodes have identical min_on_path values, causing greedy matching to assign miners incorrectly if not careful about tie-breaking. Example: star tree with root height 5, all leaves height 10, and miners with heights [6,6,...,6] (many 6's). The min_on_path for leaves is min(5,10)=5, so all leaves have value 5. If we raise the root to 6, all leaves become 6, and all miners can be placed. But if we try to assign miners to leaves without considering the order, it might fail. Also, if we raise a leaf, only that leaf becomes 10, others remain 5, so only one miner can be placed. The correct answer is raising root by 1 (increment 1). Naive algorithms might test raising each leaf and think it's impossible, missing the root.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits greedy matching that doesn't consider global effect of raising internal nodes.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive greedy algorithm might try to match the smallest miners first to the smallest min_on_path values. Initially, all leaves have min_on_path=5, so no miner can be placed (since s_j=6 > 5). The algorithm might then test raising each cave individually. If it raises a leaf, the leaf's min becomes 10, so one miner (6) can be placed there, but the other three miners cannot be placed (others still 5). So it would output -1, missing the possibility of raising root by 1.
error_types_caught: greedy matching that doesn't account for multiple miners benefiting from a single raise
failing to consider raising internal nodes

key_coverage_gaps: Trees with multiple bottlenecks requiring raise of a node that affects many miners
Cases where binary search on answer is needed but naive linear search fails
Large k equal to n with all heights distinct

adversarial.description: Costs arranged so that greedy selection of cheapest from both category leads to higher total cost.
adversarial.attack_vector: Make both-category decorations expensive, but only a few are needed. Naive greedy might pick many cheap from both unnecessarily, or might skip both and pick expensive singles.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive algorithm that always picks cheapest items first might take both from both (cost 100+1) and then need 1 more M-only and 1 more A-only (cost 1+1) total 103, but actually better to take only 1 from both (cost 100) and then 2 M-only and 2 A-only? Wait m=4, k=2. Options: 1 both + 2 M-only + 1 A-only = 100+1+1+1=103, or 0 both + 2 M-only + 2 A-only? But there are only 2 M-only? Actually M-only: decorations 4,5,6? Wait ids: third line: 2 decorations for Masha: 1 and 2. Fourth line: 2 for Arkady: 2 and 3. So categories: both: 2 (cost 1); M-only: 1 (cost 100); A-only: 3 (cost 1); none: 4,5,6 (cost 1 each). So minimum is 0 both + 2 M-only? But only one M-only (id1 cost100) so need 2 from M? Not possible. So best: 1 both (id2 cost1) + 1 M-only (id1 cost100) + 2 A-only? But only one A-only (id3 cost1) and then need one more from none (cost1) total 1+100+1+1=103. But answer should be 104? Actually example output 104? Let's recalc: m=4, k=2. Must have at least 2 liked by Masha: among chosen, at least 2. Similarly for Arkady. Options: take both (id2) gives 1 for each. Then need 1 more Masha-liked and 1 more Arkady-liked. Masha-liked: id1 (cost100) is M-only. Arkady-liked: id3 (cost1) is A-only. Already have 3 items, need 4th: cheapest remaining is any none (cost1). Total=1+100+1+1=103. Alternative: take both (id2) and also take id1 (Masha) and id3 (Arkady) and then another both? Only one both. So 103. But answer in example is 104? Maybe I mis-assigned costs. Let me adjust: make costs: both: 100, M-only: 1,1, A-only: 1, none: 1. So take both: 100, then need 2 Masha-liked: but only 2? Actually M-only: 2 items cost 1 each. Then need 2 Arkady-liked? Only 1 A-only? Not enough. So must take both: 100, then 1 M-only (1), 1 A-only (1), and then need one more Masha-liked? Actually we already have 2 Masha-liked (both and M-only) so need 0 more. Arkady: both and A-only give 2, so need 0 more. Then we have 3 items, need 4, so add cheapest none (1). Total=100+1+1+1=103. But 104? Let me re-evaluate: maybe k=2, we need at least 2 liked by each. With both (1), we need at least 1 more from each. So total from both and required singles: 1 (both) + 1 (M-only) + 1 (A-only) = 3, then add cheapest from any to reach m=4: cheapest none (1) -> total 103. But maybe there is a better: take 0 both, then need 2 M-only and 2 A-only. But only 2 M-only and 1 A-only -> impossible. So 103 is min. But example says 104? Let me adjust: make both cost 100, M-only two items cost 2 and 2, A-only one cost 1, none cost 1. Then take both 100, M-only one of 2, A-only 1, none 1 = 104. That works. So this pattern catches algorithms that don't consider the trade-off between using expensive both vs cheap singles.

adversarial.description: Many expensive both decorations, but only need few; many cheap singles. Naive algorithm might unnecessarily take many expensive both.
adversarial.attack_vector: Both category has many items but high cost, M-only and A-only have many cheap items. Optimal solution uses few or no both items.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive algorithm that iterates over number of both items might incorrectly pick too many both because it sees many available. But optimal uses 0 both: need 2 M-only (e.g., 4,5 cost 1 each) and 2 A-only (6,7 cost 1 each) and one more cheapest from any (any 1), total 5 items with cost 5? Wait m=5, need 2 from each, with 0 both: need 2 M-only and 2 A-only (4 items) and one extra from none or any, cheapest none (cost1) total 5. So 5. But example output 7? Let's compute: M-only: ids 4,5 cost 1 each, A-only: ids 6,7 cost 1 each, both: ids 1,2,3 cost 100 each, none: 8,9,10 cost 1 each. To get 2 Masha-liked: could take 2 from both (cost 200) but also 2 from M-only (cost 2) or 1 from both and 1 from M-only. Option 0 both: take 2 M-only, 2 A-only, and 1 extra (any none) cost 5. So answer 5, not 7. Let me adjust: make M-only and A-only each have only 1 cheap item? Actually to make it tricky, maybe both category has many but not enough singles. For example, M-only has 2 cheap but A-only has only 1 cheap. Then we need at least 1 both. Let's design: n=10, costs: both: 100,100,100; M-only: 1,1; A-only: 1; none: 1,1,1,1. m=5, k=2. Required: at least 2 liked by each. If we take 0 both, need 2 M-only (2) and 2 A-only, but only 1 A-only, impossible. So we need at least 1 both. Options: 1 both (100) + 1 M-only (1) + 1 A-only (1) + 2 cheapest (1,1) = 104. Could also 2 both (200) + 0 M-only + 0 A-only + 3 cheapest (1,1,1)=203, or 1 both + 2 M-only + 0 A-only? But need 2 Arkady-liked: if we have 1 both, we need 1 more Arkady-liked, so we must take at least 1 A-only. So minimal is 104. So answer 104. This pattern catches algorithms that might mis-allocate when singles are insufficient.
error_types_caught: wrong answer due to incorrect enumeration of required items

key_coverage_gaps: Cases with large number of both and singles with varied costs

Cases with very large costs triggering overflow

adversarial.why_effective: Helistic DP O(N*M) might still be fine, but if solving per column with Gaussian elimination O(M^3) it fails. Also tests boundary handling at edges.

adversarial.why_effective: Expected number of steps can be very large; iterative methods may accumulate errors if not careful.

Maximum values: n=100000, k=10^9, all wi=10000.
k=1, varying n and wi to test slot computation when each pocket holds exactly 1 pebble.
boundary.test_values: k=1, n=1..5, wi=1 each
error_types_caught: incorrect ceil division for small values

boundary.description: Single type with a large number of pebbles, testing that both pockets can be used for same type.
error_types_caught: assuming only one pocket per day for a type

adversarial.description: Multiple types that each require multiple slots, testing the correct combination of slots across days. Designed to catch solutions that sum individual days (ceil(wi/(2k))).
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits the difference between sum of individual days and actual days due to leftover capacity when combining types.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive: individual days: ceil(12/10)=2, ceil(1/10)=1 each -> sum 4, but correct is 3 because slots: ceil(12/5)=3, ceil(1/5)=1 each, total 5, days=3.

adversarial.description: Edge case where total pebbles divided by (2k) gives a lower bound but is not achievable due to type mixing constraints. Targets solutions that use total pebbles / (2k) directly.
adversarial.attack_vector: Uses a combination of a large type and small types that require extra slots beyond what the total pebbles count suggests.
adversarial.why_effective: Total pebbles =13, 2k=10, ceil(13/10)=2, which matches; but a more extreme case: n=4, k=5, w=[12,1,1,1] -> total=15, 2k=10, ceil=2, but correct slots: 3+1+1+1=6, days=3. So this pattern can be extended to show failure.
error_types_caught: using sum_{wi} / (2k) without considering slot constraints

key_coverage_gaps: Cases with extremely small k (k=1) and large n
Cases where many types have wi just above k causing multiple slots
Cases with alternating large and small wi

adversarial.description: Test case that exploits incorrect modulo handling for negative numbers in languages like C++.
adversarial.attack_vector: Use a permutation where (b_pos - shift) becomes negative for some shift, which if not handled correctly (e.g., using % in C++) yields wrong result.
adversarial.why_effective: For shift 2, value 3 has b_pos=1, shift=2, so b_pos - shift = -1. In C++, -1 % 3 = -1, leading to incorrect new position. A correct solution adds n before modulo.

adversarial.description: Test case with identical permutations to ensure zero distance is found for the first shift and other shifts are computed correctly.
adversarial.attack_vector: When a and b are identical, the distance is 0 only for shift 1 (original). Some naive solutions might miss the zero or miscount shifts.
adversarial.why_effective: For shift 1, distance 0. For other shifts, distances are non-zero and symmetric. This tests that the minimal distance is correctly computed when zero exists.

key_coverage_gaps: Large n with all identical values? Not possible in permutations.
Very large n with specific symmetry? not required.

boundary.description: Smallest n (m=1, n=2) with t=0. Verifies identity transformation.
boundary.test_values: m=1, n=2, t=0 (minimum t). p can be any value; using p=2 for simplicity.

boundary.description: Maximum m (20) with t=1 and p even (4) to test division by n (2^20) mod p where no inverse exists. Many solutions fail.
boundary.test_values: m=20, n=1048576, t=1, p=4 (a power of 2). b and e0 chosen arbitrarily.
boundary.example_output: Expected output should be computed modulo 4. For b=[1,0,...,0], transformation is identity, so output equals e0 mod 4.
error_types_caught: assumption of modular inverse of n
using WHT without handling non-coprime p

boundary.description: Extreme t=1e18 with p=2 (smallest p). Tests exponentiation modulo even number and handling of large exponent.
boundary.test_values: m=2, n=4, t=10^18, p=2. b and e0 chosen so that output is non-trivial.

adversarial.description: p even and not coprime to n. Many implementations assume modular inverse of n exists.
adversarial.attack_vector: p even, e.g., p=2,4,8,10. The modular inverse of n (power of 2) does not exist mod p.
adversarial.why_effective: Standard WHT approach requires dividing by n mod p. If p is even, division is impossible, leading to incorrect result or runtime error.

adversarial.description: All b[i]=0. This makes transformation matrix zero for any t>=1. Naive solutions may still compute incorrectly due to exponentiation of zero.
adversarial.attack_vector: b array all zeros leads to all eigenvalues zero. For t>=1, e_t is zero vector. But t=0 case must be handled.
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions that compute eigenvalues via WHT may incorrectly handle 0^t (especially 0^0 for t=0). Also, some may forget to check for zero matrix.

adversarial.description: Huge t with p prime but eigenvalues may overflow during exponentiation if not using fast exponentiation mod p.
adversarial.attack_vector: t=10^18 forces iterative exponentiation O(t) to TLE. Also tests modular exponentiation correctness.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that simulate t steps will timeout. Solutions using binary exponentiation must handle exponent modulo (p-1) if applying Fermat's little theorem incorrectly, but here p is prime but not related to eigenvalues. So proper exponentiation is needed.

key_coverage_gaps: Testing with p having small factor 2 that is not coprime to n is critical.
Large t with p=2 (minimum) is not covered by other patterns.
b all zero case is covered but ensure t=0 also tested.
Need to ensure solutions handle non-prime p correctly.

Actually if u<v, then u>=v-1 is only true if u=v-1 (adjacent). So only adjacent pairs satisfy? Wait, check: For u=1, v=3: ds[1]=0, dt[3]=997? For u=1, v=2: existing edge, not counted. For u=1, v=3: fails. So no new pair satisfies? Actually pairs like (2,4): ds[2]=1, dt[4]=996 => Sum=1+1+996=998 <999 -> fails. adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that use integer arithmetic might mistake strict vs non-strict inequality. The condition uses >=, not >.
adversarial.why_effective: The graph is path 1-2-3-4-5. s=2, t=4. Distances: ds: [?,0,1,2,3] actually from 2: to 1:1, to 2:0, to 3:1, to 4:2, to 5:3. dt from 4: to 1:3, to 2:2, to 3:1, to 4:0, to 5:1. d(s,t)=2. (1,4): ds[1]=1, dt[4]=0 => 1+1+0=2 >=2; ds[4]=2, dt[1]=3 => 2+1+3=6>=2 => valid. (1,5): ds[1]=1, dt[5]=1 => 1+1+1=3>=2; ds[5]=3, dt[1]=3 => 3+1+3=7>=2 => valid. (2,4): ds[2]=0, dt[4]=0 => 0+1+0=1 <2 => invalid. (2,5): ds[2]=0, dt[5]=1 => 0+1+1=2>=2; ds[5]=3, dt[2]=2 => 3+1+2=6>=2 => valid. (3,5): ds[3]=1, dt[5]=1 => 1+1+1=3>=2; ds[5]=3, dt[3]=1 => 3+1+1=5>=2 => valid. So valid pairs: (1,3),(1,4),(1,5),(2,5),(3,5) = 5. Wait (1,4) is valid? Yes. But we also need to count only non-edges: So 5. But example output above says 3? I made mistake. Let's recalc: Actually (3,5) is valid? Yes. So 5. But I'll correct: In this path, s=2,t=4, d=2. The only invalid non-edge is (2,4) because that would create path 2-4 direct distance 1 <2. So all other non-edges are valid. There are total possible non-edges = n(n-1)/2 - m = 10 - 4 = 6. One invalid, so answer=5. So example output should be 5. But I had 3 earlier mistakenly. So correct example output is 5. This pattern tests borderline where condition with equality matters: for (1,4), ds[1]+1+dt[4]=1+1+0=2 which equals d, so it's valid. Solutions that use > instead of >= might miss it.

adversarial.description: Large n with many zeros and a single positive that gives just enough coins for some zeros but not all.

adversarial.description: Array with all ones and zeros mixed, where zeros outnumber coin supply only slightly.

But a naive solution might think that by reducing ones to 1 (no change) they gain nothing, so must remove all zeros (3). But if they incorrectly think they can reduce ones to 0? No, ideal requires >=1. So they might think they can use ones to provide coins by reducing them to 0? That's invalid. So they might underestimate removals.

adversarial.description: Maximum digits (18) with many distinct digits and m=100. Stress test for DP memory (2^18 * 100 states) and time (O(d * 2^d * m)).

adversarial.description: Input with repeated digits leading to many identical permutations

boundary.description: Minimum n (2), single edge. p order: only two vertices: source (vertex 1) and other. Since source distance 0, it must be popped last, so p[0] must be vertex 2. Test extreme small graph.

boundary.description: Maximum n (100000) as a tree (m=n-1). Tests linear chain or star. p order must be decreasing distance from source. In a tree, distances are unique typically, so p is fixed by weights. Boundary on size.

boundary.description: p order with ties (equal distances). Since max-heap breaks ties by larger vertex index first, p can have blocks of decreasing vertex indices. Test that solution handles ties correctly.
boundary.test_values: Graph where many vertices have the same distance from source, e.g., star graph with center 1 and leaves 2..n with equal edge weights. Distances: d(1)=0, d(2)=w, ..., d(n)=w. So all leaves have same distance. The popped order should be leaves in decreasing vertex index: n, n-1, ..., 2, then source 1. Input p = [n, n-1, ..., 2, 1] and expect feasible.

adversarial.description: Impossible p: p[0] is source vertex 1. Since source distance 0 is smallest, it must be popped last. So p starting with 1 indicates impossibility.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits the property that source (vertex 1) has distance 0 and must be the last popped vertex. A naive solution might not check this and try to assign weights.
adversarial.why_effective: The ordering p = [1,2,3] places source first, but source should be last. Even if weights are assigned, the max-heap would pop larger distances first; source distance 0 is smallest, so it cannot be first. Immediate impossibility.

adversarial.description: Contradiction in distances: Suppose p order implies that d(u) > d(v) but the graph structure forces d(u) <= d(v) given edge weight constraints. For example, a path with two edges: u and v are both neighbors of source? Actually consider triangle inequality. In a graph, if there is a short path from source to u via v, then d(u) cannot be too large relative to d(v). A naive solution might assign arbitrary weights without considering these constraints.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits necessary conditions from triangle inequality: for any edge (u,v), |d(u)-d(v)| <= w(u,v). But since w>=1, we need d(u) and d(v) to be at least 1 apart. If positions in p are close but vertices are far apart in graph, might be impossible.
adversarial.why_effective: There is a path from 1 to 3 via 2, so d(3) >= d(2)+1 > d(2). Hence d(3) > d(2), so in max-heap order, 3 should be popped before 2. But p has 2 before 3, so impossible. This checks whether the solution verifies the necessary condition that along any path, distances are strictly increasing from source.

adversarial.description: Large tie-breaking scenario: many vertices have same distance, requiring correct handling of vertex indices. Also potential for impossible if tie-breaking order is not decreasing vertex indices.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits the tie-breaking rule: for equal distances, larger vertex popped first. If p has a block of equal distances but not in decreasing vertex order, it's impossible. Example: star graph with source 1 and leaves 2,3,4 with equal weight on all edges. Distances all equal to w. Max-heap order should be 4,3,2 then 1. If p is [2,3,4,1] (increasing vertex index among leaves), it's impossible.
adversarial.why_effective: Distances of leaves are equal. In max-heap, tie-breaking by larger vertex index, so leaves should be popped in decreasing order: 4,3,2. But p has 2,3,4. This violates the tie-breaking rule. Naive solution might ignore tie-breaking or not enforce it strictly.
error_types_caught: overlooking necessary condition for equal distances

error_types_caught: incorrect greedy decision on equal costs

adversarial.description: Only PS/2 mice but both computers exist. Some solutions might incorrectly assign USB-only mice (none) and waste both computers, but here both computers can use PS/2 mice.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits assumption that both computers can only be used after filling specific ones. Actually both should be used for either type.
adversarial.why_effective: If algorithm first assigns USB mice to USB-only and both, then PS/2 mice to PS/2-only, it might assign the cheapest USB mouse (5) to both computer, leaving only 2 PS/2 mice for PS/2-only and both? Actually there is one PS/2-only and one both. The best: assign USB mouse to USB-only (cost 5), then two PS/2 mice to PS/2-only and both (cost 6+7=13), total 3 computers cost 18. But if algorithm mistakenly uses both for USB first, it might assign USB to both (cost5) and then PS/2 to PS/2-only (cost6) and no mouse for remaining both? That would be 2 computers only. So it catches mistakes in order of assignment.
error_types_caught: not considering both ports for both types

key_coverage_gaps: Cases with only one type of mouse available for many computers
Cases where both computers are more than sum of USB and PS/2 mice
Cases with very large costs causing overflow if using 32-bit int

random.description: Small random intervals with exactly one valid removal
random.generation_strategy: Generate 4-5 intervals where exactly one interval overlaps with all others, which are mutually disjoint. Output indices of that single interval.

random.description: Large random intervals (n=5000) with varying overlap
random.generation_strategy: Generate 5000 intervals with random l and r in [1,1e6]. Ensure some intervals are valid removals by construction (e.g., make a few intervals that overlap with all conflicting pairs). Output can be computed by reference solution.

boundary.description: Single interval (n=1)
boundary.test_values: n=1, single interval. Output should be 1 and its index.

boundary.description: All intervals non-overlapping (touching allowed)
boundary.test_values: n=5000, intervals sorted and touch exactly (r_i = l_{i+1} - 1? Actually touching: r_i = l_{i+1}). All intervals are valid removals. Output all indices.

boundary.description: All intervals overlapping (clique)
boundary.test_values: n=5000, all intervals contain a common point. No single removal works. Output 0.
error_types_caught: failing to detect that no removal works in clique

boundary.description: Touching intervals (chain of non-overlapping)
boundary.test_values: n=5000, intervals like [1,2], [2,3], [3,4], ... [5000,5001]. All non-overlapping, all valid.
error_types_caught: false positive overlap detection when l_i == r_j

adversarial.description: Single critical interval overlapping all other mutually disjoint intervals
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive O(n^3) might check removal of each interval, but if many intervals, O(n^3) too slow. Efficient solution must correctly identify the critical interval.
adversarial.target_error: TLE or WA if algorithm incorrectly identifies multiple intervals as valid
adversarial.why_effective: Only interval 1 overlaps with all others; others are disjoint. Removing any other leaves interval 1 still overlapping with some. Algorithm must find minimal set of intervals that cover all overlapping pairs.
error_types_caught: incorrect logic for finding valid intervals
failing to identify unique critical interval

adversarial.description: All intervals overlap (clique) - no valid removal
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive might try to remove any interval and check, but if clique, all removals fail. Efficient algorithm must detect that overlapping pairs graph is a complete graph, thus no single removal works.
adversarial.why_effective: All intervals share common point, so any two intersect. No single removal leaves all non-overlapping. Misguided algorithm might think removing a middle interval works.

adversarial.description: Chain of overlapping intervals (each overlaps next, no other)
adversarial.attack_vector: Overlap graph is a path. No single removal breaks all edges. Naive might output some intervals that are articulation points in the interval graph, but still removal leaves edges among remainder.
adversarial.why_effective: Overlapping pairs: (1,2), (2,3), (3,4). Removing any single interval leaves at least one overlapping pair (e.g., remove 2, left with 1,3,4 -> (3,4) still overlap). Correct output should be 0.
error_types_caught: incorrectly identifying valid intervals in a path
failing to check all pairs after removal

key_coverage_gaps: specific large n with all intervals having same start/end
intervals with maximum range size (1e6) and many pairs

random.description: Small random test with small n, l, t for manual verification and debugging.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n random distinct positions in [0, l-1], sort them. Use small n (≤10), l (≤20), t (≤10). Compute expected value by enumerating all 2^n direction assignments and simulating collisions exactly, then compare.

random.description: Large random test with n close to 1e6, l and t up to 1e9 to stress test performance and numerical stability.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=500000 random distinct positions uniformly in [0, l-1], sort. Use l=1e9, t=1e9. Expected result computed from O(n log n) algorithm (two pointers). Check for TLE, O(n^2) worst-case, and floating-point errors.

boundary.description: Only one runner on the track. Expected number of bumpings is 0.
boundary.test_values: n=1, any l, t. Minimal n. Checks if code handles n=1 without errors.

boundary.description: Smallest possible circle (l=1) so all runners start at same point? But positions must be distinct and < l, so only possible if n=1. For n>1, l must be > n. So l=2, n=2, t=1e9 large relative to l causing many collisions.
boundary.test_values: n=2, l=2, t=1e9. Two runners at positions 0 and 1. They will collide many times. Tests handling of large number of collisions per pair (t/l large).

adversarial.description: Runners evenly spaced around the circle. This pattern maximizes collisions in expectation because many pairs are at optimal distances.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive O(n^2) simulation or inefficient counting. Also tests correctness of two-pointer or binary search solutions with many equally-spaced points.
adversarial.why_effective: Even spacing leads to many pairs with collisions; a O(n^2) algorithm would time out. Also, the two-pointer solution must handle modulo arithmetic correctly.
error_types_caught: wrong collision count due to modulo errors

adversarial.description: Time t is an exact multiple of circle length l. This creates edge cases where collisions happen exactly at boundaries (e.g., after full laps).
adversarial.attack_vector: Floating-point precision errors when computing number of collisions using division and ceil/floor.
adversarial.why_effective: The number of collisions per pair can be integer (t/l = 10). Naive use of floating point may yield 9.9999999 due to precision, leading to wrong floor/ceil and final answer.

key_coverage_gaps: very large t with small l causing many wraps
positions close to l-1 and 0 (wrap-around)
all runners moving same direction (0 collisions)

random.description: Small random test cases with n between 2 and 10, values moderate for manual verification
random.generation_strategy: Generate n uniformly in [2,10]. For each team, generate ti and wi such that 0 ≤ ti ≤ wi ≤ 1000. Ensure first team has a reasonable number of balloons.

random.description: Large random test cases with n up to 300000 and values up to 10^18, stress-test performance and memory
random.generation_strategy: Generate n uniformly in [100000, 300000]. For each team, generate ti and wi uniformly in [0, 10^18] with ti ≤ wi. Use 64-bit integers.
error_types_caught: MLE due to large data structures

boundary.description: Minimum number of teams (n=2), test tie and basic logic
boundary.test_values: n=2, Limak's opponent either above, below, or equal in balloons

boundary.description: Limak has zero balloons initially (t1=0), cannot give any away
boundary.test_values: t1=0, w1 arbitrary (≥0). Other teams have positive balloons.
error_types_caught: division by zero or incorrect handling of zero balloons
assuming Limak can always give balloons

boundary.description: All teams have ti = wi, meaning any additional balloon disqualifies them
boundary.test_values: All ti = wi, so cost = 1 for each team. Limak's initial balloons determine how many he can disqualify.
error_types_caught: greedy not considering equal teams as non-threat

boundary.description: Maximum values for ti and wi (10^18), test overflow and large number handling
boundary.test_values: Values close to 10^18, including edge cases like wi - ti + 1 = 1 or large
error_types_caught: incorrect comparison due to floating point

adversarial.description: Many teams with ti just above Limak's initial t1 and small cost, forcing multiple disqualifications
adversarial.attack_vector: Large number of teams with ti = t1 + 1 and wi = ti + 1, so cost = 2. This requires Limak to disqualify many to improve rank, but each reduces his balloons.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might not consider that after disqualifying some teams, Limak's balloons drop enough that he cannot continue, or they might incorrectly compute the threshold.
error_types_caught: missing update of current balloons after each step

adversarial.description: Teams with ti just below Limak's initial t1 that become ahead after he gives away balloons
adversarial.attack_vector: Initially no team ahead, but disqualifying a cheap team reduces Limak's balloons, causing many behind teams to become ahead and worsen rank.
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions that always try to disqualify the cheapest team without checking if it's beneficial will get a worse rank (3 here). The correct greedy should only disqualify teams that are currently ahead and only when it improves the rank.
error_types_caught: not comparing current best rank with potential new rank
failing to re-evaluate heap after disqualification

key_coverage_gaps: Large n with specific cost distribution (e.g., all costs equal)
Mixed scenario where some teams have ti just above and some just below simultaneously

random.description: Small random test case with few elements and queries, covering basic operations and mixed query types.
random.generation_strategy: Generate array of length n (e.g., 5) with random values in [1,10]. Generate q (e.g., 5) random queries: type 1 with random l,r; type 2 with random p,x.

random.description: Medium random test case with more updates and queries, testing compression and frequent modifications.
random.generation_strategy: Generate array of length n (e.g., 6) with distinct values. Generate q queries alternating between type 1 and type 2, with values from a larger range to test compression.

boundary.description: All array elements are the same value. Tests handling of uniform distributions and missing frequency 1.
boundary.test_values: n=5, all elements equal to 7. Queries include full range, single element, and update to a different value.

boundary.description: Single element array. Tests minimal array size and single element subarray queries.
boundary.test_values: n=1, array has a single value. Queries on that element and update.

adversarial.description: Test with high Mex value by constructing frequencies 1..k. Forces scanning of large range to find Mex.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that assume Mex is small or scan O(sqrt(n)) lazily by making Mex large (e.g., 5 for n=10).
adversarial.why_effective: The Mex of frequencies is 5, requiring scanning up to 5 if using incremental pointer. Naive O(n) per query would be too slow for large n.
error_types_caught: TLE due to O(n) Mex search
incorrect Mex calculation when many frequencies present

adversarial.description: Many updates on the same index with new values, interleaved with queries. Tests update correctness and time travel in Mo's with updates.
adversarial.attack_vector: Frequent changes at a single position cause many state modifications, testing if solution correctly handles version changes and frequency updates.
adversarial.why_effective: Each update changes the frequency distribution drastically. Incorrect handling of updates (e.g., order of applying changes) can lead to wrong Mex.

key_coverage_gaps: Large value compression (1e9) not explicitly tested in examples but covered in generation strategy
Queries with l=r and updates on same index combined

random.description: Small random test case with few boxes (n=5). Useful for verifying correctness of DP and logic.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n between 1 and 10, a_i between 1 and 10, b_i random 0/1, l and r random within [0, total height]. Ensure sum of a_i <= 10000 (automatically).

random.description: Large random test case (n=10000) to stress-test performance and memory usage.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=10000, a_i random between 1 and 10000, b_i random 0/1, l and r random within [0, total height]. Ensure sum of a_i <= 10000 (by generating heights that sum to at most 10000, e.g., using Dirichlet distribution).

boundary.description: Single box, interval at origin. Tests handling of single element and interval boundaries.
boundary.test_values: n=1, l=0, r=0, box height=5, important=1. Bottom at 0, counted.

boundary.description: All boxes unimportant. Convenience always 0 regardless of order.
boundary.test_values: n=3, all b_i=0, any l,r. Should output 0.
error_types_caught: logic errors where important boxes are incorrectly counted

adversarial.description: Narrow interval requiring precise bottom placement. Greedy that picks smallest important boxes fails because they cannot achieve exact bottom.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits algorithms that try to pack small important boxes without considering need for exact cumulative sum to hit a single point interval.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive greedy would attempt to place the three small important boxes, but their bottoms (0,1,2) are outside interval. Only the large important box can be placed at bottom 100 by using the small ones and the unimportant box to reach exact sum 100. Greedy that does not consider this misses the single possible count.

adversarial.description: Interval length zero (single point) and no subset sum can achieve that point. Tests DP's handling of impossible configurations.
adversarial.attack_vector: Algorithms that assume you can always place some important boxes if there are enough small boxes fail when exact height constraints are not met.
adversarial.why_effective: All boxes are important except one unimportant. Subset sums of heights placed before any important box cannot be exactly 3 (since possible sums are 0,2,5,7,10,12). Hence no important box can have bottom at 3. A naive algorithm that does not verify exact sums might incorrectly think it can achieve at least 1 by placing the small unimportant box before some important box, but it cannot reach 3.

key_coverage_gaps: very large interval (l=0, r=total height)
all boxes important with large heights
mixed importance with interval that partially overlaps

random.description: Random small strings with lengths from 2 to 10, random lowercase letters.
random.generation_strategy: Generate two strings s and t of random length between 2 and 10. Ensure s != t. Use random.choice from 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz'.

random.generation_strategy: Generate two strings of random length between 50 and 100, random letters. Ensure distinct.
random.example_input:
s: 'a'*50 + 'b'*50 (but random)
More concrete: s=''.join(random.choice('abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz') for _ in range(100))
t=''.join(random.choice('abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz') for _ in range(50))

boundary.description: Minimum length: both strings are length 1 and different.
boundary.test_values: s and t both length 1, distinct letters

boundary.description: Maximum length: both strings length 100, same multiset but different order, so only swaps needed.
boundary.test_values: s and t both length 100, same frequency of each letter but not identical strings
error_types_caught: incorrect detection when lengths equal but multiset same
false positive for automaton or both

boundary.description: Maximum length difference: s length 100, t length 1. If t character exists in s, automaton; else need tree.
boundary.test_values: s length 100, t length 1
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of length difference extremes
miss that removal only is enough

adversarial.description: t is a subsequence of s but not an anagram, so automaton only. Tests if algorithm incorrectly prioritizes anagram check over subsequence.
adversarial.attack_vector: Common mistake: check if anagram first, leading to array output when automaton is correct.
adversarial.why_effective: t is a subsequence (indices 1,2,4 or 1,3,4) so removal only. But multiset of s has extra 'b', so if algorithm checks anagram first, it might output 'array' (since multiset different), but actual correct is automaton.
error_types_caught: wrong classification when subsequence possible but not anagram

adversarial.description: Both operations needed: t is not a subsequence, but s contains all characters of t with extra characters and wrong order.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solutions may think it's impossible (need tree) because not subsequence and multiset not equal, missing that both operations can fix.
adversarial.why_effective: t is not a subsequence of s (cannot get 'aec' in order). Multiset of s has extra 'b' and 'd' and order mismatch. So need to remove 'b' and 'd', then swap 'c' and 'e'. Solutions that only check subsequence or anagram will output 'need tree' incorrectly.
error_types_caught: incorrect logic for combining removals and swaps

adversarial.description: Array only but with repeated letters to test correct handling of multiset equality when not subsequence.
adversarial.attack_vector: Common mistake: treat same multiset as automaton if some order condition holds, but here array is needed.
adversarial.why_effective: s and t have same multiset (2a,2b) but t is not a subsequence of s because 'bbaa' requires two b's before a's, but s has all a's first then b's. So only swaps possible. Algorithm might incorrectly output 'automaton' if it checks subsequence using any order? Actually it's not subsequence, so automaton fails. But if algorithm thinks automaton can reorder via removals? No, removals can't reorder. So correct is array.
error_types_caught: wrong detection of subsequence when characters are identical

key_coverage_gaps: Very small lengths (1) are covered; maximum lengths covered; both operations case covered; subsequence check priority covered. Missing: empty strings (not allowed), non-lowercase (not allowed). Also missing case where array only but t is subsequence? Not possible due to problem guarantee. Coverage seems adequate.

random.generation_strategy: n=100000, m=100000, q=100000. Generate words as random strings of length up to 20. Half relations with t=1, half t=2. Ensure no contradictions (by building consistent DSU). Queries random pairs.
random.example_input: (omitted due to size; would be generated programmatically)

boundary.description: Minimum input size n=2, minimal relations and queries
boundary.test_values: n=2, m=1, q=1. Two words. Relations: first synonym, then antonym.
boundary.example_input:
2 1 1
word1 word2
1 word1 word2
query: word1 word2
error_types_caught: Edge case handling for small n

boundary.description: Maximum constraints with a chain of relations to test performance on long path compression
boundary.test_values: n=100000, m=99999, q=0. Words are strings 'w1' to 'w100000'. Relations: all synonyms linking i to i+1, creating a huge DSU set. No queries.
error_types_caught: TLE due to deep find without path compression

boundary.description: All words have maximum length (20) and same prefix, testing string comparison and hashing
boundary.test_values: n=100000, words like 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa1', 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa2', etc. Relations and queries include many same-prefixed words.
boundary.example_input:
100000 1 1
(100000 words of length 20)
1 aaaa...1 aaaa...2
query: aaaa...1 aaaa...3

adversarial.description: Long alternating chain of synonym/antonym to cause deep recursion or stack overflow in DFS-based DSU
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits recursive implementations of find or union that use recursion instead of iterative path compression
adversarial.why_effective: If find uses recursion without tail recursion, the depth can reach n, causing stack overflow for n=1e5. Iterative find or path compression reduces depth.

adversarial.description: Many relations that are contradictory but the contradiction is only detected after many unions, testing that algorithm correctly handles and ignores wrong relations
adversarial.attack_vector: Attempts to confuse the algorithm by adding relations that initially seem consistent but later contradict, checking if the algorithm properly marks them as wrong and ignores them for future relations
adversarial.target_error: WA (wrong answer) by incorrectly accepting a wrong relation or by recording it and causing later relations to be misjudged
adversarial.example_input:
4 5 0
w1 w2 w3 w4
1 w1 w2
1 w2 w3
2 w3 w4
1 w1 w4 (should be wrong because w1 and w4 are opposite via chain)
2 w1 w4 (should be correct after ignoring previous? Actually previous was wrong so ignored, so this antonym is correct)
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might add the wrong relation and then later queries become false. Need to check that the algorithm ignores the wrong relation and doesn't use it to infer others.
error_types_caught: Failure to ignore wrong relation for future inferences

adversarial.description: Many queries with no prior relations, testing that unknown outputs are correctly given
adversarial.attack_vector: Large number of queries (1e5) after zero relations, checking if algorithm can handle many unknown queries efficiently and without false positive
adversarial.target_error: WA or TLE due to unnecessary processing
adversarial.example_input:
2 0 100000
word1 word2
(query word1 word2) repeated 100000 times
adversarial.why_effective: If the algorithm initializes DSU for all words but never uses it, it might still be fast. However, naive solutions that precompute all pairs could TLE. This tests that the algorithm only processes queries lazily or efficiently.

key_coverage_gaps: Random patterns may not cover very deep recursion; adversarial covers that
Boundary covers min/max, but not permutations of many disjoint sets
All patterns assume input words are valid; no need for invalid input

random.description: Random small set of non-overlapping intervals to test basic removal and ordering of remaining numbers.
random.generation_strategy: Generate N=5 random intervals that do not overlap, each between 1 and 1000. Ensure no interval exceeds 1000.

random.description: Random large set of fully overlapping intervals to test handling of many overlapping intervals (stress on removal marking).
random.generation_strategy: Generate N=100 intervals with A and B randomly chosen, allowing heavy overlap. This ensures all numbers from 1 to 1000 are removed multiple times.
error_types_caught: performance issues with naive set operations

boundary.description: No intervals to subtract (N=0). Output should be all 1000 numbers.
boundary.test_values: N=0, the minimal input.
error_types_caught: output format error when count is 1000

boundary.description: Single interval covering the entire range [1,1000]. Output should be empty.
boundary.test_values: A=1, B=1000, covering all numbers.
error_types_caught: incorrect output when result set is empty

boundary.description: Single-element intervals covering the first and last numbers (1 and 1000) plus a middle number.
boundary.test_values: A=B=1, A=B=1000, A=B=500. These test removal of exact endpoints.

boundary.description: Maximum number of intervals (N=100) with all being single-element intervals covering distinct numbers, leaving exactly 900 numbers.
boundary.test_values: N=100, each interval is a distinct number from 101 to 200, leaving the rest.

adversarial.description: Nested overlapping intervals that create complex gaps, e.g., intervals that cover only even numbers or patterns that might confuse merging algorithms.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits incorrect interval merging by providing intervals that overlap in non-trivial ways, causing merged intervals to be incorrect if not careful with boundaries.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive interval merging might combine intervals incorrectly if not handling full coverage correctly; after merging all intervals, the union covers everything, so output should be 0. A buggy merge might leave some numbers.

adversarial.description: Intervals that are all disjoint but placed such that they leave only few numbers remaining, testing the output format with a small non-empty set.
adversarial.attack_vector: Tests the ability to output exactly the remaining numbers in sorted order with correct count, especially when the result set is small (e.g., 1 number).
adversarial.why_effective: Only number 500 remains. A solution that incorrectly handles the boundaries of intervals or makes off-by-one errors might remove 500 or include extra numbers.
error_types_caught: missing numbers in small result set

adversarial.description: Intervals that are given in decreasing order of A and B to test if sorting is assumed. Since input order doesn't matter, this should not affect correct implementation, but a solution that assumes sorted input might fail.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits assumption that intervals are given in increasing order or are sorted.
adversarial.why_effective: If a solution sorts intervals by A and processes in that order, it will still work. But if a solution incorrectly assumes sorted input without sorting, it may produce wrong results. However, since removal is idempotent, order doesn't affect final set. So this tests only poor implementations that depend on order for correctness (e.g., if they use a running pointer).

key_coverage_gaps: Intervals that are out of range (though not allowed by constraints)
Very large number of intervals (N>100) not covered
Non-integer inputs (not applicable)

random.description: Random small test cases for verification, with varying n,m,k (including impossible cases).
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, randomly choose n,m in [0,10] and k in [0,max(n,m)] (if possible) or k outside that range to test impossibility. Also include cases where |n-m| > k and where construction is possible.

random.description: Random large test cases to stress test performance and correctness up to the sum constraints.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n,m each up to 2e5 total sum, and k within appropriate range. Ensure total n+m across test cases does not exceed 2e5.
error_types_caught: TLE due to O(n^2) substring checks
MLE from storing large strings inefficiently

boundary.description: Minimum values: n=m=0 (empty string) and k=0. Also n=0,m>0.
boundary.test_values: n=0,m=0,k=0 (should output empty string or -1? Problem likely expects non-empty? But constraints allow 0. Also n=0,m=5,k=3
error_types_caught: edge case where n or m is zero

boundary.description: Maximum imbalance: k equal to max(n,m) and also k equal to |n-m|.
boundary.test_values: n=0,m=200000,k=200000; n=100000,m=100000,k=100000? Actually max is 100000, but |n-m|=0, so k=100000 is >|n-m| but <=max. Test cases where k = max(n,m) and where k = |n-m|.
error_types_caught: failing to handle single character substring maximum

boundary.description: Large n and m with k exactly between |n-m| and max(n,m).
boundary.test_values: n=100000, m=100000, k=1 (minimum positive) ; also n=200000, m=0, k=1 (but max is 200000, so k=1 possible? Yes, by constructing with at least one one? Actually with m=0, string is all zeros, max balance is 200000, so k=1 impossible because every substring has balance >=1, but max is 200000 >1, so condition fails. So impossible unless k=200000. So careful.
error_types_caught: failing to check that k must be >=1

adversarial.description: Cases where a naive greedy algorithm that builds string with maximum run length equal to k might fail.
adversarial.attack_vector: Construct case where run-length approach constructs a substring with balance > k due to prefix/suffix effects.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive algorithm might produce '0011' (run of two zeros then two ones), but then substring '00' gives balance 2 >1. So correct construction must alternate to keep max balance 1.
error_types_caught: ignoring substring starting from inside a run

adversarial.description: Case where k is small but n and m are both large, testing if solution correctly handles the need for perfect alternation.
adversarial.attack_vector: Large imbalance between n and m with small k.
adversarial.why_effective: With m=0, all zeros, any substring of zeros has balance equal to its length, so max balance is 100, cannot be 1. So impossible. Naive might try to insert ones but m=0 forces no ones.

adversarial.description: Case where k is exactly |n-m| but construction might inadvertently produce a substring with larger balance.
adversarial.attack_vector: Incorrect placement of majority characters causing a local imbalance larger than |n-m|.
adversarial.why_effective: If you put all zeros first, substring '000' gives balance 3>2. So zeros must be distributed to avoid long runs. Correct string might be '0011010' or similar.

key_coverage_gaps: n+m=0 case not fully covered (empty string handling)
exact k = |n-m| with unequal zeros and ones
k=0 when n=m>0 (impossible)?

random.description: Small random test cases with n between 2 and 5, random splits and card orders.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly select n in [2,5], then randomly choose k1 in [1, n-1], randomly permute cards 1..n and assign first k1 to player1, rest to player2. Simulate game with cycle detection until termination or -1.

Better to use a known cyclic example from discussions: n=5, player1: [1,2,3,4], player2: [5]? That ends. adversarial.description: Laptop exactly at flat center (d=0) to test division-by-zero handling.

adversarial.description: Laptop on flat boundary (d=R) to test strict vs non-strict inequality.
adversarial.attack_vector: Using d > R for outside instead of d >= R gives wrong result.
adversarial.why_effective: Common mistake: treat d == R as inside case, leading to non-optimal radius and center.

adversarial.description: Laptop inside flat but far from center, with coordinates not aligned to axes, to test vector direction correctness.
adversarial.attack_vector: Using incorrect direction (e.g., from flat center to laptop instead of vice versa) gives wrong center.
adversarial.why_effective: Easy to swap direction; this test forces correct vector orientation.

adversarial.description: Large R and coordinates near limits to test overflow/wrapping in integer calculations.
adversarial.attack_vector: If using integers without careful casting, (R+d) may exceed int limit? But within 2e5, fine. However, using float, no overflow.
adversarial.why_effective: Large negative coordinates combined with large R can produce intermediate values that might overflow if using fixed-point or int in some languages.
