random.description: Random test cases with small n (up to 10) to verify correctness and lexicographically minimal property.
random.generation_strategy: Generate 5-10 test cases with n between 1 and 10, x between 1 and n. Ensure some with x=1 and some with x>1. For x=1, expected output is identity permutation; for x>1, output -1.

random.description: Random test cases with large n (up to 100000) to test performance and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Generate 3 test cases with n near 100000, x either 1 or a value >1. Ensure large input to test I/O and array handling.

boundary.description: Minimum constraints: n=1, x=1.
boundary.test_values: n=1, x=1. This is the smallest possible input. Output should be [1].

boundary.description: Maximum constraints: n=200000, x=1 (sum of n over test cases ≤ 200000).
boundary.test_values: n=200000, x=1. This tests large output and performance.

boundary.description: x equals n (x>1) – should always be -1 because p[x]=1 requires x=1.
boundary.test_values: Various n, x=n where n>1. E.g., n=5, x=5.

boundary.description: Minimal n>1 with x=1 and x>1.

adversarial.description: Large test case with x=1 but with many test cases to stress I/O and construction.
adversarial.attack_vector: Multiple test cases with large n, all x=1, to test if the program can output identity quickly.
adversarial.example_output: (10 lines of identity permutations for n=20000)
adversarial.why_effective: If the program constructs the permutation inefficiently or uses too many operations, it may TLE.

adversarial.description: Test case with x=1 and n=200000, but with additional test cases to reach sum n limit.
adversarial.attack_vector: Edge of constraint: single test case with n=200000, x=1.
adversarial.why_effective: Large array allocation might cause memory issues if not handled properly.

adversarial.description: Test case where x>1 but n is a multiple of x (or not) to check if any solution mistakenly thinks permutation exists.
adversarial.attack_vector: Check if program incorrectly assumes existence when n%x==0.
adversarial.why_effective: Some naive solutions might think permutation exists if n%x==0, but actual condition is x must be 1.

key_coverage_gaps: Testing with x=1 and n values that are prime or composite
Testing with multiple test cases where sum n approaches limit
Testing with x=1 and very large n to ensure no integer overflow in index

random.description: Small grid with small odd area to verify basic correctness
random.generation_strategy: Choose n and m small (≤5) and s a small odd number. This pattern tests the ability to count crosses correctly on a tiny grid where brute-force verification is easy.

random.description: Moderate grid with arbitrary area to test general counting
random.generation_strategy: Select n,m up to 50 and s random within [1, n*m]. This pattern checks the algorithm on non-trivial sizes where brute force is still feasible for verification but may expose subtle bugs.

random.description: Large grid with large area to stress performance and overflow
random.generation_strategy: Set n=m=500 and pick s close to n*m/2. This pattern pushes the algorithm to handle the maximum constraints and many possible tuples.

boundary.description: Minimum grid size: 1x1
boundary.test_values: n=1, m=1, s=1. The only possible cross is (0,0,0,0,1,1).

boundary.description: Maximum grid size with minimum area
boundary.test_values: n=500, m=500, s=1. Only (0,0,0,0) crosses, so answer = n*m = 250000. Tests correct counting of centers and large output value.
error_types_caught: integer overflow (when using int for count)

boundary.description: Even area input (impossible)
boundary.test_values: s=2 (even) on a large grid. Area of any cross is always odd, so answer must be 0. Tests parity detection.
error_types_caught: parity error (assuming all s are valid)
incorrect area calculation leading to non-zero

adversarial.description: Even area on large grid to force zero detection
adversarial.attack_vector: Parity: the cross area formula always yields an odd number. Solutions that do not check this will output a large non-zero number, causing WA.
adversarial.why_effective: Because area = odd+odd-odd = odd. Naive solutions that iterate over all tuples and compute area may incorrectly count when area is even due to integer division or truncation errors.

adversarial.description: Small odd area on large grid to generate huge count and test overflow
adversarial.attack_vector: Large output value: s=3 on 500x500 grid yields a very large number of crosses (potentially > 2^31). Solutions using 32-bit integers will overflow.
adversarial.why_effective: The number of centers is 250k, and for each, many (a,b,c,d) combos produce area 3. The total count easily exceeds 2^31. 32-bit overflow leads to WA.

key_coverage_gaps: area values that are products of two small odd numbers
cases with a=b=c=d=0 but different centers
cases where one rectangle dominates (a or c large)

random.description: Small random test case for manual verification
random.generation_strategy: Generate n between 1 and 10, k between 1 and n, and a random string of n uppercase letters. Compute optimal answer using greedy sorting of frequencies.

random.description: Medium random test case with varied frequencies
random.generation_strategy: Generate n between 10 and 100, k between 1 and n, and a random string ensuring some letters have high frequency. Use typical random generator.

boundary.description: Minimum k (k=1) with distinct letters
boundary.test_values: k=1, any n; answer should always be 1 regardless of letter chosen.

boundary.description: Maximum k (k=n) with all same letter
boundary.test_values: k=n, all letters same; answer should be n^2.

adversarial.description: Unsorted frequencies causing naive alphabetical processing to give suboptimal result
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that process letters in fixed order (e.g., A to Z) without sorting frequencies.
adversarial.why_effective: If the algorithm iterates letters in alphabetical order, it will take 5 from A first (instead of 10 from B), leading to total 50 instead of optimal 100.

adversarial.description: Oversubscription from a large frequency if algorithm subtracts full frequency instead of min(freq, remaining)
adversarial.attack_vector: Triggers negative remaining value or incorrect sum when algorithm naively subtracts entire frequency.
adversarial.why_effective: If the algorithm subtracts the full frequency (10) from the first letter when remaining is 5, remaining becomes -5, leading to incorrect subsequent calculations.

key_coverage_gaps: very large n (1e5) with k nearly n
all distinct letters with varying k
single letter case (n=1, k=1)

random.description: Random small test cases for verification of correctness and basic functionality
random.generation_strategy: Generate random k between 1 and 10, pa and pb between 1 and 10. Use brute force or known correct solution to compute expected value for verification.

random.description: Random medium-sized test cases with moderate ranges
random.generation_strategy: Generate random k between 50 and 200, pa and pb between 1 and 1000. Test DP performance and correctness.

boundary.description: Minimum value of k (k=1) with various pa and pb
boundary.test_values: k=1, pa and pb at extremes (1 and 1e6) to test base case behavior

boundary.description: Maximum value of k (k=1000) with extreme pa and pb values
boundary.test_values: k=1000, pa=1, pb=1e6 and pa=1e6, pb=1 to stress test large states and modular arithmetic
error_types_caught: time limit due to large DP

boundary.description: Equal probabilities pa=pb
boundary.test_values: pa=pb, e.g., 1, 100, 1000000. Tests symmetry.

adversarial.description: Very large pa relative to pb, causing many 'a's before any 'b'
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive DP that does not handle infinite series for large i will be slow or overflow recursion/stack.
adversarial.why_effective: The process tends to add many 'a's before a 'b', so i can become arbitrarily large. Solutions that iterate i up to a huge number or use recursion without memoization will time out or stack overflow.
error_types_caught: incorrect base case for large i

adversarial.description: Extremely large pb relative to pa, causing immediate stop after one 'b'
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that incorrectly compute expected value when pa is very small may have precision loss or modular division errors.
adversarial.why_effective: With pb huge, probability of adding 'b' is almost 1. Expected 'ab' is just 1 if first char is 'b', but if first is 'a' (rare), then next 'b' gives 'ab'. Naive solutions might compute dp incorrectly with large inverse values.

adversarial.description: k=1000 with pa=pb=1, check for moderate but tricky recurrence
adversarial.attack_vector: Some solutions may use dp[i][j] with i up to k only, but if i >= k, they may have formula error.
adversarial.why_effective: Standard solution requires handling states where i >= k correctly. Many implementations set a limit on i and use a formula for i >= k. This test checks if that formula is correct.

key_coverage_gaps: Tests with pa and pb both very large (1e6) and k=1000 to stress modulo operations
Tests where pa and pb are not coprime to check gcd reductions in probabilities

random.description: Small random test with n=10, q=3, values and colors randomly generated within small ranges for manual verification.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=10, v_i in [-10,10], c_i in [1,5], q=3 queries with a,b in [-5,5]. Compute expected outputs using brute-force O(2^n) for verification.

random.description: Large random test with n=100000, q=500, values and colors random within full range to stress test performance and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=100000, v_i random in [-100000,100000], c_i random in [1,100000], q=500 queries with a,b random in [-100000,100000]. Expected output computed by efficient solution.
error_types_caught: integer overflow in product or sum

boundary.description: Test with n=1, single ball. All combinations of a,b positive, negative, zero. Also v_i=0.
error_types_caught: wrong decision to include ball when negative profit

boundary.description: All balls have same color. Tests whether DP correctly uses a (same color bonus) or b (for first ball).
boundary.test_values: n=100000, all c_i=1, v_i alternately 100000 and -100000 to maximize complexity.
error_types_caught: wrong update of best for same color
incorrect handling of negative values with same color

boundary.description: All colors distinct. So every ball is first ball of its color, only b matters. Tests global best tracking without color interference.
boundary.test_values: n=100000, c_i=i, v_i random. Query with large positive b to ensure selection of all positive values.

boundary.description: Large negative a and b. All values negative. Optimal is empty sequence (answer 0).
boundary.test_values: n=100000, v_i=-1, a=-100000, b=-100000. Sum would be negative, but answer should be 0.
error_types_caught: integer overflow when adding large negative numbers

adversarial.description: Alternating colors to force many color changes. Tests efficiency and correctness of second-best tracking when same color appears with large gaps.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits poor implementation of second-best color update: for each ball, the best dp for its color might not be updated correctly when the previous best is from the same color but separate occurrence.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that only keep one best per color may fail when same color appears later with a better value but previous best was from the same color and cannot be used consecutively due to negative a? Actually a=1 positive, so consecutive same color is beneficial. The correct answer: choose all balls: 10+9+8+7+6+5 = 45. But a poorly implemented DP might miss updating after seeing color 1 again because it might incorrectly use old best from same color that includes previous ball of same color? The trick is to maintain two best colors globally. This pattern tests if the algorithm correctly handles multiple occurrences of same color.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect second-best logic
incorrect handling of same color repeat

adversarial.description: Large positive a but negative v_i. Only the first ball of each color might be chosen due to b being smaller. Tests decision to skip negative values even with large same-color bonus.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits greedy solutions that always include a ball if it increases sum, ignoring that later same-color balls may have negative value and reduce total.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive DP might incorrectly choose both balls of color 1: first ball value -1000, second ball value -1000 but with bonus a=1000, so second gives -1000*1000?? Actually formula: if same as previous, add v*a; else v*b. With b=-1, a=1000. For color 1: first ball (beginning) adds v1*b = (-1000)*(-1)=1000. Second ball (same color) adds v2*a = (-1000)*1000 = -1000000, total negative. So optimal is to take only first ball of color 1? But then color 2 first ball gives 1*(-1)=-1, so not taken. So best is just first ball of color 1: 1000. Actually answer should be max(0,1000)=1000. But some might erroneously take both due to large a.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect DP update order
overlooking negative v_i with large a

adversarial.description: Large n with many colors and repeated pattern to cause integer overflow in 32-bit if using int.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits use of 32-bit integers for sum or product.
adversarial.example_output: null (too large to compute here, but expect large positive number)
adversarial.why_effective: The sum can be up to n*|v|*|a| = 1e5 * 1e5 * 1e5 = 1e15, requiring 64-bit. Using int will overflow.

key_coverage_gaps: negative a,b combined with negative v_i
all colors same but v_i large magnitude mixture
q=500 with extreme a,b

random.description: Small random test cases with diverse configurations to verify basic correctness.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random n and m between 1 and 10, a_i between 1 and 100, b_j between 1 and 20. Compute expected output by brute-force game simulation (or using the derived formula).

random.description: Large random test cases to stress test performance and verify O((n+m) log max) solution.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n and m up to their maximum (2e5 each, sum over test cases also bounded), a_i and b_j up to 1e6. Use formula to compute outcome.

boundary.description: Single element arrays: n=1 and m=1. Test extremes of divisibility.
boundary.test_values: n=1,m=1 with a1 divisible by b1 (Alice wins), not divisible (Bob wins).

boundary.description: All a_i divisible by all b_j (a= n, b=0). Alice always wins because she has more exclusive moves.
boundary.test_values: n large, all a_i are multiples of lcm(b) or simply set b_j to 1 so all a_i divisible by all b.

boundary.description: No a_i divisible by any b_j (a=0, b=n). Bob always wins.
boundary.test_values: n large, all a_i coprime to all b_j, e.g., b_j all even and a_i all odd.

boundary.description: Equal exclusive counts with varying shared counts: a == b, test parity of shared.
boundary.test_values: Construct cases where a=b=0,1,2 with c=0,1,2 to verify parity rule.

adversarial.description: Large shared pool where naive count comparison fails. Exploit that with a=b, outcome depends on c parity.
adversarial.attack_vector: Target solutions that only compare exclusive counts without considering parity of shared moves.
adversarial.why_effective: Here a=b=0? Actually, all a_i are divisible by some but not all? Let's compute: a1=6 divisible by 2, not by 5 => shared. a2=15 divisible by 5, not by 2 => shared. So a=0,b=0,c=2. Since a=b and c even, Bob wins. But a naive rule that says Alice wins if c>0 would fail.

adversarial.description: Case where exclusive counts are very large but equal, with one shared. Forces correct handling of large numbers.
adversarial.attack_vector: Performance and overflow when computing gcd or lcm over large arrays.
adversarial.example_input:
1
100000 2
<50000 numbers that are all multiples of both b, 50000 numbers that are multiples of none>
2 3
adversarial.why_effective: Computing all divisibility relations naively O(n*m) will TLE. Need efficient classification using gcd or factorization.

adversarial.description: Alice-only moves count exactly one more than Bob-only moves, with zero shared. Tests if solution correctly handles a>b without shared.
adversarial.attack_vector: Edge case where a = b+1, c=0. Should be Alice win.
adversarial.why_effective: Here a=3 (all divisible by 2), b=0, so a>b, Alice wins. Simple solution might incorrectly think Bob wins if a<=b.

key_coverage_gaps: Test with very large a_i and b_j values (up to 1e6) to check for overflow
Test with repeated values in arrays
Test with m=1 only

random.description: Generate valid paths by random selection of start, peak, and end indices
random.generation_strategy: Pick random s length (5-10), random s. Choose random i, p, k with 0≤i≤p<|s|, 0≤k≤p. Construct t = s[i..p] + reverse(s[k..p-1]) (if k<p) else just s[i..p]. Output s and t, expected YES.
random.example_input:
3
abcde
bcdc
xyz
xy
a
a

random.description: Generate invalid paths by random mismatches or impossible lengths
random.generation_strategy: Generate random s and random t of length ≤ 2|s|-1 but ensure t is not a valid path. E.g., insert a character not in s, or create a string that breaks the pattern. Output s and t, expected NO.
random.example_input:
3
abc
abd
xyz
xzy
a
b

boundary.description: Minimum length: both s and t length 1
boundary.test_values: s length 1, t length 1. Cases: matching and non-matching.

boundary.description: Maximum valid length: t length = 2|s|-1 (full path from leftmost to rightmost and back)
boundary.test_values: s length up to 500, t length = 2|s|-1. Construct s as random, then build t by starting at 0, moving right to end, then left to 0.

boundary.description: t longer than maximum possible (2|s|-1) -> automatically NO
boundary.test_values: t length > 2|s|-1, e.g., |s|=3, t length=6 (max possible is 5).

adversarial.description: Test case where t is the reverse of a substring that is not a substring itself
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that only check if t is a substring of s or of s+s will incorrectly reject valid cases where the path uses left moves only.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive substring check fails because 'edc' is not a substring of 'abcde', but it can be obtained by starting at index 4 and moving left 2 times.

adversarial.description: Test case requiring a specific turning point that is not the midpoint or any symmetric position
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that assume the path is symmetric (e.g., the right part and reverse of left part are equal) will fail on this case.
adversarial.why_effective: t='abab' is obtained from s='abac' by starting at 0, moving right to index 2 (s[2]='a'), then left to index 1 (s[1]='b'). The right part is 'aba', left part reversed is 'b', sum = 'abab'. It is not symmetric.

key_coverage_gaps: No test with very large number of test cases (e.g., 500 cases each small)
No test where s contains repeated characters causing multiple valid paths
No test where t is the same as s but with zero moves? (already covered by boundary_1)

random.description: Uniformly random integers between 1 and 10^9 to test general correctness and performance under typical conditions.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random integer n in [1, 10^9] using a uniform distribution. Repeat for each test case.

random.description: Random numbers with a high digit sum (e.g., all digits 9) to test digit command usage and ensure the player can handle repeated digit operations.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random length L between 1 and 10, then create a number consisting of L random digits 1-9 (not all 0 to avoid leading zero issues), but ensure digit sum is large (e.g., use only 7-9). For example, generate L digits uniformly from 7 to 9 and concatenate.

random.description: Random numbers that are exact powers of 2 or 3 to test division by primes and multiplicative strategies.
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, randomly choose a base (2 or 3) and exponent such that base^exp <= 1e9. Alternatively, generate random integers that are divisible by many small primes.

boundary.description: Minimum value n = 1 to test edge case behavior.
error_types_caught: infinite loops when n is small

boundary.description: Maximum value n = 10^9 to test handling of large numbers.
Powers of 10: 10^k for k=1,...,9 to test digit sum properties and division by 10.

adversarial.description: Large prime numbers near the upper bound to exploit strategies that rely on factorization or division by small primes.
adversarial.attack_vector: Primes have no divisors other than 1 and themselves, making division operations ineffective for reducing the number; forces reliance on add/digit commands, which may be slower.
adversarial.why_effective: If the player's strategy aggressively uses division to reduce large numbers, they may waste operations on primes, leading to command limit exceeded.
error_types_caught: failure to adapt to non-divisible numbers

adversarial.description: Numbers with a large number of trailing zeros (e.g., 10^9) to test the player's handling of digit sum when digits include many zeros.
adversarial.attack_vector: A naive digit sum implementation might be too slow or incorrect for numbers with many zeros repeatedly.
adversarial.why_effective: Digit sum of 1000000000 is 1, but after repeated digit operations (or other operations), the player may miscount or mis-handle zeros, causing wrong final value.

key_coverage_gaps: Very small primes (e.g., 2,3,5) not specifically covered
Numbers that are one more than a power of 2 (e.g., 2^k+1) could be interesting

random.description: Small random graph with few vertices and edges, easy to manually verify connected components in complement graph.
random.generation_strategy: Set n between 1 and 10, m between 0 and min(20, n*(n-1)/2). Generate random unordered pairs of distinct vertices, ensuring no duplicates. Output n and m, then the pairs.

random.description: Larger random graph with n=1000, m=2000, to test performance and correctness on moderate input sizes.
random.generation_strategy: Set n=1000, m=2000. Generate m random unordered pairs of distinct vertices using reservoir sampling or rejection to avoid duplicates. Output n, m, then the pairs.

boundary.description: Minimum n: n=1, m=0. Graph has a single vertex, so one component of size 1.
boundary.test_values: n=1, m=0. This is the smallest possible input.

boundary.description: Maximum n with no missing edges: n=200000, m=0. Graph is complete, so one component of size n.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, m=0. Tests handling of large complete graph.

boundary.description: Maximum n with maximum m: n=200000, m=200000. Random non-edges. Tests memory and performance at upper limits.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, m=200000. Both parameters at maximum allowed values.

adversarial.description: Complement graph is a perfect matching (n even, m=n/2 non-edges forming a matching). The resulting graph is still connected because all other edges exist.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive BFS that iterates over all vertices for each vertex may still pass if implemented poorly, but it tests that the algorithm correctly determines connectivity even when many direct edges are missing.
adversarial.why_effective: A wrong algorithm might incorrectly think that missing edges break the graph into two components of size 2 each, but the actual graph is connected via edges like 1-3, etc.

adversarial.description: One vertex has many non-edges (star pattern). This tests that the algorithm efficiently processes vertices with high non-edge degree without causing O(n^2) behavior.
adversarial.attack_vector: If the algorithm iterates over all vertices for each BFS expansion, it will be O(n^2). The correct algorithm using a set of unvisited vertices and iterating over non-neighbors should handle this in O(m).
adversarial.why_effective: The vertex 1 has degree 3 (non-edges), but the set of unvisited vertices is large. A naive BFS that checks every vertex for adjacency will be slow.

adversarial.description: Graph with no edges (complement of complete graph). All vertices are isolated, so each is a component of size 1. This tests the handling of a degenerate case where the input lists all possible unordered pairs.
adversarial.attack_vector: If the algorithm stores all non-edges, it must handle the maximum number. Also, if it tries to build adjacency lists for each vertex, it may create many entries. This can cause MLE or TLE if not optimized.
adversarial.why_effective: The input has m=n*(n-1)/2, which is the maximum possible for given n. A solution that allocates memory proportional to n + m but inefficiently may run out of memory for n large.

key_coverage_gaps: No pattern specifically tests very small m with large n (e.g., m=1, n large) - this is covered by boundary_2 in a sense; missing pattern for disconnected graph with multiple components (hard to achieve with m constraints)

random.description: Small m with solutions
random.generation_strategy: Pick m from [1, 100] that have solutions (e.g., m=2). Generate random such m.

random.description: Medium m with solutions
random.generation_strategy: Pick m from [100, 1000] that have solutions (e.g., m=100).

random.description: Large m near maximum
random.generation_strategy: Pick m near 100000 that have solutions (e.g., m=100000).

boundary.test_values: m=1, the smallest valid input

boundary.description: Maximum input value m=100000
boundary.test_values: m=100000, the largest valid input

boundary.description: Hole value m=5 (no solution)
boundary.test_values: m=5, a hole where no n exists
error_types_caught: incorrectly outputting 5 numbers for all m

adversarial.description: Hole at m=5
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solutions may assume exactly 5 n's per m, or use formula n=5*m
adversarial.why_effective: For m=5, n=25 gives zeros=6, not 5. Naive algorithm outputs 25-29, but correct is 0.

adversarial.description: Hole at m=11
adversarial.attack_vector: Binary search off-by-one or incorrect zero counting
adversarial.why_effective: Jump at n=50 (zeros 12) and n=49 (zeros 10) skips 11. Naive binary search might find n=49 and incorrectly output 49-53, but zeros not equal.

adversarial.description: Hole at m=29
adversarial.attack_vector: Incorrect handling of large jumps (e.g., at n=125)
adversarial.why_effective: Jump from zeros 28 at n=124 to 31 at n=125 skips 29 and 30. Algorithm using formula n=5*m would output 145-149, but zeros there are 34, not 29.

key_coverage_gaps: m values with no solution near max
very large m causing n > 2^31

random.description: Small random test case for correctness verification. n up to 10, q up to 10.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate n (5-10), k (1 to n), a (5-10), b (1 to a-1), q (5-10). For each query, randomly choose type 1 (update) with d in [1,n] and a_i in [1,10], or type 2 (query) with p in [1, n-k+1]. Ensure at least one query.
error_types_caught: logic errors in computing prefix/suffix sums

random.description: Large random test case for performance stress. n=200000, q=200000.
random.generation_strategy: Set n=200000, k=n/2, a=10000, b=5000, q=200000. Generate queries: 70% type 1 updates with random d in [1,n] and a_i in [1,10000]; 30% type 2 queries with random p in [1, n-k+1]. Ensure at least one query.

boundary.description: Test boundary values for k: k=1 and k=n. Verifies correct handling of repair interval length extremes.
boundary.test_values: k=1 (single day repair) and k=n (entire period repair, then maybe no after-repair days). Since p ranges 1..n-k+1, when k=n, p can only be 1.
boundary.example_output:
0
0
Explanation: With k=5, repair takes all days, so no production. Orders placed but cannot be filled. After update on day 3, still 0.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of zero capacity interval

boundary.description: Test with extreme values of a and b. a=10000, b=1. Also many orders exceeding capacity.
boundary.test_values: a=10000 (max), b=1 (min difference), many orders large to test min function.

adversarial.description: Many updates to the same day to test update aggregation and efficiency.
adversarial.attack_vector: Repeated updates on a single day force the data structure to handle many increments on one index, which could cause overflow if using simple array without proper sum.
adversarial.example_input:
100000 50000 10000 5000 100000
For i in 1..50000: 1 1 1
For i in 50001..100000: 2 1
Note: Actually we need exactly q=200k but here 100k. Let's make 200k: 100k updates to day1, 100k queries. But example size too large. So give small: n=5,k=2,a=10,b=5,q=10: updates: 1 1 1000, 1 1 2000, 1 1 3000; then queries: 2 1, 2 1. Expect: day1 orders=6000, capacity before repair? p=1, repair days1-2, so before repair days? Actually p=1 means repair starts day1, so no before repair days. During repair: days1-2 0, after: days3-5 capacity=10 each, but no orders. So answer=0. But if b=5, day0? No day1 itself is repair, so no production. So answer 0. Works.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that recompute sum from scratch each query will be slow. Also solutions that don't handle multiple updates to same day correctly might miscount.
error_types_caught: TLE due to O(n) per update
wrong accumulation of orders on same day

adversarial.description: Alternating updates and queries to stress the ability to handle frequent query-after-update patterns.
adversarial.attack_vector: Frequent queries after each update force the data structure to keep state consistent and respond quickly.
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions that recompute prefix sums from scratch each time will be slow. Efficient BIT updates are needed.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of multiple queries after updates

adversarial.description: Orders far exceed capacity on many days, testing the min with capacity and sum over large ranges.
adversarial.attack_vector: All orders set to maximum 10000 on all days, and capacity a is also 10000, but b smaller. So before repair, only b can be filled; after repair, all orders filled. This tests correct computation of prefix and suffix sums with large numbers.
adversarial.example_input:
10 3 10000 1 5
1 1 10000
1 2 10000
1 3 10000
1 4 10000
1 5 10000
2 2
 (query p=2). Expected: repair days 2-4. Before repair: day1 capacity=b=1, fill 1. During repair: days2-4 fill 0. After repair: days5-10 capacity=10000 each, orders on day5=10000, so fill 10000. So total=10001.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that don't use min or incorrectly compute sums may overflow 32-bit int (max sum = 200k * 10000 = 2e9, fits in 32-bit signed? 2e9 < 2^31-1=2.147e9, borderline but okay. But with many queries, sum of many such values could exceed if not careful. Actually each query independent. But if they accumulate, might overflow. Use 64-bit recommended.

key_coverage_gaps: Very small n and k combinations
Large number of queries of only type 2
Mix of updates and queries with large ranges

random.description: Small random test with a few operations to verify correctness of the zigzag function and update operations.
random.generation_strategy: Generate an array of size n (1 ≤ n ≤ 10) with random values. Then generate m (1 ≤ m ≤ 10) random operations (type 1 or 2) with valid parameters. Compute expected outputs manually or via a brute-force script.

random.description: Larger random test with n and m up to 100000 to stress-test performance and ensure no TLE or memory issues.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=100000 with random values between 1 and 1e9. Generate m=100000 operations with random types and parameters. Expected output is not computed due to size, but the test checks that the solution runs within time limits.
error_types_caught: runtime errors due to recursion or stack overflow

boundary.description: Test with minimum array size n=1 and multiple operations to verify edge-case behavior.
boundary.test_values: n=1, a1=100, m=2: first query on the only element, then update, then second query.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of single element arrays

boundary.description: Test with maximum array values (1e9) and extreme z values (2 and 6) to check for integer overflow.
boundary.test_values: n=2, a1=a2=1e9, query with l=1,r=2,z=6. The sum should be 1e9*1 + 1e9*2 = 3e9, which fits in 64-bit but may overflow 32-bit.

adversarial.description: Sequence of alternating updates and queries on the same positions to ensure updates are applied correctly and queries return updated values.
adversarial.attack_vector: Forces the solution to handle multiple updates without losing previous updates or incorrectly caching values.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might not propagate updates correctly if they use lazy propagation or incorrect data structures.

adversarial.description: Query with z=6 and a range that tests the off-by-one in the zigzag weight sequence, especially at boundaries of the period.
adversarial.attack_vector: Misalignment of weights due to incorrect modulo or index calculation.
adversarial.why_effective: The period for z=6 is 10. An off-by-one in the weight assignment (e.g., starting at 0 instead of 1) would give a different sum.

adversarial.description: Multiple queries with different z values on the same array to test that the zigzag weights for each z are correctly precomputed or computed on the fly.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that reuse a single weight array without resetting for different z values can produce wrong results.
adversarial.why_effective: If the solution uses a static weight array, it might not update when z changes, leading to incorrect sums.

key_coverage_gaps: no test with all operations type 1 (only updates) to test performance under heavy updates
no test with z=2 and n=100000 to stress periodic queries

random.description: Random permutation and query order for small n to verify correctness.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random permutation of size n (small, e.g., 5-10) and a random permutation of indices as queries. Compute cycle decomposition and answer for each prefix.

random.description: Random permutation and query order for large n (e.g., 200000) to stress test performance.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random permutation of size n (large) and a random permutation of indices as queries. Use efficient algorithm to compute answers quickly.
error_types_caught: TLE due to O(n^2) per query

boundary.description: Minimum n (=1) and n=2 cases.
boundary.test_values: n=1 and n=2, including identity and swap permutations.
error_types_caught: incorrect cycle handling for small n

boundary.description: Permutation is identity (p[i]=i for all i).
boundary.test_values: n=5 identity; each query activates a new cycle of size 1.
error_types_caught: miscomputing answer when all cycles are size 1

adversarial.description: Identity permutation with queries in increasing order; each query activates a new cycle.
adversarial.attack_vector: If solution processes each query by iterating over all cycles or all indices, it will be O(n^2).
adversarial.why_effective: For identity permutation, each query activates exactly one new cycle, so answer increments by 1 each time. A naive O(n) per query would be O(n^2) and TLE for n=200000.

adversarial.description: Permutation with cycles of varying sizes, queries ordered to activate each cycle exactly once in order of decreasing size.
adversarial.attack_vector: Tests if solution correctly adds cycle sizes when first zero appears, and handles multiple zeros in same cycle.
adversarial.why_effective: The permutation has cycles: (1) size1, (2,3) size2, (4,5,6) size3, (7,8,9,10) size4. Queries activate cycles in order of decreasing size? Actually first activates cycle1, then cycle2, etc. But after first zero in a cycle, subsequent zeros in same cycle should not increase answer. A naive solution might double-count or miscount cumulative sums.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect cycle tracking

key_coverage_gaps: permutations with many small cycles mixed with large cycles
queries that activate all cycles early
queries that activate cycles slowly

random.description: Small random arrays with n between 1 and 10 to allow brute-force verification.
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, choose n uniformly in [1,10], then generate a_i uniformly in [1,n].

random.description: Large random arrays with n up to 200000 to test performance and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a single test case with n=200000, a_i random in [1,200000].
error_types_caught: MLE from storing large DP table

boundary.description: Minimum n: n=1.
boundary.test_values: n=1, a1=1 (any value in [1,1] is 1). Expected answer is 2 (empty and the single element).

boundary.description: n=2 with both equal and distinct values.
boundary.test_values: Case 1: a=[1,1] -> expected 4 (all subsequences valid). Case 2: a=[1,2] -> expected 3 (missing [1,2]).

boundary.description: Large n with all elements equal to 1.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, all a_i=1. This tests performance and combinatorial count. Expected output is unknown but should be computed efficiently.

boundary.description: n large with values forming a permutation of 1..n.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, a_i = i (increasing permutation). This tests if algorithm handles distinct values properly.

adversarial.description: Sequence where each element is the sum of all previous elements: e.g., powers of 2.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that try to match prefix sums naively by causing many valid subsequences.
adversarial.why_effective: In a subsequence, any element that equals the sum of its left prefix (which may be a subset of original prefix) creates many valid configurations. A naive DP storing prefix sums may count incorrectly.
error_types_caught: wrong counting of subsequences with prefix-sum property

adversarial.description: Multiple small test cases to test input parsing and initialization overhead.
adversarial.attack_vector: Large number of test cases with n=1 each, total n sum up to 200000. E.g., 200000 test cases of n=1.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution allocates per test case memory or has high constant factor, it may TLE. Also, if solution has bug when resetting global variables, it may cause WA.

adversarial.description: Sequence where every element equals the sum of all elements to its right (reverse prefix sum).
adversarial.attack_vector: Similar to adversarial_1 but opposite direction; solutions that only consider left sums may miss.
adversarial.why_effective: The condition requires checking both left and right sums. A solution that only checks left sums will underestimate valid subsequences.

key_coverage_gaps: values outside [1,n] (not allowed by constraints)
n=0 (not allowed)
negative numbers (not allowed)

random.description: Points placed on a circle (convex position) to ensure many empty triangles. All points lie on the convex hull, so any triple forms an empty triangle.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n points on a circle of radius R by random angles. Ensure no two points coincide and no three collinear by construction.

random.description: Random points within a square, not all on convex hull, to stress test detection of empty triangles amidst points inside triangles.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n points uniformly in [-1000,1000]^2, then perturb to avoid collinearity. Include points that are inside large triangles formed by hull points.

boundary.description: Minimum number of points (n=3). The only triangle is trivially empty.
boundary.test_values: n=3 ensures algorithm handles smallest possible input correctly.

boundary.description: n=4 with one point inside the triangle of the other three. Forces algorithm to find an empty triangle that does not include the inside point.
boundary.test_values: n=4, three outer points and one interior point. Typical scenario where algorithm must query to find a triangle that excludes the interior point.

adversarial.description: Points on a convex polygon (circle) with one point significantly inside the hull. The adversary can always return the interior point when a triangle contains it, forcing many queries to find an empty triangle (one that does not contain the interior point).
adversarial.attack_vector: Adaptive adversary always chooses the interior point when available, making it hard to identify empty triangles because many triangles contain the interior point.
adversarial.why_effective: The interior point lies inside most triangles formed by hull vertices, so naive algorithms may waste queries or incorrectly assume a triangle is empty. Algorithm must carefully pick points to avoid the interior.
error_types_caught: failure to adapt to adversarial point selection

adversarial.description: Points arranged in two clusters such that many triangles contain points from the other cluster. The adversary alternates between clusters to mislead adaptive strategies.
adversarial.attack_vector: By having two separated clusters, the adversary can always pick a point from the cluster not represented in the current triangle, forcing the algorithm to expand its search.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive algorithms that only consider triangles from a single cluster may repeatedly get points from the other cluster, leading to many queries. This tests the algorithm's ability to quickly find a triangle that avoids all points.

key_coverage_gaps: Large n with points on convex hull only
n=4 with two points inside triangle
Points with collinearity near-misses (though strictly disallowed)

random.description: Small n with no constraints, to verify baseline count
random.generation_strategy: Set n small (e.g., 1 to 4), k=0. Use known formula (double factorial (2n-1)!!) or manual enumeration to compute expected output.

random.description: Random constraints on medium n (n=5) with some equality and inequality constraints
random.generation_strategy: Generate n in [4,7], k in [1,5]. Randomly choose x,y, sign. Ensure consistency (e.g., no contradictory chain). Use a brute-force for small n to get output, or for this example we can compute manually.
error_types_caught: bug in constraint satisfaction in DP

boundary.description: Minimum n (n=1) with various constraints
boundary.test_values: n=1 → only 2 blocks, heights both 1. Sequence must be [1,1]. So constraints like 1<2 would be false, so answer 0. Equality works.

boundary.description: Maximum n (n=35) with no constraints (k=0)
boundary.test_values: n=35 → 70 blocks. Output should be (69)!! = product of odd numbers from 1 to 69. This is a huge number, test big integer handling if language requires.
error_types_caught: performance issue with large DP table

boundary.description: Maximum k (k=100) with simple constraints at extreme indices
boundary.test_values: n=35, k=100, all constraints are equality between consecutive positions (e.g., 1=2, 2=3, ...) which forces all heights equal, but since there are exactly two of each height, impossible (contradiction).

adversarial.description: Chain of strict inequalities forcing a total order that contradicts the unimodal shape
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit DP that assumes constraints are independent; a chain like 1<2, 2<3, ..., 2n-1<2n forces strictly increasing sequence, which is impossible because shape has decreasing part.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive DP might not detect contradiction early, or might count sequences that are strictly increasing overall, but unimodal requires non-increasing after peak.

adversarial.description: Constraints that force a specific symmetry (e.g., h[i] = h[2n+1-i] for all i) which might be hard for DP that builds from ends
adversarial.attack_vector: Symmetry constraints cause many interdependencies across positions, potentially exponential state growth if not handled properly.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive DP that treats each position independently might explode. Efficient DP uses symmetry reduction.

key_coverage_gaps: Constraints with same indices (x=y)
Constraints involving > and < on equal heights
Large n with many random constraints

random.description: Small random string of length up to 10 for functional verification
random.generation_strategy: Generate random string of lowercase letters with length between 1 and 10. Compute expected output using brute force enumeration of all substrings.

random.description: Medium random string of length 100 to test performance and correctness on moderate input

random.generation_strategy: Generate random string of lowercase letters with length 300000. Expected output must be computed by an O(n * alphabet) or O(n log) solution.

boundary.description: String of length 1 (minimum length)
boundary.test_values: Length = 1. Only one substring possible.

boundary.description: String consisting of a single repeating character (minimum diversity = 1)
boundary.test_values: All characters same. This maximizes number of substrings for given length. For length N, total substrings = N(N+1)/2, all with diversity 1.
error_types_caught: TLE if naive O(N^2) method used

boundary.description: String with all characters distinct up to 26 (maximum diversity = 26)
boundary.test_values: Diversity = 26 (max possible). For a string of length 26 with all distinct letters, substrings of length k have diversity k, so count = 27 - k.
error_types_caught: incorrect computation of diversity for higher distinct counts

boundary.description: Maximum length (300000) with all same character
boundary.test_values: Length = 300000, all 'a'. Total substrings = ~4.5e10, which exceeds 32-bit integer. Requires 64-bit output.

adversarial.description: Very long string of all same character to cause TLE/overflow in naive solutions
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that count substrings by iterating all possible substrings O(N^2) or use int for counts.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive O(N^2) enumeration of substrings will time out. Using 32-bit integer for count will overflow.

adversarial.description: Long string alternating between two characters to stress test sliding window updates
adversarial.attack_vector: Frequent changes in distinct character count force many operations in sliding window approach.
adversarial.why_effective: For a sliding window solution, the distinct count flips between 1 and 2 frequently, causing many adjustments. Inefficient implementations may degrade.
error_types_caught: TLE due to inefficient distinct tracking

adversarial.description: Long string repeating the full 26-letter alphabet many times
adversarial.attack_vector: High diversity and long substrings cause many distinct characters to track. Tests correctness of counting substrings with many distinct letters.
adversarial.why_effective: Substrings may cross cycle boundaries, requiring careful tracking of distinct set size. Naive solutions may miscount distinct characters when windows span multiple cycles.
error_types_caught: incorrect diversity calculation for long windows

key_coverage_gaps: strings with many repeated patterns causing heavy distinct count changes
very long strings with exactly 26 distinct letters in non-sequential order

random.description: Random small boards (n from 1 to 10) using the diagonal configuration (identity matrix).
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, set n randomly between 1 and 10. Output the n x n identity matrix (1 on diagonal, 0 elsewhere). This satisfies the condition with exactly n pieces.

random.description: Random large boards (n up to 100) using the all-ones configuration, which is also valid.
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, set n randomly between 10 and 100. Output an n x n matrix filled with 1s. This satisfies the condition with n^2 pieces (≥ n).

boundary.description: Minimum board size (n=1). Only one cell. The condition is trivially satisfied if a piece is placed (since no other cells to attack).
boundary.test_values: n=1: the smallest possible board. Must place at least one piece.
error_types_caught: incorrect attack count for single cell

boundary.description: Smallest even board (n=2). Testing the diagonal configuration works.
boundary.test_values: n=2: small board to verify parity condition manually.

adversarial.description: Large board (n=1000) to test output generation efficiency and memory.
adversarial.attack_vector: Generate an extremely large board to stress memory and time.
adversarial.example_output: A 1000x1000 matrix of all ones (or diagonal). For brevity, only showing the pattern: all entries are 1.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might allocate too much memory or iterate over all cells multiple times, leading to time/memory limits.

adversarial.description: n=3 (odd, small) but with a non-identity configuration that is also valid. Could catch solutions that only work for diagonal.
adversarial.attack_vector: Use an alternative valid configuration (e.g., all ones) to ensure the solution can handle different patterns.
adversarial.why_effective: Some solvers might assume only the diagonal works, but all ones is also valid. If their algorithm rejects it, they fail.

key_coverage_gaps: n=2 with all-ones configuration
n=0 (not allowed)
multiple test cases with varying n

random.generation_strategy: Generate random integers n, m, z between 1 and 10000.

random.description: Small random values for easy manual verification.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random integers n, m, z between 1 and 20.

boundary.description: Minimum values: all inputs equal to 1.
boundary.test_values: n=1, m=1, z=1 (smallest possible), n=1,m=1,z=10000 (small n,m with large z).

boundary.description: Maximum values: n,m,z all at 10000.
error_types_caught: incorrect lcm when numbers are large

boundary.description: Edge cases where n and m are divisors or multiples.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling when lcm equals one of the numbers

adversarial.description: High density of common multiples: n and m are both small and coprime, z is max, resulting in many overlaps.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit solutions that loop through all minutes (O(z)) but still within limits; also test lcm calculation with large product.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive loop over z=10000 is fine, but incorrect lcm formula (e.g., using n*m instead of lcm) would give 10000*2? Actually lcm(1,2)=2, floor(10000/2)=5000. If solution uses product n*m without dividing by gcd, it would overflow or give wrong result. Also tests large output.

adversarial.description: No common multiples: n and m are coprime and large, z less than both n and m, so answer 0.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that assume at least one overlap or miscompute GCD/LCM when lcm > z.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might incorrectly count if they don't check lcm <= z. Some might loop and never hit, but answer is 0. Also tests proper handling of condition when lcm > z.
error_types_caught: division by zero in gcd? No

adversarial.description: Extremely large lcm case: n and m are such that lcm is just above z, causing floor division to yield 0 even though both numbers are less than z.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that only consider individual multiples and not common multiples via lcm.
adversarial.why_effective: lcm(100,99)=9900, >100, so no common multiples. Proper solution returns 0. Naive might incorrectly count if they think common multiple exists because both are <=z (but not same minute).

key_coverage_gaps: Large values with n=m=z=10000 covered, but not combined with non-coprime extremes.
Test cases where lcm overflows 32-bit? Not needed as product <=1e8, but could test if someone uses long long unnecessarily.
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: At least 10 test cases covering all boundaries and adversarial patterns.

random.description: Small random strings and queries for hand verification and correctness testing.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random strings of length n between 4 and 10 with digits 0-9, then generate q between 1 and 5 random substring queries. Compute answers manually or with a brute-force solution.

random.description: Large random strings with many queries to stress test time and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=200000, q=200000 random string of digits 0-9, random queries. Expected to run within time limits with O((n+q) log n) solution.

boundary.description: Minimum n=4 and q=1 with various strings to test edge cases.
Very long string with all same character (e.g., '0') to test processing of uniform strings.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, all characters same digit, many queries. All substrings should return -1 (cannot form '2017').

boundary.description: Strings missing at least one of the digits 2,0,1,7, so impossible to form '2017'.
boundary.test_values: String consisting only of digits from {3,4,5,6,8,9} and possibly '6' (since '6' is in '2016' but not in '2017'). But if there's no '2', no '0', no '1', or no '7', answer -1. Test each missing case.

adversarial.description: String with many '2016' subsequences to force high removal count and test optimal DP transitions.
adversarial.attack_vector: Repeated pattern '2016' makes it hard to get '2017' without breaking many '2016's. A simple greedy removal might fail.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive approaches may remove too many or too few characters. The optimal is to remove the '6' in the first '2016' to break that subsequence while keeping the '2017'.

adversarial.description: Interleaved '2017' and '2016' patterns to test automaton on overlapping subsequences.
adversarial.attack_vector: Strings like '20172016' where a single substring contains both '2017' and '2016'. The minimal removal might be non-trivial.
adversarial.why_effective: Removing the '6' at the end breaks '2016' but also could break '2017' if not careful. Actually in this string, '2017' is at start, '2016' at end, so removing the '6' works. But a greedy that removes from conflict might fail if not considering order.

adversarial.description: Many queries of length 4 (minimum possible to contain '2017' or '2016') to test base cases and corner handling.
adversarial.attack_vector: Queries on substrings of exactly length 4 that could be '2017', '2016', or other combinations. Forces solution to handle many small segments efficiently.
adversarial.why_effective: Small substrings require precise handling of boundaries. A segment tree that doesn't handle leaf values correctly might give wrong answers. Also many queries can expose performance issues if not optimized.

key_coverage_gaps: Additional patterns for different digit distributions
Patterns with all digits relevant (2,0,1,6,7) but no conflict
Queries with many overlapping ranges to test segment tree lazy (if applicable)

x much larger than y

Expected output is number of trees (components).

random.generation_strategy: Generate many small trees (e.g., random tree sizes from 1 to 50) summing to 10000. Build each tree as a random tree (e.g., random parent for each new vertex) and assign ids consecutively. Compute p similarly. Output in hacking format. Expected output is number of trees.

boundary.description: Minimum n=1: single vertex tree. Tests minimal input.
Maximum n=10000 with all trees of size 1 (isolated vertices). Tests maximum number of trees.
boundary.test_values: n=10000, m=0 (no edges, each vertex isolated)

boundary.description: Large single tree (line) with n=10000. Tests DSU on a large connected component with depth.
boundary.test_values: n=10000, m=9999, edges form a line. p array computed: p[1]=10000, p[10000]=1, and for others p[i]=1 except near ends? Actually for a line, p[i]=1 if i-1 >= n-i, else n. Many nodes will point to 1.

adversarial.description: Star tree: center vertex 1 with leaves 2..n (n large). Creates tie-breaking scenario: center points to smallest leaf (2), leaves point to each other (smallest among others). This results in p[1]=2, p[2]=3, p[3]=2, p[4]=2,...,p[n]=2. Only two distinct p-values (2 and 3) but only one tree.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that count trees as number of distinct p[i] values.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might think each distinct p-value corresponds to a separate tree, but here only two distinct values (2 and 3) yet only one tree. DSU-based solution correctly unifies all vertices.
error_types_caught: incorrect component count via distinct values

adversarial.description: Two symmetric stars with tie-breaking: tree1: center 1, leaves 2,3; tree2: center 4, leaves 5,6. p values: [2,3,2,5,6,5]. Distinct values: 4, but trees: 2.
adversarial.attack_vector: Same as above, but with two trees to catch counting distinct values.
adversarial.why_effective: Distinct p count = 4, but actual trees = 2. This also tests tie-breaking across components.
error_types_caught: incorrect component count via distinct values

adversarial.description: Chain of odd length (3 nodes: 1-2-3). p: [3,1,1]. Distinct values: 2, trees: 1.

adversarial.why_effective: The center node (2) has tie between ends (1 and 3), smallest id is 1, so p[2]=1. This is a simple but tricky case.

adversarial.description: Graph consisting of a single long cycle of 100000 nodes. Tests cycle detection on large cycles.
adversarial.attack_vector: Cycle detection algorithms that use recursion may cause stack overflow or TLE if they explore entire cycle without pruning.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive DFS without cycle detection or iterative approach may overflow stack or take too long.

adversarial.description: DAG where nodes are not topologically sorted by index; DP must compute in topological order.
adversarial.attack_vector: Algorithms that process nodes in numerical order without topological sorting will produce wrong answers.
adversarial.why_effective: If DP processes nodes in order 1..4, it will miss contributions from nodes 2 and 3 to node 4.

adversarial.description: DAG with many nodes having the same letter, designed to force high path value. Tests correctness of max frequency computation.
adversarial.attack_vector: Misimplementation of frequency counting might not update correctly for all letters.
adversarial.why_effective: The path 1-2-3-4-5-6 has letters a,b,a,a,b,a; most frequent is 'a' with count 4. Some algorithms might only track count per node rather than max along path.

key_coverage_gaps: Graphs with multiple cycles
Disconnected components with cycles in some
Extreme letter distribution (e.g., all same letter)

random.description: Small random functions, both idempotent and non-idempotent
random.generation_strategy: For n in [1..10], generate random f arrays. Then test if idempotent. If yes, compute answer; else output -1. Include both cases.

random.description: Large random idempotent functions with moderate number of distinct values
random.generation_strategy: For n=100000, choose m ~ sqrt(n) = 316. For each i, assign f(i) a random value in a set of fixed points (pre-chosen). Ensure f(f(i))=f(i).

random.description: Large random non-idempotent functions
random.generation_strategy: For n=100000, generate f completely randomly. Since probability of idempotent is extremely low, most will be -1. Stress test the -1 detection.

boundary.description: Minimum n = 1
boundary.test_values: n=1, f(1) can be 1 or any. Idempotent only if f(1)=1.

boundary.description: All f(i) equal to same constant
boundary.test_values: n up to 100000, all f(i)=c. Idempotent only if c=c (always true), so valid. Distinct values count =1. m=1.

boundary.description: Maximum n = 100000 with all fixed points (f(i)=i for all i)
boundary.test_values: n=100000, f(i)=i. This is idempotent. m=n. g and h are identity. Stress large m output.

adversarial.description: Non-idempotent but f(f(x)) cycles quickly (e.g., f(1)=2, f(2)=1). This fails condition.
adversarial.attack_vector: False positive: solution might consider f idempotent if it sees f(1)=2 and f(2)=2? No, but here f(2)=1, so f(f(1))=f(2)=1 != f(1)=2. So it's non-idempotent. Test if solution incorrectly checks only f(1)=1 or something.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solution might ignore full idempotence condition and think because it can map? No, but can catch if solution only checks if f is onto set of fixed points.

adversarial.description: Idempotent but f has multiple fixed points not all in image
adversarial.attack_vector: Suppose f is idempotent but the set of fixed points is larger than image. That's fine, we only need image. But if solution incorrectly uses all fixed points, may get m too large. However, we output any valid answer. So this might not cause WA but could cause large m.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution uses all fixed points (2,1) plus maybe others? Actually fixed points are {1,2}. But image is {1,2}. So same. To really exploit, make extra fixed points that are not in image. E.g., f(1)=2, f(2)=2, f(3)=3, f(3)=3 is fixed but not in image. Then image is {2}, fixed points {2,3}. Valid solution: m=1, g(1)=g(2)=g(3)=1, h(1)=2. But if solution tries to include 3, m=2. That is also valid. So not really adversarial. Let's try another: f(x)=x for all x. That's fine.

adversarial.description: Large n with many repeated values, all idempotent but m is large (e.g., n=100000, each f(i) is i%100 + 1 but ensure idempotent? That would not be idempotent. Need idempotent: f(i)=i for i<=100, else f(i)=i%100+1? Not idempotent. Better: make f(i)=i for i in [1,m] and for i>m, f(i)=some fixed point from [1,m]. Then m distinct fixed points. This is large m.
adversarial.attack_vector: Test memory and output performance when m is large (up to 10^5).
adversarial.target_error: MLE or TLE due to large m output
adversarial.why_effective: If solution allocates O(m) space or prints incorrectly, may fail.

key_coverage_gaps: Edge case where f is idempotent but image is not a subset of fixed points (impossible: if f(x)=y then f(f(x))=f(y)=y, so y is fixed). So no gap. Also check when m=0 (impossible since m>=1).

random.description: Random valid strings constructed from a Hamiltonian cycle on the 2x13 grid. The repeated letter always appears at the first and last positions (distance 26).
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random permutation of the 26 unique letters, fill the grid row by row (first row with first 13 letters, second row with next 13 letters), then take a Hamiltonian cycle starting at some tile. The resulting path spells a 27-letter string with start and end same letter. Output the string as input; the expected grid is the one used.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of repeated letter at ends

random.description: Random valid strings with repeated letter not at ends. The distance between repetitions is even and not 13. Generated by taking a valid grid and a Hamiltonian path that revisits one interior tile.
random.generation_strategy: Start with a known valid grid (e.g., first row A-M, second row N-Z). Choose a starting tile S and a target repeated tile R (different from S). Construct a path that goes from S through all tiles exactly once except R which is visited twice, and ends at some tile E. The resulting string has two occurrences of R at some positions p and q (q-p even, not 13). Output the string; the expected grid is the original.
error_types_caught: inability to handle interior repeated letter

boundary.description: Distance between repeated letters is exactly 13 (odd), which is impossible due to bipartite parity. This is a known impossibility condition.
boundary.test_values: The two occurrences of the repeated letter are exactly 13 positions apart (e.g., positions 0 and 13).

boundary.description: Minimum even distance (2) between repeated letters. This is the smallest possible even distance and tests whether the solution can handle a short loop.
boundary.test_values: Two identical letters adjacent? Actually distance 2 means one letter between them (positions p and p+2).

boundary.description: Maximum even distance (26) with repeated letters at first and last positions. This is the simplest solvable case.
boundary.test_values: Repeated letter at index 0 and 26.
error_types_caught: failure to produce any valid grid

adversarial.description: String where the repeated letter is exactly in the middle (distance odd? Actually distance 13 is odd->impossible) but here distance even=12? Let's use distance 12. Naive solutions might try to place the middle substring in a straight line but fail because the path needs to snake.
adversarial.attack_vector: The substring between the two occurrences has length 12, which is one less than the number of columns. Some solutions might incorrectly assume it fits in a single row without wrapping.
adversarial.why_effective: A common mistake is to try to place the middle 12 letters in a row of 13, but then the repeated letter would need to be at a corner, which is not adjacent to the previous tile.

adversarial.description: String where the repeated letter is such that the distance is odd (e.g., 1 or 3). This should be impossible, but naive solutions that do not check parity might output a grid.
adversarial.attack_vector: Parity check is often forgotten.
adversarial.why_effective: The distance between the two 'A's is 1 (odd), so no closed walk of odd length exists. A solution missing parity would attempt to construct a grid and fail.

key_coverage_gaps: Strings with multiple repeated letters? Not possible per problem constraints.
Strings where the repeated letter appears more than twice? Not allowed.
Test cases with non-alphabetical order to stress adjacency constraints.
Large number of test cases (stress) for time limit.

random.generation_strategy: Generate n and m between 2 and 5. Fill board with random uppercase letters. Compute expected output via brute force.

random.generation_strategy: Generate n=50, m=50. Fill board with random uppercase letters. Expected output is determined by brute force (or known correct algorithm).
error_types_caught: incorrect cycle detection on large grids

boundary.description: Minimum board size (n=2, m=2) with a 2x2 block of same color; should output Yes (cycle of length 4).
boundary.test_values: n=2, m=2, all four cells same color
error_types_caught: missing cycle due to neglecting small board

boundary.description: Maximum board size (n=50, m=50) with all cells same color; should output Yes (many cycles).
Narrow board (n=50, m=2) with a 2x2 block of same color; should output Yes.
boundary.test_values: n=50, m=2, create a 2x2 block somewhere

adversarial.description: Deep recursive DFS stack overflow: 50x50 grid of all same color, forcing a long path like a snake that covers all cells.
adversarial.attack_vector: Depth of recursion in DFS may exceed language recursion limit (e.g., ~1000 in Python).
adversarial.why_effective: A naive recursive DFS will try to traverse the entire grid in one path, causing a call stack depth of 2500, which crashes in Python and other languages with limited recursion.
error_types_caught: time limit exceeded if iterative but incorrect

adversarial.description: No cycle but many same-color adjacent cells in a spiral pattern that might mislead BFS/DFS into thinking there is a cycle.
adversarial.attack_vector: Common bug: treating a visited neighbor that is not parent as cycle without checking distance (minimum 4 cells). Even though no cycle, algorithm might report Yes if it encounters a visited cell that is not parent but is actually part of a different branch? In grid, this could happen if the algorithm marks visited incorrectly.
adversarial.why_effective: The grid has many adjacent same-color cells but no cycle of length >=4. A naive DFS might incorrectly detect a cycle when backtracking to a node that is actually a sibling (not parent) but distance is 2 steps? Actually in undirected grid, back edge always indicates cycle of length >=4, so this pattern might not break correct algorithm. But let's think of a alternative: grid with a false cycle due to forgetting to check color? Actually if algorithm doesn't check color, it might find cycle across colors. So design a grid where colors interweave: two colors each forming a path that touches but no cycle. But more effective: grid where a color forms a 'C' shape (3 cells) that almost closes but not, and another color fills the gap, causing false positive if algorithm doesn't handle multiple colors correctly.

adversarial.description: Grid with a cycle of length exactly 4 but placed at the boundary to test edge handling.
adversarial.attack_vector: Boundary conditions: cycle on the edge might be missed if loop condition checks neighbor existence incorrectly.
adversarial.why_effective: The 2x3 grid has a 2x2 block at left (cols 0-1) forming cycle. But if algorithm incorrectly checks boundaries or uses modulo, it might miss the cycle. Also tests that cycle can be at edge.

key_coverage_gaps: all same color diagonal? No, only orthogonal
cycle of length >4
multiple cycles same color

adversarial.why_effective: The stack grows to full length before popping, testing memory

random.description: Random small pyramid and moderate pouring time
random.generation_strategy: Randomly select n between 1 and 10 and t between 0 and 10000, but ensure at least some glasses are partially filled. Use simulation to compute expected output.

random.description: Random small pyramid with fairly small t to test partial fill dynamics
random.generation_strategy: Choose n small (e.g., 3-5) and t moderate (e.g., up to n*(n+1)/2) to ensure many glasses partially filled.

boundary.description: Maximum pyramid height and maximum pouring time (beyond total capacity)
boundary.test_values: n=10 (largest pyramid) and t=10000 (much larger than total capacity 55) -> output 55 (all glasses full)

adversarial.description: Pouring exactly total capacity of the pyramid (test exact full case)
adversarial.attack_vector: t equals total capacity n*(n+1)/2, which for n=10 is 55. Some solutions may have floating point precision issues or off-by-one when checking fullness.
adversarial.why_effective: If the solution uses floating point comparisons without epsilon, it may incorrectly count a glass as not full due to rounding errors. Also, if using integer arithmetic, overflow amounts may not sum correctly.

adversarial.description: Small pyramid with t such that multiple overflow layers are filled exactly
adversarial.attack_vector: n=2, t=3 leads to all three glasses full. This requires correct handling of overflow from top to bottom and accumulation of multiple seconds.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might count only top glass or second-level glasses incorrectly, or fail to propagate overflow beyond one level after multiple seconds.

random.description: Small random queries with small bases and ranges to verify correctness via brute force.
random.generation_strategy: Generate 5 queries with base in [2,10] and l,r in [1,1000] randomly. Ensure small enough to brute force for verification.

random.description: Large random queries with many queries and large ranges to stress test performance and caching.
random.generation_strategy: Generate 100000 queries with base random in [2,10] and l,r random in [1,1e18]. Provide first few lines as example.

boundary.description: Single number at the minimum lower bound (l=1, r=1) for base 2.
boundary.test_values: b=2, l=1, r=1. The only number is 1 (binary '1'), which has one '1' (odd) and zero '0's (even), so not magic.

boundary.description: Single magic number at the smallest magic number (3 in base 2).
boundary.test_values: b=2, l=3, r=3. 3 in binary is '11' has two '1's (even) and zero '0's (even), so magic.

adversarial.description: Repeated identical queries to test caching and state reset between queries.
adversarial.attack_vector: DP caching across queries: if the DP state is not properly reset or if a global cache is used incorrectly, repeated identical queries may produce wrong results.
adversarial.why_effective: A buggy DP that modifies cached values during computation may return different outputs for the same query on successive calls.

adversarial.description: Alternating bases to test DP reset per base.
adversarial.attack_vector: If the DP cache is shared across different bases without resetting, results for one base may incorrectly affect another.
adversarial.example_output: alternating outputs: answer for base2, base10, base2, base10, ...
adversarial.why_effective: A naive DP that uses a single cache keyed only by range and not base will produce wrong results when base changes.

adversarial.description: Maximum range for base 10 to test large answer and overflow.
adversarial.attack_vector: The answer may be very large (up to 1e18) and could overflow if using 32-bit integers.
adversarial.why_effective: Many DP implementations use 32-bit integers for counts; the answer for full range in base 10 can exceed 2^31-1.
error_types_caught: use of int instead of long long

key_coverage_gaps: queries with l=r=1 for all bases 2-10
ranges that are powers of the base
queries with b=2 and large ranges

random.description: Small random strings (n up to 10) with a few queries to verify correctness of the solution against brute force.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random string of length n (even, between 2 and 10) consisting of characters '(', ')', '[', ']'. Generate a random number of queries (1 to 5) with l and r such that substring length is even. Compute the correct answer using brute force considering all possible sequences of operations (though exponential, but for small n it's feasible).
error_types_caught: Wrong answer due to incorrect logic in cost calculation

random.description: Large random string (n=1000) with many queries (q=1000) to stress test performance and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random string of length 1000 with equal probability for each bracket type. Generate 1000 random queries with even length substrings. Expected output is not provided as it requires computation, but the pattern is used to ensure the solution runs within time and memory limits.
error_types_caught: Runtime errors due to large input

boundary.description: Minimum length substrings (length 2) with various bracket combinations to test basic cases.
boundary.test_values: Substring length = 2, the smallest even length. Test all 16 possible pairs of brackets to ensure correct handling of all combinations.
error_types_caught: Incorrect handling of type conversion direction
Edge case when substring is already correct

boundary.description: Maximum length string (n=1e6) consisting entirely of the same bracket type to test memory and time, and correctness of cost calculation for homogeneous strings.
boundary.test_values: Length = 10^6, string composed of all '(' or all '['. Queries cover the entire string and smaller substrings. For all '(', the cost for a substring of even length L is L/2 (flip half to ')'). For all '[', cost is also L/2 because we can either flip direction or convert to round? Actually conversion doesn't help if all opening, so cost = L/2 as well.
error_types_caught: Incorrect cost calculation for homogeneous strings

adversarial.description: String with high imbalance between round and square brackets, forcing many type conversions. For example, many opening round brackets followed by many closing square brackets.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that treat both bracket types symmetrically or ignore type conversion costs may underestimate the cost.
adversarial.why_effective: The substring '(([[' has two opening round and two opening square. To make it correct, we need to close them. Options: change two round to closing (direction change) cost 2, or change square to round and then close? Actually we can convert both square to round (type change) giving '((((' and then flip two of them to closing: total 4 operations. So minimal is 2 direction changes. Naive solution that ignores type conversions might compute incorrectly.
error_types_caught: Wrong answer due to ignoring type conversion

adversarial.description: String that creates alternating positive and negative balances in prefix sums, causing naive greedy or stack-based solutions to fail. For example, a substring like '[(])' where the correct matching is not obvious.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that rely only on total balance or simple prefix sums may incorrectly compute the cost.
adversarial.why_effective: The substring '[(])' length 4. One optimal solution: change the ']' to ')' (type change) gives '[(])' becomes '[()]' which is correct? Actually '[()]' is correct bracket sequence: '[' opening, '(' opening, ')' closing, ']' closing. So cost 1. A solution that only considers direction changes might think need 2 operations (e.g., flip both square brackets to round? That would give '(())', also cost 2). The correct minimal is 1, testing if solution finds type conversion.
error_types_caught: Wrong answer for sequences requiring mixed operations
Incorrect handling of type conversion priority

key_coverage_gaps: Large variety of bracket combinations (random)
Performance under many queries
Edge cases with minimum and maximum lengths
Instances where both type and direction changes are needed

random.generation_strategy: Generate n=5 rows with random distinct widths (e.g., 1..10) and a random string of length 10 with exactly five '0' and five '1', ensuring feasibility by construction.

random.generation_strategy: Generate n=100000 rows with random distinct widths (e.g., random permutation of 1..100000) and a random binary string of length 200000 with exactly 100000 zeros and 100000 ones, e.g., via random shuffle of 100000 zeros and 100000 ones.
