100000
<100000 distinct random integers>
<200000 random binary string with equal 0/1 count>
random.example_output: <200000 row indices in order of passengers>

boundary.description: Minimum size n=1.
boundary.test_values: n=1, only one row. String must be '01' because equal introverts and extroverts.

boundary.description: n=2 with widths in increasing order, and alternating pattern 0101. Tests that the algorithm correctly picks smallest for introvert and largest for extrovert among options.
boundary.test_values: n=2, widths = [1,2] increasing. String '0101' (introvert, extrovert, introvert, extrovert). First introvert takes row1 (width1). Then extrovert takes row1 (the one occupied). Second introvert takes row2 (only empty row). Then extrovert takes row2. Output: 1 1 2 2.

boundary.description: Maximum n with all introverts first then all extroverts. Tests handling of full resort after all introverts.
boundary.test_values: n=100 (or 100000) with widths increasing, string = '0'*n followed by '1'*n. Introverts occupy rows 1..n in order of increasing width. Then extroverts occupy rows n..1 in order of decreasing width (since among occupied rows, choose largest width).

adversarial.description: Alternating introvert and extrovert with widths in decreasing order. Common mistake: using only one priority queue or not clearing correctly.
adversarial.attack_vector: The pattern forces frequent switching between introvert and extrovert selections. A naive implementation that does not reset state or wrongly handles already filled rows may produce incorrect order.
adversarial.why_effective: With decreasing widths, first introvert takes smallest width (row3, width1). Next extrovert takes that same row (largest among occupied, only row3). Next introvert takes next smallest empty row (row2, width5). Next extrovert takes row2 (now occupied). Last introvert takes last empty row (row1, width9). Last extrovert takes row1. Output must be: row3, row3, row2, row2, row1, row1. If algorithm picks largest empty for extrovert or doesn't update correctly, it fails.

adversarial.description: All introverts first, then all extroverts, but widths are in random order. This tests whether the algorithm correctly sorts after introverts and then uses a stack-like or queue-like structure for extroverts.
adversarial.attack_vector: After all introverts have chosen, the set of occupied rows (with one seat) must be used by extroverts in decreasing width order. A common mistake is to use a queue instead of a stack or to sort incorrectly, leading to wrong output order.
adversarial.why_effective: The introverts will pick rows in ascending width order: row4(width1), row2(width2), row3(width5), row1(width7), row5(width8). The extroverts then pick rows in descending width order: row5(width8), row1(width7), row3(width5), row2(width2), row4(width1). Output order is: introvert stops: row4, row2, row3, row1, row5; then extrovert stops: row5, row1, row3, row2, row4. This requires correct ordering. If algorithm uses LIFO from introvert order, it would give wrong answer.
error_types_caught: incorrect data structure (e.g., queue instead of stack)

key_coverage_gaps: Patterns with duplicate widths (not allowed)
Non-integer widths (not allowed)
Edge case where extrovert cannot find row (guaranteed not to happen)

boundary.test_values: n=1, first event is speed change with speed=50.
error_types_caught: off-by-one errors when processing initial condition

boundary.test_values: Speed changes and speed limits all set to 300; overtake signs present.

boundary.test_values: n=1000, all type 1 events with random speeds.
error_types_caught: mishandling of state when no signs present

adversarial.description: Many speed limit signs followed by a single speed change that violates all of them, testing optimal ignoring (should ignore only the necessary ones).
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solutions might ignore all previous speed limit signs instead of just the ones causing violation.
adversarial.why_effective: After speed change to 250, the current speed limit is 150 (top of stack) but 250 > 150, so only the last sign (150) needs to be ignored. Ignoring earlier ones would be suboptimal. Naive solution might overcount.

adversarial.description: Alternating overtake allowed and disallowed with many overtakes in prohibited state, testing that ignoring one no-overtake sign can fix multiple overtakes.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solutions might treat each overtake violation independently and ignore multiple signs, but optimal is to ignore the single no-overtake sign that covers them.
adversarial.why_effective: The first no-overtake sign (type 6) prohibits overtakes from that point onwards. The next three overtakes (type 2) are violations. By ignoring that single no-overtake sign, all three overtakes become legal. A naive solution that ignores each violation individually would count 3 ignored signs.
error_types_caught: not considering effect of ignoring signs on multiple events

adversarial.description: Many no speed limit signs and speed limit signs, with speed changes that would cause violations, but the optimal strategy is to ignore speed limit signs that are later overridden by no speed limit signs.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solutions might not handle the cancellation of speed limits correctly, leading to over-ignoring.
adversarial.why_effective: After the no speed limit sign (type 5), all previous speed limits are cleared. Then a new speed limit 110 is set. The speed change to 130 violates that limit. Only the last speed limit sign (110) needs to be ignored. Ignoring earlier ones is unnecessary. Naive solution might count more if not resetting stack correctly.
error_types_caught: incorrect stack handling with no speed limit signs

boundary.test_values: n=20, V=10000, a_i=100, b_i=100. Also could test V smaller than ingredient limit.

adversarial.description: Test targeting integer division error: all a_i and b_i such that b_i / a_i are non-integer and the true answer is fractional. If solution uses integer division, it will get wrong answer.
adversarial.attack_vector: Integer division of b_i by a_i when computing x.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions may compute x = min(b_i // a_i) = 1, then volume = 1*5=5, but correct is min(5/2=2.5,5/3≈1.6667)=1.6667, volume=8.3333. This large discrepancy will be caught.

adversarial.description: Test where the pot volume V is exactly equal to the ingredient-limited volume. This checks floating point comparison equality.
adversarial.attack_vector: Floating point equality when comparing with V.
adversarial.why_effective: The ingredient limit: b1/a1 = 100/10 = 10, so x=10, volume = 10*10 = 100 > V=10, so answer should be V=10. If solution computes min(b_i*S/a_i, V) using floating point, it's straightforward; but if they compute x first, then compare x*S with V, rounding might cause issue. This tests exact equality.

key_coverage_gaps: No test with all b_i=0 except one? Actually boundary covers zero. Also no test with n=20 where b_i=0 for many. Could add more but sufficient.

random.description: Small balanced binary tree (n=7) for verification of correct computation of times for each starting node.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a perfect binary tree of height 2 with 7 nodes. Root as 1, left child 2, right child 3; children of 2: 4 and 5; children of 3: 6 and 7. All leaves have children 0 0.

random.description: Random unbalanced binary tree with n=11, ensuring internal nodes have exactly two children. Tests performance on small but irregular shapes.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random full binary tree by randomly attaching new nodes. For node i from 1 to n, assign two children randomly chosen from unassigned subsequent IDs, ensuring full structure. For n=11, a possible tree: root 1 with children 2 and 3; 2 with children 4 and 5; 3 with children 6 and 7; 4 with children 8 and 9; 5 with children 10 and 11; all leaves have 0 0.

boundary.description: Minimum n: n=1 (single node, root). Only one vertex, answer must be 0.
boundary.test_values: n=1, only root with no children, so children lines: '1 0 0'.
error_types_caught: edge case for leaf (root also leaf)

boundary.description: Maximum n within sum constraint: n=100000 in a single test case, creating a large full binary tree. Tests modulo operations and large output.
boundary.test_values: n=100000, sum of n <= 10^5. Construct a complete binary tree as full as possible (since n is odd, last level may be partial but still full internal nodes). Use simple sequential assignment: for i from 1 to (n-1)/2, assign children 2i and 2i+1; for leaves, children 0 0. Input too large to list fully, but example shows first few lines.

boundary.description: Degenerate but full binary tree (spine): n=11 where each internal node has one leaf and one internal child, forming a path. This pattern stresses depth and may cause large traversal times.
boundary.test_values: n=11, root 1 with children 2 (internal) and 3 (leaf); node 2 with children 4 and 5 (leaf); etc. Example: 1:2,3; 2:4,5; 3:0,0; 4:6,7; 5:0,0; 6:8,9; 7:0,0; 8:10,11; 9:0,0; 10:0,0; 11:0,0. This is a left-skewed tree.

adversarial.description: Tree designed to cause exponential number of moves before reaching root, to test modulo correctness and potential overflow in intermediate calculations.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit naive simulation that doesn't use modulo properly, causing integer overflow. Use a full binary tree where the root's subtrees are large, causing many back-and-forth moves.
adversarial.why_effective: Even small trees can produce large counts if naive simulation doesn't stop early. For n=3, times are small, but for deeper trees, time grows exponentially in depth. A naive recursive simulation without memoization will overflow stack or time.

adversarial.description: Tree with many leaves that cause repeated visits to the same nodes, testing if solution correctly handles repeated states and uses dynamic programming.
adversarial.attack_vector: Stress test DP or memoization by forcing many paths. Use a balanced tree of height 10 (n=2047). The number of steps from a leaf to root is huge (exponential). A solution that recomputes for each node independently will be exponential; DP should compute in O(n).
adversarial.why_effective: For n=7, expected times are not trivially small. A naive recursive simulation without caching will recompute many subproblems, leading to explosion. The correct solution uses tree DP to compute times bottom-up.

adversarial.why_effective: Naive simulation (removing smallest each step) would take O(n^2) time as array shrinks slowly. Also, always removing the smallest element is not optimal anyway.

boundary.test_values: k=1, n=1, a_1=0 or extreme, b_1=0 or extreme

boundary.description: Zero values: a_i=0, b_j=0, etc.
boundary.test_values: k=5, n=2, all a_i=0, b_j=0 and another distinct like 5. Should have infinite? Actually initial score must be such that after each step score is one of b_j. If all a_i=0, scores are constant. So only if that constant appears in b_j then infinite? But b_j are distinct and n ≤ k. Note: The problem expects finite count because initial score must be unique? Actually if all a_i=0, then all scores are equal to initial. If that initial appears among b_j, then any initial that equals that value works? But b_j are distinct, so only one initial? Wait, the participant's initial score is unknown, and the remembered scores are after each mark. If all marks are zero, then the score never changes. So if the initial score is x, then all announced scores are x. Polycarp remembers some of these scores, all equal to x. Since b_j are distinct, there can be only one remembered value. So if that value is x, then x is the initial. So there is exactly one option. So zero case can be handled.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of constant prefix sums

adversarial.description: All jury marks positive or negative, causing many possible initial scores. Tests if algorithm correctly counts only those where the set of remembered b_j appear in the prefix sums shifted by initial.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits naive algorithm that iterates over all possible initial scores from -4e6 to 4e6 without using set of prefix sums.
adversarial.why_effective: If algorithm naively checks each possible initial score, it would loop over 8e6 values times 2000 prefix sums, causing timeout. Correct solution uses set of prefix sums and only considers initial scores that align with b_j minus prefix sums.

adversarial.description: Duplicate prefix sums after shift, causing multiple initial scores to align with same b_j set. Tests if algorithm correctly counts unique initial scores (not duplicate counts).
adversarial.attack_vector: Prefix sums can have duplicates. When computing possible initial scores from each b_j and each prefix sum, we must consider all initial scores, but if two different pairs give same initial, it should be counted once.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive algorithm might count initial scores multiple times if they appear from multiple pairs. Correct algorithm uses set of possible initial scores or ensures uniqueness.
error_types_caught: incorrect use of set vs list

adversarial.description: All b_j values are the same? But problem says distinct, so not allowed. Instead, make b_j appear at multiple positions in the prefix sums, testing if algorithm handles the condition that each b_j must appear at least once, not exactly once.
adversarial.attack_vector: Remembered scores are not necessarily all scores; they are a subset. So some b_j may appear multiple times in the sequence, but that's fine. Algorithm should only check that each b_j exists at least once.
adversarial.why_effective: A common mistake is to require that each b_j appears exactly once or that the set of scores is exactly the b_j set. Here, initial -2 gives scores [ -1,1,4 ] so b_j=1 appears but 6 does not. So no initial. But a naive algorithm might think initial -2 works because b_j=1 is present? Need to check all b_j.
error_types_caught: forgetting that all b_j must be present

For i in 1..M: if i==1: dance = [1,2,3]; next_dancer=4. else: reuse a dancer from previous dance (e.g., dance[i-1][0]), and two new dancers: dance = [reuse, next_dancer, next_dancer+1]; next_dancer+=2. If next_dancer > N, then reuse a fixed hub (say dancer 1) and two random dancers from those already assigned (ensuring they haven't appeared together with the hub in the same dance before). This generates a valid input. Example omitted for brevity.

adversarial.description: Long linear chain: first dance uses three new dancers; each subsequent dance reuses exactly one dancer from the immediate previous dance and introduces two new dancers. This forms a chain of length m, resulting in a total of 3 + 2*(m-1) dancers. For n=100001, m=50000 (approx). Tests the algorithm's ability to handle a long sequence with minimal branching.

1 2 3
3 4 5
5 6 7
7 8 9
... (continues with pattern: a_i = last dancer of previous dance, then two new)

Also, if implemented recursively, may cause stack overflow.

adversarial.attack_vector: Brute-force checking all permutations would TLE for n=10 arrays each of size 1 (10! = 3.6M, might pass? but n up to 200k, so definitely TLE). This pattern uses n=200000 arrays of size 1, which is too many for permutation generation but easy for greedy.

adversarial.description: Arrays with large element values to test integer overflow in score computation (relevant for C++ solutions using int)
adversarial.attack_vector: Element values up to 1e6, n*m up to 2e5, total sum up to 2e11, total weight up to (2e5)^2/2 ~ 2e10, product up to 2e21 > 2^63 (~9e18) so exceed 64-bit? Actually 2e5 * 1e6 = 2e11, weight max about 2e5, so max product 2e11 * 2e5 = 4e16, which is within 64-bit signed (9.22e18). But if weights accumulate, total score = sum of weights * elements, worst-case all large: each weight up to 2e5, element up to 1e6, sum up to 2e5 * 2e5 * 1e6 = 4e16, so fits in 64-bit. However, if using 32-bit int, overflow. So we include pattern to catch overflow.
adversarial.example_output: 2000010000000000? Actually compute: score = sum_{i=1}^{200000} i * 1e6? But careful: weight for element at position i (1-indexed) is (200000 - i + 1). So total score = 1e6 * sum_{j=1}^{200000} j = 1e6 * (200000*200001/2) = 1e6 * 20000100000 = 2.00001e16, which fits in 64-bit. So output is correct. But for 32-bit int, would overflow. So this catches overflow if using int.
adversarial.why_effective: Large values combined with large length cause intermediate sums to exceed 2^31-1, leading to incorrect results in languages with fixed-width integers if not using 64-bit.

error_types_caught: incorrectly thinking fixed valid string has multiple completions

boundary.description: Adjacent same fixed color makes zero ways
error_types_caught: forgetting to check adjacent fixed colors

adversarial.description: Single '?' between two different fixed colors (exactly one way)
adversarial.attack_vector: This exploits a common misunderstanding: that any '?' automatically gives at least two ways.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution might think because there is a '?' there are multiple ways, but here the only valid color for '?' is Y, so exactly one way.

adversarial.description: Multiple isolated '?' each with exactly one way, total one completion
adversarial.attack_vector: To test if algorithm correctly counts number of ways when each '?' is forced.
adversarial.why_effective: Each '?' is sandwiched between two different fixed colors, leaving only one possible color for each, so total completions=1. Naive algorithm might count incorrectly or think multiple '?' give multiple ways.

adversarial.description: Valid string with no '?' (exactly one way)
adversarial.attack_vector: Some solutions might incorrectly output Yes for valid strings with no '?' because they think exactly one way qualifies as at least one, but problem requires at least two.
adversarial.why_effective: The string is valid but only one coloring exists (the given one). The problem asks for at least two different ways, so output should be No.

key_coverage_gaps: Strings with multiple isolated '?' each having exactly one choice (adversarial_2 covers but could be extended)
Strings with a mix of forced and free '?'
Performance on maximum length with all '?'

random.description: Small random queries with n, f up to 10 for correctness verification via brute force.
random.generation_strategy: Generate q=10 queries with n and f uniformly random from 1 to 10, ensuring f ≤ n.

random.description: Large random queries with n, f up to 10^5 to test performance and correctness for larger inputs.
random.generation_strategy: Generate q=1000 queries with n and f uniformly random from 1 to 100000, ensuring f ≤ n.

boundary.description: Minimum values: n=1, f=1; also small cases where f=1 or n=f.
Maximum values: n and f at upper bound 100000.
Edge cases with prime n or n having many small divisors, and f=1 or n.
boundary.test_values: n=99991 (prime), f=1; n=99991, f=2; n=720720 (highly composite), f=360360

adversarial.description: Many queries with the same highly composite n to test divisor caching efficiency.
adversarial.attack_vector: Repeated computation of divisors for the same large n across many queries.
adversarial.why_effective: If the solution recomputes divisors for each query independently, it will be too slow for 1e5 queries with n having many divisors.

adversarial.description: Queries where answer is 0 due to n/d < f for all d (e.g., n small, f large).
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploiting early termination conditions or incorrect handling of zero cases.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might miss the condition that n/d must be at least f, leading to incorrect binomial coefficients or index errors.

adversarial.description: Queries where n and f are both large and close to each other, e.g., n=f or n=f+1.
adversarial.attack_vector: Testing large combinatorial values with small difference; potential overflow in binomial computation.
adversarial.why_effective: Binomial coefficient C(n/d-1, f-1) may be large; modulo handling and factorial precomputation must be correct.

key_coverage_gaps: Combinations of very large n and small f
Multiple queries with different n values each having many divisors
Edge case where n is a perfect power of a prime

boundary.description: Single vertex tree (n=1) to test base case
boundary.test_values: n=1, only one vertex, threat equals its danger
error_types_caught: empty output or index out of bounds

boundary.description: Star tree centered at root to test performance on shallow but wide tree
boundary.test_values: n=5 (but can scale), root connected to all other vertices. Tests alternating sums for paths of length 1 or 2.
error_types_caught: incorrect alternating sum for short paths

boundary.description: Chain (path) tree to test linear descendants
boundary.test_values: n=5, chain from root to leaf, dangers alternating small and large to test sum accumulation

adversarial.description: All dangers equal on a chain to test uniform values
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solutions might incorrectly compute threat if they assume distinct values or fail to handle ties
adversarial.why_effective: For uniform values, the alternating sum cannot exceed the danger of the starting vertex itself, as adding subsequent terms reduces the sum. Simple greedy might incorrectly compute larger sums.

adversarial.description: Deep chain with alternating large positive and negative dangers to test overflow in 32-bit integers (but Python fine; target C++ solutions)
adversarial.attack_vector: If solution uses int (32-bit) for sum, it may overflow when summing many large values
adversarial.why_effective: Alternating sum can become very large, causing overflow if using 32-bit integers. Solutions using Python's big ints or 64-bit are safe, but many C++ solutions use int and fail.

key_coverage_gaps: No pattern for large star tree with many leaves
No pattern for binary tree (balanced) to test recursion

random.description: Small random test cases with known initial array, modifications, and final array. Useful for verifying correctness of solution logic.
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, generate n up to 10, q up to 10. Create an initial array a_initial with random values in [1,10]. Generate q modifications: each with p in [1,n], x in [1,n], y in [1,10] (assuming operation a[p] = a[x] + y or similar). Apply modifications to get final array. Output modifications and final array. The solution should recover a_initial or alternative.

random.description: Large random test cases to stress test performance and memory. n up to 2e5, q up to 2e5. Random modifications.
random.generation_strategy: Generate t test cases (e.g., t=10). For each, n and q max (sum over all cases <= 2e5). Create random initial array. Generate random modifications (p, x, y). Compute final array. Provide modifications and final. Expect solution to run within time.

boundary.description: Test case with n=1 (minimum size) and various q values including 0 and max.
boundary.test_values: n=1, q=0, q=1, q=100000 (if possible). Verify handling of single element array.

boundary.description: Test case with all modifications having p=n or p=1, to test edge indices.
boundary.test_values: n large, p always 1 or n, x and y at extremes (1 or n).

adversarial.description: Case where modifications create a cycle, making naive reversal produce infinite loop or wrong answer.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solution may try to reverse operations by iterating backwards, but if operations form a dependency cycle, it may break. Requires proper handling of cycles.
adversarial.why_effective: Cycle in operation dependencies: a1 depends on a2, a2 on a3, a3 on a1. Without cycle detection, solution might incorrectly output an array.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect cycle handling

adversarial.description: Large number of modifications (q near maximum) with all distinct p, to test scalability of data structures.
adversarial.attack_vector: O(n q) solutions will TLE. Requires efficient processing like building a graph.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive reverse simulation would be O(q * n) if each modification updates many values. But here each modification independent. Still, if solution uses inefficient data structures, large q may cause TLE.

key_coverage_gaps: Large random with hierarchical constraints
Zero modifications (q=0) with large n
Multiple test cases boundary

random.description: Small random permutations (n from 1 to 10) to verify correctness of bipartiteness check.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a few test cases with n between 1 and 10. For each, use a random permutation of 1..n (by assigning ranks to distinct numbers). Compute expected output by constructing the graph of original and sorted adjacencies and checking bipartiteness via BFS/DFS.

random.description: Large random permutations (n=1000) to stress test performance and ensure bipartiteness algorithm scales.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a single test case with n=1000 using a random permutation of 1..1000 (or distinct random integers, then compress). Compute expected output via efficient bipartite check.

boundary.description: Minimum n=1: Only one card. Conditions are vacuously true (no adjacent pairs).
boundary.test_values: n=1, any distinct integer.

boundary.description: Minimum n=2: Two cards. Conditions reduce to a single edge (adjacent in original order, and adjacent in sorted order since the two numbers are consecutive in value). Always bipartite.
boundary.test_values: n=2, both increasing and decreasing order.
error_types_caught: assumption that answer can be NO for n=2

boundary.description: Large n at maximum constraint (10^5) with sorted order (increasing) to test input reading and processing speed.
boundary.test_values: n=100000, array sorted increasingly (1..100000). This is always YES.

adversarial.description: Odd-length cycle permutation for odd n. The array is a cyclic shift: [n, 1, 2, ..., n-1]. This creates a single odd cycle in the adjacency graph, making coloring impossible.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits naive assumption that answer is always YES or that only sorted order matters.
adversarial.why_effective: The graph formed by original and sorted adjacencies is a 5-cycle (odd). Many solutions incorrectly output YES because they only check one condition or don't detect odd cycles.
error_types_caught: incorrect conclusion that answer is always YES

adversarial.description: Many test cases (t=1000) with small n (n=1 to 10) to stress test handling of multiple test cases and potential timeouts from re-initialization.
adversarial.attack_vector: Large number of test cases can cause slow solutions to time out if they allocate new data structures per test case or have high constant factors.
adversarial.why_effective: Some solutions use O(n^2) per test case or have high overhead; repeated small cases amplify the issue.
error_types_caught: timeout due to inefficient per-test-case handling

adversarial.description: Worst-case permutation for bipartiteness check: a permutation that produces many cycles of various lengths, including even cycles, to test correctness of cycle detection.
adversarial.attack_vector: Permutation that is a product of many disjoint cycles, some even, some odd. Solutions that only check for odd cycles using a flawed method may misclassify.
adversarial.why_effective: This permutation gives three 2-cycles (even cycles). The graph is bipartite. Some solutions might incorrectly think that any cycle means NO.
error_types_caught: incorrect assumption that any cycle implies impossible
missed bipartiteness due to misinterpretation of cycles

key_coverage_gaps: N/A - patterns cover typical edge cases and common mistakes
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: At least 10 test cases to cover small and large, boundary, and adversarial cases.

random.description: Simple forward only: a appears earlier in s, b appears later, no other occurrences.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random string s of length 10-100, random non-empty a and b (length 1-5) such that first occurrence of a ends before first occurrence of b starts in s. Ensure b not present in reverse order.

random.description: Both directions: a appears before b in s and b appears before a in s (due to multiple occurrences).
random.generation_strategy: Generate palindrome or symmetric string s such that both a and b appear multiple times, with a before b in at least one occurrence and b before a in at least one occurrence, all disjoint.

boundary.description: Minimal s length: s length 1, both substrings length 1. Cannot fit two non-overlapping substrings.
boundary.test_values: s length 1, a and b length 1 (non-empty minimum).

boundary.description: Maximum s length with a and b at extremes. s has 50000 'a's followed by 50000 'b's, a = 100 'a's, b = 100 'b's.
boundary.test_values: |s| = 100000, |a| = |b| = 100, patterns at opposite ends.

boundary.description: One of the substrings not present in s.
boundary.test_values: a or b absent from s.
error_types_caught: missing the case where substring not found

adversarial.description: Overlapping substrings: a and b appear but their occurrences overlap. Since Peter slept between, overlapping is invalid.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive algorithm might accept overlapping occurrences if it doesn't check that a ends before b starts.
adversarial.why_effective: Common mistake: only check that a appears before b in string, not that a end < b start. Overlap invalidates the sequence.

adversarial.description: Same substring repeated: a and b are identical and appear many times. Both directions possible due to multiple occurrences.
adversarial.attack_vector: Algorithm might incorrectly identify only one direction if it doesn't consider multiple occurrences.
adversarial.why_effective: If algorithm only finds the first occurrence for each direction, it might miss the other direction if the first occurrence coincides? Actually for both directions, need a before b in forward and b before a in backward. With identical substrings, it's easy to find both if there are at least two occurrences. Naive algorithm might only check one occurrence and miss the other direction.

adversarial.description: Repeated pattern with overlapping possibilities: s is alternating 'ab', a='ab', b='ba'. Disjoint occurrences are hard to find.
adversarial.attack_vector: Algorithm that simply checks existence of a and b without proper index constraints may accept overlapping occurrences.
adversarial.why_effective: The only occurrences of 'ab' and 'ba' overlap (e.g., 'ab' at 0-1, 'ba' at 1-2). Since they cannot be disjoint, output should be fantasy. Naive substring search without index check might incorrectly think they appear non-overlapping if it finds 'ab' at 0 and then 'ba' at 2? But 'ba' at 2? s[2-3]='ab' not 'ba'. So actually 'ba' only occurs at positions 1,3,... So all overlap. So fantasy.

key_coverage_gaps: very long a and b (length 100) with s of moderate length
both a and b present but only backward direction
s with all same characters and a,b different

random.description: Small random test case with moderate n to verify correctness of construction.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n uniformly between 2 and 10. Generate a_i uniformly from 1 to 100. Then compute the optimal permutation by sorting indices by a in ascending order and assigning p in descending order (largest p to smallest a). Output the permutation.

random.description: Large random test case with many elements to stress test performance.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n = 200000, a_i uniformly from 1 to 10^9. Compute permutation using O(n log n) sorting. Ensure sum of n over test cases <= 200000.

boundary.description: Minimum n = 2, test with two elements to check edge case logic.
boundary.test_values: n=2, a=[x,y] with varying x,y. Test both increasing and decreasing order.

boundary.description: Maximum n with all a equal. This tests if solution correctly handles ties (no inversions needed).
boundary.test_values: n=200000, all a_i = 1. The optimal permutation is any; output identity (1..n) is valid.
error_types_caught: long long overflow in sum calculations? (no sum needed)

adversarial.description: Strictly increasing a array. This tests if solution correctly assigns decreasing p to avoid negative inversions.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive sorting of a and assigning p in same order may produce many negative inversions. Optimal solution should assign p in decreasing order.
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions that naively assign p as increasing order (1..n) will produce no inversions (beauty=0), missing optimal beauty.

adversarial.description: Decreasing a array. This tests if solution correctly assigns increasing p to avoid negative inversions (since inversions would give negative value).
adversarial.attack_vector: If solution assigns p in reverse order of a sorted ascending, for decreasing a, it would assign p in increasing order, which is correct.
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions that always create inversions (e.g., p descending) will produce many negative contributions, leading to suboptimal beauty.
error_types_caught: failure to consider sign of difference

adversarial.description: Large number of duplicates. Tests tie-breaking: for equal a, any permutation works; but some solutions might incorrectly enforce strict ordering.
adversarial.attack_vector: If solution assumes strict inequality, it might fail on equal values. Potential off-by-one in ranking.
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions that assign p based on rank with ties might have incorrect ordering among equal a. Our output: sorted indices by a ascending: indices: 3,4,1,2,5,6 assigning p: 6,5,4,3,2,1 -> p[3]=6, p[4]=5, p[1]=4, p[2]=3, p[5]=2, p[6]=1 yields array [4,3,6,5,2,1] but that's not permutation 1..6? Actually it is: p values are 4,3,6,5,2,1, that's a permutation. So example output: 4 3 6 5 2 1. Let's use that.

random.description: Small random test with few reindeer and queries, for correctness verification.
random.generation_strategy: Generate small n (1-5), strengths between 1 and 10, few queries (5-10) mixing add, remove, and count.

random.description: Large random test with up to 2000 reindeer and 2000 queries, to stress performance and correctness on larger data.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=2000 initial strengths in [1, 1e9], then 2000 random queries with probabilities: 30% add, 30% remove, 40% count. Strengths for add/remove chosen uniformly from existing set or from full range.

boundary.description: All strengths equal to 1 (minimum allowed strength) and small k, test base case.
boundary.test_values: strengths=1 for all reindeer, k from 0 to n.
error_types_caught: wrong combination count when strengths are equal

boundary.description: All strengths very large (1e9) and k very large (close to sum), test overflow and large numbers.
boundary.test_values: strengths=10^9 for all, n up to 2000, k up to n*10^9, also k=0.

adversarial.description: All strengths equal to the same value, with many type 3 queries asking for various k.
adversarial.attack_vector: Combinatorial explosion: the number of subsets achieving capacity depends on binomial coefficients modulo 998244353. Naive counting would be O(2^n).
adversarial.why_effective: With all identical strengths, the capacity depends only on the number of reindeer chosen, not their identities. A solution that recomputes from scratch per query or uses meet-in-the-middle without memoization will be slow.

adversarial.description: Heavy add/remove of the same strength value repeatedly, interleaved with count queries, to test dynamic multiset update correctness.
adversarial.attack_vector: Alternating add and remove of same value can cause incorrect counts if deletion removes the wrong instance or if the multiset state becomes corrupted.
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions that use a simple counter for strengths (e.g., array index) might miscount when the same strength is added and removed repeatedly. Also, if the data structure does not handle multiple identical values correctly, the answer for k where only one reindeer is needed can be wrong.
error_types_caught: count off by one after alternating adds/removes

key_coverage_gaps: Mixed strengths with large spread
Many query type 3 after many adds/removes
k = 0 edge case

random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate a length L in [4,10]. Start with a list containing at least one of each digit 1,6,8,9. Fill remaining positions with random digits (0-9) except avoid leading zero. Shuffle the list to create the number string.

boundary.test_values: Number consisting of many zeros and exactly four non-zero digits (1,6,8,9) somewhere.
error_types_caught: Incorrect placement of special digits when prefix is zero

adversarial.description: All digits zero except the four special digits. Many zeros, special digits at the end. Tests if solution incorrectly outputs 0 or produces leading zero.
adversarial.attack_vector: Common mistake: If the prefix (non-special digits) is all zeros, some algorithms may try to put zeros first, causing leading zero. They might also fail to adjust remainder correctly.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that sort the non-special digits in descending order will put zeros first (if all are zero) leading to a leading zero. They need special handling.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect modulo adjustment

adversarial.description: Multiple copies of digits 1,6,8,9. Tests if solution correctly uses only one copy of each in the special block and treats the rest as normal digits.
adversarial.attack_vector: Some algorithms may take all occurrences of 1,6,8,9 as part of the special block, leading to an unmanageable number of permutations or incorrect remainder.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution that tries all permutations of all occurrences of 1,6,8,9 would have factorial complexity (9! = 362880) which is too large. A correct solution should select exactly one of each and treat the rest as ordinary.
error_types_caught: WA if remainder correction fails due to multiple special digits

key_coverage_gaps: Extreme length exactly 10^6 with all same digit
Input with only one non-zero digit besides specials

boundary.description: All chips have same color and same range (e.g., all can only go to edge (1,2)). This limits permutations significantly.
boundary.test_values: n=5, m=4, all chips range=2 (only edge (1,2)). Colors all 0. Then only relative order changes allowed by swapping same-color adjacent chips? Actually because they are all same color, swapping is allowed anywhere. But movement restricted to single edge, so no movement needed. Final order can be any permutation? Wait: chips are initially on edge (1,2) from top to bottom in label order. They can only stay on that edge. Operations that move chips require two edges; cannot move if only one edge. So no operations except swapping adjacent same-color chips. Since all same color, any adjacent swap is allowed. This means any permutation is reachable? Actually swapping adjacent same-color chips repeatedly can achieve any permutation because chips are distinguishable but color condition is satisfied (they are all same color). So number of permutations is m! (since all colors same). This tests combinatorial counting.
error_types_caught: DP not accounting for full factorial when all colors same

boundary.description: Maximum n and m with all ranges identical (e.g., all chips have range covering entire tree). This tests the case where chips can move freely among edges, leading to maximum number of permutations.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, m=200000, all chips range = n (the last node). All colors alternating. This generates large state space.

adversarial.description: Chain tree with chips having increasing ranges that cause a large number of possible permutations, potentially overwhelming DP memory.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit combinatorial explosion by creating many chips with overlapping ranges in a chain tree. Each chip's range is a prefix of the tree. This may cause DP states to be huge.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive DP that enumerates all permutations or uses large state vectors will hit exponential growth.

adversarial.description: Tree where many chips have the same range and same color, but the tree is a star (root 1, node 2 as child, then many children of node 2). This tests whether the solution correctly handles multiple chips with identical constraints causing many symmetries.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit symmetry in colors and ranges to cause overcounting or undercounting if not properly factored.
adversarial.example_input:
1
1001 500
1 (for node 2) then for nodes 3..1001 parent=2
(all chips color 0)
(all chips range=2)
adversarial.why_effective: If the DP treats chips with identical constraints as distinct without considering symmetry, it may count permutations incorrectly.
error_types_caught: WA due to combinatorial counting errors

adversarial.description: Tree with deep branching and chips with different colors and ranges that create many constraints, testing complex DP interactions.
adversarial.attack_vector: Create a tree where some chips have ranges that are subsets of others, forcing ordering constraints that may be missed.
adversarial.why_effective: Complex dependencies between chips may cause incorrect DP transitions if not properly handled.

Tests with large branching factor
