random.description: Random inputs with large x (50-60) and random times, to test efficient computation and wrapping behavior.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random x in [50,60], random hh in [0,23], random mm in [0,59].

boundary.description: Minimum x=1 and midnight time 00:00, testing the smallest step and the start of the day.
boundary.test_values: x=1, hh=00, mm=00. The smallest possible input values.

boundary.description: Maximum x=60 and last minute of day 23:59, testing large step and time just before wrap.
boundary.test_values: x=60, hh=23, mm=59. The maximum x and time just before midnight.
error_types_caught: incorrect hour wrap when minute underflow

adversarial.description: Time with minute digit 7 but no hour digit 7, to catch solutions that only check hour digits for lucky condition.
adversarial.attack_vector: The lucky digit appears only in the minutes field, so a solution that only checks hours will incorrectly say not lucky and return a non-zero y.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution checking only hours would start from 00:07 and see no 7 in hours, then subtract x minutes (1 minute) to 00:06, etc., possibly returning a positive y, while correct answer is 0.

adversarial.description: Time at midnight with x=59, testing proper handling of minute and hour borrowing when subtracting large steps.
adversarial.attack_vector: When subtracting 59 minutes from 00:00, the result should be 23:01 the previous day. A common off-by-one error is to incorrectly compute the hour or minute after borrow.
adversarial.why_effective: Many implementations fail to correctly compute the time after subtract when minutes become negative, e.g., setting hour to 23 but minute to 1 incorrectly. This input forces that edge calculation.

key_coverage_gaps: No pattern specifically testing times where the lucky digit appears in the tens place of hours or minutes (e.g., 17:00, 00:70 is invalid, but 07:00 is covered).
No pattern with x=60 and time that already contains 7 (y=0).

random.description: Small random directed graph constraints to verify correctness
random.generation_strategy: Generate n between 5 and 20, m between 1 and n*(n-1)/2, random distinct pairs (a_i,b_i) with a_i != b_i. Compute answer using standard algorithm (SCC condensation, DAG analysis). Ensure coverage of both cyclic and acyclic components.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect cycle detection
WA due to incorrect component handling

random.description: Large random constraints to stress test performance and memory
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=100000, m=100000 random distinct pairs (a_i,b_i) with a_i != b_i, using random number generation. Ensure edges are uniformly distributed to create multiple components of varying sizes.
error_types_caught: MLE due to excessive recursion or storage
WA due to overflow or incorrect logic

boundary.description: Minimum n and m
boundary.test_values: n=2, m=1. This is the smallest possible input.
error_types_caught: edge case where component size is 2 and acyclic

boundary.description: Maximum n and m with a large cycle to test full coverage
boundary.test_values: n=100000, m=100000. All edges form a single directed cycle covering all nodes.

adversarial.description: Long chain causing deep recursion
adversarial.attack_vector: Deep DFS recursion without iterative stack
adversarial.why_effective: Naive recursive DFS for cycle detection will recurse 100,000 times, causing stack overflow in most languages.
error_types_caught: TLE if recursion depth is large but not overflow

adversarial.description: Many small cycles to test component summation
adversarial.attack_vector: Incorrect calculation of required edges per component
adversarial.why_effective: Each 2-node cycle requires 2 edges, total edges = 2*50000 = 100000. A naive algorithm might incorrectly count edges or miss cycles in small components.
error_types_caught: WA due to miscounting edges for cycles
WA due to incorrect component detection

key_coverage_gaps: Empty graph (n>2, m=0)
Self-loop (not allowed by constraints)
Multiple edges (disallowed)
Maximum n and m with all possible edges (dense graph)

random.description: Random secret with all distinct digits randomly chosen from 0-9.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly select 4 distinct digits from 0-9 and permute them randomly.

random.description: Random secret using digits from a limited range to test digit coverage.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly select 4 distinct digits from {0,1,2,3,4} and permute.

boundary.description: Secret with smallest possible digits (0,1,2,3) in increasing order.
boundary.test_values: Digits 0,1,2,3 in order

boundary.description: Secret with largest possible digits (9,8,7,6) in decreasing order.
boundary.test_values: Digits 9,8,7,6 in order

boundary.description: Secret with digits in consecutive order (1,2,3,4) as a common guess.
boundary.test_values: Consecutive digits starting from 1

adversarial.description: Secret that is far from a typical first guess (e.g., 4567) to test if algorithm can quickly narrow down.
adversarial.attack_vector: May cause first guess to yield 0 bulls and 0 cows, leaving many candidates; some algorithms might not update correctly.
adversarial.why_effective: Many naive strategies start with a fixed guess like 0123; if secret is 4567, first response is 0 bulls 0 cows, which might not help distinguish among many remaining possibilities; if algorithm doesn't efficiently prune, it may exceed query limit or make mistakes.

adversarial.description: Secret designed to expose errors in counting cows when solution makes a guess with repeated digits.
adversarial.attack_vector: The solution might incorrectly count cows when its guess contains duplicate digits; the secret is chosen so that a typical repeated-digit guess (e.g., 1111) would yield a response that a buggy algorithm misinterprets.
adversarial.why_effective: If the solution guesses 1111 at some point, correct response is 1 bull 0 cows. A buggy algorithm might count 1 bull 3 cows and incorrectly eliminate the true secret.
error_types_caught: incorrect cow counting with duplicate digits

key_coverage_gaps: Secrets with digits in non-numeric order (e.g., 1023)
Secrets that are permutations of a common set

random.description: Small random test cases with n between 2 and 10, heights between 1 and 10. Useful for correctness verification and debugging.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n uniformly random in [2,10]. Generate h array of length n with each element uniformly random in [1,10]. Output the test case input and expected output (if computed by a known correct solution).

random.description: Medium random test cases with n up to 50, heights up to 100. Tests moderate scalability and logic.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n uniformly random in [10,50]. Generate h array with each element uniformly random in [1,100]. Output test case and expected output if available.

boundary.description: All heights equal. Since all partitions are the same height, the maximum sum for any empty vessel is (n-1)*h (since all other vessels can be filled to exactly h).
boundary.test_values: n=4, h=[5,5,5,5]. Expected outputs all 15.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of equality case (max > h vs max >= h)

boundary.description: Minimum n (n=2). Tests the simplest non-trivial cyclic case.
boundary.test_values: n=2, heights h1=3, h2=5. Expected output for both k: min(h1,h2)=3.

boundary.description: Maximum heights (up to 10^9). Tests integer overflow and large number handling.
error_types_caught: runtime error due to large values

boundary.description: Monotonically decreasing heights. Tests behavior when partitions get lower along the circle.
boundary.test_values: n=5, h=[5,4,3,2,1]. Expected output unknown but can be computed.

adversarial.description: V-shaped heights: low in the middle, high on ends. This can force the empty vessel to be isolated, while others can be filled high.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits naive algorithms that assume monotonicity or fail to consider circular propagation of equality constraints.
adversarial.why_effective: The low partitions (height 1) create barriers. If the empty vessel is at index 1 (height 10 partition before it), vessels 2 and 3 might be forced to low levels due to connection through low partitions. Naive greedy might fill too high.

adversarial.description: All heights equal to 1, except the empty vessel's adjacent partitions. This tests the extreme where almost all vessels can be filled only up to 1, but the empty vessel might force others to be 0.
adversarial.attack_vector: Triggers equalities due to low heights, forcing many zeros if emptiness propagates.
adversarial.why_effective: If the solution incorrectly handles the condition (e.g., using < instead of <= or vice versa), it might produce wrong answers. Also tests symmetry.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of edge case max = h

adversarial.description: Chain of low heights connecting all vessels to the empty vessel, so all vessels must be empty. Tests if solution correctly forces all zeros when the empty vessel is in a low-height component.
adversarial.attack_vector: Forces the entire circle to have zero water if the empty vessel is connected via low partitions to all others.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might allow some vessels to have water above the low partitions, but condition would force equality, so if k is empty, all must be empty.

adversarial.description: Large n (up to 2000) with random heights, but many test cases. Tests time complexity of O(n^2) or O(n^2 log n) solutions.
adversarial.attack_vector: A large number of test cases with n near 2000 each can cause TLE if solution is not O(n log n) or O(n).
adversarial.why_effective: Many test cases with large n can cause time limit exceeded for O(n^2) per test case. The problem ensures sum of n over all test cases ≤ 2000, but we can generate within that limit.

key_coverage_gaps: Cases with n=1 (if allowed)
Cases with zero heights (possibly invalid)
Cases with repeated identical heights causing large components
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: At least 10 test cases per pattern, with varying parameters, to ensure robustness.

random.description: Small random values of m up to 1000 to verify basic correctness and brute-force comparison.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly choose m in range [1, 1000]. For each m, compute correct answer via brute force (try all X from 1 to m, simulate greedy, count blocks, choose best). Generate 10-20 such cases.

random.description: Large random values of m up to 10^15 to stress test recursion depth and performance.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly choose m in range [10^12, 10^15]. Use the correct recursive solution to compute expected output. Generate multiple cases.

boundary.description: Minimum value m=1 and small values just above cube roots.
boundary.test_values: m=1 (only cube 1), m=2 (only ones), m=7 (largest cube 1), m=8 (exact cube 2^3), m=9 (just above cube). Also m=15 (classic case).

boundary.description: Maximum value m=10^15 and nearby values to test edge cases of large cubes.
error_types_caught: incorrect cube root for large numbers

adversarial.description: Case where using a smaller first cube yields more blocks than using the largest possible.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits the fact that greedy choice of X (largest cube) may lead to fewer blocks; the optimal X may be less than the maximum cube.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution that always picks X = m (the largest possible volume) will get 2 blocks (2^3+2^3=16) while optimal is 8 blocks with X=15 (1x2^3 + 7x1^3). Many incorrect implementations fail to consider using a smaller first cube.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of two branches in DP

adversarial.description: Case where the optimal involves using a large cube after a smaller one, but the DP might miss the second branch.
adversarial.attack_vector: Test near a perfect cube boundary, e.g., m = a^3 + something small, to see if algorithm correctly compares both options.
adversarial.why_effective: For m=23, a=2 (2^3=8). Option 1: use 8, then remaining 15, best for 15 gives 8 blocks (total 9). Option 2: use 1 (a-1=1), then remaining bound min(23-1, 1^3-1=0?) Actually careful: Option 2: use (a-1)^3 = 1^3=1, then bound is min(23-1=22, 1^3-1=0) =0, so only 1 block. So best is 9 blocks from option 1. But some naive implementations might incorrectly compare and choose option 2, giving fewer blocks.

key_coverage_gaps: cases where m is exactly a cube
cases where m is between cubes but optimal uses multiple of same cube
cases with large number of cubes (like many ones)

random.description: Small random tree with few criminals to verify correctness of algorithm
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random tree with n between 3 and 10, m between 1 and 3, edge weights between 1 and 5, policeman at a random vertex, criminals at random distinct vertices not equal to s.

random.description: Large random tree with m=n=50 to test performance and DP state explosion
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random tree with n=50, edge weights random 1-50, m=50, policeman at a random vertex, criminals at random vertices (can repeat) with at least one criminal per leaf to stress test.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of large DP tables

boundary.description: Chain tree with policeman at one end and a single criminal at the other end. Minimum n=2.
boundary.test_values: n=2, edge weight=1, m=1, s=1, x=2

boundary.description: Star tree with policeman at center and all criminals on leaves. Tests optimal police strategy to catch multiple criminals on different branches.
boundary.test_values: n=51? Actually n ≤ 50, so star with 50 leaves? n=51 is not allowed. So n=50, center s, 49 leaves, m=49 all criminals on distinct leaves.
boundary.example_input:
50
... (star edges with weight 1 each) ...
centroid_vertex
49
... (all leaves) ...
error_types_caught: incorrect DP for tree with multiple branches

boundary.description: All criminals at the same vertex far from policeman. Tests that police catches all at once.
boundary.test_values: n=50, chain, s=1, all criminals at leaf n, m=50.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of multiple criminals at same node

adversarial.description: Balanced binary tree with policeman at root and criminals distributed in left and right subtrees. Tests that DP correctly decides which subtree to clear first.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits naive greedy that always goes to the closest criminal first; optimal may be to go to far side to trap criminals.
adversarial.why_effective: If police goes to closest criminal (distance 11), he catches one but other escapes to another branch, causing longer total time. Optimal is to go to the root's other child first.

adversarial.description: Tree with one leaf that has many criminals and another leaf with few, but edge weights are set so that going to many first is suboptimal.
adversarial.attack_vector: Criminals can move to other branches when police is far; DP must consider that after catching some, remaining can redistribute.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive might think to go to leaf with 2 criminals (node 3) first, but then criminal at node 5 can move away, causing longer time. Optimal is to go to node 5 first (distance 106) then to node 3 (2).

adversarial.description: Tree where policeman is at a leaf and all criminals are at other leaves, forcing policeman to traverse the tree multiple times.
adversarial.attack_vector: Tests handling of large m and policeman starting at a leaf; DP must consider that policeman must go back and forth.
adversarial.test_values: n=50, chain or star, m=49, s at one leaf.
adversarial.example_input:
50
(chain: 1-2-...-50, each weight 1)
1
49
... (all vertices 2..50, each appears once? Actually m=49, can have repeats, but chain leaves only two ends, so must repeat? Actually chain has only two leaves, so to have 49 criminals, we need multiple on same vertices. But problem allows repeats. So put all criminals at farthest leaf? That would be trivial. So put them spread along chain to force many steps.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive BFS or simulation would be exponential. Proper DP should handle it.
error_types_caught: timeout due to exponential state enumeration

key_coverage_gaps: n=1 edge case (but s cannot equal x, so n must be >=2)
edge weight 50 extreme
criminal repeats on many vertices

random.description: Random small values for A and B (both between 1 and 12) to test basic correctness.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random integers A and B uniformly in [1,12].

random.description: Random values where one of A or B is up to 1e9 and the other is small (min ≤12).
random.generation_strategy: Generate random large A in [1e8, 1e9] and random small B in [1,12], ensuring min(A,B)=B≤12. Similarly swap roles.
error_types_caught: overflow when computing factorial of large number

boundary.description: Minimum possible value of min(A,B) = 1, with various large/small partners.
Maximum allowed value of min(A,B) = 12, with various partners including both equal and large.
error_types_caught: integer overflow for factorial of 12 using 32-bit int

boundary.description: Equal values for A and B, including small and large, but with min ≤12.
error_types_caught: logical error in GCD when numbers are equal

adversarial.description: Input that tests overflow in int if factorial is computed up to 13, but min is only 12, so no overflow should occur, but naive implementation might use 32-bit int and compute factorial as int, which is fine for 12! but could overflow if they attempt to compute both factorials fully? Actually 12! fits. However, some solutions might compute factorial of A or B up to 12 safely. No overflow. So this pattern tests robustness against off-by-one in loop: e.g., loop from 1 to min(A,B) inclusive. Also tests that they use correct min(A,B) rather than max.
adversarial.attack_vector: Attempt to cause incorrect result by having A and B both large but min 12, and someone takes max instead of min.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution might compute GCD by calculating both factorials or by iterating from max(A,B) down, leading to incorrect result or timeout. Since min is 12, correct answer is 12!.
error_types_caught: wrong choice between min and max

adversarial.description: Input with A=12, B=12, but some solutions might compute factorial of 12 incorrectly due to integer overflow if they use 32-bit signed integer? 12! = 479001600, which fits in 32-bit signed (max 2,147,483,647). So no overflow. However, if they use unsigned 32-bit, it's still fine. This pattern checks for correct handling of largest allowed factorial.
adversarial.attack_vector: Edge case of maximum factorial result.
adversarial.why_effective: Ensures that the factorial calculation is correct for the maximum possible result. A naive loop that multiplies from 1 to 12 should work, but if there is a typo or off-by-one, it might produce wrong value.
error_types_caught: overflow if using wrong data type

key_coverage_gaps: Testing with min(A,B)=0 not allowed
Testing with A or B exactly at 10^9
Testing with both A and B very large but min small already covered

random.description: Small random test cases with n from 1 to 10, b_i from 1 to 300. Generated by first creating a strictly increasing sequence of random positive integers with digit sums within 1..300, then output b_i.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n random strictly increasing integers a_i (e.g., random step sizes) ensuring digit sum of each is between 1 and 300. Then output n and b_i = digit sum of a_i.

random.description: Large random test with n=300, b_i randomly generated from 1 to 300. To ensure existence, generate b_i and then compute a_i using a correct greedy algorithm.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random n (1..300) and random b_i (1..300). Then run a correct implementation to obtain a_i. Output b_i as input and a_i as expected.
error_types_caught: handling of many b_i in range 1..300

boundary.description: Minimum input: n=1, b_i = 1 (minimum possible digit sum) and b_i = 300 (maximum possible digit sum). Tests the smallest and largest single number.
boundary.test_values: n=1, b=1 gives a=1; n=1, b=300 gives a=3 followed by 33 nines (34 digits).

boundary.description: All b_i equal to 1 with maximum n=300. This creates an exponentially growing sequence: 1, 10, 100, 1000, ... up to 10^299.
boundary.test_values: n=300, all b_i=1. Extreme size of output numbers.
error_types_caught: timeout due to large number computation
incorrect handling of numbers with many digits

boundary.description: All b_i equal to 300 with maximum n=300. Each number has maximum digit sum. First number minimal (3 followed by 33 nines). Tests ability to generate strictly increasing numbers with same large digit sum.
boundary.test_values: n=300, all b_i=300. Large numbers with same digit sum.
error_types_caught: incorrect generation when digit sum is large and fixed

boundary.description: Mixed extreme values: first b=300, then b=1. Transition from a huge number to a number with small digit sum, requiring a large increase in magnitude.
boundary.test_values: n=2, b1=300, b2=1. Smallest a1 with sum 300 is 3 followed by 33 nines; smallest a2 > a1 with sum 1 is 10^(34) (1 followed by 34 zeros).
error_types_caught: handling of large jumps in number size
carrying over when digit sum decreases

adversarial.description: Monotonic decreasing digit sums: b = 300, 299, 298, ..., 1 (n=300). Forces algorithm to generate numbers that increase in value but decrease in digit sum, requiring careful construction to avoid going backward.
adversarial.attack_vector: Greedy algorithm must find next number with smaller digit sum but larger value. Naive methods might try to increase digits from previous, but decreasing sum while increasing value often requires going to a higher number of digits.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive iterative algorithms that add 1 and check digit sum will be extremely slow. Greedy algorithms may fail to correctly handle the case where digit sum decreases, leading to incorrect or non-minimal numbers.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect handling of decreasing digit sums

adversarial.description: All b_i = 1 with n=300. Creates geometric progression of powers of ten. Tests overflow (if using integer types) and performance (if naive increment).
adversarial.attack_vector: Overflow and performance: using 64-bit integers causes overflow after 10^19; naive incrementing is exponentially slow.
adversarial.why_effective: First number is 1. Each subsequent number must be larger and have digit sum 1, minimal are powers of 10. Integer overflow occurs early; increment-based searches are hopelessly slow.

adversarial.description: Alternating small and moderate digit sums: e.g., b = [1, 10, 1, 10, ...] repeated. Tests transitions from small to larger sums and back, requiring correct handling of carries and magnitude jumps.
adversarial.attack_vector: Algorithm must handle extreme changes in digit sum while maintaining increasing order. Small sum then moderate sum may require adding many digits; then next small sum must be even larger, causing exponential growth.
adversarial.why_effective: The pattern forces multiple transitions: from 1 (a1=1) to 10 (a2=19) to 1 (a3=100) to 10 (a4=109). Naive approaches that assume monotonic b_i or don't handle carries properly will produce incorrect numbers.
error_types_caught: TLE due to large number generation

key_coverage_gaps: patterns with repeated same large digit sums
patterns with non-monotonic b_i but not extreme

random.description: Small random tree with moderate constraints for verification of correctness.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n between 5 and 10, m between 1 and 5. Assign random L_i between 1 and 100, random A_i between 1 and n, random H_i between 0 and 100. Compute expected output by brute force (O(n^2)) for small n and verify against solution.

random.description: Large random tree with maximum constraints to stress test performance and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Set n=1e6, m=1e5. Generate L_i randomly between 1 and 1e5. Generate A_i uniformly from 1 to n, H_i uniformly from 0 to 1e7. Expected output not given; this tests TLE and MLE.
error_types_caught: TLE due to O(n log n) per query

boundary.description: Minimum n (n=1) with various H values.
boundary.test_values: n=1, smallest possible tree. Only one city, distance 0. H can be 0 or positive. Tests base case of tree structure.

boundary.description: Extreme L and H values: all L_i=1 (minimum), all H_i=0 or H_i=1e7 (maximum).
boundary.test_values: n=100, m=100. All L_i=1 (min). Half queries with H_i=0 (all zero happiness), half with H_i=1e7 (very large). Tests sum correctness for extreme happiness and distances.

adversarial.description: All queries from leaf node (n) with large H to maximize number of ancestor checks.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits O(log^2 n) per query if solution does binary search on each ancestor's sorted list. With many queries from same leaf, repeated ancestor traversal may cause TLE.
adversarial.why_effective: Leaf has many ancestors (log n). Each query requires updating distances along path and binary searching all ancestor subtrees. If solution does O(log n * log size) per query, repeated identical queries stress cache and may still be slow.

adversarial.description: Overflow attack: maximum n, maximum L_i, maximum H_i, and queries from root to trigger sum over all nodes.
adversarial.attack_vector: Sum of positive happiness from root with H_i=1e7 : total happiness = n*1e7 - sum_distances. sum_distances is about n * log n * maxL (approx 1e6*20*1e5=2e12). So total sum ~ 1e13 - 2e12 = 8e12, which exceeds 32-bit integer max (2.1e9). Solutions using 32-bit will overflow.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions using int instead of long long will produce wrong answers due to overflow.

key_coverage_gaps: Multiple queries from different leaves to test different ancestor paths
Queries where H is exactly equal to some distance (zero happiness threshold)
Very large n with all queries from root to test full tree traversal

random.description: Small random test cases with n and q up to 10 to verify correctness of brute force implementations.
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, randomly choose n (1-10) and q (1-10). Generate random array a of length n with values 0-5. For each query, randomly choose type 1 (update) or type 2 (query). For type 1, random index and value. For type 2, random l,r with 1-indexed. Compute expected output via brute force enumeration of all valid sequences b for small n (since n small, brute force possible).

random.description: Large random test cases with n up to 200000 and q up to 200000 to test performance and memory. Mixed updates and queries.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a single test case with n=200000, q=200000. Randomly initialize a with values in [0, 10^9]. Generate random queries: type 1 updates (30% of queries) with random indices and values, type 2 queries (70%) with random l,r and k (k maybe in [0, 10^9]? problem specifies k for query type 2: compute g(a,l,r) modulo mod, but k is given? Actually input format: for type 2, three integers l,r,k. So k is also a parameter. So include random k. Output just the computed values.

random.description: Test cases with extremes of k: very small (0) and very large (10^9). Also arrays with all zeros and all large numbers.
random.generation_strategy: Generate 10 test cases with varying n and q but focusing on edge values for k and a_i. For each, set a_i all 0, or all 10^9, or alternating. Include queries with k=0 and k=10^9.

boundary.description: Minimum array size (n=1) with various queries and updates.
boundary.test_values: n=1, array element a_1, queries: type 2 on full range (l=1,r=1) with various k, type 1 update to change a_1.
boundary.example_output: For k=0: g for sequence length 1? Output maybe 0?

boundary.description: Maximum array size (n=200000) and maximum queries (q=200000) with only type 2 queries (no updates) to test query-only performance.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, q=200000, all queries type 2 on random ranges with random k. Array a random.
error_types_caught: memory overuse from storing precomputed data

boundary.description: All a_i equal to 0 (minimum value) and all a_i equal to large number (10^9). Check for overflow or modulo issues.
boundary.test_values: a_i = 0 for all i; a_i = 10^9 for all i. Both should be handled correctly.

adversarial.description: Extreme update pattern: alternate updates to the same element many times to test update path performance.
adversarial.attack_vector: Many updates to a single element cause repeated propagation in segment tree if not lazy properly, or cause many recalculations in naive solutions.
adversarial.example_input:
1
2 200000
1 1
1 1 0
2 1 2 0
... (alternate update on index 1 and query on full range)
adversarial.why_effective: If solution uses brute force per query, it will recompute from scratch each time. If segment tree updates are not efficient, many updates to same leaf cause O(log n) each time but cumulative is fine. However, if solution stores per node something that changes on update, it's fine. But maybe some solutions precompute dp for each prefix? This pattern tests handling of repeated updates.

adversarial.description: Range queries on entire array repeatedly to stress full range processing.
adversarial.attack_vector: Many queries on same large range (l=1,r=n) forcing full array computation each time.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution recomputes g from scratch for each query, it will be O(n) per query leading to O(n*q) which is too large. The intended solution should be O(log n) per query or precomputed.
error_types_caught: TLE due to O(n) per query

adversarial.description: Queries with k=0 and large k on arrays with alternating large and small values to test combinatorial explosion.
adversarial.attack_vector: k=0 may simplify formula? Or cause division by zero? Not sure. But adversarial can target mod inverses or combinatorics.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution uses formulas involving binomial coefficients or factorials, k=0 might cause invalid assumptions. Also large k may cause overflow if not modulo.
error_types_caught: WA for edge cases in combinatorial formulas
incorrect handling of k=0 or large k

key_coverage_gaps: Missing pattern with all a_i equal to large number and many updates
Missing pattern with random updates and queries interleaved in worst-case order
Missing pattern with k exactly equal to a value that causes overflow in exponentiation

random.description: Random tree with small n and random university positions; used for verifying correctness against brute force or known solutions.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random tree of n nodes (n up to 10) using Prüfer sequence or random edges, then randomly select 2k distinct nodes as universities. Output in problem format.

random.description: Large random tree (n=200000) with random university positions to stress-test performance and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random tree of n=200000 nodes (using random parent for each new node), then randomly assign 2k distinct universities (k=n/2). Ensure no recursion depth issues (use iterative DFS if needed).
random.example_output: Expected value: sum over edges of min(size_subtree, 2k - size_subtree). For a line, answer = 200000*100000? Actually need compute.

boundary.description: Minimum n and k (n=2, k=1). Only two towns and both have universities.
boundary.test_values: n=2, k=1, universities at 1 and 2, edge between them.

boundary.description: Maximum n (200000) and k=n/2 (all towns have universities). Tree can be a line or star. This tests performance and correctness when every node is a university.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, k=100000, all towns have universities. Use a line tree: 1-2-3-...-200000.
boundary.example_output: Expected sum = 100000 * 100000 = 10^10? Actually each edge contributes min(s, 2k-s) where s is subtree size. For line from left to right, subtree sizes go 1,2,...,199999. So contribution of edge between i and i+1 is min(i, 200000-i). Sum = 2 * (1+2+...+99999) + 100000? Actually symmetric. Answer = 100000^2 = 10^10. Output 10000000000.

boundary.description: Star tree: one center connected to all other nodes. Universities placed at leaves. Tests edge cases where distances are all 2.
boundary.test_values: n=100001, k=50000, universities at all leaves (nodes 2..100001). Center node 1 has no university.
boundary.example_output: Each pair of leaves has distance 2. The maximum sum is achieved by pairing leaves optimally. Since all distances are 2, total = 2*k = 100000.

adversarial.description: Balanced binary tree where all universities are in one half. This tests if solution correctly accounts for distribution across edges.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solutions might incorrectly sum distances assuming uniform distribution.
adversarial.example_output: Maximum sum? Universities at 4,5,6,7. Pairing (4,5) and (6,7): distances 2+2=4. But better? (4,6) distance 3 via 2-1-3, (5,7) distance 3, total 6. Actually best is 6. So answer 6.
adversarial.why_effective: For each edge, contribution is min(universities in subtree, total_universities - that). If all universities in one side of an edge, that edge contributes 0. Naive algorithm might ignore this.
error_types_caught: overlooking that universities must be paired within tree

adversarial.description: Deep line tree with universities at both ends. Tests recursion depth (stack overflow) and integer overflow in sum.
adversarial.attack_vector: Recursive DFS on deep tree can cause stack overflow; also sum may be large.
adversarial.why_effective: Recursive DFS on a chain of 200k nodes will overflow recursion stack if not handled with iterative approach or increased stack limit.

adversarial.description: All universities are on the same node? Not allowed because they are distinct towns. But can place universities such that many edges contribute zero. For example, a star with university at center and leaves? Actually universities must be distinct. So center cannot have multiple. Instead, make a tree where one node has many children with universities. This tests edge case of zero contribution edges.
adversarial.attack_vector: If all universities are in one subtree, many edges contribute zero. Naive solution might incorrectly assign positive contribution.
adversarial.example_output: Universities at 1,2,3,4 on one end. The only edge that contributes is edge 4-5? Actually universities are in subtree of 4? Let's compute: tree is a line, universities at leftmost 4 nodes. For edge between i and i+1, universities on left side are 4 for first 3 edges? For edge 4-5, left side has 4 universities, right side 0, min(4,4-4)=0? Actually total universities=4, left=4, right=0 => min(4,0)=0. So all edges contribute 0? But obviously distances between universities are 1 or 2 (1-2:1, 1-3:2, etc). Pairing can give sum up to? For 4 nodes, best pairs: (1,4) distance 3, (2,3) distance 1, total 4. Wait check: edge contributions method: The sum of distances for a set of pairs is not simply sum of edge contributions? Actually known result: For any pairing, sum of distances = sum over edges of (number of pairs whose path uses that edge). And the maximum sum is achieved by maximizing each edge's contribution: it can't exceed min(universes on one side, total_universes - that side). So for each edge we take that min. For line with universities at nodes 1,2,3,4: Consider edge 1-2: left side node 1 has 1 university, right side 3, min=1. Edge 2-3: left side nodes 1-2 have 2 univ, right 2, min=2. Edge 3-4: left 3, right 1, min=1. Sum=1+2+1=4, matches. So output 4.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution assumes that edge contributions are independent and always positive, this case shows that many edges can have zero contribution.

key_coverage_gaps: trees with high degree (star) combined with specific university placements
large k near n/2 on non-line trees
multiple components? Not applicable because tree is connected

random.description: Small n values (1 to 100) with all possible x queries to verify correctness against brute-force simulation.
random.generation_strategy: For each n from 1 to 100, generate all x from 1 to n. Compute expected output using a known correct O(n^2) simulation or derived formula for verification.

random.description: Large n (up to 1e18) with random queries (q=200000) to stress time and overflow.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate n between 10^15 and 10^18, and q=200000 random x in [1,n]. Ensure no repeated queries to maximize coverage.

boundary.description: Minimum n=1 and n=2, with all possible x.
boundary.test_values: n=1 (single element), n=2 (smallest non-trivial)

boundary.description: Maximum n value (10^18) with extreme queries: x=1, x=n, x=n-1, x=n/2, and large even/odd numbers.
error_types_caught: infinite loop in while (x%2==0) for large numbers
incorrect handling of large n near power of two

adversarial.description: All queries are even numbers: some solutions handle odd positions correctly but fail on even due to improper transformation.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits common mistake of treating even positions with a simple formula or forgetting to adjust for n.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions may incorrectly assume even positions follow a pattern like (x/2)+something, but correct answer for even requires iterative reduction until odd.

adversarial.description: Large n that is a power of two (e.g., 2^60) with queries near the end: tests for potential infinite loops or overflow due to repeated halving.
adversarial.attack_vector: Power of two leads to many iterations if x is also power of two, causing time blowup in naive iterative simulation.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive O(log n) loop per query is fine, but if solution uses simulation of the whole process (O(n)), it will TLE. Also, if solution incorrectly handles very large even numbers, it may loop infinitely.
error_types_caught: infinite loop in while(x%2==0) if not careful about n

adversarial.description: n is odd (e.g., 10^18+1) and queries target positions that are powers of two: tests for correct handling of odd n.
adversarial.attack_vector: Some solutions assume n is even or rely on symmetry.
adversarial.why_effective: Odd n changes the pattern? Actually, the process works for any n. Some derived formulas might assume n is even.
error_types_caught: incorrect formula for large odd n

key_coverage_gaps: Testing with n that is not a power of two and has many factors
Testing with queries that are consecutive numbers to detect off-by-one
Testing n=10^18-1 (close to max) with various queries

random.description: Random strings with moderate length and some question marks, where a nice substring exists.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a string of length between 26 and 100. Ensure there is at least one contiguous segment of length 26 where each letter appears exactly once after filling question marks with appropriate letters. Fill other positions with random letters or '?'.

random.description: Random strings where no nice substring is possible due to duplicate letters in every window of length 26.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a string of length between 26 and 200. Insert repeated letters such that any window of length 26 contains duplicates. A simple way: fill the entire string with only one letter, e.g., all 'A's, or create a pattern with cycles shorter than 26.

boundary.description: Minimum input length (1 character). Since length < 26, it is impossible to have a nice substring.
boundary.test_values: String of length 1, containing any letter or '?'.

boundary.description: Maximum input length (50000). The string contains only '?' so a solution exists (fill first 26 with A..Z, rest with any). Ensure algorithm handles large input efficiently.
boundary.test_values: String of length 50000 consisting entirely of '?'.
boundary.example_output: ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ... (first 26 as alphabet, then remaining filled with e.g., 'A')

adversarial.description: String where naive greedy filling of '?' without considering the window leads to failure, but a careful choice yields a solution.
adversarial.attack_vector: Greedy replacement with the first available letter may break the only possible nice window.
adversarial.why_effective: The only window of length 26 starts at position 1. The missing letter is 'Z', but a naive algorithm might fill '?' with 'A', causing duplicate 'A' in the window.
error_types_caught: greedy fill leading to invalid solution

adversarial.description: Long string with no solution because every window contains duplicates (e.g., all same character). Tests that algorithm correctly identifies impossibility without making assumptions.
adversarial.attack_vector: Optimization assuming solution always exists for long strings may lead to false positive.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive algorithms might incorrectly try to fill '?' (none here) or assume that with many '?' a solution always exists, but here there are no '?' and duplicates break all windows.

key_coverage_gaps: Strings with multiple windows that could be nice, ensuring the algorithm picks one correctly.
Strings with exactly 26 characters where all are '?' (solvable) or with duplicates (unsolvable).
Strings where the nice window is at the very end or beginning.
Strings with mixed case? Problem specifies uppercase only.

error_types_caught: Incorrect formula for number of merges

boundary.test_values: n=1, m=0, k=5. Only one component, no roads needed.

adversarial.why_effective: Naive solution might think adding fewer roads works because it sums endpoints incorrectly.

adversarial.attack_vector: Components have limited stubs (min(size,k)), so large component might not help much if k is small.

random.generation_strategy: Generate a random tree of n nodes (n up to 10^5) using Prufer sequence or random parent-child assignment. For each edge, assign type 1 with probability 0.7, type 2 with probability 0.3. Ensure tree connectivity.
error_types_caught: Wrong answer due to missing problem edges coverage

random.generation_strategy: Generate a chain of length n/2, then attach remaining nodes as branches from random nodes on the chain. Assign problem edges only to branches or chain ends.
error_types_caught: Stack overflow due to deep recursion
Handling of multiple problem edges on same path

boundary.description: Minimum n = 2 with a single problem edge.
boundary.test_values: n=2, edge (1,2) type 2. Since root is 1, candidate must be node 2 to cover the problem edge.

boundary.description: Maximum n = 100000 as a chain with all edges problem (type 2).
boundary.test_values: n=100000, edges i-(i+1) type 2 for i=1..99999. Only candidate needed is node n (covers all edges).
error_types_caught: Memory limit error storing large input
Time limit due to O(n^2) algorithm

boundary.description: Star graph with root 1 and many children, all edges good (type 1).
boundary.test_values: n=100000, root 1 connected to all others, all edges type 1. No problem edges, output should be 0 with empty second line.
error_types_caught: Missed edge case of no problem roads

boundary.description: Large n with all edges problem, but tree is a perfect binary tree.
boundary.test_values: n=2^20-1 (approx 1e5), complete binary tree, all edges type 2. The minimal candidates are all leaf nodes? Actually leaf nodes cover all edges on their paths; only leaves needed? Check: root covers only edge to first child; leaves cover entire path. But if a leaf covers its path, its sibling's path shares edges? No, they share only root edge. So each leaf must be selected? Actually consider root has two children, both leaves with problem edges: leaf1 covers edge root-left, leaf2 covers edge root-right; but root-left edge is covered by leaf1, root-right by leaf2. So both leaves needed. In a perfect binary tree of depth d, number of leaves = 2^(d-1). But internal nodes also could cover multiple leaf paths? For example, a node at depth d-1 covers its two leaf children edges, but not the sibling's edges. So each leaf's path is distinct except root. So minimal set is leaves? Possibly yes, because each leaf covers its path, and any internal node's set of covered edges is a subset of its descendants' union. So leaves are sufficient. So output size = number of leaves (approx n/2). This tests memory and time for large output.
error_types_caught: Slow output for large k (up to n)
Incorrect logic for selecting nodes when many candidates

adversarial.description: Deep chain with alternating problem and good edges, designed to test if solution correctly selects the deepest nodes that cover multiple problem edges.
adversarial.attack_vector: Misunderstanding that problem edges separated by good edges require separate candidates. Naive solution might select all nodes adjacent to problem edges, leading to too many candidates.
adversarial.why_effective: Node 4 covers both problem edges (1-2 and 3-4) because path 4-3-2-1 includes both. Naive greedy might select nodes 2 and 4, but minimum is 1.
error_types_caught: Greedy selection that doesn't consider path overlap

adversarial.description: Branching tree where a node has multiple children with problem edges, testing that solution selects the deepest nodes (leaves) rather than intermediate nodes.
adversarial.attack_vector: Selecting a parent node instead of its child, leading to larger set because parent's coverage is redundant if child is already selected.
adversarial.why_effective: Node 3 covers edge 1-2 and 2-3. Nodes 5 and 6 cover their own edges to 4. If solution selects node 2 instead of 3, it would still need nodes 5 and 6, but node 2 also covers edge 1-2; however node 3 already covers that, so including node 2 is extra. Naive might select node 2 because edge 1-2 is problem and no child of 2 has problem edge? But node 2's child node 3 has a problem edge (2-3) which is not covered by node 2? Actually node 2 covers edge 1-2 only, node 3 covers both. So optimal is to use node 3. The pattern catches algorithms that incorrectly stop at a node when its parent edge is problem without checking deeper children.
error_types_caught: Incorrect handling of problem edges on path to root
Not considering that a child may cover parent's problem edge

adversarial.description: Very large n with a deep chain of problem edges, designed to cause recursion stack overflow in DFS (typically 10^5 depth may crash in recursion).
adversarial.attack_vector: Using recursive DFS without increasing stack limit, leading to runtime error on deep trees.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution uses recursion with depth equal to n, it will overflow the call stack on many programming environments (e.g., default stack size ~8MB, each frame ~100 bytes => 10^5 frames ~10MB, can overflow). Iterative DFS or increased stack size is needed.
error_types_caught: Memory limit (if using large local arrays)

key_coverage_gaps: Random patterns do not cover extreme skewness in problem edge distribution (e.g., all problem edges on one branch)
Boundary patterns missing cases with n=1? (but n>=2 per problem)
Adversarial should also include cases leading to TLE via O(n^2) path checking

random.description: Random intersecting cases where the two squares overlap in various ways (partial overlap, one inside another, touching at a point or edge).
random.generation_strategy: For each test case, randomly generate an axis-aligned square by picking a center (cx, cy) and side length s, then compute vertices: (cx-s/2, cy-s/2), (cx+s/2, cy-s/2), (cx+s/2, cy+s/2), (cx-s/2, cy+s/2). For the rotated square, generate a center (rx, ry) and diagonal length d (distance from center to vertex), then compute four vertices by rotating (0, d) by 45° intervals: (rx + d*cos(θ), ry + d*sin(θ)) for θ = 45°, 135°, 225°, 315°. To ensure intersection, adjust parameters so that the bounding circles overlap significantly. Alternatively, randomly decide intersection status and generate accordingly.

random.description: Random non-intersecting cases where squares are clearly separated.
random.generation_strategy: Generate an axis-aligned square and a rotated square far apart. Ensure minimum distance between their bounding circles exceeds sum of half-diagonals. Also include cases where squares are close but not touching (e.g., separated by a small gap).
error_types_caught: bounding box over-approximation leading to incorrect Yes

boundary.description: Squares sharing exactly one point (tangent). For axis-aligned square, one vertex touches a vertex of the rotated square, or an edge touches a vertex, etc.
boundary.test_values: Coordinates such that the squares just kiss at a single point. Testing precision of point-in-square detection.

boundary.description: One square completely inside the other. The axis-aligned square inside the rotated square, and vice versa.
boundary.test_values: Small square centered inside larger square. For axis-aligned inside rotated: the rotated square's axes are at 45°, so the inscribed square will be axis-aligned with corners touching rotated edges. For rotated inside axis-aligned: the rotated square's vertices touch the axis-aligned edges.

boundary.description: Minimum coordinate range: very small squares (side length 1) at the smallest possible integer coordinates (e.g., -1000, -1000). Also maximum coordinate range: large numbers near 10^9 to test overflow in multiplication or area calculations.
boundary.test_values: Use coordinates near the extremes of the allowed range. For example, squares at (-1000,-1000) with side 1, and at (1000,1000) with side 1. Also large squares covering almost the entire coordinate range.

adversarial.description: Squares that are very close but not intersecting, with small gap. Designed to catch solutions that use floating point comparison without epsilon.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits lack of epsilon tolerance in floating point computations. Two squares separated by a distance smaller than floating point precision may be falsely classified as intersecting.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that compute distances or check point-in-square using exact arithmetic might incorrectly consider the shared point (0,1) as outside if they consider boundaries strictly. But problem says shared point counts, so this case actually intersects. For a non-intersecting close case: adjust so that the gap is 0.0000001, but with integer coordinates, the smallest non-zero gap is 1. So use coordinates that are integer but close, e.g., axis-aligned square from (0,0) to (2,2), rotated square from (2,2) to (2,4) to (0,4) to (0,2) - they share point (2,2). That's intersecting. For non-intersecting, shift rotated square slightly: axis-aligned square (0,0)-(2,2), rotated square with vertices (3,3), (3,5), (1,5), (1,3). They have a gap of 1 unit (since nearest points (2,2) and (3,3) distance sqrt(2)>1). That's fine.

adversarial.description: Squares where the bounding boxes overlap but the actual squares do not intersect. This exploits solutions that first check bounding box overlap and then skip detailed intersection tests.
adversarial.attack_vector: Axis-aligned bounding box of the rotated square is large and may overlap with the axis-aligned square even when the rotated square is far away. Solutions that use only bounding box test will give false positive.
adversarial.why_effective: The axis-aligned bounding box of the rotated square (with vertices (8,0),(10,0),(10,2),(8,2)) is exactly the same as the rotated square itself? Actually rotated square is axis-aligned? No, it's given as rotated, but here vertices are (10,0),(10,2),(8,2),(8,0) which is axis-aligned! So that's not rotated. We need a true rotated square whose axis-aligned bounding box overlaps with the axis-aligned square. For example, axis-aligned square (0,0)-(2,2). Rotated square centered at (2,2) with diagonal 4, vertices at (2+2√2,2) ≈ (4.828,2), (2,2+2√2) ≈ (2,4.828), (2-2√2,2) ≈ (-0.828,2), (2,2-2√2) ≈ (2,-0.828). This rotated square's bounding box is approximately (-0.828 to 4.828, -0.828 to 4.828), which overlaps with (0,0)-(2,2). But do they intersect? The rotated square's center is at (2,2), which is at the corner of the axis-aligned square, so they share that point, so they do intersect. To make them non-intersecting, move the rotated square away. Use a rotated square with center at (5,5), diagonal 2, vertices approx (5+√2,5) ≈ (6.414,5), (5,5+√2) ≈ (5,6.414), (5-√2,5) ≈ (3.586,5), (5,5-√2) ≈ (5,3.586). Its bounding box [3.586,6.414] x [3.586,6.414] does not overlap with axis-aligned square (0,0)-(2,2). So that doesn't cause false positive. Need a case where bounding boxes overlap but squares do not. For example, axis-aligned square (0,0)-(2,2). Rotated square with vertices at (0,4), (2,4), (4,2), (2,0). Wait, that's a diamond shape centered at (2,2). Its bounding box is [0,4] x [0,4], overlapping with (0,0)-(2,2). But do they intersect? The diamond's edges: from (0,4) to (2,4) is horizontal at y=4, x in [0,2]; from (2,4) to (4,2) is a line y = -x+6; from (4,2) to (2,0) is y = x-2; from (2,0) to (0,4) is y = -x+4? Actually (0,4) to (2,0) is line y = -2x+4? Let's compute: slope = (0-4)/(2-0) = -4/2 = -2, equation y = -2x+4. So the diamond's interior is all points inside these four lines. The axis-aligned square (0,0)-(2,2) is entirely below y=2? Actually its top is y=2. The diamond's bottom vertex is (2,0), so they touch at that point? (2,0) is a vertex of diamond and also a point on the bottom edge of axis-aligned square? Axis-aligned square bottom edge from (0,0) to (2,0), so (2,0) is a corner of the square. So they share that point, so they intersect. To avoid intersection, shift the diamond so that its bounding box still overlaps but it doesn't touch. For example, axis-aligned square (0,0)-(2,2). Diamond with center (3,3), diagonal 2*√2? Specifically, vertices: (3+1,3) = (4,3), (3,3+1) = (3,4), (3-1,3) = (2,3), (3,3-1) = (3,2). Bounding box [2,4] x [2,4] overlaps with [0,2]x[0,2]? The overlap is just the line x=2? Actually [0,2] and [2,4] share point x=2. So bounding boxes touch at x=2. But do squares intersect? The axis-aligned square's right edge at x=2 from y=0 to 2. The diamond's leftmost point is x=2 at vertex (2,3) and (3,2). The diamond's left edge from (2,3) to (3,2) is line y = -x+5? For x=2, y=3; for x=3, y=2. So for x=2, y=3, which is above the axis-aligned square's top (y=2). For y=2, x=3, which is to the right. So they do not intersect; the point (2,2) is inside the diamond? Check (2,2): distance from center (3,3) is √2, diamond's half-diagonal is 1 (since vertices at distance 1 from center), so (2,2) is outside. So no intersection. So this is a good adversarial case: bounding boxes overlap but squares do not intersect.

adversarial.description: Squares that intersect only at a single point (tangent) but with the point being a vertex of one square and lying on an edge of the other (not at a vertex). This catches solutions that only check vertex-to-vertex touch.
adversarial.attack_vector: Some implementations only check if any vertex of one square lies inside the other or if vertices overlap. They may miss intersections where a vertex of one square lies exactly on an edge of the other.
adversarial.why_effective: The axis-aligned square's right edge from (2,0) to (2,2). The rotated square has a vertex at (2,1) which lies on that edge. Solutions that only check if any vertex of one square lies strictly inside the other (ignoring boundary) would miss this. Also solutions that check edge-to-edge intersections might catch it, but some naive vertex-in-polygon tests with < instead of <= would fail.

key_coverage_gaps: Very large numbers (10^9) to test overflow in area or distance calculations
Squares with side length 1 and nearly degenerate shapes
Multiple test cases in a single run (though problem has only two lines per test)

adversarial.description: Test case that discriminates between the correct condition (max/min ≤ 2) and a common misinterpretation (absolute difference ≤ 2). Includes a path with r=3,b=1 (ratio 3, invalid) and another with r=2,b=0 (diff=2, invalid under correct but valid under misinterpretation).
adversarial.attack_vector: Misinterpretation of 'differ at most twice' as absolute difference rather than ratio.
adversarial.why_effective: Path 1-3: r=2,b=0 invalid (ratio infinite), but if misinterpreted as |2-0|≤2 would be considered valid. Path 1-4: r=2,b=1 valid (ratio=2). But product of all valid paths: only path (1,4) has product 1*1*1=1, and (2,4) path (2-3-4) has r=1,b=1 valid product=1; (1,2) and (2,3) and (3,4) invalid. So total product=1. If misinterpreted, (1,3) would also be included, giving extra factor 1*1=1, but still product=1? Actually all weights 1, so any product is 1. To make it decisive, use non-unit weights: e.g., edges: (1-2) weight 2, (2-3) weight 3, (3-4) weight 5. Then path (1,3): r=2,b=0 invalid, product=2*3=6; path (1,4): r=2,b=1 valid, product=2*3*5=30; path (2,4): r=1,b=1 valid, product=3*5=15; total product=30*15=450. If (1,3) included, product becomes 450*6=2700. So a solution misinterpreting condition would output 2700 instead of 450. Use that as example.

adversarial.description: Star tree with n=10 (center node 1 connected to leaves 2..10). Many paths go through center, testing centroid decomposition handling of many paths with mixed colors and weights. Also includes paths with ratio exactly 2 and 0.5 to check condition boundaries.
adversarial.attack_vector: Centroid decomposition may mishandle multiplicative accumulations or overlook some paths. Also tests large number of valid paths.
adversarial.why_effective: Star tree creates many paths through center. The condition on each path depends only on the color of the two edges if path includes two leaves? Actually path between two leaves goes through center, so has two edges: one from leaf A to center, one from center to leaf B. So each such path has exactly 2 edges. Colors can be (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1). For (0,0): r=2,b=0 invalid; (1,1): r=0,b=2 invalid; (0,1) or (1,0): r=1,b=1 valid. So only paths with one red and one black are valid. Each valid path product is product of two weights. Total product is product over all unordered leaf pairs with one red and one black of (weightA * weightB). This can be computed efficiently. Provided example: red edges: 1-2 (w1), 1-4 (w3), 1-6 (w5), 1-8 (w7), 1-10 (w9). Black edges: 1-3 (w2), 1-5 (w4), 1-7 (w6), 1-9 (w8). Number of red=5, black=4. Number of valid paths = 5*4 = 20. Product = (w1*w2)*(w1*w4)*...? Actually product of all (product of two weights). So total product = (product over red weight)^black_count * (product over black weight)^red_count. Let's compute: red product = 1*3*5*7*9 = 945; black product = 2*4*6*8 = 384; total = 945^4 * 384^5 mod MOD. That's a large number; we can compute expected output mod 1e9+7 for verification. This tests modulo exponentiation and accumulation. A naive algorithm that enumerates all leaf pairs would be O(n^2) and TLE for n=100000, but here n=10 it's fine. For large star, centroid decomposition must handle it efficiently. This pattern can catch errors in multiplicative counting with prefix products.

Compute expected output by simulating anchoring: at each second, check if current wind direction is needed and if anchoring is better? Actually compute prefix counts of needed directions. boundary.description: Minimum t (t=1). Tests if the algorithm handles the smallest input size correctly. One wind direction either matches the needed move or not.
boundary.test_values: t=1, coordinates such that a single wind can or cannot reach destination.

boundary.description: Maximum coordinate magnitude (10^9). Tests ability to handle large differences without overflow. The required moves are huge (up to 2e9), but t is limited, so output is -1.
boundary.test_values: sx, sy = -1e9; ex, ey = 1e9; t <= 1e5, so impossible.

boundary.description: Max t (100000) with all needed directions at the very end of the wind string. Tests that the algorithm correctly waits for the last second and doesn't early exit prematurely.
boundary.test_values: t=100000, wind contains many opposite directions, then exactly needed directions in the last few seconds.

adversarial.description: First wind direction is opposite to the needed direction. Tests if the algorithm correctly anchors to avoid moving away from destination.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that do not allow anchoring or that move with every wind (even opposite).
adversarial.why_effective: A naive simulation that moves with every wind would first move west to (-1,0), then east to (0,0), never reaching (1,0) and output -1, while the correct answer is 2 by anchoring at the first second.

adversarial.description: Required directions appear only at the very end of the wind string, with many irrelevant or opposite wind in between. Tests if the algorithm correctly computes the earliest time as the last second when all counts are satisfied.
adversarial.attack_vector: Tests solutions that might pick the earliest occurrence of any needed direction without waiting for all needed directions to appear.
adversarial.why_effective: A solution that only checks when the first needed direction appears would output 4 (time of first E), but reachable only after both E and N have occurred (time 5). Also tests that anchoring earlier is mandatory to avoid moving in wrong direction.

adversarial.description: Exactly the needed number of each direction, but they are scattered throughout the wind string, with some opposite directions in between. Tests if the algorithm correctly counts occurrences and ignores opposite winds.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that simulate movement without using prefix counts, which may get lost or overshoot.
adversarial.why_effective: A simulation that never anchors would end at (0,0) after 5 seconds (west then east) and output -1, while the correct answer is 5 by anchoring the first 4 and using the last E.

boundary.description: Single node tree (n=1). No edges. Candy at node x, spiders cover paths. The covered set must be connected and contain an edge adjacent to x, but there are no edges. So answer should be 0.

Two-node tree (n=2) with a single edge of length 1000. Test y=1 and y=2. For any candy node x, with y=1 the best is to cover the only edge (length 1000). With y=2, the only edge is still the maximum (union of two paths must include edge incident to x, and connectivity forces covering that edge, other path cannot add more edges). So answer should always be 1000.
error_types_caught: misunderstanding of y spiders can cover duplicates
incorrect handling of y=1 vs y=n

boundary.description: Maximum values: n=100000, all edges weight=1000, and the tree is a line (path). Queries with y=1 and y=n for various x. This tests whether algorithm can handle extreme tree shape and large y.
boundary.test_values: n=100000, all edges weight=1000, line tree. y=1: answer is max distance from x to any leaf? Actually with one path, you can cover any simple path that includes an edge incident to x. The best is the longest path starting at x and going to one end. So answer is max distance to leaf. For y=n, you can cover entire tree? But must include an edge incident to x. Since tree is a line, union of n paths can cover all edges. So answer = total sum = (n-1)*1000. But careful: with n=100000, total sum is 99999000, fits in 32-bit.
boundary.example_output: answer for first: distance from 1 to farthest leaf (n-1? actually farthest from node1 is node100000 with distance (100000-1)*1000 = 99999000. For node50000: farthest leaf is either node1 or node100000, distance max(49999, 50000)*1000 = 50000000. For y=n: total sum = 99999000.
error_types_caught: overflow if using 32-bit int for total sum (though within range)

adversarial.description: Star tree: one center node (1) connected to many leaves (2..n). Edge weights = 1000. Candy at a leaf, say node 2. With y spiders, the optimal plan might be to cover paths from the leaf to other leaves via the center. However, connectivity requires that all covered edges form a connected component including the edge (1-2). The best is to cover all edges (all leaves) because the union of paths from leaf 2 to every other leaf covers all edges exactly twice? Actually paths: (2-1-3), (2-1-4), ... cover edges (1-2) and all other edges (1-i). They all share edge (1-2), so total covered edges = (n-1)*1000. So answer = (n-1)*1000. For any y>=1, the same is achievable? Not exactly: with y=1, only one path, best is (2-1-any leaf) covering edge (1-2) and one other edge, total = 2000. For y=2, can cover two such paths, covering three edges? Actually two paths: (2-1-3) and (2-1-4) cover edges 1-2, 1-3, 1-4 (total 3000). So answer increases with y up to n-1. Many solutions might incorrectly compute optimal for star.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits naive greedy that doesn't consider that paths can share edges. May overcount or undercount.
adversarial.why_effective: The star tree simplifies structure; many solutions might try to find y longest paths from the candy node but ignore that paths can be chosen to cover all edges efficiently. For y=4, the union of paths from leaf 2 to every other leaf covers all 4 edges. So answer is 4000. A naive max-weight path selection might choose paths that overlap in a non-optimal way.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect path selection strategy

adversarial.description: Deep chain with a branch near the end. Tree: nodes 1-2-3-...-100000 chain, plus node 100001 attached to node 100000. Candy at node 100001. With y=1, the optimal path is (100001-100000-...-1) covering the entire chain (length ~100000*1000). With y=2, can also cover a path from leaf 100001 to some else? But must remain connected. A common bug: assume y paths can be disjoint, but here they must connect via candy edge. Some algorithms might double count edges or fail to include the branch.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that use centroid decomposition or heavy-light but incorrectly handle the connectivity constraint near the candy node.
adversarial.example_output: For y=1: best is the whole chain? Actually from leaf 100001, the longest path includes the entire chain to node 1, length = 100000*1000 = 100,000,000. For y=2: can cover the same chain plus what? The only other edge is the branch? No other branches. So best is still 100,000,000 because union of two paths can't exceed total edges. So answer same. But a buggy solution might overestimate.
adversarial.why_effective: The deep chain tests recursion depth (may stack overflow) and also forces algorithm to handle the case where y paths cover the same set; many solutions might incorrectly assume that more paths always increase coverage.
error_types_caught: stack overflow due to deep recursion
incorrect handling of y>1 when tree is a path

adversarial.description: Online query encoding test: many queries (q=100000) with large numbers to ensure correct decoding of x and y using previous answer. The encoding uses modulo and addition; a bug in reading or computing previous answer can propagate errors.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits incorrect implementation of the online formula or integer overflow in decoding.
adversarial.example_input:
100000 100000
(complete tree of 100000 nodes, random)
100000 100000
100000 100000
... (all queries same initial values but after first answer they change accordingly). Need to compute actual answers to generate proper sequence, but for pattern we can just note that any off-by-one in formula leads to WA.
adversarial.why_effective: If the solution misreads the input or incorrectly updates x,y, the queries become wrong. This pattern ensures that the online decoding is correctly implemented.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect input parsing
WA due to integer overflow in decoding
WA due to using wrong previous answer
