boundary.test_values: n=2, m=2. Coordinates such that line segments intersect at a point.
error_types_caught: missing edge case when n=2 or m=2

boundary.description: Minimal case with no intersection: exactly 2 pumps and 2 reservoirs, but lines do not intersect (parallel or disjoint).
boundary.test_values: n=2, m=2. Coordinates such that segments do not intersect.
error_types_caught: incorrectly reporting intersection when there is none

boundary.description: Large coordinate values near 10^9 to test overflow and precision.
boundary.test_values: Coordinates at extremes: -10^9 and 10^9. Ensure intersection exists with points far apart.

boundary.description: Maximum number of points: n=200000, m=200000 but all collinear to test degenerate cases.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, m=200000. All points on a line (e.g., x=0, y varying). Pumps at even y, reservoirs at odd y. Then any two pumps and any two reservoirs will form collinear segments that overlap? Need intersection. Since collinear and overlapping, they intersect. So answer exists.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of collinear overlapping segments

adversarial.description: Many points collinear with no intersection: all pumps and reservoirs on same line but no overlapping segments.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that use orientation test incorrectly for collinear cases, or that check only one pair.
adversarial.why_effective: Many solutions assume intersection must occur at a non-collinear configuration; collinear overlapping is tricky. Here, all points are collinear, but the segments from pumps (0,0)-(1,1) and reservoirs (0,3)-(1,4) are parallel and disjoint. Naive orientation test might treat collinear as intersecting incorrectly (e.g., returning true for any orientation=0).

adversarial.description: Large dense grid causing many potential intersections but solution must be efficient.
adversarial.attack_vector: Forces O(n*m) solutions to TLE by making many points but answer exists early. However, if solution does exhaustive search without early exit, it will TLE.
adversarial.example_input:
1
100000
<100000 points on a line>
100000
<100000 points on another line crossing the first>
adversarial.example_output: Exists if lines cross, e.g., pumps on x=0, reservoirs on y=0. But solution must find it quickly. Example: pumps: (0, i) for i=0..99999; reservoirs: (j, 0) for j=0..99999. Then segment between first two pumps (0,0)-(0,1) and reservoirs (0,0)-(1,0) intersect at (0,0). So answer exists early. But if solution checks all pairs, it will be slow.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive O(n^2 m^2) or O(n*m) per pair check is too slow. This pattern catches solutions that do not use efficient data structures or early break.

adversarial.description: All points are in convex position (no three collinear) but with a specific arrangement that makes intersection impossible.
adversarial.attack_vector: Some solutions might assume a convex hull will always have intersection, but with separate sets it might not.
adversarial.why_effective: Points form two separate triangles that do not intersect. A solution might incorrectly report that any two segments from convex sets intersect.

adversarial.description: Large random points with many collinear but no intersection; test handling of collinearity in orientation.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that use floating point orientation and suffer from precision errors.
adversarial.why_effective: All pumps and reservoirs are collinear on the same line. Segments from pumps (0,0)-(1,1) and reservoirs (0,1)-(1,2) are parallel and disjoint. Using integer orientation (cross product) might incorrectly treat collinear points as intersecting if not checking overlap. Also floating point might give inexact zero.

key_coverage_gaps: points with same x or y
points overlapping exactly
single pump or single reservoir (but constraints require at least 2 each)
multiple test cases sum to large numbers

random.description: Small random valid test cases for verification
random.generation_strategy: Generate small n (1 to 10) and random frequencies that sum to n (valid). For each test case, shuffle the frequencies to avoid sorted order bias.

random.generation_strategy: Generate n up to 2e5 (multiple test cases summing to 2e5). Randomly distribute frequencies such that sum = n. Include cases with many zeros and one large frequency.
error_types_caught: output formatting errors for large arrays

boundary.description: Minimum n (n=1) with both valid and invalid sums
boundary.test_values: n=1, a1=0 (sum 0 !=1, invalid) and a1=1 (valid)

boundary.description: Maximum n and maximum frequencies (a_i = n for some i)
boundary.test_values: n=200000, a_1=200000, all others 0. Sum=200000 valid. Output should be 200000 times 1.

Also, if they allocate a list of size n, it's fine. But if they treat each i separately and create a list of lists, it may be slow.

adversarial.description: Alternating valid and invalid cases to test reset of state between test cases
adversarial.attack_vector: If solution uses global variables not reset properly, they might produce wrong output.
adversarial.why_effective: The pattern has small n but different structures; if the solution holds state across test cases, it may misprint.

adversarial.description: Large n with all frequencies zero except last one, which is n (maximal)
adversarial.attack_vector: Some solutions might allocate arrays of size n+1 and loop from 1 to n, causing time but not TLE. However, if they use O(n^2) algorithm for checking, it will TLE.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution tries to validate by building a frequency array from output and comparing, it is O(n). But if they double-loop over i and j, it will TLE.

Negative or out-of-range a_i values (though not allowed by constraints) not covered

adversarial.attack_vector: Input a power of a small prime (2^k) to test φ(2^k)=2^{k-1}. Many algorithms might have off-by-one errors for prime powers.
adversarial.why_effective: Algorithms that incorrectly handle repeated factors or use subtraction without considering exponent may produce wrong result.

adversarial.description: Product of many distinct small primes (primorial), to test algorithms that factor by trial division and may struggle with many factors
adversarial.attack_vector: Input n = product of first several primes (e.g., 2*3*5*7*11*13*17*19 = 9699690) but limited to easy version, so maybe up to 10^6: 2*3*5*7*11*13*17 = 510510.
adversarial.why_effective: Some implementations might incorrectly compute totient for numbers with many prime factors due to overflow or incorrect inclusion-exclusion.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of multiple prime factors

key_coverage_gaps: n = 0 is not in domain (positive integers)
very large numbers beyond easy version limit (e.g., 10^9) not covered
special cases like n = 2^a * 3^b

random.description: Small random cases with small n and t to verify correct rounding and carry propagation.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random n between 3 and 10, t between 1 and 3. Generate a positive decimal number with integer part from 1 to 9, a decimal point, and fractional digits of length n-2. Ensure last fractional digit is non-zero. Optionally include digits >=5 to allow rounding.

random.description: Large random case with maximum n and moderate t to test performance and sequential rounds.
random.generation_strategy: Set n=200000, t=100000. Create integer part '1', then fractional part consisting of 100000 '4's followed by 99998 '9's. Total fractional digits = 199998. This creates a chain of 100000 possible rounds, exactly matching t.

boundary.description: Minimum input size n=3 and t=1 with grade '1.5'.
Maximum n and t, no digit >=5 after decimal, but last digit non-zero.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, t=1000000000, grade '1.' + '0'*199997 + '4' (199998 zeros? Actually total fractional digits = 199998, last digit '4', so string: '1.' + '0'*199997 + '4' )

boundary.description: Integer part with 9's leading to overflow, n=7, t=1.

adversarial.description: Chain of 9's with a trailing 5 to test carry propagation.
adversarial.attack_vector: Single rounding operation that must propagate a carry through multiple 9's to the integer part.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions may fail to propagate carry beyond one digit, resulting in '1.9999' or '1.99910'.

adversarial.description: Large number of digits with first >=5 far to the right, testing floating-point precision.
adversarial.attack_vector: Use a grade with many digits so that floating-point representation loses precision, causing incorrect rounding.
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions that convert to double will truncate the number, not detecting the 5 at the end.

adversarial.description: Multiple sequential rounds required to reach maximum grade.
adversarial.attack_vector: Grade with pattern of digits that requires multiple rounds, each producing a new rounding opportunity.
adversarial.why_effective: Some solutions only attempt one rounding per second and stop after the first, but here multiple rounds are needed to achieve the maximum.

random.description: Small full binary tree with n=5 (odd) to verify basic functionality. The tree is randomly generated with balanced shape.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly assign each node as leaf or internal, ensuring total nodes odd and tree full. For n=5, create a root with two children; one child is leaf, the other internal with two leaves.

random.description: Large random full binary tree with n=100001 (odd) to test performance and memory. Tree shape is random (balanced on average).
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random full binary tree of odd size by a recursive procedure: for a given node, decide with probability 0.5 to make it leaf (if remaining nodes can form a full tree) else internal. Use a pool of nodes. Ensure total nodes equals n.
error_types_caught: memory overflow from storing full sequences
recursion depth stack overflow if deep recursion in generation

boundary.description: Minimum size full binary tree: n=1 (root only leaf). Tests edge case of single node.
boundary.test_values: n = 1, the smallest possible odd full binary tree. Only leaf node.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of leaf as root

boundary.description: Maximum size full binary tree: n=999999 (odd, largest under 1e6). Tests scalability and limits.
boundary.test_values: n = 999999, maximum odd number < 1e6. Tree with many nodes.
error_types_caught: integer overflow for node indices (if using 32-bit ints)
runtime error due to large recursion depth

adversarial.description: Deep chain full binary tree where each internal node has left child as leaf and right child as next internal node, until the last internal node has two leaves. This creates a tree with depth O(n) (n=99999).
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits recursion depth in naive implementations that recursively compute f_u or compare by recursion. Also causes long sequences in f for internal nodes, leading to huge memory if storing full strings.
adversarial.target_error: RE (stack overflow due to deep recursion) | TLE (due to O(n^2) comparison if each comparison traverses the entire depth) | MLE (if storing full function sequences)
adversarial.why_effective: The recursive computation of f_u will traverse the entire depth for every node, leading to O(n^2) time if not memoized. Also, if using recursion, the call stack depth reaches O(n) which causes stack overflow for n=1e5 or more.

adversarial.description: Perfect full binary tree (complete) with n=2^h-1, e.g., n=2^20-1 = 1048575 (just over 1e6? Actually 2^20=1048576, minus 1 = 1048575 < 1e6? 1e6=1000000, so 1048575 > 1e6, so we use h=19: n=2^19-1=524287, which is <1e6). This tree has minimal depth (log2(n)) but many leaves. Tests handling of large branching factor and many leaf comparisons.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits memory consumption if each leaf stores a full function string or if comparison creates many temporary copies. Also tests hashing collisions if many leaves have similar f.
adversarial.target_error: MLE (if storing large structures) | TLE (if comparisons are O(length) and lengths are large due to many internal nodes) | WA (if hash collision leads to incorrect ordering)
adversarial.why_effective: In a perfect tree, the function f for internal nodes becomes large quickly. If the comparison computes f recursively without memoization, it will repeatedly compute the same f for subtrees, leading to exponential blow-up. Naive implementations may time out or run out of memory.
error_types_caught: WA (incorrect handling of equal f? but they are all distinct)

key_coverage_gaps: Trees with repeated subtrees? (but problem says all f distinct)
Very deep tree with small n? Already covered in chain
Multiple test cases? Should include multiple t cases; but examples show single test case per run. Could add pattern with many small trees to test overhead.

random.description: Small random test cases for verification of correct logic
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate n and m in range 0..20, compute expected answer as min((n+m)//3, n, m), include diverse combinations

random.description: Large random test cases for stress testing performance and correctness
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate n and m up to 5e5, ensure both large and unbalanced ratios

boundary.description: Both n and m are zero
One of n or m is zero, the other large
error_types_caught: ignoring that each team needs both types

boundary.description: Both at maximum possible value (500000)
Extreme ratio with one very small and one very large
Both n and m are 1
error_types_caught: assuming at least one team possible

adversarial.description: Case where naive min(n,m) overestimates the answer
adversarial.attack_vector: Solution that returns min(n,m) without considering total people constraint
adversarial.why_effective: min(n,m)=3 but total people 7 allows at most 2 teams, so naive output 3 is wrong
error_types_caught: overestimating due to ignoring total people

adversarial.description: Case where naive (n+m)//3 overestimates the answer
adversarial.attack_vector: Solution that returns (n+m)//3 without considering individual counts
adversarial.why_effective: (n+m)//3=33 but only 1 experienced participant, so answer 1, naive output 33 is wrong
error_types_caught: overestimating due to ignoring one type

adversarial.description: Case where both constraints are active and balanced
adversarial.attack_vector: Solution that uses only one constraint (e.g., min(n,m) or (n+m)//3) but not both
adversarial.why_effective: min(n,m)=499999, (n+m)//3=333333, correct answer is 333333; any single constraint gives wrong answer
error_types_caught: missing the minimum of both constraints

key_coverage_gaps: very large n and m with large difference
cases where n and m are both near max but not equal

random.description: Random grid with small dimensions for quick verification. Generator chooses each cell as working with probability 0.5.
random.generation_strategy: Set n=m=k=3. For each cell, independently assign 1 with probability 0.5, else 0. Then compute answer via brute-force enumeration of all pairs and all paths (since small).

random.description: Large random grid with low density to stress connectivity computation. Generator creates a 100x100x100 grid with 10% working CPUs.
random.generation_strategy: For each cell, assign 1 with probability 0.1, else 0. This often yields many isolated components and few critical nodes.

boundary.description: Smallest possible grid: n=m=k=1. Only one CPU. No pair of distinct CPUs exists, so answer must be 0.
error_types_caught: assuming at least one critical exists

boundary.description: Largest possible grid with all CPUs working. In a full grid, no node is critical because there are always alternative paths between any two nodes (except possibly endpoints, but endpoints have no incoming or outgoing). Answer should be 0.
error_types_caught: assuming many critical nodes in dense graph
TLE due to O(n^3) or similar

boundary.description: One-dimensional line: n=5,m=1,k=1 with all working. This creates a linear chain where each internal node is critical because it is the only connection between left and right.
boundary.test_values: n=5,m=1,k=1, all '1'. The three internal nodes (x=2,3,4) are each critical.
error_types_caught: undirected articulation point algorithms giving different counts

adversarial.description: Dense grid with a single critical node in the middle. Create a 3x3x1 grid where all cells in layer 1 and layer 3 are working, but layer 2 has only one working cell at the center (2,2). Then all paths from layer 1 to layer 3 must go through that center node, making it critical.
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive solutions might count all nodes with both incoming and outgoing edges as critical, but here the center node is truly critical despite being one of many. Alternatively, some solutions might miss this because they consider only local properties.
adversarial.why_effective: The center node is clearly critical, but many solutions that do not check all pairs may incorrectly mark other nodes as critical or miss this one. Also, the graph is symmetric and small, making manual verification easy.

adversarial.description: A 3x3x1 grid with all working cells (full 2D grid). Despite having many nodes with indegree and outdegree, no node is critical because for any node there exist alternative paths between some pair that avoid it.
adversarial.attack_vector: Some naive solutions might incorrectly label nodes like the center as critical because its removal would break many paths, but there exist alternative paths that bypass it.
adversarial.why_effective: This directly challenges algorithms that overcount. A correct solution must output 0; any positive answer is wrong.
error_types_caught: assuming any node with high betweenness is critical

key_coverage_gaps: grids with only one working CPU
grids with many isolated components
grids with multiple critical nodes forming a chain

random.description: Random test cases with small n (n between 5 and 10) to allow manual verification and detect basic errors.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n between 5 and 10. For each book, randomly assign ti in {1,2} and wi in [1,100]. Compute expected output via DP solution for verification.
error_types_caught: wrong handling of books with thickness 2

random.description: Random test cases with maximum n=100 and random ti, wi to stress test performance and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=100. For each book, randomly assign ti in {1,2} and wi in [1,100]. Use DP solution to compute expected output.

boundary.description: Test with only one book (n=1), the smallest possible input size.
boundary.test_values: n=1, any ti (1 or 2) and wi (1-100). The answer should be ti because the book must be placed vertically if placed horizontally, sum of widths would exceed thickness (since no other books).

boundary.description: All books have thickness 1, which simplifies the DP because only one type of thickness.
boundary.test_values: n=100, all ti=1, wi varying. This tests the ability to combine many thin books.
error_types_caught: DP dimension off when thickness is small

boundary.description: All books have thickness 2, the other extreme for thickness.
boundary.test_values: n=100, all ti=2, wi varying. Tests handling of only thickness 2 books.

adversarial.description: Books with high width and thin thickness (ti=1, wi=100) mixed with low width and thick thickness (ti=2, wi=1). This tests whether the solution correctly prioritizes putting high-width thin books vertically to minimize vertical thickness.
adversarial.attack_vector: Greedy by width/thickness ratio might incorrectly place thick books vertically because they have small width, but optimal is to place thin books vertically.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive greedy that selects vertical books based on thickness-to-width ratio or weight might choose the thick books (thickness 2, width 1) because they seem 'thin', but that would force a larger vertical thickness. The optimal solution puts both thin books (thickness 1, width 100) vertically, achieving thickness 2.

adversarial.description: All books have width equal to 100, the maximum possible width. This forces the solution to place all books vertically, so answer = total thickness.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that attempt to place books horizontally may fail because the sum of widths is too large relative to thickness.
adversarial.why_effective: Any horizontal placement will immediately violate the constraint because each book has width 100, so even a single horizontal book would require vertical thickness at least 100, but total thickness is only 3. Hence all books must be vertical, giving answer = total thickness. A solution that tries to save thickness by placing books horizontally will fail.

key_coverage_gaps: mix of thickness 1 and 2 with specific sums
cases where dp[t] exactly equals total_width - t
n=100 with all identical books

random.description: Small field with few trees, for manual verification
random.generation_strategy: Choose small n (e.g., 5-10), dx and dy coprime to n, random m (e.g., 3-5) apple coordinates, compute expected output via brute force.

random.description: Moderate field with many trees, common vector (1,1)
random.generation_strategy: Set n=10, dx=1, dy=1, m=4, choose trees so that one key appears multiple times.

boundary.description: Minimum field size n=1
boundary.test_values: n=1, m=1, dx=1, dy=1, apple at (0,0)
error_types_caught: division by zero in modular inverse

boundary.description: Maximum n=10^6, dx near n, dy=1, m=1
boundary.test_values: n=1000000, dx=999999 (coprime with n), dy=1, m=1, apple at (0,0)
error_types_caught: incorrect modular inverse for large numbers

adversarial.description: Many trees on the same path (all same (x-y) mod n)
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits grouping by key; if grouping is wrong, output will not be optimal
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solution might try to simulate all starting points (O(n*m)) but this is too slow; this tests that grouping correctly aggregates count per path.

adversarial.description: Multiple trees on the same cell
adversarial.attack_vector: If multiple trees per cell are not handled correctly, count might be undercounted
adversarial.why_effective: Without counting duplicates, the answer might be (0,0) but with count 2 vs 1; grouping must sum occurrences.
error_types_caught: failure to count multiple trees per cell

key_coverage_gaps: very large m (100k) with all trees on different paths
n prime with dx,dy random
dx=1, dy=n-1 scenario

random.description: Small random test with n=3 for verification of basic functionality.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate 3 stones with edge lengths from 1 to 10.
error_types_caught: incorrect comparison of single vs pair

random.description: Small random test with n=2 where a pair gives better radius than singles.
random.generation_strategy: Generate 2 stones that share a common face and have large third dimensions compared to face dimensions.

random.description: Small random test with n=4, multiple stones with same face, including a better single stone.
random.generation_strategy: Generate 4 stones: two pairs of stones with common face but one pair's pair radius is same as single, and another stone with larger min dimension.
error_types_caught: incorrectly preferring single over better pair

boundary.description: Minimum n=1, single stone.
boundary.test_values: n=1, edges are (1,1,1).

boundary.description: n=2 stones that can be glued, pair gives larger radius.
boundary.test_values: n=2, both stones (2,2,1) so single radius=0.5, pair radius=1.

boundary.description: n=2 stones that cannot be glued, must output best single.
boundary.test_values: n=2, stones with no common face dimensions.

adversarial.description: Stones with large common face but small third dimension versus a single stone with large min dimension.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that overvalue pairs or forget to consider single stones may output the pair.
adversarial.why_effective: The pair radius is only 1, while the single stone has radius 25. Naive solutions that only consider pairs or incorrectly rank radii will fail.

adversarial.description: Stones that require orientation to match face: stone with dimensions (1,10,10) can be oriented with face (10,10) to pair with another (1,10,10).
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that do not consider all three orientations for each stone may miss valid pairs.
adversarial.why_effective: If algorithm only uses original order or only two orientations, it may not find the face (10,10) and think no pair exists, outputting single with radius 0.5 instead of pair radius 1.

adversarial.description: Many stones with identical face dimensions but varying third dimension, to test grouping and selection of top two.
adversarial.attack_vector: Solutions that use O(n^2) pairing will TLE; also tests correct selection of two largest third dimensions.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive O(n^2) will be too slow for larger n; also some solutions may incorrectly pair non-optimal stones (e.g., not the two largest z) or forget to consider that stones are distinct.

key_coverage_gaps: Large n performance with diverse face groups
Edge case where exactly one stone has a certain face (no pair possible)
Overflow in sum of third dimensions? Already safe

random.description: Small random case for verification: small n, p, q, and small values to easily compute expected outputs manually or via brute force.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n up to 5, p up to 5, q up to 3. Randomly choose c_i, h_i, t_i within 1-5. Randomly choose a_j up to 10, b_j up to 10.

random.generation_strategy: Generate n=4000 items with c_i,h_i up to 4000, t_i up to 10000, p=10000. Generate q=20000 queries with a_j up to 20000, b_j up to 4000. Use seeded random for reproducibility.

boundary.description: Minimum constraints: single item, single query, minimal p and values.
Maximum constraints: n=4000, p=10000, q=20000 with all parameters at upper bounds to test limits.
All items available at only one time (p=1), each query at a different time.
boundary.test_values: n=5, p=1, each item at distinct t_i; queries at each time.

boundary.description: Budget exactly matches cost of an item or sum of items, to test edge of knapsack.
boundary.test_values: n=2, items with costs 1 and 2, budget=2

adversarial.description: Many items with overlapping time windows (p large) and many queries at same time, to test DP reuse and offline processing efficiency.
adversarial.attack_vector: High overlap forces many items per query, potentially O(n*b) per query if not handled with divide and conquer or offline DP.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive per-query DP would recompute for each query, which is expensive with many overlapping items. Efficient solution should reuse calculations.

adversarial.description: Items with cost=1, happiness=1, many items, large p, many queries with budget small, to test if solution correctly handles many items but small budget constraint.
adversarial.attack_vector: Large number of items with low cost and low happiness may cause DP array to be huge but budget small; memory or time issues if not optimized.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive DP with dimension up to 4000*4000 would be huge. Solutions need to handle large n but small budget efficiently (e.g., using DP only up to budget).
error_types_caught: MLE due to large DP array

adversarial.description: Randomly generated items with high variance in cost/happiness and time windows that are barely overlapping, forcing many disjoint intervals.
adversarial.attack_vector: Divide and conquer DP may have many small intervals; inefficient merging could cause overhead.
adversarial.why_effective: Items are spread across time with small windows; each query sees only a few items. A naive solution might still process all items for each query.
error_types_caught: TLE from not pruning items by time

adversarial.description: Queries with time outside any item's availability, to test empty result handling.
adversarial.attack_vector: Edge case where no items are available at query time.
adversarial.why_effective: Some solutions might incorrectly output non-zero or fail to handle empty item sets.

key_coverage_gaps: No pattern specifically tests items with zero cost? (cost min is 1 so not needed)
No pattern with p=10000 and t_i=1 (longest windows)
Multiple queries with same time but different budgets tested in adversarial_1
Large number of queries (20000) with many items per query tested in random_2

random.description: Multiple test cases with small lengths (n <= 20) for quick verification, including edge cases like all same characters and alternating patterns.

Edge case where n=0 (if allowed)

adversarial.description: Single high-degree source vertex (out-degree 2999) to cause O(n^3) time in naive solutions or integer overflow if using 32-bit integers.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit naive enumeration of all pairs (b,d) from a high-degree source and checking common neighbors by iterating over all vertices. This leads to O(deg^2 * n) operations, which is about 4.5e6 * 3000 ≈ 1.35e10, causing TLE. Also, the answer can be large (approx 4e13) causing overflow in 32-bit int.
adversarial.why_effective: The source vertex (1) has out-degree 2999. All its out-neighbors have no outgoing edges (except possibly themselves, but no self-loops). So common neighbors for any pair (b,d) is 0, so answer 0. However, the naive algorithm still iterates over all C(2999,2) pairs and for each checks all n vertices for common neighbors, resulting in 4.5e6 * 3000 ≈ 1.35e10 operations, which is too slow for 1 second time limit. Additionally, if the algorithm uses int for counting intermediary steps, it might overflow. This pattern tests time efficiency and overflow handling.

adversarial.description: Graph where source vertex a is also a common out-neighbor of b and d, testing if solution correctly excludes a=c.
adversarial.attack_vector: Create a structure where a points to b and d, and b and d both point back to a. This causes an invalid rhombus (a=c) if not handled. Many naive solutions might count it.
adversarial.why_effective: Here, a=1, b=2, d=3, c=1. But c must be distinct from a, so this is not a valid rhombus. The common out-neighbors of b and d include a (vertex 1), so the count should be 0 after subtracting a. Without subtraction, the solution would count 1 rhombus.

adversarial.description: Mixing depths: one task at depth 1 and two tasks at depth 2 to satisfy Kraft sum=1
adversarial.attack_vector: Optimal solution requires combining tasks at different depths, exploiting the binary tree structure constraint that sum_{leaves} 2^{-depth}=1.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive DP that does not enforce Kraft equality or treats tasks independently may either put the large task at depth 0 (missing the chance to use it at depth 1 with two small tasks) or try to pack too many tasks.

adversarial.description: Greedy by ratio fails: high interest large time task beats many low interest small tasks
adversarial.attack_vector: A greedy algorithm that selects tasks based on interest/time ratio would pick many small tasks, but the optimal is a single large task.
adversarial.why_effective: Greedy by ratio picks the two small tasks (ratio 20) over the large (ratio 16.67), but binary tree constraints limit the small tasks to depth 1 (only two leaves possible), giving total 40 < 50. The optimal is the single large task at depth 0.
error_types_caught: not accounting for tree structure limiting number of leaves

adversarial.example_output: YES (possible: take left 'a', then right 'b', then left 'b', then right 'a'? Actually T='abab'. Sequence: left 'a', right 'b' (now T='bab'? Wait careful: initial T='abab'. Step1 left: output 'a', T='bab'. Step2 right: output 'b' (last char of 'bab' is 'b'), output 'b', T='ba'. Step3 right: output 'a', T='b'. Step4 left: output 'b', S='abab'? Sequence: L,L,R,L gives: output a (left), T becomes 'bab'; then L gives b (left of 'bab' is b), T becomes 'ab'; then R gives b (right of 'ab' is b), T becomes 'a'; then L gives a, S='abba'. Yes possible. So many solutions may miss this.)
adversarial.why_effective: Naive DP that doesn't cache states may time out, but here we want WA: solutions that only consider simple patterns might reject this.

adversarial.description: Exploit naive assumption that walking alone is always beneficial by creating a scenario where tunnels are limited and early walks block later critical paths.
adversarial.attack_vector: Force the optimal solution to require a specific order of using tunnels; a naive greedy might use a tunnel early and later be unable to reach the goal.
adversarial.why_effective: Walking alone uses a one-directional tunnel; if the algorithm uses the tunnel from 1 to 2 early, it might later need to go back via the opposite tunnel, but that tunnel is still available. However, if it uses the walk from 2 to 3 early, it might block the ability to bring the dragon from 3 to 2 later. The example design may force a solution using walking in a specific order.

adversarial.description: Exploit stamina management: require multiple swims but limited stamina increases, forcing careful scheduling of shrine visits.
adversarial.attack_vector: Set d high and S low, but shrines provide just enough stamina if visited in order; an algorithm that doesn't plan shrine visits may get stuck.
adversarial.why_effective: Starting stamina is 1, but swim requires 5. First shrine gives 0, second gives 5. So you must reach island 2 with dragon to get stamina. But to reach island 2, you might need to walk alone? Possibly use fly? Fly sets stamina to 0, not helpful. So you must walk alone from 1 to 2 without dragon, then return? But tunnels are one-way. This forces a complex sequence that naive DP might miss.

adversarial.description: Exploit that fly sets stamina to zero and see if algorithm incorrectly treats it as a reset but forgets that stamina cannot be negative.
adversarial.attack_vector: Force the algorithm to fly at a critical moment and then need stamina immediately after, but no shrine available.
adversarial.why_effective: Start stamina 3. Swim cost 2. If you swim from 1 to 2, stamina becomes 1, then you can fly to 3? But fly sets stamina to 0, then you need to land on 3 with dragon. But you flew to 3? Actually fly moves to adjacent island. So from 2 you could fly to 3 with stamina 1 (since fly requires stamina>0), setting stamina to 0. Then you are at 3 with dragon, stamina 0. Goal reached. But if algorithm tries to swim again from 2 to 3, it would need stamina 2 but has 1. So optimal is fly. If algorithm misorders, it might try to walk alone which is expensive (t_w=10). So test if algorithm correctly chooses fly.

adversarial.description: Full binary tree of depth 10 (n=2047) with all vertices except root having '?'. This causes exponential memory in naive DP because number of distinct traversals could be huge, but modulo counting should be efficient if DP is polynomial. Targets naive brute force solutions that enumerate all colorings (2^{2046} impossible) or store all traversals.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exponential blowup in number of colorings and traversal lists. Naive enumeration or storing all permutations will cause TLE/MLE.
adversarial.why_effective: A full binary tree of depth d has 2^d-1 vertices. With all '?', there are 2^{n-1} colorings. For depth 10, n=2047, 2^{2046} is astronomically large. Any algorithm that enumerates colorings will not finish. Proper DP must count distinct traversals without listing them.
error_types_caught: incorrect DP ignoring merging of identical subtrees

adversarial.description: Tree where colors are all fixed (no '?') but the structure is such that the traversal order is a mix of DFS and BFS. Tests whether the algorithm correctly computes the only traversal list. Common mistake: assuming that for fixed colors, the traversal is deterministic and simple, but the algorithm's behavior on push front/back can be tricky when a node has both 0 and 1 children.
adversarial.attack_vector: Misunderstanding of the traversal process: especially when a node is visited later after its children are queued in different order.
adversarial.why_effective: This tree: root 1 has children 2,3,4,5 in order. Colors of children: 2=0, 3=1, 4=0, 5=1. After root, we process children: first child 2 (color0) pushed to front, so deque becomes [2]. Then 3 (color1) pushed to back -> [2,3]. Then 4 (color0) pushed to front -> [4,2,3]. Then 5 (color1) pushed to back -> [4,2,3,5]. Then pop front 4, etc. The traversal list might be [1,4,2,3,5]? Actually need to simulate fully. This tests whether algorithm correctly handles multiple children of same node with different colors. An incorrect implementation might treat all children the same or ignore the push order.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect simulation of deque operations
incorrect handling of 'already in p or q' condition

adversarial.description: Threshold conflict – queues can produce small values but share the same threshold, preventing consecutive values.
adversarial.attack_vector: Designs a set of queues where specific small values (1 and 2) come from different queues but require the same threshold (i=2), making it impossible to have both. This forces MEX=2, but a naive greedy might think MEX=3.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive algorithms that try to assign target values to queues without considering threshold uniqueness may attempt to assign 1 to queue1 (threshold 2) and 2 to queue2 (threshold 2) simultaneously, but they conflict. Correct solution must recognize that 2 can only come from queue2 at threshold 2, but that threshold is already used for 1. Thus max MEX is 2 (0 and 1).

adversarial.description: Large arrivals all equal – but small n, max MEX=1
adversarial.attack_vector: All arrivals are huge numbers (>10^9) so the only small final count achievable is 0 (by serving at last moment), and all other final counts are huge. Thus MEX=1. Solutions that assume we can always achieve MEX up to n will fail.
adversarial.why_effective: Checks if the algorithm correctly identifies that no small positive final count can be produced besides 0. If it overestimates MEX, it fails.
error_types_caught: failure to consider suffix sum size

boundary.description: Minimum n and m: n=2, m=1. Graph must have exactly one edge connecting 1 and 2.
boundary.test_values: n=2, m=1: vertices 1 and 2 connected by a single edge. Weight must be prime because both shortest path and MST sum are that weight.
boundary.example_output: First line: sp and mstw both equal the prime weight. For example, weight=2: output '2 2' then '1 2 2'. But ensure weight is prime (2). Alternative weight=3,5,... But 2 is smallest prime and within 1e9. So example: 2 2\n1 2 2

boundary.description: Maximum n and m (dense graph): n=100000, m=n*(n-1)/2 (complete graph). This is extreme but within constraints? m up to ~5e9? Actually n=10^5 gives m ~5e9, too large output. So instead use moderate dense: n=1000, m=500000 (complete graph for 1000 is 499500, so m close to max). This tests handling of dense graph construction.
boundary.test_values: n=1000, m=499500 (complete graph). Need to construct such that shortest path and MST sum prime. Use construction: make a path from 1 to n with appropriate weights, and all other edges have very large weight (e.g., 10^9) to not affect MST. But careful: with complete graph, there are many edges, but we need exactly m edges. We can add all missing edges with large weight. This tests ability to generate many edges without duplicate or missing.
boundary.example_output: First line: sp and mstw computed. For n=1000, n-2=998. Choose p such that p+998 is prime. p=3 gives 1001, composite. p=5 gives 1003, composite? 1003=17*59? Actually 17*59=1003, composite. p=7 gives 1005, composite. p=11 gives 1009, check: 1009 is prime. So p=11, sp=mstw=1009. Then edges: path edges: (i,i+1) for i=1..999 with weight 1 except last edge weight 11. Then all other possible edges (i,j) with i<j not in path have weight 10^9. This outputs many edges. Example output lines: first line '1009 1009', then 499500 edges.
error_types_caught: shortest path calculation on dense graph

adversarial.description: Star graph: n vertices where vertex 1 is connected to all others, and no other edges. But must have exactly m edges. For star, m = n-1. This tests whether solution handles graph where shortest path from 1 to n is direct edge, and MST is also star (all edges in tree). Need to set weights so that both sums prime.
adversarial.attack_vector: Some naive constructions may fail when graph is a tree or star because they assume a path structure. Also, in star, shortest path is single edge, so weight must be prime. MST sum is sum of all edges, which may not be prime if we just set all to 1.
adversarial.example_output: Star: edges 1-2, 1-3, 1-4, 1-5. Need shortest path from 1 to 5 weight prime, and MST sum prime. Set edge 1-5 weight p (prime) and other edges weight 1. Then MST sum = p + 3*1 = p+3, which must be prime. So choose p such that p and p+3 are both prime. Example: p=2 gives p+3=5 (prime). So edges: 1-2:1, 1-3:1, 1-4:1, 1-5:2. Then sp=2, mstw=5. Output: '2 5' then edges.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solution assuming path from 1 to n may fail on star because shortest path is single edge, not multi-edge path. Also, if solution uses a different tree for MST, star might cause trouble.

adversarial.description: Graph with multiple edges between same vertices? No multi-edges allowed. We'll generate a case where the construction must avoid duplicate edges when adding extra edges.
adversarial.attack_vector: Some solvers might generate extra edges by iterating over all pairs and adding if not already in tree, but they might accidentally add an edge that is already present if not careful with ordering.
adversarial.target_error: WA (due to duplicate edges in output)

1 2 1
2 3 1
3 4 5
1 3 10
1 4 10. Check no duplicate: all distinct.

For each trainer, generate a random set of 20 distinct teams from 1..T, but ensure teams are consecutive? Actually problem says teams are numbered consecutively from 1 to T, so all teams 1..T appear in at least one wish list. So we need to ensure coverage. With n=4, l_i=16, each list 16 teams, total distinct might be up to 64 but T must be consecutive from 1. So set T=64. Create hate pairs: only two pairs, e=2.

error_types_caught: integer overflow in counting total hate

boundary.description: Edge case with T=1 (all teams same) but wish lists must be distinct? Actually teams are numbered consecutively, but if all trainers want the same team, T would be 1. But l_i >=16, so each list must have 16 distinct teams? They said each team no more than once per list. So with T=1, cannot have 16 distinct teams. So T minimum is at least 16. But we can set T=16 and all trainers want exactly all 16 teams.
boundary.test_values: n=4, e=2, T=16, each trainer's wish list is exactly 1..16.

adversarial.description: Graph with high hate density but limited team choices to force suboptimal splits
adversarial.attack_vector: The problem requires at least e/2 hate between conferences. If graph is dense but trainers have few common teams, naive assignment may fail to achieve the threshold.
adversarial.why_effective: Many hate pairs involve trainers from different team groups; assignment may need to put all trainers from same team in same conference to maximize cross-conference hate? Actually we need at least e/2 between conferences. If we put all in one conference, between conference hate is 0. So we need to split teams. With limited team overlap, some hate pairs cannot be made cross-conference if trainers are forced into same team? Wait, team assignment is free as long as each trainer gets a team from his list. So we can assign trainers to different teams to enable cross-conference hate. But if all trainers have disjoint team sets, we can put each team in a different conference, maximizing cross hate. The challenge is when trainers share teams. This case tests if the algorithm can find a valid assignment.

adversarial.description: Large T with small wish lists relative to T, causing many teams unused but still consecutive
adversarial.attack_vector: If T is huge (1e6) but each trainer only lists 20 teams, the algorithm might iterate over all teams unnecessarily, causing TLE.
adversarial.example_input:
50000 100000
(edges)
For i=1 to 50000: list of 20 teams: ( (i-1)*20+1 to i*20 ) but must be consecutive? Actually teams are numbered 1..T, so if T=1e6, we can partition into 50000 groups of 20. So each trainer gets a unique set of 20 consecutive teams? Not necessarily consecutive, but can be. Example: trainer1: 1..20, trainer2: 21..40, etc. Then T=1000000, but last trainer gets 999981..1000000. This ensures all teams appear. Then hate edges can be arbitrary.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive algorithms that create arrays of size T for each team may cause memory or time issues. Also, initializing large arrays for team conferences might be heavy.
error_types_caught: TLE due to large T loops
MLE from storing all team info

adversarial.description: All hate pairs form a complete graph on a subset of nodes, but those nodes have no common teams
adversarial.attack_vector: If a clique of trainers have no common team, they must be assigned to different teams. But then teams can be placed in different conferences to achieve cross-conference hate. However if all teams are in same conference, cross-conference hate is 0. The algorithm must ensure at least e/2 hate between conferences. With a clique of size k, e = k*(k-1)/2, so need at least k*(k-1)/4 between conferences. This is achievable if we put half teams in conference 1 and half in 2, and assign the clique members to teams accordingly. But if the clique members have disjoint team sets, we can assign each to a different team and place those teams in alternating conferences. This test checks if algorithm can handle such balancing.
adversarial.why_effective: The algorithm might ignore the need to split teams properly if it focuses only on individual trainers' preferences. It might assign all trainers to same conference because they are all in different teams, but then cross-conference hate is e (if all teams in same conference, cross=0). Actually if all teams are in same conference, hate between conferences is 0. So we need to split teams. This test ensures that the algorithm can correctly assign conferences to achieve threshold.
error_types_caught: conference assignment not considering hate pairs
incorrect count of hate between conferences

adversarial.description: Tree where root has cat, and some branches have cats at children but then no cats; tests reset after break.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that do not reset the consecutive cat count when encountering a vertex without a cat.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive BFS/DFS might count both leaf4 and leaf5 (since root and child have cats, but child's child has no cat, so consecutive count resets to 0 at child, but then leaf is reached; however, the path includes root(1) and child2(1) -> two consecutive before encountering non-cat at leaf? Actually leaf4: path: 1(1),2(1),4(0). Consecutive cats are exactly the first two vertices -> 2 > m=1, so not allowed. Leaf6: 1(1),3(0),6(0) -> consecutive cats: only root -> 1 <= m, allowed. So only leaf6 is valid. Incorrect solutions might count leaf4 as well if they don't properly accumulate consecutive cats.

adversarial.description: Star tree: root with cat, all leaves without cat, m=1. Tests that path from root to leaf has exactly 1 consecutive cat (root only), so all leaves should be counted.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that treat leaf cats differently or miscount consecutive when leaf is immediately after root.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution might think that since root has cat and leaf has no cat, the consecutive count is 0 (resetting incorrectly) or 0? Actually many solutions correctly count, but if they set current consecutive to 0 when cat absent, they might not add root's cat. Correct: at root, consecutive=1. Then go to leaf (no cat), consecutive=0 (resets). But the path to leaf includes root, so we must have recorded that max consecutive along path was 1. So correct. However, a solution that does not propagate the max correctly might still count it as 0 consecutive, error.

For instance, selecting all four streets results in all vertices degree 2 (even) and beauty from alternating sums: need compute. Actual optimal might be different. This tests if algorithm correctly solves the parity-constrained optimization.

boundary.test_values: a=m=100 ensures no remaining votes. Tests if algorithm correctly computes final outcome without any uncertainty.

boundary.description: k=n, meaning all candidates with votes are elected. Tests if algorithm correctly handles seats equal to candidates.

boundary.description: k=1, only top candidate gets seat. Tests tie-breaking when multiple candidates tie for first.
boundary.test_values: k=1, a=2, m=3, votes [1,2] so each has 1 vote. Remaining 1 vote can break tie or create new tie. Candidate with earlier last vote is higher.

adversarial.description: Tie-breaking exploit: create a scenario where candidate A has many votes but very late last vote, candidate B has fewer votes but early last vote. With remaining votes, it's possible for B to tie A and win on tie-breaker, but algorithm might not consider this.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits insufficient consideration of last vote time in determining guaranteed status.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might think candidate 1 is guaranteed because they have 2 votes vs candidate 2's 1, but remaining 2 votes could go to candidate 2, making both 2 votes, and candidate 2's last vote (from time 3) is later than candidate 1's last vote (time 2), so candidate 2 is higher. Thus candidate 1 is not guaranteed, only chance.

adversarial.description: Zero-vote candidate chance: a candidate initially with 0 votes can still be elected if they get all remaining votes and tie-breaking favors them. Algorithm might incorrectly mark them as impossible.
adversarial.attack_vector: Overlooking that zero votes at current time does not mean zero votes at end.
adversarial.why_effective: Candidate 3 currently has 0 votes, but with 3 remaining votes they can get 3 votes and become top. However, candidates 1 and 2 each have 1 vote and earlier last votes. If candidate 3 gets all 3, they have 3 votes and are first. So candidate 3 has chance. Naive solutions might output 3 for candidate 3.
error_types_caught: incorrect marking of impossible for zero-vote candidates

adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that require strictly greater weights for non-MST edges will fail because equal weight is allowed.

random.description: Graph with no hydra, to test false positive rejection
random.generation_strategy: Generate a graph where no edge (u,v) has enough distinct non-common neighbors to form a hydra. For example, a complete bipartite graph K_{100,100} has many edges but for any edge (u,v), all neighbors of u are also neighbors of v? Actually in bipartite, no edge between partitions, so u's neighbors are all in opposite partition, v's neighbors also in opposite; they share many? Let's design simpler: a star graph with center node 1 connected to all others, and another node 2 connected to a few. For any edge (1,2), heads from 1: all others except 2, but those are all shared with 2? No, 2 is only connected to 1 and maybe some others. Actually star: node1 connected to nodes 2..n; node2 connected only to node1. For edge (1,2), node1 has neighbors 3..n, node2 has neighbor 1 only. So node2 has degree 1 < t if t>1. So no hydra. But need to ensure all edges fail. So make a graph where for every edge, at least one of the vertices has insufficient degree or too many common neighbors. Use a line graph.

adversarial.attack_vector: Degrees of u and v are high but all neighbors are shared, so no hydra exists. Naive algorithm that only checks degree conditions would incorrectly output YES.

1 2

(Note: 1-2 edge also present? Actually need edge 1-2. So edges: 1-2, 1-3,1-4,1-5,1-6, 2-3,2-4,2-5,2-6. That's 9 edges? Let's count: 1-2,1-3,1-4,1-5,1-6 (5 edges); 2-3,2-4,2-5,2-6 (4 edges) total 9. So n=6, m=9, h=2,t=2. For edge (1,2), neighbors of 1: 3,4,5,6; neighbors of 2: 3,4,5,6; all common. So no head can be chosen that is not adjacent to 2, and no tail not adjacent to 1. So NO.
adversarial.why_effective: Algorithm might see degree(1)=5 >=2 and degree(2)=5 >=2 and output YES without checking that required neighbors are not adjacent to the other center.
error_types_caught: false positive due to missing adjacency check

adversarial.description: Overlapping neighbor sets: u and v have some common neighbors, and algorithm must select disjoint sets from non-common neighbors
adversarial.attack_vector: If algorithm does not ensure that heads and tails are disjoint and not adjacent to the opposite center, it might pick overlapping nodes or nodes that are adjacent to the wrong center.
adversarial.example_input:

1 2
1 3
1 4
1 5

(Note: u=1, v=2. Neighbors of 1: 3,4,5; Neighbors of 2: 5,6,7. Common neighbor: 5. So possible heads: from {3,4} (not adj to 2); tails: from {6,7} (not adj to 1). So h=2,t=2, we can choose heads={3,4}, tails={6,7}. Output YES. But if algorithm incorrectly picks heads={3,5} or tails={5,6}, it's invalid. The adversarial aspect is that the sets must be chosen carefully; algorithm must handle overlap correctly.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive algorithm that picks first h neighbors of u and first t neighbors of v without checking disjointness or adjacency to opposite center may fail.

adversarial.description: Edge between two heads, making the induced subgraph not a tree
adversarial.attack_vector: Algorithm that only checks adjacency to u and v but ignores edges among heads/tails will output YES for a graph that is not a hydra because of extra edges among heads.

1 2
1 3
1 4
2 5
3 4
(Explanation: u=1,v=2. Heads candidate: 3,4 (both connected to 1, not to 2? Actually check: 3 not connected to 2? Edge list: 3 not connected to 2; 4 not connected to 2; so they are valid heads for adjacency to u? But there is an edge between 3 and 4. So if we choose heads={3,4}, there is an edge among heads, making the induced subgraph have a cycle (1-3-4-1). So it's not a hydra. However, we could choose heads={3,??} but we need exactly 2 heads; only choices are 3 and 4. So no valid hydra because any two heads will include the edge. So answer should be NO. But if algorithm doesn't check edges among heads, it would output YES with heads={3,4}.
adversarial.why_effective: Many solutions only check that heads are not adjacent to v and tails not to u, ignoring the tree structure requirement. This test catches that.
error_types_caught: false positive due to missing inter-head/tail edge check

adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit common assumption that answer for k=2 might be related to global maximum or something else.
adversarial.why_effective: The global maximum is 100 at index 2, but answer is max(a1, an)=5. Naive solutions that pick the max element might output 100, which is wrong.

adversarial.description: k=3 (or more) with array where max element appears multiple times and at different positions. Ensure answer is global max regardless of position.
adversarial.attack_vector: Check if code correctly handles k>=3 by maybe computing min of concatenated segments incorrectly.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive approach that tries to compute something like min of some range might fail because they could isolate 10 as one segment, achieving min=10. But they might incorrectly think they need to include all elements? Actually must split into exactly k segments. Here k=3, we can do [-5], [-5], [-5,10] -> mins -5,-5,-5 -> max=-5. Wait that gives -5, not 10. Is 10 achievable? Need to isolate 10 alone. But we have 4 elements and k=3. We can do: [-5], [-5], [-5], [10] but that's 4 segments. If k=3, we cannot have 4 segments. So we need exactly 3 segments covering all 4 elements. One valid split: [-5,-5] and [-5] and [10] -> mins -5,-5,10 -> max=10. Yes possible. So answer 10. But if someone tries to do greedy of making segments with min as large as possible, they might miss that they can isolate 10 by grouping three negatives together. This tests correct handling of k>=3.

adversarial.description: Large negative numbers only, k=1. Answer is the minimum (most negative). Stress test for negative handling.
adversarial.attack_vector: Array all negative, varying size, k=1. Ensure answer is min (i.e., most negative).
adversarial.why_effective: Naive initialization of min with 0 would fail because all values are negative.

But we want minimal distances, so we could set distances to 1,2 in all sectors? But then between sector1 and sector2, they have same distances? That would violate guarantee. So if sector1 has 1..100000, sector2's single distance must be outside that range, e.g., 100001. Similarly for other sectors, we can assign them distances that are unique relative to their adjacent sectors. For simplicity, make each sector have exactly one bridge? But then no cells, total unstable=0. That doesn't test. So we want at least one sector with many bridges to create many cells, and adjacent sectors with varying bridge counts. Since total bridges limit 100k, we can allocate one sector with 50000 bridges, and others with few bridges such that distances are unique between adjacent sectors.

adversarial.description: Two clusters of points far apart. Each cluster has points densely packed. This forces the algorithm to process many large inter-cluster edges without forming triangles, stressing the bitset intersection step.

For two components with sizes s1 and s2, the optimal orientation on the tree edges gives contribution. Here sizes s1=5, s2=3, n=7. The maximum pairs is s1^2 + s2^2 + 2*s1*s2 = (s1+s2)^2 = 49. So answer=49. Naive solutions that don't compress may get less.

So shortest subsegment is for number 2 of length 4? But beauty is 4, so we need a subsegment containing an element 4 times. So only number 3 qualifies. The minimal window for number 3 is 4 to 9 (length 6). But maybe there is a smaller subsegment containing 4 occurrences of 3? The earliest 4 occurrences: indices 4,6,7,9: the span is 4-9 = length 6. Alternatively indices 6,7,9,? there is no fourth after 9? So length 6. So answer would be 4 9. That's fine. Need a better adversarial: make two numbers both have max frequency, one with tight cluster. Example: n=8: 1 1 1 2 2 2 2 3. Frequencies: 1:3, 2:4, 3:1 -> beauty=4 only for 2. Minimal window for 2: positions 4,5,6,7 -> length 4 (4-7). Another: 1:3, 2:3, 3:3: e.g., 1 1 2 2 3 3 1 2 3? Then minimal window for block number is length 3, for spread ones longer. That would catch bugs where solution picks the first most frequent number without checking minimal window.

Actually for a block, first and last occurrence is the block itself, so that's fine. The bug is if the solution only considers the first number with max frequency encountered, or if it uses a global first and last of all numbers? Another bug: incorrectly computing minimal window that contains a given count of a number. This pattern tests the correctness of finding minimal window for each number that achieves max frequency.

adversarial.description: Large array where the maximum frequency is achieved by many numbers all spread out, but the minimal subsegment is very short because one number appears many times in a small interval. This forces a solution to compute the minimal window efficiently.

We want short: make a number appear very frequently in a small interval, e.g., 1000 occurrences in a row, and other numbers have the same max frequency but spread out. But if they have same max frequency, then shortest window is the small interval. Example: n=2000, number 1 appears 1000 times in positions 1-1000, number 2 appears 1000 times in positions 1,3,5,... spread throughout. Then minimal window for 1 is length 1000, for 2 is length >1000. So answer is 1 1000. This tests that solution finds the tight cluster.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution that takes the entire range of the most frequent number might pick a much larger segment if it happens to check the spread number first. Also O(n^2) solutions will timeout on large n.

adversarial.why_effective: The intersections of lines between (-2,-1), (0,0), (2,1) all yield the same x (0) but each small ship placed at 0 destroys all 6 enemies because all rays pass through the center? Actually, careful: Many pairs produce x=0, but the actual destroyed set is all enemies. Solution might incorrectly combine multiple candidate x but not realize that one position suffices.

adversarial.description: Case where one group has all enemies at the same x coordinate, and the other group has spread out coordinates, testing if solution handles when many rays coincide.
adversarial.attack_vector: Group 1 all at same x, Group 2 scattered. The small ship can be placed at intersection with any b_j, but the best might be to place at a position that hits many from group 2 via collinearity with group 1.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solution might enumerate all intersections (only (0,b_j) lines) and miss that a small ship at (0,0) destroys all group 1 plus some from group 2? Actually, careful: Rays from group 1 to small ship at (0,0) go straight up; they only hit group 1 itself. But group 2 rays to small ship at (0,0) hit only group 2? The problem is symmetric. The best is to place small ship at (0,0) destroys all group1 (5) and all group2? Not necessarily, because rays from group1 to small ship are vertical, they don't hit group2. Rays from group2 to small ship: from (-10, -100) to (0,0) line passes through (0,0) only, so no other enemies. So total destroyed=5+3=8? Actually, each ray from each enemy destroys the target small ship? No, rays destroy enemies they pass through. A ray from group1 to small ship passes through other group1 enemies if they are on the same vertical line? Yes, all group1 are at same x=0, so vertical ray hits all group1. Similarly, ray from group2 hits only itself. So total 5+3=8. So answer 8. This tests if solution accounts for rays that hit multiple enemies from same group.

adversarial.description: Case with many points but no three collinear with any small ship candidate except trivial ones, forcing the solution to handle many candidate positions and bitmasks efficiently.
adversarial.attack_vector: Coordinates chosen such that each pair generates a distinct intersection x (no duplicates), so the number of candidates is O(n*m) and bitmask enumeration is heavy.
adversarial.why_effective: With 2500 candidates, a solution that processes each candidate by checking all n+m enemies would be O((n+m)*n*m) ≈ 5e5, which is fine. But if solution uses pairwise check among enemies for each candidate, it may become O(n*m*(n+m)^2) too large. This catches inefficient algorithms.

+-+-
(Since k=4, n=4, period full. b_3 = -1, term = -1 * 0^0 * 2^3 = -8 mod 10 = 2. But careful: formula: b_i * a^{n-1-i} * b^i. For i=0: a^{3}=0 term=0; i=1: a^{2}=0; i=2: a^{1}=0; i=3: a^{0}=1, term = b_3 * 1 * b^3 = -1 * 8 = -8 mod 10 = 2. So output 2.
error_types_caught: division by zero when computing ratio

boundary.test_values: n multiple of k, e.g., n = 2*k. Tests proper handling of full periods.

adversarial.description: Geometric ratio equals 1 modulo m, requiring special handling of division by zero
adversarial.attack_vector: When (b^k * inv(a^k)) mod m = 1, the geometric series formula needs to use sum = Q * first term mod m instead of (ratio^Q - 1)*inv(ratio-1). Naive implementations that compute modular inverse of (ratio-1) will fail if ratio=1 mod m because denominator 0 has no inverse.
adversarial.target_error: WA | RE (division by zero) | runtime error if not handled
adversarial.example_input:
6 2 4 7
+++
(k=3, n=6, a=2, b=4, m=7). Compute: a^k mod m = 2^3=8 mod7=1, b^k=4^3=64 mod7=1, so ratio = (1*inv(1)) =1 mod7. So sum = 2 periods * first period sum. First period: i=0: +1*2^5*4^0=32 mod7=4; i=1: +1*2^4*4^1=16*4=64 mod7=1; i=2: +1*2^3*4^2=8*16=128 mod7=2; sum=4+1+2=7 mod7=0. So total=0. Many naive solutions might incorrectly compute denominator inv(0) and crash.
adversarial.why_effective: Common solution uses modular inverse of (ratio-1). If ratio=1, denominator is 0, causing division by zero or infinite loop.

adversarial.description: Large n with k=1 and ratio=1 mod m, causing sum = n * (first term) mod m, testing overflow in multiplication
adversarial.attack_vector: When k=1 and s[0] is '+' and a=b mod m, then ratio = (b^1 * inv(a^1)) = 1 mod m. Sum = n * a^{n-1} mod m. For large n, multiplication may overflow if not using modular multiplication. Also naive exponentiation may be slow if not fast.
adversarial.example_output: Let's compute: a=b=2, m=1e9+9, ratio=1. Sum = n * 2^{n-1} mod m. 2^{n-1} mod m using fast exponentiation. Then multiply by n mod m. Expected: 2^{999999999} mod m * 1e9 mod m. Hard to compute manually but we can reference. Example output should be some number.
adversarial.why_effective: If solution iterates linearly over n, it will TLE. If it uses geometric series but forgets to handle ratio=1, it will use division formula incorrectly.

adversarial.description: m is composite, a or b not coprime with m, causing modular inverse to not exist
adversarial.attack_vector: In the geometric series, we need to multiply by inverse of (a^k mod m) and inverse of (ratio-1). If a is not invertible modulo m (gcd(a,m)>1), the computation of inv(a^k) fails. However, the correct approach is to recognize that the formula involves a^{-k} as part of ratio, but we can rewrite the sum without inverse by computing directly? Actually the typical solution computes the sum for the first period multiplied by geometric series of ratio = (b^k * inv(a^k)) mod m. If a is not invertible, we cannot compute inv(a^k). But we can instead compute the sum by iterating over each period? Might be too slow. So this input breaks solutions that assume m is prime or that a and m are coprime.
adversarial.target_error: RE (modular inverse not found) | WA (incorrect result if using non-invertible)
adversarial.example_input:
4 2 3 6
+-+
(k=3, n=4, a=2, b=3, m=6). Compute manually: i=0: +1 * 2^3 * 3^0 = 8 mod6=2; i=1: -1 * 2^2 * 3^1 = -4*3=-12 mod6=0; i=2: +1 * 2^1 * 3^2 = 2*9=18 mod6=0; i=3: b_0 again? Since n=4, period k=3, i=3 gives b_0? Actually n=4, indices 0,1,2,3. b_3 = b_0 because period 3. So i=3: +1 * 2^0 * 3^3 = 1*27=27 mod6=3. Sum = 2+0+0+3=5 mod6=5. So output 5. Naive solution that inverts a^k=2^3=8 mod6=2, gcd(2,6)=2, inverse doesn't exist. So it will fail.
adversarial.why_effective: Many solutions assume m is prime (as in typical CF problems) but m may be composite. This input exposes reliance on modular inverse of a.

adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution might consider that vertices 4 and 5 are in a tree (bipartite) attached to triangle, but because component is non-bipartite, no vertex can be beautiful. Incorrect solution would output 2 (size of tree part).
error_types_caught: WA (incorrectly counting vertices in non-bipartite components)

key_coverage_gaps: Graphs with multiple odd cycles
Graphs with self-loops (not allowed)
Very large m but small n

random.description: Small random test with all values small, used for verifying correctness by brute force or manual checking.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate n, m, q between 1 and 5. Generate t_i and d_i randomly between 1 and 10. Generate episode lengths e_i between 1 and 5. Generate query times T_j randomly between 1 and 20. Ensure feasibility: all tasks can be scheduled by deadlines without episodes; adjust if necessary.

random.description: Large random test with constraints near limits, used for performance and stress testing.
random.generation_strategy: Set n=100000, m=100000, q=100000 (but sum over test cases ≤1e5, so only one test case). Generate t_i, d_i, e_i, T_j uniformly within allowed ranges (1 to 1e9). Ensure feasibility by generating deadlines sufficiently large: e.g., d_i = sum of all task times before i + random slack. Or use a known feasible generator: first generate episode lengths, then set deadlines large enough to allow all tasks.
error_types_caught: time limit exceeded (TLE) due to O(n^2) algorithm

boundary.description: Minimal values: n=1, m=1, q=1, smallest task time and episode length.
boundary.test_values: n=1, m=1, q=1. t=1, d=1, e=1, T=1. Expected: Since episode takes 1 minute, and task must be done by time 1, it's impossible to watch the episode before time 1 (since then task would be late). So answer 0.
error_types_caught: logic error when n=1 or m=1

boundary.description: All deadlines very large relative to task times and T, so any number of episodes up to m can be watched before T (if time allows).
boundary.test_values: Tasks with very large deadlines (e.g., 1e9) and small processing times. Episodes short. T large. Expectation: answer is min(m, floor(T / sum_e) )? Actually need to also consider task mandatory sum. But since deadlines huge, all tasks can be done after T, so condition reduces to total homework time before T can be 0, so mandatory_sum=0, so only constraint is S_k ≤ T. So maximum k with S_k ≤ T.

boundary.description: Zero episodes (m=0). Output should be 0 for all queries.
boundary.test_values: m=0, n>0, q>0. No episodes, so answer is always 0.

boundary.description: Single episode length larger than T, so before T cannot complete any episode.
boundary.test_values: m=1, e_1 > T so answer always 0.

boundary.description: Multiple tasks with deadlines exactly equal to T. This forces mandatory tasks to be done before T, potentially limiting episodes.
boundary.test_values: n=2, tasks; deadlines both = T=10; t1=3, t2=5. Episodes: e1=4, e2=2. Total mandatory time 8, S_1=4 ≤ 10, feasible; S_2=6? Actually S_2=4+2=6, mandatory+episodes=8+6=14>10, so only 1 episode possible. Answer for T=10 is 1.

adversarial.description: Many tasks with tight deadlines that are just above T, causing a large mandatory sum, but episodes are short. Exploits solution that incorrectly assumes all homework can be postponed after T.
adversarial.attack_vector: cause solution to underestimate mandatory homework time before T
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions may assume that if deadlines are greater than T, then all tasks can be postponed after T, but due to tight deadlines after T, watching episodes before T reduces the available time after T, causing infeasibility.
error_types_caught: incorrect logic for tasks with deadlines > T
missing check of feasibility after T

adversarial.description: Very large number of episodes, and query times that require binary search on k. Exploits solutions that do linear search per query.
adversarial.attack_vector: force O(n*m) or O(q*m) by causing many iterations in binary search due to large m
adversarial.example_output: For each T, answer is min(k where S_k ≤ T) because homework trivial. But only one task with deadline huge so mandatory sum=0. So answer is max k with S_k ≤ T. Output many zeros. Since m and q up to 1e5, binary search per query is O(log m) okay, but if solution does O(m) per query, TLE.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution might iterate over episodes for each query, resulting in O(m*q) time.
error_types_caught: TLE due to O(m*q) or O(n*q)

key_coverage_gaps: Multiple test cases with varying sizes
Episodes with total length exceeding large T
Tasks with deadlines very close to each other causing scheduling conflicts
Very large T that allows all episodes up to m

error_types_caught: WA from incorrect DP or memoization
