adversarial.description: A number one greater than the maximum long value, which should be BigInteger but may cause overflow if parsed.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that try to parse the number into a 64-bit integer, causing overflow and incorrect comparison.
adversarial.why_effective: If the code attempts to convert the string to a long long, it will overflow (since it's one more than max long). The comparison might then be incorrect.

adversarial.description: A 19-digit number that is lexicographically larger than max long string, but not by much; tests string comparison correctness.
adversarial.attack_vector: Targets solutions that only compare length or do naive lexicographic comparison without considering leading digits.
adversarial.why_effective: The number has the same length as max long (19 digits) but is larger. Some naive solutions might compare strings and incorrectly think it's still within long because they only check length, or they might convert to unsigned incorrectly.

key_coverage_gaps: Numbers exactly at the boundary between int and long (2147483648)
Numbers with many digits but not exceeding long max (e.g., 19-digit numbers less than max long)

random.description: Small random test with minimal number of friends (n=2) for verification.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=2 with random positions in [1,100] and speeds in [1,10].

random.description: Large random test with n=60000, positions and speeds uniformly distributed over full range.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=60000 with positions uniformly in [1,1e9] and speeds uniformly in [1,1e9].

boundary.description: Minimum n=2 with extreme positions and speeds; testing min and max boundaries.
boundary.test_values: n=2, x1=1, x2=1e9, v1=1, v2=1; the optimal meeting point is at 5e8 resulting in time ~5e8 seconds.

boundary.description: All friends have same position; answer should be 0.
boundary.test_values: n=5, all xi=42, vi arbitrary; the meeting time is 0.

adversarial.description: Extreme asymmetry: one friend far away with very low speed, others close with high speed. Tests if binary search correctly narrows to the constrained friend.
adversarial.attack_vector: The answer is dominated by the slow friend; solutions that naively use average or midpoint may fail.
adversarial.why_effective: The middle friend at 1e9 with speed 1 dictates the time; the other friends can reach anywhere quickly. A faulty interval intersection might not correctly handle this imbalance.

adversarial.description: Precision stress test: large n with positions clustered very close together, causing the feasible time interval to be extremely narrow. Tests floating-point precision in binary search.

adversarial.description: Case where naive combination fails due to wrap-around not handled
adversarial.attack_vector: Sum of two halves can exceed m, requiring to consider both L+R and L+R-m. Solutions that only check L+R may miss the max.
adversarial.why_effective: The optimal subset gives sum 19, modulo 10 = 9, but sum of individual halves might be e.g., 6+4=10 (0 mod 10) and 5+2+3=10 (0), requiring combination of sums that exceed m to achieve 9.

adversarial.description: Maximum n with all a_i = m-1
adversarial.attack_vector: All a_i equal to m-1. Then any non-empty subset sum modulo m is either (m-1)*k mod m. Since (m-1) ≡ -1 mod m, sum of k elements ≡ -k mod m. To maximize, we want k such that (m - (k mod m)) mod m is large. For n=35, m large (e.g., 1000), maximum is m-1 = 999 if odd number of elements, else 0. Solutions that don't consider all subsets might miss.
adversarial.why_effective: Only odd number of elements give modulo 6, even give 0. Brute-force for n=6 is small but for n=35, naive meet-in-the-middle must correctly combine counts.
error_types_caught: overflow in number of subsets (though small for half)

adversarial.description: Sequence with many repeating small values, e.g., t = [0,0,0,...]. This exploits a common mistake where one might think that duplicates allow frequent revisits, but actually only the first occurrence of each value can be a revisit; subsequent occurrences force new rooms because the last visit time changes.
adversarial.attack_vector: Misleads solutions that count frequencies or think duplicates always allow revisits.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solution might think answer is 1 (only one distinct value) or 2 (first revisit, then new? but actually each 0 after first forces a new room).
error_types_caught: incorrect answer due to misinterpretation of revisit condition

adversarial.description: Sequence where a value appears but not at the right time to be reused, e.g., t = [0,1,0]. This breaks solutions that assume any previous occurrence of the same number allows a revisit.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits confusion between 'value' and 'last visit time'.
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution might think since 0 appears twice, one could be a revisit, but actually after the first revisit, the last visit time becomes 1, so the second 0 does not match any last visit time, forcing a new room.

adversarial.description: Large alternating pattern: t = [0,1,0,1,0,1,...] for n=200000. This tests the set operations and might cause many insertions and deletions.

adversarial.why_effective: While algorithm is O(n log n), some suboptimal implementations could become O(n^2) if they use lists or scans.
error_types_caught: TLE due to inefficient data structure

adversarial.description: Many vertices have inefficient cards (low power per cost) while one vertex on a critical path has extremely good efficiency. Naive solutions might waste budget on weak cards before reaching the good vertex.

adversarial.example_output: For k=1000: you can buy 1000 cards at vertex 4 (cost 1 each, power 1000) giving 1000000 power, but you have to buy at least cost 1 from each earlier vertex (since you must pass them, but you don't have to buy anything? Actually you can skip buying. So you can go directly to vertex 4 and spend all money there. So output 1000*1000=1,000,000. For k=2000: similarly 2000*1000=2,000,000. But naive DP that treats path as forced to buy something might incorrectly subtract costs from earlier vertices.

adversarial.example_output: For k=10: path 1->2->4->5: buy at 2 (cost 5, power 10) and at 4 (cost 20>5 remaining? Actually after buying at 2, remaining 5, can't buy at 4. Alternative path 1->3->4->5: buy at 3 (cost 1, power 1) and at 4 (cost 20>9) no. Best is buy at 1 only? But you must go to t, so you can buy at 1: cost 10, power 100, then go directly? But from 1 you can go to 2 or 3, and eventually to 5? Yes. So buy at 1: power 100. So output 100. For k=200: you can buy at 1 (100), at 2 (10), at 4 (200? cost 20, power 200) actually you can buy multiple. Possibly buy 10 at 1? but each card costs 10. So with 200, buy 20 at 1 gives 2000 power. So output 2000. So optimal might not use other vertices. But the point is path selection.
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions that do not consider all paths may miss the best combination of items.
error_types_caught: WA due to incorrect path exploration

adversarial.description: Queries with very large k (up to 1e9) but only small intermediate vertices. Tests if algorithm correctly handles large k in unbounded knapsack without iterating over k.

adversarial.example_output: For each query with k=1e9, optimal is to buy at vertex 2 only: cost 1 each, power 1e9, so max power = 1e9 * 1e9 = 1e18, which fits in 64-bit. So output huge number. Naive O(k) DP would be too slow.
adversarial.why_effective: Large k forces algorithms to handle unbounded knapsack efficiently, e.g., via convex hull trick or slope optimization. Simple DP by cost would fail.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of very large numbers

adversarial.description: Vertices with decreasing efficiency (power/cost) along the path, so optimal strategy is to buy only from the first vertex if budget is small, but from later vertices if budget is large. Tests ability to select proper combination across multiple vertices.

adversarial.example_output: For k=1: only vertex 1 is affordable, power=100. For k=1000: best is to buy 1000 copies at vertex 4? cost 4 each, power 200, but you cannot afford 1000*4=4000>1000. Actually you can buy 250 copies at vertex 4 (cost 4 each) for 1000 cost, power 250*200=50000. Meanwhile buying at vertex 1: 1000 copies cost 1000, power 1000*100=100000, which is better. So optimal might be to buy all at vertex 1. Actually efficiency of vertex 1 is 100 per cost, vertex 4 is 50 per cost, so vertex 1 is best. So output 100000 for k=1000. The adversarial part is that vertex efficiency decreases, but naive might think later vertices are better due to higher power per card, but cost is higher.
adversarial.why_effective: Solutions that only compare power per card (not per cost) will make mistakes.
error_types_caught: WA due to using power per card instead of power per cost

random.description: A set of consistent guesses that uniquely determine the secret number. Typically 2-5 guesses with varying bull/cow counts, leading to a single candidate after filtering.
random.generation_strategy: Pick a random 4-digit number with distinct digits (including leading zero). Generate 2-5 guesses by choosing random 4-digit distinct-digit numbers and computing their bull/cow counts against the secret. Ensure the set of guesses is sufficient to uniquely identify the secret (i.e., only the secret remains after filtering all 5040 possibilities). If not, add more guesses until unique.

random.description: A set of guesses that are inconsistent (no possible secret matches all guesses). This tests the detection of 'Incorrect data'.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random secret and a few guesses. Then modify one guess's bull or cow count by 1 or change a digit while keeping counts, ensuring no secret satisfies all guesses. Alternatively, create two guesses that conflict (e.g., first guess: 1234, bulls=4, cows=0 is invalid because game not over, but bounds prevent that; so use other contradictions like a digit appearing in wrong counts).

boundary.description: Minimum number of guesses (n=1). With only one guess, the secret cannot be uniquely determined (unless bulls=4, which is not allowed). The output must be 'Need more data'.
boundary.test_values: n=1, guess with any valid bulls and cows (sum ≤ 4, not 4 bulls). Should result in need more data.

boundary.description: Maximum number of guesses (n=10) but still ambiguous, to test that the algorithm correctly outputs 'Need more data' even with many guesses.
boundary.test_values: n=10, all guesses consistent but leave multiple candidates (e.g., all guesses have the same bull/cow pattern against different numbers, so many secrets satisfy).
error_types_caught: incorrect termination on ambiguous high n

boundary.description: Maximum guesses with inconsistency. Use 10 guesses where the last one contradicts the previous, testing that the algorithm correctly identifies 'Incorrect data' with many inputs.
boundary.test_values: n=10, first 9 consistent, last one conflicting.
error_types_caught: incorrect inconsistency detection with many guesses

adversarial.description: Guesses with zero bulls and zero cows. This eliminates many digits quickly but still leaves many candidates (e.g., if guess is 0123, any secret with digits 0,1,2,3 is ruled out, leaving 5040 - combos of 4 from other 6 digits = 360? Actually combinations: choose 4 from remaining 6 digits: 15 combos, each can be arranged in 24 ways = 360. With multiple such guesses, candidate count may still >1. This tests if algorithm handles large candidate enumeration efficiently and correctly outputs 'Need more data' when multiple remain.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploit that many 0-bull 0-cow guesses drastically reduce candidate set but still may not yield a unique solution; implementation might mistakenly think it's unique if it doesn't iterate over all remaining possibilities correctly.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might cut off early if they only consider guesses that eliminate all but one candidate, but here two guesses still leave many candidates. Also, implementation might incorrectly compute complement intersection.
error_types_caught: performance issues with large candidate set

adversarial.description: Guess with leading zero (e.g., '0123'). This tests that the algorithm treats the input as a 4-digit string and does not convert to integer losing the leading zero. Especially important when iterating over all 4-digit numbers from 0000 to 9999 (only those with distinct digits).
adversarial.attack_vector: If the program reads the guess as an integer, leading zero is lost, and later when comparing to candidate numbers, it may compare '123' to '0123', causing incorrect matching.
adversarial.why_effective: Some implementations may parse the guess as integer, storing as 123 instead of 0123. Then when checking candidates, they compare 0123 (as a string of length 4) to 123 (as 3 digits), leading to wrong bull/cow counts.

adversarial.description: A set of guesses that create many possibilities with the same bull/cow counts, forcing the algorithm to exhaustively check all 5040 numbers. This tests both correctness and performance (no TLE).
adversarial.attack_vector: Use a sequence of guesses that each have bull count 0 and cow count 0 for a subset of digits, gradually narrowing but leaving a symmetric group of candidates. For example, guess with digits 0-3, then 4-7, etc., leaving at least 4 digits. With up to 10 guesses, there can still be multiple candidates.
adversarial.why_effective: This input is likely inconsistent because after first 5 guesses (each 0 bulls 0 cows), all digits are covered, making any secret impossible. Then the next guesses add bulls, creating contradictions. A naive brute-force might still iterate over all 5040 candidates and check all 10 guesses, which is fine for 5040*10=50400 operations, but if implementation is poorly coded (e.g., repeated expensive checks), it could be slow. Also, it tests that contradiction is detected correctly.

key_coverage_gaps: Edge case where secret has all zeros? Not allowed because digits must be distinct, so at most one zero. So 0000 invalid.
Guesses where bull+cow=4 but bulls<4, testing that implementation correctly limits sum.
Large number of candidate enumeration with many consistent guesses leading to unique solution (e.g., 10 guesses uniquely determine). Our patterns don't include that, but it's covered by normal case.
Test with all possible bull/cow combinations (0-4, sum ≤4) to ensure exhaustive counting works.

random.description: Large random graph with n=5000, m=20000 to test performance and memory usage.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=5000, m=20000. Each split has 1-10 outputs, with at least one -1. Ensure some cycles but also many terminating paths. Use adjacency lists. Total sum of l_i ≈ 100000.

boundary.description: Single monster with a single split producing only diamonds.
boundary.test_values: n=1, m=1, split: '1 1 -1' -> min=max=1

boundary.description: Single monster with a split that produces itself and a diamond, leading to infinite loop.
boundary.test_values: n=1, m=1, split: '1 2 1 -1' -> should output -1 -1 because process never terminates

boundary.description: Monster with a split that produces a huge number of diamonds (close to cap) to test overflow and capping.
boundary.test_values: n=1, m=1, split: '1 314000001' with 314000000 diamonds? But l_i is number of outputs, cannot be that large. Instead, make a chain that sums to >314000000. Use small splits but many steps. For example, 2 monsters: monster1 splits into monster2 and 200000000 diamonds; monster2 splits into monster1 and 200000000 diamonds. That would sum arbitrarily large, so max=-2. To get finite large number, create a chain of length 100000, each producing 1 diamond, then terminating. Then total = 100000, which is < cap. To exceed cap, need more. Actually constraints allow sum of l_i up to 1e5, so total diamonds from a path cannot exceed 1e5 unless there are cycles. So to test cap, we need cycles that produce many diamonds per cycle. But that gives -2. So boundary: individual diamond count per split is at most 1e5? No, l_i can be up to sum l_i overall, but each split can have many -1s. So we can have a split with 100000 diamonds and no monsters (terminate). That gives min=max=100000. That's less than cap. To test cap, we need multiple splits that sum to >314000000, but sum l_i overall is 1e5, so impossible. Actually the cap is only for finite numbers. If finite, max diamonds are at most sum of diamonds along a path, and each split contributes at most sum of its diamonds. Since total sum of l_i is 1e5, the maximum finite diamonds is bounded by 1e5 (if each output is diamond). So cap of 314000000 will never be reached. So we can ignore this cap in practice, but still test that -2 is output for infinite loops. So this boundary is not needed. Replace with something else: extreme large n and m with many edges.

adversarial.description: Monster with two splits: one terminating (diamond only) and one self-loop (itself + diamond).
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits decision to choose non-terminating path to get arbitrarily many diamonds.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive BFS/DFS might think there is no termination because of loop, but terminating split exists so min is 1. Loop allows infinite, so max is -2. Solutions not correctly handling choices may output -1 for max.
error_types_caught: incorrect distinction between infinite loop and arbitrarily large
failure to consider multiple splits per monster

adversarial.description: Long chain of monsters each splitting into next monster and a diamond, with last monster splitting into diamond only.
adversarial.attack_vector: Forces deep recursion or long iteration.
adversarial.why_effective: If using recursion without tail recursion optimization or iterative approach, stack depth equals chain length. With n=1e5, recursive solution would crash. Also tests time if recalculating many times.
error_types_caught: poor performance due to repeated computation

adversarial.description: Two monsters forming a cycle, but one also has a terminating split. Tests cycle detection and handling of multiple paths.
adversarial.attack_vector: Complex dependency graph that may cause infinite loops in DP if not handled properly.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive approaches may mark a monster as infinite if it is part of a cycle, but if there is an escape, it might still be finite. Here, both 1 and 2 only have cycle (since split to each other) and no terminating split, so -1. But if we add a terminating split to one, it becomes finite. This pattern tests solving with DP and cycle analysis. The example above has no escape, so -1. To show escape, modify: 1 has split to 2 and -1, and 2 has split to 1 and -1, but also 2 has split to -1 alone. Then 2 can terminate, so min and max? Actually if 2 can terminate alone, then from 1, choose split to 2 and diamond, then from 2 choose diamond only, so min=2. Max: from 1, choose split to 2 and diamond, then from 2 choose split to 1 and diamond, loop. So max = -2. So pattern with escape gives -2. We'll include both variants.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of cycles with multiple exits
failure to compute finite min when cycle exists

key_coverage_gaps: large finite numbers near cap are impossible due to sum constraint
cases where multiple cycles interact
cases with many monsters that are unreachable from others

adversarial.attack_vector: Greedy might change a character that destroys subsequences; e.g., s='ab', t='ab' with k=1; best is no change (1), but greedy may change something and get 0

adversarial.description: Case where optimal solution requires multiple small divisors on one side to achieve a much cheaper cost than a single large divisor.
adversarial.attack_vector: Greedy algorithm that uses the smallest possible k to reduce the larger number may fail because using multiple small k's can be cheaper.

adversarial.why_effective: Checks if solution correctly enforces the constraint that each k can be used only once overall.

random.description: Small random instance where heights are consistent and easy to verify manually
random.generation_strategy: Choose small n (e.g., 10), small m (3-5), generate random days and heights satisfying |h_i - h_{i+1}| ≤ gap, then manually compute expected max
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of missing days between notes

random.description: Large random instance with n up to 1e8 and m up to 1e5, heights up to 1e8, ensuring consistency
random.generation_strategy: Set n = 100000000, m = 100000. Start with day=1, height=random(0,1e8). For each next note, pick day increment slightly larger than height difference, set new height within feasible range. Finally add last note close to n.

boundary.description: Single day n=1, single note with height 0
boundary.test_values: n=1, m=1, h=0. No other days, max must be 0.
error_types_caught: off-by-one errors in handling first/last day

boundary.description: First note at day 1, last note at day n, large gap with zero height difference
boundary.test_values: n=100000000, m=2, d1=1, h1=0, d2=100000000, h2=0. The maximum height occurs in the middle: floor((100000000-1)/2) = 49999999.5? Actually max = floor(gap/2) = 49999999. So answer 49999999.

boundary.description: Contradictory notes with large height difference in small gap
boundary.test_values: n=5, m=2, d1=2, h1=0, d2=3, h2=10. Gap=1, height diff=10 > 1 => IMPOSSIBLE.

adversarial.description: Alternating heights over many notes to force naive solutions to compute large intermediate values incorrectly
adversarial.attack_vector: Many notes with small gaps and heights that alternate between 0 and 1, but the maximum height from the path may be much higher than the notes suggest; also tests for off-by-one in computing max from endpoints.
adversarial.example_input:
100000 50000
1 0
3 1
5 0
7 1
... (odd days with 0, even gaps but notes on odd days) ...
99999 0
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might incorrectly compute max between notes as max(note heights) + floor(gap/2) but note that heights are small, so the actual maximum achievable might be just 1 because you cannot go higher than 1 from the given points. Some might think you can go arbitrarily high if gaps are large, but here gaps alternate 2 days, so max = max(0,1)+ floor(2/2) = 1+1=2? Actually compute: between day1 (h=0) and day3 (h=1), gap=2, diff=1, max possible = 1 + floor((2-1)/2)=1, so no 2. But careful: overall max might be 2 if you can go high between day1 and day3? Let's recalc: you can go from 0 up to 1 max in 2 days? Since step 1 per day: day1=0, day2=1, day3=1 (or 0? Actually to go from 0 to 1 in 2 days, you could do 0,1,1 so max=1). So indeed max remains 1. This pattern catches solutions that incorrectly compute max as max(h_i, h_{i+1}) + floor((gap - |diff|)/2) without considering that if diff is large relative to gap, formula still works but here diff=1, gap=2 -> (2-1)/2=0, so max=1. So it's correct. But still it's a good stress for handling many intervals.

adversarial.description: Two notes with a huge difference that just barely satisfies the constraint, causing overflow in languages with 32-bit integers if computing gap*diff
adversarial.attack_vector: Use n up to 1e8 and heights up to 1e8, with gap also large. For example, d1=1, h1=0, d2=100000000, h2=100000000 - 1 = 99999999? Actually max diff allowed is gap, so set h2 = h1 + gap = 0 + (100000000-1) = 99999999. That is valid. Then max height = h2 + (n - d2) = 99999999 + 0 = 99999999, but also from start: h1 + (d1-1)=0, so answer 99999999. Compute intermediate: gap=99999999, diff=99999999, formula gives max = max(0,99999999) + floor((99999999-99999999)/2)=99999999. No overflow. Actually could cause overflow if using int (32-bit) as 99999999 is <2^31, but still close. Better: set heights to near 1e8 and gap large so that addition exceeds 2^31. For example, h1 = 1e8, d1=1, h2=1e8, d2=1e8, then max = h1 + (d2-d1) = 1e8 + 99999999 ≈ 2e8, which fits in 64-bit but not 32-bit. So target C++ solutions using 32-bit int.
adversarial.why_effective: Catches solutions that do not consider both ends

key_coverage_gaps: no pattern specifically tests for large m with many notes that force many iterations
lack of pattern for very large heights in combination with very large gaps
no pattern for zero height in note

boundary.description: Minimum number of players (n=1). Only one player, who must be the winner.
boundary.test_values: n=1, token value ranges from 1 to 1e9. Ensures the algorithm handles single-player input correctly.

boundary.description: All players have identical tokens. Every player has a nonzero probability of winning because any tie can lead to a win.
boundary.test_values: n up to 200000, all tokens equal to same integer (e.g., 5). Tests whether the algorithm correctly identifies that all players can win.

adversarial.description: Strictly decreasing tokens. This tests if the algorithm correctly handles the case where the largest token is first, which may cause naive in-order processing to fail.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that process players in input order without sorting or that assume the largest token can only beat smaller ones immediately.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that do not sort may conclude only the first player (token 5) can win, but actually players with tokens 2,3,4 also have a chance because they can absorb smaller tokens and eventually tie with the largest. Sorting is essential.
error_types_caught: wrong answer due to incorrect winner determination
failure to sort or maintain original indices

adversarial.description: All players can win despite some having small tokens. The tokens are such that the smallest player can absorb others and eventually tie with the largest.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that prematurely exclude players based on a threshold without considering that small tokens can combine to become large.
adversarial.why_effective: The smallest player with 1 can absorb another 1 to become 2, then absorb the 2 to become 4, and then tie with the 4. Solutions that check only immediate prefix sums may incorrectly exclude the first player.

boundary.example_input:
100 100
1 5 1 5 ... (pattern: 1->5 gives distance 4, then 5->1 gives distance 96? Actually 96 mod100=96, but from 1 to 5 distance 4, so a[1]=4 if first step, later step from 1 to something else must be consistent; if next step is 1 to 1, distance 0 -> a[1]=100, conflict with 4)
error_types_caught: permutation assignment when values out of range

adversarial.description: Distance zero case: leaders repeat causing a[l_j] = n requirement, but later another distance contradicts for same leader
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits that when l_j = l_{j+1}, the distance is 0 mod n, so required a[l_j] = n. If same leader later appears with non-zero distance, conflict arises.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might not handle the modulo wrap correctly: distance from 1 to 1 is 0, should set a[1]=3. Then distance from 1 to 2 is 1, but a[1] already set to 3, contradiction. If code sets a[1]=1 instead (ignoring zero case), it might produce a wrong permutation that doesn't match the leaders.

adversarial.description: Multiple leaders requiring same a value (conflict because permutation must have distinct numbers)
adversarial.attack_vector: Leaders l_j and l_k (j≠k) both require the same number as their a value, e.g., both need a=2. Since a must be a permutation, this is impossible. Should output -1.
adversarial.target_error: WA (outputting a permutation when conflict should have been detected)
adversarial.why_effective: Distance from 1 to 3: d=2, so a[1]=2. Distance from 3 to 1: d= (1-3+4)%4 = 2, so a[3]=2. Both require value 2. Since permutation, 2 can only appear once. Naive solutions might assign both and later fail to fill permutation, or overwrite and produce invalid.

key_coverage_gaps: large m with small n (many steps vs few children) causing repeated constraints
cases where the distance is exactly n (should be n but modulo 0)

random.description: Small random graph with moderate density, used for verifying correctness against a brute-force solution.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n random nodes (n between 5 and 10). For each pair of nodes, add an edge with probability 0.5, with random integer weight in [1,10]. Ensure graph is connected (if not, add extra edges). Compute expected output using Floyd-Warshall and then for each pair count edges on any shortest path by iterating over all edges.

random.description: Large random graph with n=500, m approximately n*log2(n) to stress performance without being worst-case.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=500 nodes. For each pair (i,j) with i<j, add an edge with probability 0.02 (approx 2500 edges). Weights random in [1,1000]. Ensure graph is connected by adding a spanning tree first. Then run Floyd-Warshall and counting algorithm.
random.example_input:
500 2500
 (list of edges omitted due to length, but it's a random sparse graph)
error_types_caught: memory issues with adjacency matrix of size 500x500

boundary.description: Minimum number of cities (n=2) with a single road. Tests base case.
boundary.test_values: n=2, m=1, edge between 1 and 2 with length 1. Expected output: c12 = 1.

boundary.description: Maximum number of cities (n=500) with no roads. All pairs disconnected, output zeros.
boundary.test_values: n=500, m=0. All pair distances are infinity, so c_st=0 for all.
error_types_caught: infinite distances causing issues in counting algorithm
overflow when summing large numbers of zeros

adversarial.description: Complete graph with uniform edge weight (1). All pairs have direct edge as the only shortest path, so c_st = 1 for all. This exploits naive O(n^2 * m) counting: m = n*(n-1)/2, iterating over all edges per pair leads to O(n^4) time.
adversarial.attack_vector: Dense graph causes TLE if counting algorithm loops over all edges for each pair.
adversarial.why_effective: For n=500, m=124750, naive pair-edge loops yield about 15.6e9 operations, causing TLE.
error_types_caught: wrong output if counting condition mishandled

adversarial.description: Complete bipartite graph with uniform edge weight (1). Partition into two sets of equal size (250 each). For vertices in the same set, there are 250 shortest paths (each of length 2), so c_st = 500. For vertices in opposite sets, only direct edge, so c_st = 1. This tests large counts and also stresses O(n^2 * m) counting.
adversarial.attack_vector: Large number of edges on some shortest paths, and dense graph leading to TLE.
adversarial.why_effective: For n=500, m=62500, same-set pairs have count 500, requiring correct computation. Naive counting iterating over all edges per pair gives O(n^4) ~ 7.8e9 operations.
error_types_caught: double counting of edges in condition check

key_coverage_gaps: Graphs with zero-weight edges (not allowed)
Negative weights (not in problem)
Multiple edges between same nodes (not allowed)

random.description: Small random test with moderate n, m (≤10) and small block sizes to manually verify correctness.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly choose n and m between 1 and 10. Generate random block lengths between 1 and 10 for both sequences. Adjust the second sequence's last block to make total sums equal (by setting difference).

random.description: Large random test with n,m near 10^5, and block sizes up to 10^6, total sum ≤ 10^6. Stress test for performance and potential overflow.
random.generation_strategy: Choose n,m up to 100000. Generate random block sizes summing to ≤ 10^6. Use random partitions: first generate a random total sum S, then split into n parts, similarly for m, but ensure sums equal by using the same S. Alternatively, generate random blocks for first sequence, then for second sequence generate prefix sums and create blocks that align with first sequence's cumulative sums at random points.
random.example_input:
100000 100000
(100000 random integers summing to 1000000)
(100000 random integers summing to 1000000)

boundary.description: Minimum input: n=1, m=1, single block of size 1.
boundary.test_values: n=1, m=1, block=1

boundary.description: Maximum total sum: sum = 10^6, with many blocks. Also n,m large. Also extreme block size: single block of 10^6 in one message, many small blocks in the other.
boundary.test_values: total sum = 10^6, n=100000, m=100000, max block size = 10^6, min block size = 1
error_types_caught: integer overflow if using int in some languages
incorrect sum tracking when sums are large

adversarial.description: Case where no intermediate prefix sums match except at the end. This forces the algorithm to process entire arrays without early cuts.
adversarial.attack_vector: Greedy algorithm that resets sums only when equal; if sums never match early, it runs through all elements. This can test performance and correctness when the answer is 1.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might incorrectly split at some point if they don't correctly compute cumulative sums or if they create segments when sums are equal but not properly aligned. In this case, only final sum matches.

adversarial.description: Case with alternating sums that match frequently, but greedy algorithm must correctly increment count each time. This tests handling of many cuts.
adversarial.attack_vector: Many small blocks that cause repeated matches. For example, both sequences consist of alternating 1 and 2 such that after every block the cumulative sums are equal.
adversarial.why_effective: If greedy algorithm incorrectly merges consecutive segments or misses a match due to off-by-one, the output will be wrong.

key_coverage_gaps: Extremely uneven block sizes (e.g., one huge block vs many tiny) could be added
Random tests with n,m not equal
Case where total sum is exactly 1 but many blocks? not possible because each block ≥1

random.description: Small path graph (n up to 10) to verify correctness
random.generation_strategy: Generate a path from 1 to n with edges i-i+1. Randomly assign weights w_i between 1 and 10^4. Sum over all non-adjacent pairs (i,j) with i<j and j-i>1.

random.description: Larger graph that is well-designed: a series-parallel graph built by replacing edges with series or parallel compositions. Ensures all vertices lie on a 1-n path and ordering is consistent.
random.generation_strategy: Start with a path from 1 to n. For each edge (u,v) with u<v, replace it with a parallel path u-x-v (adding a new vertex x) or series-compose by splitting into u-y-v and then parallel. Ensure the graph remains well-designed. Use up to n=2e5, m=2e5.
random.example_output: Sum over all non-adjacent pairs that respect the order. (Computed manually or by algorithm)
error_types_caught: missing edge cases in path existence

boundary.description: Minimum n=2 with one edge (must be well-designed).
boundary.test_values: n=2, m=1, edge 1-2. w_1, w_2 arbitrary.

boundary.description: Maximum n=2e5 with path graph (linear). Stress test for large input.
boundary.test_values: n=200000, m=199999, path from 1 to n. Weights random up to 10^4.
boundary.example_output: Computed sum modulo? Problem does not mention modulo; output as integer. Sum can be large (up to ~10^14 for n=200k, weights up to 10^4 -> max sum ~ 10^9 * 10^8? Actually number of pairs O(n^2) ~ 2e10, times weight product ~1e8, so overflow risk for 64-bit? 2e10 * 1e8 = 2e18, fits in 64-bit signed (9e18). So no modulo, but must use 64-bit.

adversarial.description: Graph that is almost well-designed but has a pair of vertices with both orderings possible. Tests detection of 'bad'.
adversarial.attack_vector: Create a graph with two parallel paths between 1 and n that share a vertex other than 1 and n, causing reversal of order for some pair.
adversarial.why_effective:
Naive algorithm might only check that every vertex is on some path but miss condition 2. Here, vertices 2 and 3 each lie on a path, but also appear together? Actually, paths: 1-2-4 and 1-3-4. No path contains both 2 and 3, so condition 2 is not violated. This graph is actually well-designed? Wait, for pair (2,3), no common path, so condition 2 holds. So this graph is well-designed. Need a pair that appears in two paths with different orders. Example: add edge between 2 and 3 to create two paths: 1-2-3-4 and 1-3-2-4. Then both orders exist for (2,3). So input: 1
4 5
1 1 1 1
1 2
2 3
3 4
1 3
2 4
 That graph has edges: 1-2,2-3,3-4,1-3,2-4. Paths: 1-2-3-4 (2 before 3), 1-3-2-4 (3 before 2). Violation. So output 'bad'.
error_types_caught: missing detection of cycles that allow reversal

adversarial.description: Star graph with center 1 and leaves 2..n, where n is a leaf. This is not well-designed because leaves other than n are not on any 1-n path.
adversarial.attack_vector: Common mistake: assume all vertices are on some path because graph is connected. However, condition 1 requires a path from 1 to n, and that path cannot revisit vertices. In star, only path is 1-n.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive algorithm might think that since every vertex is reachable from 1, there is a path containing it. But for leaf 2, any path from 1 to 5 that includes 2 must go 1-2-1-5, which repeats 1, so invalid. So condition 1 fails.
error_types_caught: misunderstanding of 'successful path' requiring distinct levels

key_coverage_gaps: Graphs with cycles and chords not forming simple reversal

Graphs with multiple edges (parallel edges) - not allowed per input? Actually, problem says transitions connect levels bidirectionally, but does not forbid multiple edges. Need to test if multiple edges affect conditions.
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: At least 6 test cases (2 per type) for basic coverage; more for stress.

random.description: Random small trees (n up to 10) for correctness verification
random.generation_strategy: Generate random trees of size n=3..10 using Prüfer sequence or random edge addition ensuring no cycles. For each n, generate a few cases.

random.description: Random larger trees (n up to 2e5) for stress testing performance
random.generation_strategy: Generate random trees with n up to 200000 using Prüfer sequence or random parent array (ensuring tree). Use multiple test cases with total n ≤ 2e5.
error_types_caught: inefficient algorithms (O(n^2) or O(n log n) but with high constant)

boundary.description: Minimum n and maximum n values
boundary.test_values: n=2 (minimum) and n=200000 (maximum as per sum constraint).
error_types_caught: handle large input sizes without overflow

boundary.description: Single test case with extreme range and star tree
boundary.test_values: Star tree with center 1 and n-1 leaves. n=200000. Also path tree of same size.
error_types_caught: misclassification of star as needing operations

adversarial.description: Long path (caterpillar) to exploit greedy strategies that try to use endpoints
adversarial.attack_vector: For a path tree, the optimal number of operations is floor((n-2)/2) maybe? But naive solutions might overcount or undercount. Provide a path to force many operations.
adversarial.why_effective: If algorithm incorrectly assumes that you can reduce diameter to 2 in fewer operations by picking non-endpoints, it may produce wrong count.

adversarial.description: Tree with a very long branch and many leaves attached to one node (like a broom) to test if algorithm handles asymmetry
adversarial.attack_vector: Naive algorithm might pick the two farthest leaves each time, but optimal might require different choices. Exploit symmetry breaking.
adversarial.why_effective: If algorithm always picks the two farthest nodes, it might perform extra operations. A greedy by diameter reduction might fail.

key_coverage_gaps: Trees with diameter already 2, requiring zero operations
Trees where the optimal first operation is not on the diameter endpoints
Very large star trees to test O(n) time without crashes

random.description: Random small case with mixed positive and negative values, total points differ
random.generation_strategy: Generate n up to 10, random ai between -10 and 10 excluding 0, ensure sum first != sum second

random.description: Random large case with maximum constraints, points equal leading to lexicographic comparison
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=200000, ai with absolute values up to 1e9, ensure total points equal, and sequences differ lexicographically
random.example_output: first or second (depends on lexicographic order)

boundary.description: Single technique
boundary.test_values: n=1, positive and negative cases

boundary.description: All points from one wrestler
boundary.test_values: n large, all positive or all negative
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of missing sequence for other wrestler

boundary.description: Equal total points, equal sequences, last technique decides
boundary.test_values: sequences identical, last element determines winner

adversarial.description: Large numbers that could cause integer overflow if sum is computed with int
adversarial.attack_vector: Use ai up to 1e9 and many of them, sum may exceed 32-bit integer
adversarial.example_input:
200000
1000000000
-1000000000
... (repeat 100000 times each, total sum 0 but large intermediate sums)
adversarial.example_output: first or second depending on sequence
adversarial.why_effective: If using 32-bit int for sum, overflow may cause incorrect comparison

adversarial.description: Equal total points, sequences differ lexicographically due to early large values
adversarial.attack_vector: One wrestler has a very large early point, but total equal, naive solutions might compare strings incorrectly
adversarial.example_output: first (since sequence of first: [1000000000] vs second: [1,999999999,1]; lexicographically first wins because 1000000000 > 1)
adversarial.why_effective: If comparing sequences as strings of numbers, may compare lexicographically as strings which is wrong (e.g., '1000000000' vs '1' string comparison gives '1' > '1000000000' because '1' is greater than '1'? Actually '1' < '1000000000' because '1' is a prefix? But standard lexicographic comparison of sequences compares element by element numerically, not as strings. So this catches solutions that convert to strings and compare lexicographically.

key_coverage_gaps: Large n with many zeros? Not allowed because ai != 0
Equal sequences but last technique differs

random.description: Small random tests with a,b,c,l in [1,10] to verify brute force correctness.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate a,b,c in [1,10] and l in [0,10] uniformly.

random.description: Large random tests with all values up to 300000 to stress test performance and large number handling.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate a,b,c in [1,300000] and l in [0,300000] uniformly.

boundary.description: Minimum values: a=1, b=1, c=1, l=0.
boundary.test_values: a=1, b=1, c=1, l=0: the smallest possible input.

boundary.description: Maximum values: all parameters at 300000.
boundary.test_values: a=300000, b=300000, c=300000, l=300000: the largest possible input.

boundary.description: Extreme inequality: a is much larger than b and c, l=0.
boundary.test_values: a=300000, b=1, c=1, l=0: one side is much larger, no increase allowed.

boundary.description: Small initial sides with large l.
boundary.test_values: a=1, b=1, c=1, l=300000: all sides small but large possible increase.

adversarial.description: Degenerate initial triangle (a+b=c) with small l to catch off-by-one in counting valid increases.
adversarial.attack_vector: Tests handling of degenerate triangle where a+b=c exactly.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions may count the original degenerate case as invalid, but may incorrectly count some increases as invalid when they are valid. For example, increasing the smaller sides (a or b) can make triangle valid, but increasing c makes it worse. Must handle equality carefully.

adversarial.description: All sides equal and large l, tests the combinatorial counting for symmetric case.
adversarial.attack_vector: Tests counting of all triples minus those where one side exceeds sum of other two; symmetric case simplifies to binomial coefficients.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive O(l) simulation will TLE, but combinatorial formula must be correct. Off-by-one in formula can cause large errors.

adversarial.description: Very unequal sides with large l, test handling of multiple constraints.
adversarial.attack_vector: Tests that the algorithm correctly subtracts cases where the large side becomes even larger and also cases where the small sides might become too large.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions may only consider the longest side initially and not update after increases. But the longest side can change. Must consider all possibilities.

key_coverage_gaps: Combinations of extreme a,b,c with medium l
Cases where l is large but a,b,c are nearly equal to max

random.description: Random binary strings of moderate lengths (10 to 100 bits) with random k from 0 to 10.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random binary string of length L between 10 and 100 (first bit always 1). Choose k randomly from 0 to min(10, L). Output the input with n on first line and k on second. Expected answer can be computed by brute-force for small L or by a known correct solution.

random.description: Random long binary strings (1000 bits) with various k values (0,1,2,10,100,1000) to test performance and large combinatorial counts.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random 1000-bit binary string (first bit 1). For each k in {0,1,2,10,100,1000} compute answer (using known algorithm). This tests memory and modulo operations.

boundary.description: Smallest possible n: n=1 (binary '1'). Test k=0 and k=1.
boundary.test_values: n=1 (binary '1'), k=0 and k=1. k=0 should output 1 (number 1). k=1 should output 0 because no number ≤1 reduces to 1 in exactly 1 step (only 1 reduces in 0 steps).

boundary.description: Largest possible n: 1000-bit string of all '1's (i.e., 2^1000 - 1). Test various k: 0,1,2, and k large like 1000.
boundary.test_values: n = '111...1' (1000 ones). k=0: only number 1 is special so answer 0? Actually numbers ≤ n that reduce in 0 ops: only 1. But n is huge, so answer 1. k=1: numbers with popcount that reduces to 1 in 1 step: popcounts that are powers of 2? Actually need to compute. This tests combinatorics with max range.
error_types_caught: incorrect handling of large binary strings

boundary.description: n with leading zeros not allowed; but could have very small values like n=2 (binary '10'), n=3 ('11'), etc.
boundary.test_values: n=2 (binary '10') with k=0,1,2.
error_types_caught: DP initialization errors for small n
handling of numbers with only one zero

adversarial.description: n with alternating bits to stress digit DP: e.g., '101010...' (1000 bits).
adversarial.attack_vector: DP state transitions when bits alternate; may cause incorrect counting if not careful with prefix equality.
adversarial.why_effective: Alternating bits force many branches in DP; naive solutions may double-count or miss numbers due to incorrect handling of strict less vs equal.
error_types_caught: incorrect DP state for prefix equality
off-by-one in counting numbers with same prefix

adversarial.description: n with all zeros except first bit: n=2^{L-1} for large L (1000 bits), e.g., '1' followed by 999 zeros.
adversarial.attack_vector: Only one number (n itself) has the leading 1; all other valid numbers have fewer bits. This tests the DP's handling of numbers with exactly L bits.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might include numbers less than n with different bit lengths improperly, or miscount combinations for the fixed leading bit.
error_types_caught: off-by-one in counting numbers with same length

adversarial.description: k=0 with various n to ensure only 1 is counted.
adversarial.attack_vector: Special definition for k=0: only number 1. Many solutions might incorrectly count 0 or other numbers.
adversarial.why_effective: Test if code correctly identifies that 1 is the only number requiring 0 operations.

key_coverage_gaps: Large k values near 1000 with moderate n lengths
n with repeated patterns like all zeros except first bit
k=0 with n>1

random.description: Small random test to verify correctness on random instances with moderate constraints.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n between 1 and 10, k between 1 and 5, l between 1 and 20, and depths d_i random between 0 and l. Use brute force or known solution to compute expected output for verification.

random.description: Large random stress test with high n and large parameter values to test performance and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n=100000, k=1000000000, l=500000000, depths random between 0 and l. Ensure sum of n over test cases does not exceed 300000.

boundary.description: Single element test with minimum n and small k, l.
boundary.test_values: n=1, k=1, l=0, d=[1]. Depth exceeds l at all tidal phases, so impossible.

boundary.description: All depths zero with maximum l and moderate k.
boundary.test_values: n=2, k=1e9, l=1e9, d=[0,0]. Always safe because depth never exceeds l.

boundary.description: Large n with all depths at safety margin exactly l.
boundary.test_values: n=300000, k=1, l=10, d=[10,10,...,10]. Since depth at high tide (tide=1) becomes 11>10, and at low tide (tide=0) it's 10, but Koa cannot stay at high tide; hence impossible. This tests the greedy algorithm's handling of waiting and movement.

adversarial.description: Test for solutions that fail to utilize waiting at safe spots to cross deeper areas.
adversarial.attack_vector: A deep spot that is only safe at low tide, preceded by a shallower spot where Koa can wait for the tide to recede.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive greedy that always moves forward if possible will try to cross the deep spot too early and drown, outputting No. Correct solution waits at the shallower spot until low tide.

adversarial.description: Test for solutions that mishandle deep spots exactly at the depth limit with large tidal range.
adversarial.attack_vector: A depth exactly equal to the safety limit l, with large k, making it impossible to ever be at that spot safely except at t=0 (which is impossible to reach from shore).
adversarial.why_effective: Many solutions incorrectly assume that a depth of l is always safe (since at low tide it's exactly l), but due to the need to move through the spot, it's impossible because Koa cannot be at that spot exactly at t=0. Solutions that only check depth at landing might output Yes erroneously.

key_coverage_gaps: No test for k=0 (not allowed)
No test for n=300000 with all depths varying

random.description: Random test with short strings (length 1-5) composed of common ASCII characters (letters and digits).
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random string of length 1 to 5 using characters from 'A' to 'Z', 'a' to 'z', '0' to '9'. Then run a correct solver to produce the rectangular grid. This pattern verifies basic functionality for typical inputs.

random.description: Random test with longer strings (length 6-10) including special characters like '!', '@', '#', etc., covering full ASCII range 33-122.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random string of length 6 to 10 using characters from ASCII 33 to 122, ensuring at least one special character. Run a correct solver to produce grid. This pattern tests handling of edge cases in character set and longer sequences.
error_types_caught: state machine errors for longer sequences

boundary.description: Minimum input length: single character string. Tests base case with no loops.
boundary.test_values: Input string of length 1, e.g., 'A' or '!'
error_types_caught: incorrect neighbor handling for isolated X

boundary.description: Maximum input length: exactly 10 characters. Tests upper bound of input size.
boundary.test_values: Input string of length 10, e.g., '0123456789' or all 'z's

boundary.description: ASCII boundary values: use characters with code 33 ('!') and 122 ('z'). Tests extremal characters.
boundary.test_values: Input string containing both '!' and 'z'

adversarial.description: Toroidal wrap-aware input: design a string that forces use of toroidal neighbors (e.g., first row's top neighbor is last row). This can be achieved by placing X's on edges.
adversarial.attack_vector: toroidal topology edge case
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might ignore toroidal wrapping or incorrectly compute neighbors across boundaries, leading to wrong instruction mapping.

adversarial.description: Maximum X count: force the grid to contain exactly 500,000 X's. This tests memory and time limits.
adversarial.attack_vector: resource exhaustion
adversarial.why_effective: A naive solution that allocates too much memory or has high time complexity will fail on a grid with max X's. The grid must be carefully designed to not exceed constraints.
error_types_caught: failure to respect max X limit

adversarial.description: Single X in a huge grid: create a minimal grid (e.g., 1x1) to test base case, but also a grid with one X in a 10000x10000 grid to stress memory.
adversarial.attack_vector: sparse grid with extreme dimensions
adversarial.why_effective: Some solutions might allocate a full grid even if only a few X's are needed, causing memory blowup or invalid accesses.

key_coverage_gaps: toroidal wrap with multi-line sequences
mixture of instruction types
empty input not allowed (length >=1)

random.description: Small random test with few babies to verify correctness and check for simple bugs.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate n and m between 1 and 10, and coordinates between -100 and 100, ensuring all points are distinct.

random.description: Large random test with maximum constraints to stress test performance and memory.
random.generation_strategy: Generate n = m = 2000, random coordinates within [-1e6, 1e6] uniformly, ensuring all points distinct.

boundary.description: Minimum number of babies (n=m=1) to test edge case where rectangle is impossible.
boundary.test_values: n=1, m=1; coordinates arbitrary but distinct.

boundary.description: Maximum coordinate values to test overflow risk in time and coordinate computations.
boundary.test_values: n=m=2000, all coordinates at +1e6 or -1e6, e.g., alternating.

adversarial.description: All babies lie on two perpendicular lines, forming a rectangle only after large t, testing binary search and line sweep.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits algorithms that assume rectangle appears early or that use limited time range.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive simulation of time steps would be too slow; binary search must be used but need proper upper bound. Many collinear points may cause DSU inefficiency.

adversarial.description: Babies arranged so that a rectangle forms exactly at an integer time, but many babies overlap in a way that tests segment handling.
adversarial.attack_vector: Targets geometry calculations for segment coverage, especially handling of endpoints and overlapping.
adversarial.why_effective: At t=1, segments may form a rectangle but endpoints coincide; algorithms that don't treat segments as closed might miss coverage.

adversarial.description: No rectangle ever forms because all babies are collinear, testing that solution returns 'Poor Sereja!' correctly.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that assume rectangle always exists or have infinite loops.
adversarial.why_effective: If algorithm doesn't properly detect impossibility, it may run forever or crash.

key_coverage_gaps: Very large time steps (beyond 10^6) might not be covered
All babies at same position (not allowed due to distinct points, but near duplicates could be tested)
Performance with many babies on same line

random.description: Random small angles in degrees, including both positive and negative, within the range of typical rotation values.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random integers in the range [-360, 360]. Ensure coverage of positive, negative, and zero. Include some multiples of 90 and others not.

random.description: Random large angles up to 1e18, testing the algorithm's ability to handle large numbers without overflow or precision loss.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random integers with absolute value up to 10^18, covering both positive and negative. Use a source of randomness that ensures large magnitude.

boundary.description: Test the extreme values of the input range: -1e18 and 1e18. These test the algorithm's handling of maximum magnitude.
boundary.test_values: x = -10^18 and x = 10^18. These are the largest absolute values allowed.

boundary.description: Test angles that are multiples of 90 and 360, as well as zero, to check basic correctness.
boundary.test_values: x = 0, 90, 180, 270, 360, -90, -180, -270, -360. Also include 45 and -135 for tie-breaking edges.

adversarial.description: Test negative angles that could cause incorrect modulo results in languages with remainder sign same as dividend.
adversarial.attack_vector: Use negative angles to exploit potential modulo implementation differences.
adversarial.why_effective: Some naive solutions might compute ((360 - x) % 360) incorrectly for negative x, leading to wrong candidate angles.

adversarial.description: Angles where multiple numbers of turns yield the same minimal deviation, testing that the smallest k is chosen.
adversarial.attack_vector: Use angles like 45, 135, 225, 315 where two k values give same deviation.
adversarial.why_effective: A solution might incorrectly choose the larger k if it doesn't properly break ties.

key_coverage_gaps: Testing with extremely large negative values that are not multiples of 360
Edge case where x is exactly a multiple of 90 but not 0 modulo 360, e.g., x=90 already covered
Large positive numbers causing different modulo behavior if language uses floor division

random.description: Small random values with various n, covering both solution and no solution cases.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly pick A from -10 to 10, B from -10 to 10, n from 1 to 3. Then check if integer X exists within [-1000,1000] by brute force. Include both cases.

random.description: Larger values up to 1000, including negative A and B, n up to 10.
random.generation_strategy: Randomly pick A from -1000 to 1000, B from -1000 to 1000, n from 1 to 10. If a solution exists (integer X such that A*X^n=B) and |X| <= 1000, output that X. Also include cases with no solution.

boundary.description: Cases with A=0.
boundary.test_values: A=0, B=0 (any X works); A=0, B=5 (no solution); A=0, B=-5 (no solution).
error_types_caught: incorrectly output no solution when B=0

boundary.description: Extreme values of |A| and |B| = 1000, n=1 and n=10.
error_types_caught: overflow in exponentiation for large A

adversarial.description: Case with two possible solutions (positive and negative) for even n.
adversarial.attack_vector: Multiple solutions exist, but algorithm might only output one sign.
adversarial.why_effective: Some solutions only search positive X or only consider one root.

adversarial.description: Case where X=0 is the only solution.
adversarial.attack_vector: Algorithm might miss X=0 because 0^n=0 but may treat 0 specially.
adversarial.why_effective: Some algorithms might incorrectly output 'No solution' because they think 0 is not a valid integer coefficient, or they divide by zero.

adversarial.description: Case with A negative, B positive, odd n, requiring negative X.

boundary.description: k exactly the maximum possible distance for given string s.
boundary.test_values: String with all 'a's and k = n*25 (max). Output should be all 'z's.

adversarial.description: String with alternating 'a' and 'z' to force greedy to make proper choices when k is large but not maximum.
adversarial.attack_vector: Greedy might incorrectly assign distances if it always goes to extremes without considering future possibilities.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive greedy that tries to maximize distance at each position might fail because after changing 'a' to 'z' (distance 25) and 'z' to 'a' (distance 25) total 50, but we need 30. The correct solution must balance distances. For this case, it's possible: change first 'a' to 'z' (25), second 'z' to 'a' (25) too high, so must reduce second change to only 5 (e.g., 'u') to get total 30. Greedy without backtracking would fail.

adversarial.description: String consists of only 'a's and 'z's with large n, and k is such that full conversion is impossible but solution exists with mix.
adversarial.attack_vector: Exploits solutions that might assume only extremes are used.
adversarial.why_effective: Max distance for each 'a' is 25. To get total 10, we need small changes. Naive might try to set some to 'z' but that overshoots. Needs careful allocation.

adversarial.description: Large k that is exactly at the edge of feasibility, requiring very specific string construction.
adversarial.attack_vector: Off-by-one errors in calculating if k is possible.
adversarial.why_effective: Maximum distance for string 'az' is from 'a' to 'z' (25) plus from 'z' to 'a' (25) = 50, exactly 50. But wait: distance between 'a' and 'z' is 25, and 'z' and 'a' is 25, total 50. So 50 is possible? Actually original string 'az': first char 'a' -> change to 'z' gives 25, second char 'z' -> change to 'a' gives 25, total 50. So it is possible. The output should be 'zz' or 'aa'? Actually if we change both to extremes, we get 'zz' (distance 25+0? No, second char 'z' stays same? Let's compute: s='az', s'='zz': first: a->z =25, second: z->z =0, total 25. Not 50. To get 50, we need s'='za': first a->z=25, second z->a=25. So 'za' is valid. So k=50 is possible. So adversarial example should be k=51 to make impossible. Let's correct: n=2, s='az', k=51 -> impossible because max is 50. That would catch off-by-one.

key_coverage_gaps: Combinations of very small n with huge k
Strings with repeated patterns that may cause greedy to backtrack
Performance when n=100000 and k=0 (trivial but large I/O)

adversarial.why_effective: Without sorting, the algorithm may group 5 and 2 first (cost 8), then 4 and 3 (cost 6), then 2 (cost 2) totalling 16, while optimal is 14.

adversarial.attack_vector: If the solution uses integer types incorrectly or miscomputes product, it fails.
adversarial.why_effective: Each person requires a separate trip, so total time = n*2*(2000-1) = 10*2*1999 = 39980. A miscalculation could yield 39960 or 40000.

adversarial.description: Mixed high and low floors with duplicates to test grouping priority.
adversarial.attack_vector: If the solution incorrectly prioritizes grouping by floor order rather than highest floor first, it may produce suboptimal results.
adversarial.why_effective: Optimal groups: (10,10) cost 18, (10,2) cost 18, (2,2) cost 2, total 38. A naive grouping that pairs equal floors together would yield (10,10) 18, (10,2) 18, (2,2) 2 also 38, but if it groups 10 with 10 and 10 with 10 incorrectly? Actually it's fine. But if it groups three 10s together when k=2? That violates capacity. Harder to break. This pattern tests that solution correctly processes duplicates.

boundary.description: Prime numbers: the smallest prime (2), a large prime (999999937), and the largest prime ≤ 10^9.
boundary.test_values: Prime numbers: 2, 1000000007 (if ≤ 10^9), 999999937. Also include 1? But n>1 from constraints. So exclude 1.
error_types_caught: WA for primes (expecting 0 layers if 1 and n excluded)
WA for large primes causing incorrect modulus operations

boundary.description: Powers of primes: squares and higher powers of 2, 3, and a large prime.
error_types_caught: WA for prime powers: layers may be exponent-1

adversarial.description: Numbers that are products of many distinct small primes (primorials) to maximize the number of divisors and test chain layering.
adversarial.attack_vector: This exploits naive solutions that try to compute layers by iterating over all divisors or using simple greedy based on exponent sums.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that enumerate all divisors will have to handle many divisors (e.g., for primorial of first 9 primes, number of divisors is 2^9=512, which is manageable, but for larger? Actually 2^9=512, not huge. To cause TLE, we need many divisors: for n with many small prime factors, the number of divisors can be up to around 1344 for numbers ≤ 10^9 (e.g., 73513440 has 1344 divisors). So a primorial up to the 9th prime gives 512 divisors. Not huge but combined with many test cases could be slow. For true TLE, we need to repeat many such cases. But within a single test, 512 divisors is fine. So we need to stress the algorithm that might do O(d(n)^2) or something. Alternatively, this pattern catches WA in greedy grouping: all divisors are pairwise coprime? Actually for primorial, divisors are all square-free products of subsets. Many divisors share primes, so they can be grouped. The minimal layers might be the number of distinct primes? Possibly? But naive solutions might give wrong answer.

adversarial.description: Numbers with one large prime factor and a high power of a small prime, e.g., 2^a * p for large a and large p.
adversarial.attack_vector: This exploits solutions that might compute layers based only on the maximum exponent or only on distinct primes, causing incorrect layering.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that compute answer as max exponent + (distinct primes - 1) or similar might fail because the layers need to accommodate both the chain from the prime power and the separate prime factor. For 2^20 * 3, max exponent=20, distinct=2. A correct answer might be 20+2-1=21? Or something else. But an algorithm that only considers the maximum exponent will underestimate.

key_coverage_gaps: Numbers with repeated prime factors of the same prime (e.g., p^a * q^b with a and b both >1) are partially covered, but specific combinations like p^2 * q^2 might be missing.
Numbers that are perfect squares of composite numbers might behave differently.
Edge case n=2 (smallest prime) should be covered in boundary.

random.description: Small random tree with n=5-10, s and t arbitrary. Generate a random tree, then produce a valid permutation by ordering vertices in decreasing distance from t (BFS level order reversed).
random.generation_strategy: Randomly generate a tree with given n. Compute distances from t via BFS. Sort vertices by distance descending. For s==t, any permutation works. Output the sorted order as permutation.

random.description: Large random tree with n=200000, s and t random. Stress test for performance and correctness of permutation construction.
random.generation_strategy: Generate a random tree of size n (using random parent array for linear tree, or random Prufer code for general tree). Compute distances from t via DFS/BFS. Sort vertices by distance descending. Output permutation of size n.

boundary.description: Minimum constraints: n=2, s and t different or same. Tree of two vertices.
boundary.test_values: n=2, s=1, t=2 (or s=t=1). Ensure solution exists.

boundary.description: Star tree with center t, s at leaf. n large, all leaves connected to t. Mouse must end at center.
boundary.test_values: n=100000, s=1 (leaf), t=n (center). Edges: center connected to all leaves. Need permutation that herds mouse to center.
error_types_caught: mouse moves incorrectly when cheese at center

adversarial.description: s == t. Mouse already at trap. Any permutation should work because mouse never moves (stays if cheese at same vertex else moves? Actually if s==t, mouse starts at t. For each step, if cheese appears at t, mouse stays; otherwise moves towards cheese away from t, so may leave. So not any permutation. Need to ensure mouse ends at t. A valid permutation is one where the mouse never leaves t? Actually it can leave but must return. Common mistake: assume any permutation works when s==t. This pattern checks that.
adversarial.attack_vector: Incorrect handling of s==t case
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions might output any permutation like '1 2 3' but if cheese first at 2, mouse moves to 2, then cheese at 3, mouse moves to 3, then cheese at 1, moves towards 1 (path 3-2-1) moves to 2, ends at 2 not 1. So '1 2 3' fails. Correct permutation needs to ensure final step brings mouse back to 1. For example '2 1 3'? Let's verify: start at1, cheese2: move to2, cheese1: path to1 is 2-1, move to1, cheese3: path to3 is 1-2-3, move to2, ends at2. Not good. '2 3 1'? start1, cheese2: to2, cheese3: path 2-3, to3, cheese1: path 3-2-1, to2, ends at2. So maybe any? Actually need to think. But adversarial pattern is to show that naive solutions may fail.

adversarial.description: Chain tree where s and t are far apart and mouse must traverse many steps. Tests permutation that ensures mouse moves consistently towards t and does not overshoot.
adversarial.attack_vector: Incorrect ordering that causes mouse to move away from t in last steps
adversarial.why_effective: If permutation is anything else (e.g., reversed), mouse may end away from t. This checks that the sorting-by-distance descending works.

key_coverage_gaps: Trees with multiple branches where mouse may loop
Large depth trees causing recursion depth issues

boundary.description: Minimum n = 1, ensuring the answer is 0 if both bottles cost >1, or 1 if one costs 1.
boundary.test_values: n=1, various a,b,c with a,b >=1. For example a=1, b=2, c=1: answer is 1 (plastic). If a=2,b=2,c=1: answer 0.

boundary.description: Maximum n = 1e18, and boundary values for a,b,c. Test large values and possible overflow in subtraction.
boundary.test_values: n=10^18, a=10^18, b=10^18, c=10^18-1. Then answer is 1 (buy glass once, then you get c back but less than a? Actually after buying glass, you get c back, remaining n = n - b + c = 1, and a is huge, so no more bottles. So total 1. Alternatively, if a=1, b=2, c=1, n huge: answer is n // a (since a <= b-c?).

adversarial.description: Case where glass is cheaper per bottle (b-c < a) but n is just below b, so only plastic is possible. Designed to catch solutions that ignore the initial cost of glass.
adversarial.attack_vector: Misorder of operations: buying glass only when n >= b, else plastic.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solution might try to buy glass (since b-c=9 < a=10), subtract 9 from n, but n is only 9, less than b, so cannot buy any glass. Correct answer is 0 plastic (since a=10 > n).

adversarial.description: Case where a == b-c, so both types give same effective cost. Solution should prefer plastic because no deposit hassle, but answer same. Test both branches.
adversarial.attack_vector: Equal effective cost may cause off-by-one if using floating comparisons.
adversarial.why_effective: a=5, b=10, c=5 -> b-c=5 == a. So both options yield 4 liters (20//5=4 for plastic; glass: first buy one glass with 10, get back 5, remaining 15, then 15//5=3, total 4). Incorrect code might give 3 due to rounding.

adversarial.description: Case where b is huge but c is close to b, making effective cost tiny. Large numbers to test overflow in intermediate calculations like (n - b) // (b - c).
adversarial.attack_vector: Large b and c near b can cause (n-b) to be negative if n < b, or (b-c) very small causing large division result.
adversarial.why_effective: b-c=1, a=1e18. Since b-c=1 << a, glass is much cheaper. But n >= b only once, so you buy one glass, get back c, then remaining n=1e18-1+999...? Actually n - b + c = n - (b-c) = 1e18 - 1 = 999... , but a is still 1e18, so no more plastic. So answer=1. Naive may try to divide by b-c incorrectly.

key_coverage_gaps: Cases where a is very small (1) and b-c is also small but different
Case with multiple glass purchases and remainder

random.description: Small random test cases with n up to 10, M up to 100, a_i up to 100. Useful for verifying correctness with brute-force or small DP.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random n in [1,10], random M in [1,100], random a_i in [1,100]. Ensure that there is at least one valid assignment? Not required; output can be 0.

random.description: Large random test cases with n up to 1e5 (sum n=2e5), M up to 1e12, a_i up to 1e12. Stresses time for factorization and DP.
random.generation_strategy: Generate random n uniformly in [1, 1e5] but ensure total sum across all test cases <= 2e5. For each test case, generate random M in [1,1e12], random a_i in [1,1e12]. Use prime factorization for M to increase chance of LCM condition? Not necessary, but can be any.

boundary.description: Single voter (n=1). The only possible d1 must be a divisor of a1 and LCM(d1)=M => d1=M. So answer is 1 if M divides a1, else 0.
boundary.test_values: n=1, M various, a1 various. Includes M=1, M=prime, M=large.

boundary.description: M=1. LCM condition forces all d_i = 1. So each voter must have 1 as a divisor, which is always true (since 1|a_i). So there is exactly 1 way: all vote for 1.
boundary.test_values: M=1, any n, any a_i. Answer always 1.

adversarial.description: M is a large prime (near 1e12). Factorization of M is trivial, but prime factors of a_i may be many. The number of divisors each a_i has is limited. However, the LCM condition must be exactly M. Since M is prime, only divisors of M are 1 and M. So each d_i must be either 1 or M, and at least one d_i must be M, and all M's must be from voters whose a_i is divisible by M. Count ways: (product over i of (1 if M|a_i, else 1)) - 1? Actually each voter with M|a_i can choose either 1 or M (2 choices), others only 1. Then subtract the case where all choose 1. So answer = (2^{k} - 1) mod MOD, where k = number of voters with M|a_i. If k=0 then answer=0. This tests handling of prime M and combinatorial formula.
adversarial.attack_vector: Expect TLE if solution enumerates all divisors of M (which are only 2) but still does heavy factoring for each a_i. Or WA if it fails to realize the simple formula.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that factor M and then try to match exponent vectors may be overkill but still work; however, if they improperly handle the special case of prime M (e.g., missing the -1 for all-1 case), they get WA. Also, solutions that factor each a_i repeatedly may TLE if n large and a_i have many prime factors.
error_types_caught: slow factorization when M is prime but a_i are large

adversarial.description: M is a product of many distinct small primes, e.g., 2*3*5*7*11*13 = 30030. Each a_i is also a product of a random subset of these primes, so that each voter's divisor choices are constrained. The number of divisors of M is 2^6=64, manageable. However, the LCM condition requires that for each prime factor, the maximum exponent among chosen d_i equals the exponent in M (which is 1 for all). So each prime must appear in at least one chosen d_i. This can be solved by inclusion-exclusion or DP over subsets. This pattern forces inclusion-exclusion or DP over primes, and can catch bugs like missing primes, miscomputing number of choices per voter, or overflow in DP.
adversarial.attack_vector: Complex combinatorial counting that tests for correctness of inclusion-exclusion or DP over subsets.
adversarial.why_effective: Naive solutions that enumerate all divisor combinations are too slow (each voter up to 64 divisors, 3 voters => 64^3=262k, okay, but with n=20 it's huge). Solutions using DP over divisors of M must correctly map each a_i to the set of divisors that are divisors of a_i. Errors can occur in mapping or DP transitions.
error_types_caught: DP over divisors not covering all cases

key_coverage_gaps: Cases with M having high exponent prime factors (e.g., M=2^{10})
Cases where a_i are huge with many divisors (smooth numbers)
Cases with multiple test cases summing to exactly 2e5
pattern_summary.recommended_test_count: At least 10 random, 5 boundary, 5 adversarial for complete coverage; but for this pattern set, 6 cases are provided.

boundary.test_values: Points at (0,0), (0,1e9), (1e9,0), (1e9,1e9). Maximum Manhattan distances 2e9 per pair.

adversarial.description: All points have same x coordinate, testing reliance on x dimension only
adversarial.attack_vector: If algorithm sorts only by x, it will not achieve optimal pairing because all x equal, so pairing by x order arbitrary. Optimal requires pairing extremes in y.
adversarial.why_effective: A greedy algorithm that sorts solely by x and pairs first-last will not necessarily pair the extreme y values because x-order is arbitrary (all same). The optimal sum is 200 (|0-150|+|100-50| = 150+50=200), but a naive pairing might get only 100.

adversarial.description: Points with large coordinate values causing integer overflow if algorithm computes sum of distances
adversarial.attack_vector: If solution computes total sum as 64-bit integer, it's fine, but if using 32-bit int, overflow possible. However, output is indices, not sum. But some solutions may compute sum internally for debugging. This pattern catches those.
adversarial.why_effective: Manhattan distance is 2000000000 which exceeds 2^31-1 if signed 32-bit (max ~2.14e9). Actually 2e9 < 2^31-1, so not overflow. To trigger overflow with 32-bit signed, need sum of two distances? For n=2, only one distance. To get overflow need large n and sum of many distances, but not needed. So this pattern might not cause overflow. Let's adjust: use points that cause sum of two distances > 2^31-1? Already one distance < 2^31. So overflow unlikely. Better: pattern for TLE: points arranged to cause O(n^2) if algorithm tries all pairs. But that would be a different pattern.
error_types_caught: integer overflow (unlikely but possible if summing many distances)

adversarial.description: Points all on a line (y=x) to test if algorithm correctly handles degenerate cases
adversarial.attack_vector: If algorithm uses (x+y) and (x-y) sorting, (x-y) will be zero for all points, possibly causing issues if not handled.
adversarial.why_effective: Sorting by x+y gives order 0,2,4,6 -> pairing (0,6) and (2,4) gives distances 6 and 2, sum 8. Sorting by x-y gives all zeros, so pairing might be arbitrary if algorithm uses both. But optimal is 8, and any pairing on line gives same sum? Actually, Manhattan distance on line y=x equals 2*|x_i-x_j|, so pairing extremes gives max. So algorithm using x+y works. But if algorithm only uses x-y and gets all zeros, it might pair in arbitrary order, leading to suboptimal. So this pattern catches algorithms that rely solely on x-y.

key_coverage_gaps: Missing pattern for multiple test cases with mixed n sizes
Missing pattern for points with large duplicate counts

adversarial.description: Test where repeated use of same factor is required and naive solutions may incorrectly allow it with p too small or miss it when p is sufficient

adversarial.description: Test that triggers integer overflow when generating candidate numbers by multiplication without checking bounds

adversarial.description: Perfect square discriminant but s(x) mismatch
adversarial.attack_vector: Creates n where discriminant is a perfect square but the resulting x has a different s(x), causing unsuspecting solvers to output an incorrect x.
adversarial.why_effective: The discriminant for s=1 is a perfect square, giving x=999999999. However, s(999999999)=81, so the equation does not hold. If a program does not verify s(x) after solving the quadratic, it will incorrectly output x.
error_types_caught: missing verification of digit sum after solving
incorrect assumption that perfect square implies solution
